**Surah ash-Shu'ara'**

*Ash-Shu'ara'* is the plural of *sha'ir* (poet), and the surah is named after it because the poets are mentioned at its end.

The naming of surahs: some of it is *tawqifi* (based on revelation, i.e., on instruction from the Prophet ﷺ), and some of it is *ijtihadi* (based on scholarly reasoning). The Prophet ﷺ sometimes mentions a specific surah by name, as when he said: "Recite the two bright ones: al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran" [narrated by Muslim (804/252), from Abu Umamah al-Bahili]. And sometimes he does not mention it or specify its name, and the Companions strive to name it.

The naming of surahs may also be single, meaning a surah is named by one name, and a surah may have several names.

Among the curious claims: the surah al-Isra' is called "Surat Bani Isra'il." Some nationalists denied this, saying: it is not possible (...) the Children of Israel, especially the Jews. So they denied this matter, just as the nationalists affirmed that the Jews killed 'Isa ibn Maryam, while Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾ [an-Nisa' 157]. Therefore, when the Church gathered some years ago and issued a statement clearing the Jews of the killing of the Messiah 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon him, the nationalists rose up (...), each arguing with falsehood. The truth is that this does not harm Israel at all; rather, it harms them, by their denial of the Qur'an. Moreover, the Jews now have been in control for thirty years or more, I think more (...) and forty, and now we are at eighty; more than thirty years, thirty-two years, and they are occupying Jerusalem. These nationalists are like dogs that bark but do not reach. Nor is their aim the elimination of the Jews; they do not desire that at all. Their aim is only to remain on the thrones of rule. Otherwise, we know from the circumstances that they never want to eliminate them. Rather, they want the matter to remain as it is (...) the feelings of the naive and superficial.

(...) may Allah have mercy on him has an excellent poem on this meaning, called *Falastiniyyat* (Palestinian poems), and he mentioned that the Palestinian cause is like the doll or picture with which a child plays and amuses himself. This is correct and true.

The evidence for this is that the elimination of Israel will not occur except through conviction, because they fight out of conviction. I have been told that when they occupied the land of Palestine and entered the city of Jerusalem, they began kissing the dust of the earth and weeping, because they fight out of conviction. We, without doubt, do not fight out of conviction. Those who confronted the Jews do not fight out of conviction, except out of tribal conviction, with no victory in it. Therefore, we praise Allah that after this great, disgraceful defeat, this defeat is not a defeat of religion; otherwise its calamities would have doubled. Rather it is a defeat of tribalism, and the defeat of tribalism does not matter. What matters is that a defeat be in the name of religion, so it is said: "Islam was defeated." But they do not say, "Islam was defeated"; rather they say, "The Arabs were struck by calamity." This lightens the matter for us, although it is heavy upon us in any case. Nevertheless, the Jews are increasing (...) their footing in the city of Jerusalem, and they will not leave it except through the righteousness of the Muslims. ﴿And We had already written in the Zabur after the Reminder that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya' 105]. These are the ones who inherit the earth. As for those who are not righteous, they will not inherit it, except that one more wrongdoing than them may remove them. That may happen, but victory for truth cannot come from non-righteous people. So when the Muslims become righteous and return sincerely to Allah, then they will be given victory; otherwise there is no victory for them. Therefore, now the Jews are firmly planting their feet in Jerusalem.

Last night I heard that they will move government offices to East Jerusalem. This means they have no intention of leaving. I once heard from a preacher in Egypt called 'Abd al-Hamid Kishk that he heard that Golda Meir, the Prime Minister at the time of the Nakba, said: "If it is permissible for us to give up Tel Aviv, it is not permissible for us to give up Jerusalem." That is, even with that (she declared it in London), this means they cannot give it up. This is true. People whom Allah has given a sacred land, to whom it was said in the Torah: "It is the land which Allah has decreed for you," and Musa promised them it; therefore they call it "the Promised Land." Then they would abandon it to Arabs? This is not possible.

**Shaykh:** Just as the Messenger said: "Allah does not seize knowledge by snatching it from the breasts of men, but He seizes it by the death of the scholars" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (100) and Muslim (2673/13), from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr]. So the scholars die, and the Muslim people die little by little, until the world comes to an end.

*Ash-Shu'ara'* says: (It is Meccan. The Meccan is what was revealed before the Hijra according to the correct view; that is, the criterion is the time, not the place) except for ﴿As for the poets, the deviators follow them﴾ and so on, four verses: ﴿As for the poets, the deviators follow them. Have you not considered that they wander in every valley? And that they say what they do not do? Except those who believe and do righteous deeds and remember Allah often and defend themselves after they were wronged. And those who have wronged will know to what return they will be returned﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 224-227]. This exception, as we said previously and say now, is not accepted unless evidence points to it. The evidence may be transmitted, or it may be by meaning. The meaning may be clear, or it may be disputed. Here the author excepted these four verses based on the context, because His saying: ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds and remember Allah often and defend themselves after they were wronged﴾ was said to have been revealed when Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him, was affected by the verse when it was revealed; so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds and remember Allah often and defend themselves after they were wronged﴾. And defending oneself after being wronged, when did it take place, in Medina or in Mecca?

**Students:** In Medina.

**Shaykh:** In Medina. It took place in Medina. Therefore they said these verses are Medinan.

Then he said: (and it has two hundred and twenty-seven verses). The division of verses is also *tawqifi*. Even the Prophet ﷺ has no role in dividing the verses. The verses descend from Allah already divided, and the Messenger ﷺ commands that they be placed in their positions within the surah. So numbering is also *tawqifi*.

He says: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾. This has been discussed at length before. We said that the *basmalah* (the phrase "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful") is connected to a deleted verb that comes later. And what else? Suitable to what is being begun with. For example, "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful": when you want to recite, you say: the estimate is "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, I recite." It is estimated as a verb because it is the origin of action; and it is estimated as coming later to indicate restriction and to seek blessing by placing the name of Allah first; and it is estimated as suitable because it is more specific. Otherwise you could estimate: "In the name of Allah I begin," but when it is estimated as specific, it is more specific and more indicative of the intended meaning.

(﴿Ta Sin Mim﴾: Allah knows best what He intends by that.) This may be understood in his saying "by what He intends by that." It may mean that he intends that this word, or these letters, have meanings, and Allah knows them best. It may also mean that His intent, Allah knows best, is the purpose for which these alphabetic letters came. Do you understand now? And there is a difference between the two cases. On the first estimate, this word has a meaning, but it is not known. On the second estimate, it has no meaning, but what is the wisdom in its occurrence? That is not known.

The possibility that they have a meaning is remote. The reason is that the Quran came in clear Arabic, and these disjointed letters, by being mere letters, have no meaning. Allah, glorified and exalted, does not reveal to us disjointed letters intending a meaning by them, for that would contradict the Quran being a clarification and would depart from the requirements of the Arabic language.

As for the second possibility, that one says: "Allah knows best what He intended by the purpose for which He brought these disjointed letters," this is true. It is true when a person says: "I do not know; Allah knows."

However, some scholars offered a point of relevance (munasabah), and said: Among the points of relevance is that the Noble Quran, which is a miracle for all of mankind, did not come with something strange. Rather, it came with words made from these letters of which people's speech is composed, and yet it rendered them incapable. Had it come with new letters unknown to people, it would have been said: "Its miracle is evident, and no one can match it." But the way of the miracle and its completeness is that it comes with letters from those of the speech people use, and yet it defeats them. They found support for this relevance, or for establishing this relevance, in that if you reflect on the surahs that begin with disjointed letters, you will find that after the letters there is mentioned something related to the Quran:

﴿Alif Lam Mim. That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah 1, 2]; ﴿Alif Lam Mim. Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all. He has sent down to you the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran 1–3]; ﴿Alif Lam Mim Sad. A Book revealed to you﴾ [al-A'raf 1, 2]; ﴿Alif Lam Ra. These are the verses of the Wise Book﴾ [Yunus 1]; ﴿Alif Lam Ra. A Book whose verses are made firm﴾ [Hud 1]; ﴿Alif Lam Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ [Yusuf 1]; ﴿Alif Lam Mim Ra. These are the verses of the Book, and what has been sent down to you﴾ [al-Ra'd 1]; ﴿Alif Lam Ra. A Book We have sent down to you that you might bring mankind out of darkness into light﴾ [Ibrahim 1]; ﴿Alif Lam Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Quran﴾ [al-Hijr 1]; ﴿Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad. A mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya﴾ [Maryam 1, 2]; ﴿Ta Ha. We did not send down the Quran to you to make you wretched﴾ [Ta Ha 1, 2]; ﴿Ta Sin Mim. These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 1, 2]; ﴿Ta Sin. These are the verses of the Quran and a clear Book﴾ [al-Naml 1]; ﴿Ta Sin Mim. These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ [al-Qasas 1, 2]; ﴿Alif Lam Mim. Do the people think they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested? And We did certainly test those before them﴾ [al-'Ankabut 1–3]; ﴿Alif Lam Mim. The Romans have been defeated, in the nearest land﴾ [al-Rum 1–3]; ﴿Alif Lam Mim. These are the verses of the Wise Book﴾ [Luqman 1, 2]; ﴿Alif Lam Mim. The revelation of the Book, in which there is no doubt, is from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Sajdah 1, 2]. We proceed on this basis.

It remains that you should say: ﴿Alif Lam Mim. Do the people think they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 1, 2], and ﴿Alif Lam Mim. The Romans have been defeated, in the nearest land﴾ [al-Rum 1–3], and ﴿Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad. A mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya﴾ [Maryam 1, 2] contain no mention of the Quran.

It is said: They do contain a mention of the Quran. ﴿A mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya﴾ is revelation (wahy). And ﴿Alif Lam Mim. Do the people think they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested? And We did certainly test those before them﴾: the stories and reports of the earlier peoples were only through revelation. And ﴿The Romans have been defeated, in the nearest land﴾ is also a report of a future matter from the unseen, which is known only through revelation. Then, even if it is assumed that this is not clear, the rare case has no ruling. This meaning which we have pointed to was mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, and Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, supported it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 2:

(﴿تِلْكَ﴾ i.e., these verses are the verses of the Wise Book), the author says: "i.e., these verses," whereas the Qur'anic expression is: ﴿These are the verses﴾, and there is a difference between them. What is the difference between the Qur'anic expression and the expression of the mufassir?

* Student: (...) this thing, it is as if..

* The Shaykh: No, what is the difference? We do not say: what is the reasoning. What is the difference?

* Student: (...).

* Another student: "Tilka" is a demonstrative for the distant, and "hadhihi" is a demonstrative for the near.

* The Shaykh: A demonstrative for the near, okay?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The point is that the difference between them is this: the Qur'anic expression uses the demonstrative for the distant, while the author uses the demonstrative for the near.

Then he said: "i.e., these verses are verses of the Book," also to clarify that "verses of the Book" is the predicate.

The correct approach is to say: if the author had said, "Those verses are verses," it would have been better, because his departing from the demonstrative for the distant to the demonstrative for the near, even though Allah Most High affirmed the demonstrative for the distant, is not an explanation. So the correct view, without doubt (it needs no further proof), is that the Qur'an is correct, and the demonstrative for the distant here, despite the closeness of the Noble Qur'an and its being among our hands, indicates the loftiness of its rank, so it is for magnification. If we follow what the author said, we miss this meaning that the demonstrative for the distant intends.

And His saying: ﴿verses of the Book﴾ means the Qur'an. The annexation is in the sense of "from" (min): i.e., verses from the Book. And His saying: ﴿verses of the Book﴾, ﴿the Book﴾ means "the written," like "al-libas" meaning "the worn," "al-ghiras" meaning "the planted," "al-bina'" meaning "the built," and "al-firash" meaning "the spread."

It is called a Book because it was written in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), written in the scrolls that are in the hands of the angels, and written in the earth among people.

And His saying: ﴿verses of the Book﴾: "al-ayat" is the plural of "aya," which linguistically means "sign," and what is meant here is the sign indicating the One who sent down this Qur'an, who is Allah, glorified and exalted.

Thus every verse contains inimitability (i'jaz). From this we take that every verse contains inimitability, because if it did not contain inimitability it would not be an "aya," since the aya is the distinguishing sign, and the Qur'an is not a distinguishing sign between it and the speech of humans unless it is inimitable (mu'jiz).

﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 2].

﴿al-Mubin﴾: he said: "the one that makes the truth manifest from falsehood." Sometimes they interpret "al-mubin" as "al-bayyin" (the clear). Sometimes "al-mubin" is interpreted as "al-bayyin," as in ﴿So rely upon Allah; indeed you are upon the clear truth﴾ [an-Naml 79], meaning the clearly evident. That is because "abana" is used both intransitively and transitively: it is said "bana al-shay'" (the thing became clear) and "abana al-shay'" (he made the thing clear), and it is used transitively, as in "abantu al-haqq," meaning: I made the truth manifest.

So if "al-mubin" is interpreted as "al-bayyin," its meaning is that the context requires nothing other than that. Is it then intransitive or transitive?

* Students: Intransitive.

* The Shaykh: Intransitive. And if the meaning may be transitive, i.e., in the sense of "making manifest," it must be interpreted that way, because interpreting it as "making manifest" includes or entails interpreting it as "clear," since "mubin" means clear in itself and making others clear, whereas "bayyin" in itself may not make others clear.

So now, whenever "mubin" comes in the Qur'an, if it can be interpreted as "ibana" in the sense of "izhar" (making manifest), it is obligatory, because that is more comprehensive. If that is not possible, it is interpreted as "bayyin," the intransitive (...).

﴿And indeed they were before that in clear error﴾ [Al 'Imran 164]. Which of the two senses?

* Student: The intransitive.

* The Shaykh: Clear, intransitive, is it so? It is possible, though remote, that "al-mubin" means one that makes their error manifest, a error that makes manifest their error, but the first meaning is clearer.

In any case, we now say: "al-mubin" here means "that which makes the truth manifest," and nothing makes the truth manifest except that it is clear in itself: ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 2].

And in His saying: ﴿al-Mubin﴾, the object is not mentioned. Why was the object not mentioned? For what benefit?

* Students: Generality.

* The Shaykh: Generality and comprehensiveness: it makes clear everything. For this reason Allah Most High said: ﴿And We sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [an-Nahl 89], and this is what shows that the Qur'an encompasses everything.

As for ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [al-An'am 38], the intended meaning is not the Qur'an, although many people, as you hear, cite this verse as evidence that the Qur'an encompasses everything. Rather, the intended meaning of ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ is the Preserved Tablet. And ﴿an explanation of all things﴾ is more eloquent: it is stated in it that there is an explanation of everything. The Qur'an is an explanation of all things, and the explanation of the Qur'an is not hidden from anyone except due to a defect in the one from whom it is hidden, not in the Qur'an, because we are certain of the truth of this proposition, ﴿And We sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [an-Nahl 89]. No ruling is hidden from anyone among people except due to deficiency in his understanding, or in his knowledge, or in his intention: either he is deficient in understanding, he does not grasp, and so nothing is made clear to him; or deficient in knowledge, he has no information; or deficient in his purpose. And what is meant by his purpose? That is, his intention. For this reason we have encountered the words of Shaykh al-Islam: "Whoever reflects upon the Qur'an seeking guidance from it, the path of truth becomes clear to him." He mentioned this in al-'Aqidah al-Wasitiyyah when he spoke about the Qur'anic verses indicating the attributes, and it is a statement with its meaning: "Whoever reflects upon the Qur'an seeking guidance from it, the path of truth becomes clear to him." ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾.

So we say: it is clear for everything, and the obscurity of some matters for people from the Qur'an is not due to a deficiency in the Qur'an, but due to their own deficiency: either in understanding, knowledge, or intention.

Someone may say: we do not find everything in the Qur'an. The first objection that arises is that we do not find in the Qur'an the number of rak'at in prayer. So where is the explanation?

* Student: The Qur'an came as an explanation of all things in general, and the Sunnah (...) explains to people what was sent down to them. The Messenger ﷺ explained the Qur'an, but in a general way; the general indications are in the Qur'an, and the detailed branches were explained by the Messenger.

* The Shaykh: We say: the explanation in the Qur'an is of two kinds. One: that it explains a thing itself. Two: that it explains it through its means and method; that is, it says: the way to it is such and such, the path to knowing this is such and such. Sometimes it explains the thing itself, and usually this is for what cannot be perceived otherwise; and sometimes it explains the thing by its method and means, that is, it says: the way to such and such is such and such.

For example, it explained to us the way to knowing the number of prayers by His saying: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [al-Hashr 7], and by His saying: ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom﴾ [an-Nisa' 113], and by His saying: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [an-Nisa' 80], and by His saying: ﴿that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [an-Nahl 44], and other than these.

Many times you have heard the story reported about Shaykh Muhammad 'Abduh with the Christian man who objected to him, saying: "We do not find in the Qur'an how to prepare this food." So he summoned the owner of the restaurant and said to him: "How did you prepare this food?" He said: "I did such and such." He said: "This is how the Qur'an taught us." He said: "How did the Qur'an teach you?" He said: "Because it says: ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾ [an-Nahl 43]." So the explanation in the Qur'an is sometimes that it explains a thing itself, and sometimes that it explains the means which makes it manifest and clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 3:

He said: "﴿Perhaps﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿you will kill yourself with grief﴾, destroying yourself out of distress ﴿that they will not be believers﴾, meaning the people of Makkah."

"La'alla" (perhaps) here expresses concern (al-ishfaq), meaning: he is concerned for him, so that this distress is lightened.

﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself with grief [al-Shu'ara' 3]﴾. Here "la'alla" (perhaps) expresses concern (al-ishfaq). It can also express causation (al-ta'lil) or hope (al-tarajji). When it is attached to something disliked, it expresses concern. When it is attached to something loved, it expresses hope. When it is attached to a cause, it expresses causation.

Here it expresses concern, as when you say: "Perhaps the beloved is dying." Do you hope that your beloved will die? No, you are concerned. God, exalted is He, was concerned for His Prophet ﷺ lest he destroy himself, killing himself with grief over their unbelief. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, suffers from their unbelief, endures severe hardship, grieves, and his chest becomes constricted. But God consoles him with verses such as: ﴿And do not grieve over them, and do not be in distress about what they plot [al-Nahl 127]﴾.

Here He says: ﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself [meaning, destroy it] that they will not be believers﴾. In this there is evidence that the person who calls to God should not destroy himself with worry and grief because people do not accept the truth. For when he does what is obligatory upon him, his chest is relieved. It is sufficient that you do what has been made obligatory upon you of enjoining good and forbidding evil. Then if people comply, it is a blessing for all. And if they do not comply, do not grieve. For if you grieve, you will be occupied with others rather than yourself, and your concern becomes: if I pray, [will it be] the people's approval; if I sit, the people's approval; if I stand, the people's approval. This is not correct, because it corrupts your own worship. Attend to yourself, and to others give what God has obligated you to give them. Then if they are guided, well; otherwise, you are not a guardian over them. By this a person finds great relief and is able to devote himself to his worship, performing it well.

Allah the Exalted says: (﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them from the heaven a sign, so their necks would remain bowed before it﴾ "بمعنى المضارع" meaning the present tense, i.e., "تظل" (they remain), that is, "تدوم" (they continue), ﴿their necks would remain bowed before it﴾, so that they would believe).

﴿If We willed, We would send down﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 4]. "إن" (in) is the conditional particle, "نشأ" (nasha'a, "We will") is the protasis verb, and "ننزل" (nunazzil, "We would send down") is its apodosis. In using this form, "نشأ.. ننزل" (nasha'a... nunazzil), there is a clear exaltation by Allah, glorified and exalted is He, of Himself. He made the matter easy for Himself whenever He wills it, and that by His will He does not act. Then the use of the "نون العظمة" (nun al-'azamah, the plural of majesty) is another exaltation. Allah did not say "إذا شئنا نزّلنا" (idha sha'na nazzalna, "if We wish, We send down"), but rather ﴿If We willed, We would send down﴾.

As for His saying ﴿from the heaven a sign﴾, "آية" (ayah) means a sign. There is no doubt that no one can produce its like, as we have pointed out shortly before. Furthermore, it is a sign not only of the power of the One to whom it belongs, or of His being alone in creation, but also a sign that they will not believe, and of a warning of threat against them. For this reason He said: ﴿so their necks would remain bowed before it﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 4]. They cannot resist this sign, because Allah made it indefinite (نكّرها, nakkarahā). It is a sign not known to us, because Allah has not sent it down; yet it is a sign that they hear, and for this reason He said: ﴿so their necks would remain bowed before it﴾.

As for His saying ﴿from the heaven﴾, is what is meant the protected ceiling, or is it height? Both possibilities are open. It may mean height, i.e., "from above," and it may mean the ceiling that is over the earth. Whichever it is, the coming of a thing from above is more forceful in threat, because whoever is above you has overpowered you, and whoever has overpowered you, you have no strength against him. Unlike one who is opposite you, you may flee or you may resist him, but the problem arises when the command comes from above.

As for His saying ﴿so their necks would remain bowed﴾, he says: "بمعنى المضارع، أي: تظل" (meaning the present tense, i.e., "they remain"). The author only said "بمعنى المضارع" (meaning the present tense) because His saying ﴿If We willed, We would send down﴾ is in the present tense.

﴿so their necks would remain bowed﴾: the expected form would be the present tense, but it was turned away from that to show that it is like an event that has already occurred, as in His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl 1], even though it is yet to come. The meaning is: when it descends upon them, their necks will remain bowed before it.

As for His saying ﴿their necks ... before it﴾, i.e., before this sign. The "لام" (lam) here may be for transitivity, i.e., "bowed to it," or for causation, i.e., "because of it."

As for His saying ﴿bowed﴾, i.e., humbled, in my view. (And when the necks were described with the bowing that belongs to their owners, the descriptive word was made plural in the manner of rational beings.)

What is meant by "الصفة منه" (the descriptive word from it) here is the predicate ﴿bowed﴾, and the predicate is a descriptive in meaning, even though grammatically it is not called a "صفة" (sifah, adjective). In meaning it is an adjective. Here, regarding ﴿their necks﴾, the well-known usage in the Arabic language is to say "خاضعة" (khadi'ah, feminine singular), "أعناقهم لها خاضعة" (their necks are bowed before it), like "خاشعة أبصارهم" (their gazes are humbled). But since bowing is a quality of rational beings and not of non-rational things, and since bowing is a quality of rational beings, it was made plural in the manner of the rational plural, because the sound masculine plural (جمع المذكر السالم, jam' al-mudhakkar al-salim) is specific to rational beings. So it was made plural in the manner of the rational plural for this reason.

We cannot say that ﴿their necks ... before it﴾ with "لها" (lahā) as the predicate, and that ﴿so their necks would remain bowed before it﴾ is the predicate, with ﴿bowed﴾ being a circumstantial state (حال, hal) from the pronoun hidden in the predicate. We say this is far-fetched, because what is the meaning of "ظلت أعناقهم لها" (their necks remained before it)? It has no meaning. If someone says: perhaps the implied phrase is "ناظرة لها" (looking at it), "ظلت أعناقهم ناظرة لها" (their necks remained looking at it), we answer: this is refuted by saying that if the governed element (المتعلَّق, al-muta'allaq) is specific, it is not omitted. It is omitted only when it is general, i.e., its implied phrase is "كائن" (existing) or "مستقر" (settled). That is what is omitted. But when it is specific, like "راكب" (riding), "جالس" (sitting), and the like, it is not omitted.

* In this verse there is an affirmation of Allah's will, exalted is He, by His saying ﴿If He wills﴾.
* And in it is an affirmation of power, by His saying ﴿We would send down﴾.
* And in it is a warning to these deniers, by His saying ﴿so their necks would remain bowed before it﴾.
* And in it is evidence that causes are effective, because when the sign descends they submit, and this is evidence for the establishment of causes and that they are effective.
* And in it is evidence for the affirmation of divine wisdom, because Allah did not send down this sign. If He had sent it down, faith would have been compelled, and compelled faith has no praise or commendation in it; rather, it does not even benefit its holder. For this reason, when a person believes at the moment of meeting death, it does not benefit him, and after the sun rises from the west, it does not benefit him. It benefits only when faith is by choice. When Allah lifted the mountain over the Children of Israel, they believed, but this faith is undoubtedly weak, because it is compelled faith. So it is from the wisdom of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, that He did not send down this sign, so that faith would be by choice, not by compulsion.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 5:

In this regard he says: ("Never does there come to them a reminder (dhikr) from the Most Merciful, [any] newly revealed (muhdath) [reminder] but they turn away from it" – a descriptive clarifier (sifa kashifa)).

(Ma) is a negation, as evidenced by His saying ﴿but they were turning away from it﴾. This exception is a "mufarragh" exception from general states; meaning: nothing befalls them in any state except turning away.

And His saying ﴿Never does there come to them any reminder﴾: (min) is grammatically redundant for emphasis, and the implied meaning is: "dhikrun" (a reminder).

And His saying, blessed and exalted is He, ﴿any reminder﴾: the author said "(qur'an)", and the Qur'an was named a reminder (dhikr) because in it there is remembrance (tadhakkur) and also admonition (tadhkir). It is an admonition from Allah and a remembrance for the one who hears it, and for this reason it is called a dhikr. The Qur'an is described a second time as ﴿possessing the Reminder﴾ [Sad 1], ﴿It is nothing but a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾ [Ya-Sin 69], ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ [Sad 1]. So once He made it a reminder, and once He made it possessing a reminder, and in reality there is no difference between them, because it is a reminder in itself and an admonition, and because it is possessing remembrance, i.e., possessing remembrance (tadhakkur); whoever recites it, memorises it and reflects upon it is reminded by it. ﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ [al-Qamar 17].

* Student: It does not contain the reminder.

* Shaykh: How "contains the reminder"? "Contains the reminder," meaning what? What is the meaning of "contains it"?

* Student: There are verses in it that contain admonition.

* Shaykh: No, even if so, the intended meaning is the admonition itself. The intended meaning is that it is a reminder that admonishes, and by which whoever recites it is reminded.

And His saying ﴿from the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 5], and the other verse ﴿from their Lord﴾ [al-Anbiya' 2]. The mention of "the Most Merciful" here indicates that the sending down and coming of this Qur'an is a requirement of Allah's mercy, and that Allah, glorified and exalted, has shown mercy to His servants through this Qur'an. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya' 107], meaning, a mercy from Us to the worlds. The meaning is not, as many common people understand, "except a mercy," i.e., that you yourself are the mercy. No; the meaning is: We sent you only so that We might show mercy to the servants. That is the meaning, and he is not himself the mercy, as those who exaggerate regarding the Prophet ﷺ say, and the ignorant too.

﴿Never does there come to them any reminder from the Most Merciful, [any] newly revealed [reminder]﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 5]. He says: ("a descriptive clarifier" (sifa kashifa)). The descriptive clarifier is that which clarifies the reality and does not restrict the described thing, because descriptive attributes – as you know – include a restrictive attribute which excludes whatever is other than it, and a clarifying attribute which explains the reality of the matter. Here the author says: the word ﴿newly revealed (muhdath)﴾ is a clarifying attribute, because the Qur'an, whatever reminder comes to them, is newly revealed. The phrase ﴿comes to them﴾ indicates newness, so it has no implied restriction, because if it comes to them, it must be newly revealed, since by its coming to them it becomes newly revealed. The reasoning for this is clear: it is a clarifying attribute, because if it were not newly revealed, it would not be correct to say "and there does not come to them" when it is already coming from the origin.

As for His saying ﴿newly revealed (muhdath)﴾: does the apparent meaning of the noble verse indicate that the newly revealed thing is the reminder itself, so that the verse indicates that Allah speaks the Qur'an at the time of its sending down?

And it is not as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: that it descended to the House of Honour (Bayt al-'Izza) from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz); rather, Allah, blessed and exalted, speaks it at the time of its sending down.

It has also been said: "newly revealed" refers to its sending down, so that ﴿never does there come to them any reminder from the Most Merciful, [any] newly revealed﴾ refers to its sending down, and the attribute here is not literal but causal (sifa sababiyya), because the thing truly described by it is not the reminder but the sending down, if we say "newly revealed in its sending down".

Like when you say: "I passed by a man whose father is standing" – "standing" is grammatically an attribute of "man," but in meaning it is an attribute of his father. This kind of attribute is called the causal adjective (na't sababi). So according to the view that what is meant is "newly revealed in its sending down," the adjective here is causal, not literal.

However, if it is a matter of choosing between an adjective being a literal attribute or a causal attribute, it is obligatory that it be a literal attribute, because a causal attribute requires restriction, and everything that requires restriction requires evidence. So here we say: if we say ﴿never does there come to them any reminder from the Most Merciful, [any] newly revealed﴾ in its sending down, we have departed from the apparent wording, because its apparent meaning is that the thing newly revealed is itself, i.e., the Qur'an itself. Furthermore, "newly revealed in its sending down" has no meaning in reality after His saying ﴿never does there come to them﴾, because it is not possible for it to come to them without its sending down being new, since "came" (atā) means "occurred."

So based on this we say: the correct view is that what is meant by "newly revealed" is the reminder itself, not its sending down.

He says: ﴿but they were turning away from it﴾. ﴿From it﴾ is a prepositional phrase related to "turning away," and "turning away" is the predicate of "were." The benefit of placing it before the predicate here is both verbal and semantic. The verbal benefit is observing the rhyme endings (fawasil) of the verses. The semantic benefit is to convey restriction (hasr), as if he is saying: their state is nothing but turning away from it, not from anything else; that is, from it alone, turning away. This is more eloquent in censure than if he had said "but they were turning away from it," because that might allow that they turn away from it and from other things. But when he said ﴿from it, turning away﴾, it is as if they are characterised by turning away only from this reminder.

So the benefit of placing it first is:

* Student: observing (...) semantic and verbal.

* Shaykh: Good.

* Student: (...) the endings (...) semantic.

* Shaykh: ﴿but they were turning away from it﴾: is this turning away semantic (ma'nawi) or physical (hissi)? The answer: it includes both. They turn away even when they are present in body, and they also turn away physically by getting up from it. ﴿And those who disbelieved said: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that perhaps you may overcome"﴾ [Fussilat 26]. So they turn away – may Allah protect us – with their hearts and their bodies.

Allah, blessed and exalted, said: (﴿So they have denied﴾ it).

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿So they have denied﴾, but the author says: (it), meaning this reminder, and the sentence is confirmed by "qad" (indeed), and the meaning is that even though it is clear that this reminder is from the Most Merciful, they did not benefit from it, but rather denied it. Denial of it encompasses outright denial of it, by saying that this is not the Qur'an from Allah, as they said: ﴿It is only a human who teaches him﴾ [al-Nahl 103]; or denial of some of its verses, such as if they denied the story of one of the messengers, or a story Allah related to someone, like the one who passed by a town, and the like.

So either denial of it outright, saying: "You are not being revealed to, and this Qur'an is not revelation," or denial of some of the verses that came in it: all of it is denial.

Denial is more eloquent than turning away, because a person may turn away out of negligence, laziness, or for some reason and not deny. But the denier is more severe, because a denier cannot possibly accept, and how would one accept something he believes to be false? For this reason He said: ﴿but they were turning away from it (5). So they have denied﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 5-6]. He did not say "so they have turned away," but He said ﴿so they have denied﴾, and this includes turning away, but not the reverse.

(﴿So they have indeed denied, and there will soon come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾: consequences ﴿of that which they used to mock﴾.) The fa' is a conjunction indicating sequence, and the sin also indicates nearness. The meaning is: because of their denial, the news will come to them soon.

"Anba'" means "news." Its singular is naba', which is news of important matters. The "news" here means the consequences, as the author said: "(the consequences)," because consequences are, in reality, news.

For example, the Qur'an states that Allah, the Exalted, supports His Messenger and destroys those who deny him. These are news that will in reality become consequences: the Prophet ﷺ will be victorious, and his enemies will be defeated. This is the reality, and it is the outcome.

His saying ﴿that which they used to mock﴾ means "that which they used to ridicule." The fronting of the object in ﴿they used to mock it﴾ serves the two benefits mentioned earlier, the verbal and the semantic.

His saying ﴿that which they used to be﴾ may be understood as free of time, meaning "that which they mock," or it may be understood as tied to time, meaning "that which they used to mock in the past at the time the consequence occurs," since their mockery preceded this consequence. However, the apparent meaning is that it is free of time, and this is the most common usage of "kanu" (they used to be).

﴿Except that they used to mock it﴾ means they used to scoff at and laugh at it. Denying a true thing is a kind of mocking it, because if it contains a promise and a threat, a command and a prohibition, information and questioning, guidance and reproach, and then it is denied, this means that one mocks it, its rulings, its information, and what it includes of these matters.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The Student: What is the benefit?

* The Shaykh: The benefit, as they say, is that an increase in the form of a word indicates an increase in its meaning. So if you find extra letters in a word, this means there are extra meanings. The addition here is for intensification, like "istakbara" and "takabbara" (both meaning to be arrogant): "istakbara" is more intensive than "takabbara." Here, "istahza'a" is more intensive than "hazi'a bihi" (both meaning to mock). Therefore we say that the sin and the ta' here are for intensification.

Allah, the Exalted, said, explaining a clear proof of His signs: (﴿Have they not looked﴾: they have not observed ﴿at the earth, how much We have caused to grow therein﴾: that is, We have caused to grow much ﴿of every noble pair﴾: a good kind).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 7:

﴿Have they not seen﴾ means these deniers. The author says that "yarawā" (they see) means "yanzurū" (they look), so he takes it as sight by the eyes (al-ru'yah al-hissiyyah), not sight by knowledge (al-ru'yah al-'ilmiyyah). We have already had something similar before, and we said that it can carry both meanings: sight by the eyes when one looks with his own eyes, and sight by knowledge when one knows it from someone else. This is because there are things that grow in the earth that we do not know, meaning we do not see them, but we are informed of them. So the better view is that it includes both the seeing of the eye and the seeing of the heart, which is knowledge.

﴿to the earth, how many of every noble kind We have caused to grow therein﴾. The author says: "ay kathīran" (that is, many). "Kathīran" (many) is an explanation of "kam" (how many), so here "kam" is for multiplicity (takthīriyyah). The meaning: We caused many kinds to grow in it.

This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How many a small company has overcome a large company by the permission of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:249], meaning: many a small company has overcome a large company.

And His saying: ﴿How many of every noble kind We have caused to grow therein﴾ attributes the growing to Him, blessed and exalted is He, because He is the true doer. When the growing is attributed to rain, that is because rain is a means (sabab).

His saying: ﴿of every noble kind﴾ means: of every kind (ṣinf). "Karīm" (noble) originally means one who gives generously, but it is sometimes used to mean "good" (ḥasan). From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Mu'adh: «Beware of the most precious of their possessions» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1496) and Muslim (19/29), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas]. That is, the best of them. The meaning is not their noble (generous) ones that give much milk, since they do not give milk as beasts; rather, what is meant is the good ones. So here "karīm" we say means "good" (ḥasan).

"Zawj" (kind) means a category and a type. These good, delightful kinds and types indicate the power of their Creator, blessed and exalted is He, and His grace and kindness, and His wisdom. Look at the earth, and in it this vegetation: you find it differing in its size, differing in its color, differing in its benefit, differing in every respect, while the earth is one and the water is one. Indeed, sometimes you find that a single type of this vegetation differs. For example, if we look at wheat: wheat is one type among grains, yet it differs. If we also look at palm trees, we find them differing; and if we look at watermelon and others, we find them differing, which indicates the perfection of Allah's power, blessed and exalted is He, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:4]. The water is one and the earth is one; you take from this a thing and taste it and it is bitter, and you take from that and taste it and it is sweet, even though the earth is one and the water is one. But this is the power of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, by which those who are granted success infer the perfection of His power.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 8:

(﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ — an indication of the perfection of His power, exalted is He. ﴿And most of them would not have been believers﴾).

He says: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾. How is "āyah" (sign) in the accusative?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: It is the noun of "inna" (indeed). Where is its predicate?

* Student: "In that" (fī dhālika).

* Shaykh: "In that."

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: And the predicate is: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾; that is, in what was mentioned of the growth, and of the varieties, and of the beauty. So "āyah" here means "āyāt" (signs).

As for his saying "an indication of the perfection of Allah's power": this is correct, and the most evident thing in it is power. But there are also, in these signs, an indication of the perfect wisdom in diversifying these things and varying them, for Allah, blessed and exalted, intended a wisdom in it. So power, as the author said, is the clearest of the signs of Allah, the Exalted, in these plants, but they also point to other matters.

As for his saying ﴿And most of them would not have been believers﴾, the author said: "(in the knowledge of Allah)," intending that "kāna" (would have been) in ﴿And most of them would not have been believers﴾ refers to what they had not yet become: it does not mean that they were not believers in the past and are now believers. So the author says "in the knowledge of Allah," meaning they were not so in Allah's knowledge. But he said: "(and kāna, Sibawayh said, is redundant)," meaning that "kāna" in ﴿And most of them would not have been believers﴾ is redundant. This is the author combining one opinion with another opinion, because the one who says ﴿And most of them would not have been believers﴾ with "kāna" being redundant does not say "in the knowledge of Allah." ﴿And most of them would not have been believers﴾ means: according to the reality and the situation. As for the one who says it is "in the knowledge of Allah," he has no need to say it is redundant, and the one who says "kāna" is a past verb in its true sense needs to say "in the knowledge of Allah."

But we can dispense with all of this by saying: the intended meaning of "kāna" here is merely the event, the indication of the occurrence only. It is stripped of time, and if it is stripped of time we do not need to say it is redundant, nor do we need to say "in the knowledge of Allah." We say: the reality is that most of them are not believers, and most of them are not believers.

As for his saying ﴿And most of them﴾...

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: The words of the commentator are not open to objection except that it is another statement; because if you say ﴿And most of them would not have been believers﴾ "in the knowledge of Allah," it is not correct to say "kāna" is redundant.

* Student: (...) and Sibawayh said.

* Shaykh: (...).

* Student: And Sibawayh said (...).

* Shaykh: No, that is, he says: "and Sibawayh said (...)", but when he said "(and kāna, Sibawayh said)," it means that it is a statement branching off from what precedes it.

The point is that Sibawayh holds that it is redundant, while the author holds that it is original but in view of Allah's knowledge. We say that it is original, stripped of time, rather only to indicate the event alone.

As for his saying ﴿And most of them would not have been believers﴾, it contains evidence that some of them are believers, and so it is: some of them are believers and have actually believed.

﴿وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ [الشعراء: ٩]

﴿وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ﴾ The lordship (al-Rububiyyah) here is special, because Allah, exalted is He, is the Lord of the Prophet ﷺ and of others, but this is for the Prophet's ﷺ special care and to make clear that He will not abandon him despite this denial. Rather, He must take him under His special care and lordship.

And His saying, "﴿لَهُوَ﴾ The lam is for emphasis. ﴿الْعَزِيزُ﴾ the Mighty, who has might, who takes vengeance on the disbelievers. ﴿الرَّحِيمُ﴾ the Merciful, who shows mercy to the believers."

﴿لَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ﴾ the Mighty, the one who possesses 'izzah (might). 'Izzah means domination, as one says "'azza" meaning "overcame and subdued." It has been said that 'izzah is divided into three types: 'izzat al-qadr (the might of exalted status), 'izzat al-qahr (the might of subjugation), and 'izzat al-imtina' (the might of inviolability).

The meaning of 'izzat al-qadr is that He, glorified and exalted, is Mighty, such that no one can reach His standing.

'Izzat al-qahr: He is the Mighty who cannot be subdued; rather, He is the Overcomer.

'Izzat al-imtina': He, glorified and exalted, is protected from any deficiency in any respect. It is an expression of strength, and from it comes the phrase "al-ardh al-'azaz," where 'azaz means hard and strong ground.

In any case, 'izzah in all its types, these three, belongs perfectly to Allah, blessed and exalted. From His might comes His seizing of the deniers. For this reason the author said, "(takes vengeance on the disbelievers)." To which of the three types does this return?

* Student: To the might of subjugation.

* The Shaykh: To the might of subjugation.

"(﴿الرَّحِيمُ﴾ shows mercy to the believers)." It would have been better for the author to leave it general. But since Allah, exalted is He, said, ﴿وَكَانَ بِالْمُؤْمِنِينَ رَحِيمًا﴾ [الأحزاب: ٤٣], the author began restricting the word "al-Rahim" to the believers. However, it should be general, because His might does not necessitate vengeance; rather, this mercy that is particular to Him may prevent vengeance. So the combination here of might and mercy, these two attributes together, is for a supreme harmony, because perfection is attained through their combination. He is, by His might, the possessor of mercy. If we compare might and mercy in the attributes of created beings, we find that they generally do not combine, and that the mighty who sees himself as dominant generally has no mercy in him. So the combination of the two attributes produces perfection upon perfection: might and mercy. Then their combination is a perfection; with might He is merciful, He does not seize or take vengeance hastily. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, did not hasten punishment for the wrongdoer, but in His wisdom He gives him respite, so that when He seizes him, He does not let him go.

* Student: Is "هو" a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl)?

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, it is a pronoun of separation.

* Student: The lam.

* The Shaykh: The lam is for emphasis.

* Student: "'Izzat al-imtina'", what does it mean?

* The Shaykh: "'Izzat al-imtina'" means that deficiency is impossible for Him.

* Student: (...) the power.

* The Shaykh: Allah knows best. Rather, Allah, glorified and exalted, made the language after death Arabic, because in the Hereafter the apparent language is Arabic, as came in the hadith: "Indeed the language of the people of Paradise is Arabic,"[[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat (5583), and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (7175), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] and the apparent meaning, Allah knows best, is that in the Hereafter it will be Arabic. For this reason whoever said that the two angels question the deceased in the Syriac language was mistaken, and the apparent source of this is specifically taken from the Christians, because it is the language of the Gospel. They claimed that the two angels ask the person about his Lord and his religion in Syriac, (...) in the Arabic language.

* Student: (...) they mean (...).

* The Shaykh: I do not know; he did not mention it (...).

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The hadith is weak, but its meaning is supported, because the majority of the people of Paradise are from this Ummah, the Muslims. Either it may be said: the Qur'an, which is the most noble of the revealed books, is in the Arabic language (...).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verses 10–17 (part 1 of 2):**

**The student:** ﴿The people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear God?﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me, and my chest will be constricted and my tongue will not be loosed, so send [word] to Aaron. And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me." He said, "No! So go, both of you, with Our signs; indeed, We are with you, listening."﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 11–15].

* **The Shaykh:** I seek refuge with God from the accursed Satan. God the Exalted said: ﴿And [recall] when your Lord called Moses, [saying], "Go to the wrongdoing people"﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 10]. In the Noble Quran, God, blessed and exalted, repeats the story of Moses and what happened to him with Pharaoh and with the Children of Israel. This is so that the Prophet (ﷺ) would be prepared for the Jews who were in Medina, so that he would know about their affairs what had not been known to him. For this reason, whenever the Messenger (ﷺ) sent someone, he would inform him about the condition of the people to whom he was sent, as he said to Mu'adh: "Indeed, you are going to a people of the Scripture"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1496) and Muslim (19/29), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]], so that he would be prepared for them.

The story of Moses was repeated by God briefly and in detail for this purpose, to clarify the condition of these Jews who are (...), or who are among the inhabitants of the Abode of Migration (Medina).

In yesterday's lesson, God, blessed and exalted, explained that those who denied the Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿No reminder comes to them from their Lord, newly revealed, except that they listen to it﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 2].

The meaning of ﴿muhdath﴾ ("newly revealed") was already discussed. Did it mean: "its revelation" (i.e., its sending down), or "it is newly made" (i.e., the reminder itself)? Which of these is more preferred?

* **A student:** The more preferred is that it refers to the reminder.
* **The Shaykh:** The second answer.
* **A student:** The second answer, because if we say that it is "newly made" with respect to its sending down (...), [the verse says] "and no reminder comes to them" (...).
* **The Shaykh:** (...) is a clarification of [its being] newly sent down.

Also, if it were the third [option], the adjective would be a *sababi* (an adjective whose qualification is indirectly related to what it describes): that is, the thing it is attributed to is not (...), and the principle is otherwise. The principle is that the adjective should be a *haqiqi* (directly qualifying its noun), (...), but rather related to what is connected to it; and the matter is not like that.

It has already been stated that the meaning of "news" (*anba'*) here is the consequence, because they were informed of it. So the meaning of "the coming of the news" is "the coming of what they were informed of," which is the consequence.

It was also mentioned earlier that God, the Exalted, intended to show the completeness of His power, when He pointed to what He causes to grow on this earth of kinds and types that are good and delightful, and that in that there is a sign. But it is only for the one who is a believer: ﴿And most of them were not believers﴾. The sign is in itself a sign, but only the believer benefits from it. When no one benefits from it, it does not become a sign in relation to him.

For this reason, He qualified it: ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 8], meaning they do not benefit from it. Then He ended the verse by mentioning His might and His mercy, in order to combine encouragement and warning: warning through [His] might, and encouragement through [His] mercy. Then God began by mentioning the stories of the prophets, giving precedence to the story of Moses because of its length and because of its importance for the Prophet (ﷺ).

He said: ﴿And [recall] when your Lord called Moses﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 10]. "Idh" here is an adverb of time whose governing verb is omitted. The estimate is what the author (al-Mu'allif, i.e., al-Sa'di or the author of the Tafsir) estimated: "(And) mention, O Muhammad, to your people, when your Lord called Moses" on the night he saw the fire and the tree, and so on to the end.

﴿When your Lord called Moses﴾: "nada" means he called him, i.e., summoned him with a raised voice, because calling (*nida'*) is only with a loud voice. The saying of God: ﴿And We called him from the right side of the mount and brought him near as a confidant﴾ [Maryam 52]. So *nida'* is for the distant, and it necessarily involves a loud voice, whereas *munajah* (intimate conversation) is for the near.

﴿Your Lord, Moses﴾: he is the son of 'Imran, peace be upon him. The genitive construction here ("your Lord") is for specification, and it does not mean that there is no other lord than You. Rather, it is a particular lordship (*rububiyyah khassah*), because the lordship of God is of two kinds, just as His worship is of two kinds.

﴿Your Lord called Moses, [saying], "Go to the people"﴾: the "an" here is *tafsiriyyah* (explanatory), because it is preceded by a meaning of speech without its letters. When "an" is preceded by a meaning of speech without its letters, it is called *tafsiriyyah*. Similar is the saying: ﴿So We revealed to him, "Construct the ship"﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 27], since the revelation here carries the meaning of speech without its letters. Thus they parse such [an "an"] as *tafsiriyyah*. For this reason, the commentator (al-Sharih or al-Mufassir) said: (i.e., "that" ﴿Go﴾).

The author's statement: "(when he saw the fire and the tree)." That he saw the fire is correct: ﴿When he saw a fire and said to his family, "Stay; indeed, I have perceived a fire"﴾ [Ta-Ha 10]. Likewise, the tree. But his insistence that he saw it is open to question, because Surah al-Qasas does not indicate that he saw it. What is the wording of the verse?

* **A student:** ﴿But when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed place, from the tree﴾ [Al-Qasas 30].

* **The Shaykh:** ﴿From the tree: "O Moses, indeed I am God, Lord of the worlds."﴾ And ﴿He said to his family, "Stay; indeed, I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I will bring you from it news or a burning brand that you may warm yourselves."﴾ [29] ﴿But when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed place, from the tree: "O Moses, indeed I am God"﴾ [Al-Qasas 29, 30]. So it is not clear from the Quran that he saw the tree; rather, it is clear that he heard the voice from the direction of the tree.

(﴿Go to the wrongdoing people﴾, i.e., as a messenger), because the meaning is not merely that he comes to them, but that he comes to them with the message. "Al-qawm" means the group, and "al-zalimin" (the wrongdoers): the meaning of wrongdoing here will come in the author's words.

(﴿The people of Pharaoh﴾, with him; they wronged themselves by disbelieving in God, and the Children of Israel by enslaving them.) They are the wrongdoers who transgressed, who deprived others of their rights: the right of God and the right of people. As for the right of God, they disbelieved in Him and associated partners with Him, and God has said: ﴿Indeed, association [with God] is great injustice﴾ [Luqman 13]. As for the right of people, they enslaved the Children of Israel, and they began slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive.

In His saying ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people (10), the people of Pharaoh﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 10, 11], there is specification after generalization, or clarification after ambiguity, because "the wrongdoing people" is vague, but "the people of Pharaoh" is specified. The benefit of the ambiguity followed by clarification is: emphasis from one aspect, showing the importance of the matter from another aspect, and receptiveness to hearing it with acceptance from a third aspect.

As for emphasis: it is repeated twice, once in summary and once in detail, and this is emphasis. As for showing its importance: mentioning it with emphasis is evidence that it is important. As for receptiveness to hearing it with acceptance: when the word comes in summary, the mind keeps circling: "What is this? And who are these people?" for example. When the clarification then comes, it comes to a mind that is eager and desirous to know this vague matter, so it receives it more readily, because it is eager for it and longing for it. These are the benefits of clarification after ambiguity.

And in describing them as wrongdoers before identifying them, there is an indication of the gravity of their matter, in that the description was placed before the described in reality. When it is said, "Go to the wrongdoing people," a person imagines and knows that they are oppressors. When their identification comes, it comes after a judgment upon them with this description, which indicates the ugliness of what they are upon of this matter: ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people﴾.

(﴿The people of Pharaoh. Will they not﴾: the *hamzah* is for the interrogative of denunciation; ﴿fear God﴾ by obeying Him, so that they would single Him out.)

His saying ﴿Will they not fear God﴾ may be from what was sent with him, i.e., say to them: "Will they not fear God?" It may also be from God, the Exalted, to Moses, to make clear to him their condition and that they keep away from piety, and that what is most fitting for them is to fear God, the Exalted.

His saying ﴿Will they not﴾: the *hamzah* is for the interrogative of denunciation. The implication of his statement is that we should say: the *hamzah* is for interrogation, and "la" is a negation; that is, "Do they not fear God?" And it is not valid for us to take it as an offer, as in "Will you not descend with us and receive good?" Then the intended meaning of ﴿Will they not fear God?﴾ would be an offer of piety to them, while (...).

* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** No, it is an offer to them.
* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** (...).
* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** So the point is that, according to the author's statement, the *hamzah* is parsed alone and "la" alone; the *hamzah* is an interrogative and "la" is a negation. But according to the possibility we mentioned, that it is an offer, that is: I offer them piety, obligating them to it. It was previously stated that the meaning of piety (*taqwa*) is taking a protection against God's punishment.

* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, it is possible, and the two meanings do not contradict each other.

* **A student:** What does the author want?
* **The Shaykh:** The author wants the *hamzah* alone, and "la" as a negation. The *hamzah* is an interrogative, and "la" is a negation; that is, "Do they not fear God?"

Then he said: (﴿He said﴾, Moses, ﴿"My Lord, I fear that they will deny me"﴾). This is Moses' response to God, peace be upon him, explaining to Him his condition, so that the matter may be clear to him, i.e., to Moses, so he becomes energized and strengthened. The meaning is not to oppose God's command, for Moses did not oppose the command of God, the Mighty and Majestic. Rather, he wanted the matter to become clear: what would his situation be with Pharaoh, given that he has these qualities. The fear is in ﴿I fear that they will deny me﴾. The "an" here is verbal (*masdariyyah*), meaning: "I fear their denial of me." The meaning of fear here is (...), that is: "I expect that." ﴿That they will deny me﴾, because he, peace be upon him, knew from them this matter, their obstinacy, their arrogance, and their commitment to worshipping Pharaoh.

His saying: (﴿And my chest will be constricted﴾ from their denial of me). There is a difficulty here: it is in the nominative (*raf'*), although it follows an accusative [verb], ﴿that they will deny me﴾, because this "an" is verbal (*masdariyyah*), and "yukadhdhibuni" is in the accusative governed by it with the deletion of the *nun*; the *nun* present is the *nun* of protection, and its original form was "yukadhdhibunani." Then the first *nun*, the one of the governing particle, was deleted, and the *ya'* was deleted for lightness. But "wa-yadiqu sadri" is not in the accusative form "wa-yadiqa sadri."

* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** (...).
* **A student:** (...) the difference; that is (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Here he fears them, and says: "I fear that they will deny me, and I fear that my chest will be constricted and my tongue will not be loosed."
* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Then the meaning is: "I fear that they will deny me, and I fear that my chest will be constricted by their denial."
* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** It is a coordinate (*ma'tufah*), conjoined to "I fear" in ﴿Indeed, I fear that they will deny me﴾, and "indeed my chest will be constricted by their denial, and my tongue will not be loosed," and so on to the end.
* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** It is not contradictory; that is, because they would deny me. This [phrase] is nothing more than an object, a direct object, like "I struck Zayd and honored him."

As for his saying: (﴿And my chest will be constricted﴾ from their denial of me): constriction of the chest is its lack of expansion and openness. This is a natural matter: when a person is opposed, his chest will be constricted, just as the Messenger (ﷺ) would have his chest constricted. But God, the Exalted, consoles His messengers by not letting their hearts be constricted and not letting them grieve over these deniers, because for them there is a day on which God will call them to account, and the messengers are only conveyers.

﴿And my chest will be constricted and my tongue will not be loosed﴾. They say that constriction of the chest is among the causes of the occurrence of high blood pressure (*dagh*). For this reason, those afflicted with high blood pressure are advised to avoid anger and what grieves them and constricts their chests, because this is indeed the reality: high blood pressure entails constriction of the chest, constriction of breathing, and the earth becoming narrow for a person. When he exposes himself to what (...) that, the pressure increases upon him. But if he accustoms himself to openness, expansion, and not being troubled by calamities, he will gain much good and will always remain in joy, especially if he seeks reward and believes in divine decree.

He said: (﴿And my chest will be constricted and my tongue will not be loosed﴾ in delivering the message, because of the knot that is in it). Is this knot (*'uqdah*) figurative or literal?

* **A student:** Figurative (...).
* **The Shaykh:** No, (...). This story of the ember is false; it is an Israelite narration and not acceptable. But it is possible that it is figurative, meaning that he cannot express himself with fluency and eloquence, because of God's saying: ﴿And loosen a knot from my tongue (27), that they may understand my speech﴾ [Ta-Ha 27, 28], and Pharaoh's description of him: ﴿and he almost cannot express himself clearly﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 52]. And it is possible, and this is closer, that there is a speech impediment: either a hastiness in speech when pronouncing the letters, such that the letters follow one another until they cannot be understood (because some people are like this, having no literal knot in their tongue, but the letters pile up in their speech so that you do not know what they are saying); or because there is an impediment in which the letters are not distinguished in his speech. All of these are possible. But they indicate that this knot is not as mentioned, from the ember, because that would be a physical effect that prevents him from speaking; it is rather an innate defect, i.e., from the original creation. It is also possible that it is with respect to eloquence: that he is not eloquent in his address, his explanation, and his persuasion. But the first is preferable; that is, it is a figurative knot, namely in the quality of speech, such that the letters are not distinguished in his speech, either because of his haste, or because of a lisp (*lathgha*), or something else.

(﴿And my tongue will not be loosed, so send [word] to Aaron﴾, my brother, ﴿with me﴾). "Arsil ilayhi" means: send the message to him, so that he may be a helper and a minister to him. It has been said that no one is more deserving of such a request from his brother than Moses regarding his brother Aaron, because Aaron was the cause of Moses attaining the highest station among the descendants of Adam whom God has blessed, which is prophethood, when he said: ﴿so send [word] to Aaron﴾.

Then he mentioned another obstacle other than denial, saying: (﴿And they have a charge against me﴾ for the killing of a Coptic man from among them, ﴿so I fear that they will kill me﴾). This is a different fear, resulting from his dealings with them. The first fear relates to the message, and this fear relates to dealing with them. For this reason, in the first he said: ﴿I fear that they will deny me﴾, not "that they will kill," because he would not imagine being killed if he came with the message. Therefore, in the second he said: ﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me﴾ for what? As the author said: (for killing the Coptic man among them).

Its story is well known in Surah al-Qasas: he, peace be upon him, was a strong and powerful man. One day he went out and found in the city two men fighting, one of them from his party from the Children of Israel, and the second from his enemies, the Copts. The Israelite sought his help, so Moses struck the Copt with his fist until he died. On the next day he went out and found his Israelite companion with another man. Moses said to him: ﴿Indeed, you are clearly a misguided man﴾ [Al-Qasas 18], and he wanted to seize the enemy. The Israelite thought that he wanted to seize him, because he had reproached him and said: ﴿Indeed, you are clearly a misguided man.﴾ When he prepared to strike, he thought that he would strike him, so the Israelite said: ﴿Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?﴾ [Al-Qasas 19], "God suffices you against the evil of the one to whom you do good." When he said this, the Copt became aware of it, and he informed on Moses for this reason. Moses, peace be upon him, went out fearful, watching, and turned to God, the Exalted, saying: ﴿My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people﴾ [Al-Qasas 21], so God saved him and bestowed upon him the message.

* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** It is not related to anything. Read the verses (...).
* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Is the whole context in the context of the man who (...)? ﴿So he became in the city fearful, watching; and suddenly the one who had sought his help the day before cried out to him for help. Moses said to him, "Indeed, you are clearly a misguided man"﴾ [Al-Qasas 18]. (...) But when Moses ﴿wanted to seize the one who was an enemy to both of them, [the man] said, "O Moses, do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul?"﴾ [Al-Qasas 19].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 10–17 (part 2 of 2):

He says: ﴿And they have a crime against me, so I fear that they will kill me﴾. That is, they will kill me for it. The yā' (of the first person) has been omitted for lightness, and the nūn, which is the nūn of the verb, has been omitted because of the accusative (naṣb). ﴿So I fear that they will kill me﴾ because of it.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Never!﴾, that is, they will not kill you. ﴿So go, both of you﴾, that is, you and your brother, and in this there is the prevalence of the present over the absent.)

Also in it: Allah the Exalted answered Mūsā's supplication, as He said in Surah Ṭā-Hā: ﴿You have been granted your request, O Mūsā﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 36]. He answered him, and sent Hārūn with the message. ﴿So go, both of you, with Our signs﴾. The bā' here denotes accompaniment: those who accompany the signs of Allah, that is, the distinct signs belonging to Him alone which indicate Him to the exclusion of others. The signs that went with them were: the revelation, which is the first; the second, the staff; and the third, the hand. These are the signs that were present at the revelation to him.

Then after that nine signs followed them, as is clear. Of these, these three signs are one of meaning and two that are sensory, corresponding to the principle, because the transformation of the staff into a serpent resembles magic, but it is not magic, for this is a reality, whereas magic is illusion. Likewise, when he places his hand in his pocket it comes out white without harm, meaning without leprosy; its deficiency also resembles magic, but it is not magic. So it is one of the signs of Allah the Exalted, a miracle for these people, that they could not produce the like of it.

(﴿Indeed, We are with you, listening﴾ to what you say and what is said to you; it is treated as the plural.) As for His words ﴿Indeed We﴾, the pronoun refers to Allah the Exalted in the form of the plural of majesty. He did not say "Indeed I", although in Surah Ṭā-Hā He said: ﴿Indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 46]. But here He mentioned only ﴿listening﴾, so the emphasis is achieved by combining the two matters, hearing and seeing; here only listening is mentioned, and for this reason it came in the form of majesty in relation to the subject.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed We are with you﴾, and not "with you both" as He said in Surah Ṭā-Hā, the author says: (it is treated as the plural). The answer to this: the author did not say that the two are treated as the plural; and if we say that the least of the plural is two, then this is said, and although it is in the plural form, it indicates the two in terms of the linguistic meaning, so there is no need for interpretation.

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...). If we say that the least of the plural is two, we say this, and although it is in the plural form, it indicates the two in terms of the intended linguistic meaning, so there is no need for interpretation.

If you say: since Mūsā and Hārūn and the signs were there, it is as if they became three, although the signs are not (...) but they are supportive, because support comes through proofs and the strength of the one calling and the one arguing. It is also possible that He gathered them in view of the fact that Mūsā and Hārūn would have a people, and the listening would concern Mūsā and Hārūn with their people.

﴿So come, both of you, to Pharaoh and say: Indeed we are the messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 16]. He says: ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Pharaoh﴾. Here He said: ﴿So come to Pharaoh﴾, which shows that the people and the family, when they are attributed to a person, include him among them. So His saying ﴿Admit the family of Pharaoh to the severest punishment﴾ [Ghāfir 46] does not indicate Pharaoh's salvation, because of His saying: ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them into the Fire﴾ [Hūd 98]; so he is their first. Here too He said: ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 10], then He said: ﴿So come to Pharaoh﴾, which indicates that "the people", when attributed to someone, the one to whom they are attributed enters first among them, unless a physical obstacle prevents that, such as his death for example; for if he has died there is no benefit in coming to him, but if he is present, he is the first to enter among his people.

﴿So come, both of you, to Pharaoh and say: Indeed we are the messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾. Allah the Exalted did not specify the manner of the saying, but here specified what is said, whereas in Surah Ṭā-Hā: ﴿Speak to him gently, perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 44]. Mūsā and Hārūn were commanded, or Mūsā was commanded, to say that they are messengers from Allah, and to say that in a gentle tone rather than a harsh tone; because the harsh person, if met with a harsh tone, becomes harder still, whereas if met with a gentle tone, gentleness and harshness come together and no clash or collision occurs between them. This is among the wisdom in calling to the truth. As for the person who is arrogant and tyrannical, he should not be met with arrogance and tyranny, because that only increases the matter in severity; he is met with gentleness until the proof is established against him.

(﴿So come, both of you, to Pharaoh and say: Indeed we﴾, that is, each of us ﴿are the messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾.) The author supposed: (that is, each of us), for the sake of agreement with the subject, which is the noun of ﴿inna﴾, and the predicate, which is ''messenger'': ﴿Indeed we are messenger﴾.

In another verse: ﴿Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 47], in the dual; and here in the singular. The author supposed, or interpreted the verse, to mean: each one of us. And the saying of the Exalted earlier: ﴿and make us leaders for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Furqān 74] means: make each one of us (a leader). This is one of the aspects.

Another aspect: that "rasūl" means "risāla" (the message), in the sense of a verbal noun (ism maṣdar), and a verbal noun when described by it is the same whether singular or otherwise.

A third aspect: it may be said that the principal in the message is Mūsā, who is one; Hārūn is designated and a minister; otherwise the principle is that Mūsā is the messenger, as (...) the biography mentions Mūsā without mentioning Hārūn.

﴿Indeed we are messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾.

And His saying: ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾, and He did not say "I am the messenger of God", because they would meet a person who claims lordship, that he is the Lord; so it becomes clear to him from the outset that lordship is not his, but belongs to Allah: ﴿Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾. The "worlds" are everything other than Allah; every creature is a world. Yet they are sometimes attributed to their kinds, so it is said: the world of humans, the world of jinn, the world of camels, the world of such and such; but when put together in this way they encompass all kinds. Everything other than Allah is a world; they said: they were named "world" because they are a sign of their Creator.

(﴿Indeed we are messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ to you). The author supposed "to you" for clarification; otherwise there is no need, since they are addressing him, so their saying ﴿Indeed we are messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ would have no benefit from addressing him unless... They are the messengers of the Lord of the worlds to him.

(﴿that﴾, that is: that ﴿send with us﴾ to Shām ﴿the Children of Israel﴾; so they came to him) and so on.

His saying: ﴿that send with us the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 17]. The word "send" (irsāl) is used in the sense of release; that is, release them, because he had tightened the grip upon them and tormented them by killing their sons and sparing their women.
