The meaning of fear here is (...), that is: "I expect that." ﴿That they will deny me﴾, because he, peace be upon him, knew from them this matter, their obstinacy, their arrogance, and their commitment to worshipping Pharaoh.

His saying: (﴿And my chest will be constricted﴾ from their denial of me). There is a difficulty here: it is in the nominative (*raf'*), although it follows an accusative [verb], ﴿that they will deny me﴾, because this "an" is verbal (*masdariyyah*), and "yukadhdhibuni" is in the accusative governed by it with the deletion of the *nun*; the *nun* present is the *nun* of protection, and its original form was "yukadhdhibunani." Then the first *nun*, the one of the governing particle, was deleted, and the *ya'* was deleted for lightness. But "wa-yadiqu sadri" is not in the accusative form "wa-yadiqa sadri."

* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** (...).
* **A student:** (...) the difference; that is (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Here he fears them, and says: "I fear that they will deny me, and I fear that my chest will be constricted and my tongue will not be loosed."
* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Then the meaning is: "I fear that they will deny me, and I fear that my chest will be constricted by their denial."
* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** It is a coordinate (*ma'tufah*), conjoined to "I fear" in ﴿Indeed, I fear that they will deny me﴾, and "indeed my chest will be constricted by their denial, and my tongue will not be loosed," and so on to the end.
* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** It is not contradictory; that is, because they would deny me. This [phrase] is nothing more than an object, a direct object, like "I struck Zayd and honored him."

As for his saying: (﴿And my chest will be constricted﴾ from their denial of me): constriction of the chest is its lack of expansion and openness. This is a natural matter: when a person is opposed, his chest will be constricted, just as the Messenger (ﷺ) would have his chest constricted. But God, the Exalted, consoles His messengers by not letting their hearts be constricted and not letting them grieve over these deniers, because for them there is a day on which God will call them to account, and the messengers are only conveyers.

﴿And my chest will be constricted and my tongue will not be loosed﴾. They say that constriction of the chest is among the causes of the occurrence of high blood pressure (*dagh*). For this reason, those afflicted with high blood pressure are advised to avoid anger and what grieves them and constricts their chests, because this is indeed the reality: high blood pressure entails constriction of the chest, constriction of breathing, and the earth becoming narrow for a person. When he exposes himself to what (...) that, the pressure increases upon him. But if he accustoms himself to openness, expansion, and not being troubled by calamities, he will gain much good and will always remain in joy, especially if he seeks reward and believes in divine decree.

He said: (﴿And my chest will be constricted and my tongue will not be loosed﴾ in delivering the message, because of the knot that is in it). Is this knot (*'uqdah*) figurative or literal?

* **A student:** Figurative (...).
* **The Shaykh:** No, (...). This story of the ember is false; it is an Israelite narration and not acceptable. But it is possible that it is figurative, meaning that he cannot express himself with fluency and eloquence, because of God's saying: ﴿And loosen a knot from my tongue (27), that they may understand my speech﴾ [Ta-Ha 27, 28], and Pharaoh's description of him: ﴿and he almost cannot express himself clearly﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 52]. And it is possible, and this is closer, that there is a speech impediment: either a hastiness in speech when pronouncing the letters, such that the letters follow one another until they cannot be understood (because some people are like this, having no literal knot in their tongue, but the letters pile up in their speech so that you do not know what they are saying); or because there is an impediment in which the letters are not distinguished in his speech. All of these are possible. But they indicate that this knot is not as mentioned, from the ember, because that would be a physical effect that prevents him from speaking; it is rather an innate defect, i.e., from the original creation. It is also possible that it is with respect to eloquence: that he is not eloquent in his address, his explanation, and his persuasion. But the first is preferable; that is, it is a figurative knot, namely in the quality of speech, such that the letters are not distinguished in his speech, either because of his haste, or because of a lisp (*lathgha*), or something else.

(﴿And my tongue will not be loosed, so send [word] to Aaron﴾, my brother, ﴿with me﴾). "Arsil ilayhi" means: send the message to him, so that he may be a helper and a minister to him. It has been said that no one is more deserving of such a request from his brother than Moses regarding his brother Aaron, because Aaron was the cause of Moses attaining the highest station among the descendants of Adam whom God has blessed, which is prophethood, when he said: ﴿so send [word] to Aaron﴾.

Then he mentioned another obstacle other than denial, saying: (﴿And they have a charge against me﴾ for the killing of a Coptic man from among them, ﴿so I fear that they will kill me﴾). This is a different fear, resulting from his dealings with them. The first fear relates to the message, and this fear relates to dealing with them. For this reason, in the first he said: ﴿I fear that they will deny me﴾, not "that they will kill," because he would not imagine being killed if he came with the message. Therefore, in the second he said: ﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me﴾ for what? As the author said: (for killing the Coptic man among them).

Its story is well known in Surah al-Qasas: he, peace be upon him, was a strong and powerful man. One day he went out and found in the city two men fighting, one of them from his party from the Children of Israel, and the second from his enemies, the Copts. The Israelite sought his help, so Moses struck the Copt with his fist until he died. On the next day he went out and found his Israelite companion with another man. Moses said to him: ﴿Indeed, you are clearly a misguided man﴾ [Al-Qasas 18], and he wanted to seize the enemy. The Israelite thought that he wanted to seize him, because he had reproached him and said: ﴿Indeed, you are clearly a misguided man.﴾ When he prepared to strike, he thought that he would strike him, so the Israelite said: ﴿Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?﴾ [Al-Qasas 19], "God suffices you against the evil of the one to whom you do good." When he said this, the Copt became aware of it, and he informed on Moses for this reason. Moses, peace be upon him, went out fearful, watching, and turned to God, the Exalted, saying: ﴿My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people﴾ [Al-Qasas 21], so God saved him and bestowed upon him the message.

* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** It is not related to anything. Read the verses (...).
* **A student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Is the whole context in the context of the man who (...)? ﴿So he became in the city fearful, watching; and suddenly the one who had sought his help the day before cried out to him for help. Moses said to him, "Indeed, you are clearly a misguided man"﴾ [Al-Qasas 18]. (...) But when Moses ﴿wanted to seize the one who was an enemy to both of them, [the man] said, "O Moses, do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul?"﴾ [Al-Qasas 19].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 10–17 (part 2 of 2):

He says: ﴿And they have a crime against me, so I fear that they will kill me﴾. That is, they will kill me for it. The yā' (of the first person) has been omitted for lightness, and the nūn, which is the nūn of the verb, has been omitted because of the accusative (naṣb). ﴿So I fear that they will kill me﴾ because of it.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Never!﴾, that is, they will not kill you. ﴿So go, both of you﴾, that is, you and your brother, and in this there is the prevalence of the present over the absent.)

Also in it: Allah the Exalted answered Mūsā's supplication, as He said in Surah Ṭā-Hā: ﴿You have been granted your request, O Mūsā﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 36]. He answered him, and sent Hārūn with the message. ﴿So go, both of you, with Our signs﴾. The bā' here denotes accompaniment: those who accompany the signs of Allah, that is, the distinct signs belonging to Him alone which indicate Him to the exclusion of others. The signs that went with them were: the revelation, which is the first; the second, the staff; and the third, the hand. These are the signs that were present at the revelation to him.

Then after that nine signs followed them, as is clear. Of these, these three signs are one of meaning and two that are sensory, corresponding to the principle, because the transformation of the staff into a serpent resembles magic, but it is not magic, for this is a reality, whereas magic is illusion. Likewise, when he places his hand in his pocket it comes out white without harm, meaning without leprosy; its deficiency also resembles magic, but it is not magic. So it is one of the signs of Allah the Exalted, a miracle for these people, that they could not produce the like of it.

(﴿Indeed, We are with you, listening﴾ to what you say and what is said to you; it is treated as the plural.) As for His words ﴿Indeed We﴾, the pronoun refers to Allah the Exalted in the form of the plural of majesty. He did not say "Indeed I", although in Surah Ṭā-Hā He said: ﴿Indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 46]. But here He mentioned only ﴿listening﴾, so the emphasis is achieved by combining the two matters, hearing and seeing; here only listening is mentioned, and for this reason it came in the form of majesty in relation to the subject.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed We are with you﴾, and not "with you both" as He said in Surah Ṭā-Hā, the author says: (it is treated as the plural). The answer to this: the author did not say that the two are treated as the plural; and if we say that the least of the plural is two, then this is said, and although it is in the plural form, it indicates the two in terms of the linguistic meaning, so there is no need for interpretation.

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...). If we say that the least of the plural is two, we say this, and although it is in the plural form, it indicates the two in terms of the intended linguistic meaning, so there is no need for interpretation.

If you say: since Mūsā and Hārūn and the signs were there, it is as if they became three, although the signs are not (...) but they are supportive, because support comes through proofs and the strength of the one calling and the one arguing. It is also possible that He gathered them in view of the fact that Mūsā and Hārūn would have a people, and the listening would concern Mūsā and Hārūn with their people.

﴿So come, both of you, to Pharaoh and say: Indeed we are the messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 16]. He says: ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Pharaoh﴾. Here He said: ﴿So come to Pharaoh﴾, which shows that the people and the family, when they are attributed to a person, include him among them. So His saying ﴿Admit the family of Pharaoh to the severest punishment﴾ [Ghāfir 46] does not indicate Pharaoh's salvation, because of His saying: ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them into the Fire﴾ [Hūd 98]; so he is their first. Here too He said: ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 10], then He said: ﴿So come to Pharaoh﴾, which indicates that "the people", when attributed to someone, the one to whom they are attributed enters first among them, unless a physical obstacle prevents that, such as his death for example; for if he has died there is no benefit in coming to him, but if he is present, he is the first to enter among his people.

﴿So come, both of you, to Pharaoh and say: Indeed we are the messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾. Allah the Exalted did not specify the manner of the saying, but here specified what is said, whereas in Surah Ṭā-Hā: ﴿Speak to him gently, perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 44]. Mūsā and Hārūn were commanded, or Mūsā was commanded, to say that they are messengers from Allah, and to say that in a gentle tone rather than a harsh tone; because the harsh person, if met with a harsh tone, becomes harder still, whereas if met with a gentle tone, gentleness and harshness come together and no clash or collision occurs between them. This is among the wisdom in calling to the truth. As for the person who is arrogant and tyrannical, he should not be met with arrogance and tyranny, because that only increases the matter in severity; he is met with gentleness until the proof is established against him.

(﴿So come, both of you, to Pharaoh and say: Indeed we﴾, that is, each of us ﴿are the messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾.) The author supposed: (that is, each of us), for the sake of agreement with the subject, which is the noun of ﴿inna﴾, and the predicate, which is ''messenger'': ﴿Indeed we are messenger﴾.

In another verse: ﴿Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 47], in the dual; and here in the singular. The author supposed, or interpreted the verse, to mean: each one of us. And the saying of the Exalted earlier: ﴿and make us leaders for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Furqān 74] means: make each one of us (a leader). This is one of the aspects.

Another aspect: that "rasūl" means "risāla" (the message), in the sense of a verbal noun (ism maṣdar), and a verbal noun when described by it is the same whether singular or otherwise.

A third aspect: it may be said that the principal in the message is Mūsā, who is one; Hārūn is designated and a minister; otherwise the principle is that Mūsā is the messenger, as (...) the biography mentions Mūsā without mentioning Hārūn.

﴿Indeed we are messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾.

And His saying: ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾, and He did not say "I am the messenger of God", because they would meet a person who claims lordship, that he is the Lord; so it becomes clear to him from the outset that lordship is not his, but belongs to Allah: ﴿Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾. The "worlds" are everything other than Allah; every creature is a world. Yet they are sometimes attributed to their kinds, so it is said: the world of humans, the world of jinn, the world of camels, the world of such and such; but when put together in this way they encompass all kinds. Everything other than Allah is a world; they said: they were named "world" because they are a sign of their Creator.

(﴿Indeed we are messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ to you). The author supposed "to you" for clarification; otherwise there is no need, since they are addressing him, so their saying ﴿Indeed we are messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ would have no benefit from addressing him unless... They are the messengers of the Lord of the worlds to him.

(﴿that﴾, that is: that ﴿send with us﴾ to Shām ﴿the Children of Israel﴾; so they came to him) and so on.

His saying: ﴿that send with us the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 17]. The word "send" (irsāl) is used in the sense of release; that is, release them, because he had tightened the grip upon them and tormented them by killing their sons and sparing their women. So Mūsā, peace be upon him, asked him to send the Children of Israel with him and release them. But the discussion between him and Mūsā will come later, God willing.

* From these verses is derived, firstly: the affirmation of calling (nidā') for Allah the Exalted. From where do we take it?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: So his speech is with a voice in this sense, and that it is with a letter.
* And it is also derived from the verse that it is with a letter.
* Student: ﴿that come to the wrongdoing people﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿that come to the wrongdoing people﴾, since ﴿Come to the wrongdoing people, the people of Pharaoh, will they not fear God?﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 10–11] are all letters.

In this is evidence of the grace of Allah the Exalted upon creation. From where do we take it?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Sending the messengers, yes. The sending of messengers is evidence of Allah's grace upon creation and His care for them, because however much intelligence people are given, they cannot grasp in detail what is due to Allah the Exalted; the sensible person grasps what is due to Allah in a general way: that He has absolute perfection and deserves worship; but to grasp it in detail is possible only through the messengers. For this reason He said: ﴿So that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisā' 165]. And in this is evidence of the bad state of Pharaoh and his people. From where do we take it?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...).

And in it is evidence that there is no harm in brevity in speech, on condition that (...). From where do we take it? ﴿that come to the wrongdoing people, the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 10]. What is the benefit of stating something in brief and then detailing it after?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The meaning? Its importance; (...) because he becomes eager and looking forward to the explanation of this brief matter, so he comes to it while he is (...). Also among the benefits in this hadith is evidence that natural fear is permissible and is not shirk. From where do you take it? (...) i.e., the two fears, because he fears twice: ﴿that they will deny me﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 12] and ﴿that they will kill me﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 14].

Or we may say: the fear here means its consequence, which is expectation, because he expects this (...). He says: ﴿I fear that they will deny me﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 12]; I think they will deny me. It does not mean he feared with terror; the terror that befalls the soul is one thing, and it means expectation. In this is evidence that a person may describe his condition when he does not intend complaint. His saying: ﴿and my breast tightens and my tongue does not speak freely﴾ is a description of himself as weak, yes, and of inability to bear it psychologically through tightness of breast, and of lack of precise eloquence through his tongue not running freely. In it is also evidence that it is permissible to mention the means that make a supplication likely to be accepted, since he mentioned that he cannot do it because his breast tightens and his tongue does not speak freely; this is from the means by which the supplicant seeks nearness, mentioning his condition being among the means that make his supplication deserving of acceptance.

In this is affirmation of Allah's companionship (ma'iyya), the Mighty and Majestic. Is the companionship literal or figurative?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: If it is literal, does that not necessitate the saying (...)? That is: for example, you now (...) that companionship originally means sharing a place or not? You acknowledge that companionship originally entails sharing a place.
* Student: No doubt.
* The Shaykh: No doubt.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Does it imply (iqtiḍā'), not necessitate (istilzām)? It implies; that is (...) this or necessitates.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Necessitates.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, I say: companionship absolutely, so that one reaches the call to (...). Then why do they interpret companionship, and then object to our interpreting the hand?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It does not necessitate sharing a place nor mixing (...), because companionship in the reality of Allah means absolute accompaniment, but it is in every thing according to its nature, is it not? You say, for example: the milk is with water; he gave me milk with water. This implies mixing and blending.
(...).

And taking the evidence as a companion, due to His saying: ﴿with Our signs﴾, and knowledge of the one who defends, which is His saying: ﴿with you, listening﴾. Everything needs encouragement, so a person should show encouragement to his companion so that he becomes active and conveys the message in the most complete manner. In this is evidence that the people, the family, and the like, when attributed, include the one to whom they are attributed; we take it from His saying: ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾, then at the end of the verses He said: ﴿So come to Pharaoh﴾, which indicates that Pharaoh is among them.

And in it is also evidence that a person should be addressed according to what his condition requires: the one who denies lordship is addressed with the affirmation of lordship, and the one who denies divinity is established with the affirmation of divinity, and so on. From where is it taken? From the words of the Exalted: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them﴾ [al-Naml 14].
* Student: Those are Pharaoh's people.
* The Shaykh: No, Pharaoh is with them.
* Student: Pharaoh and his people (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. And Mūsā also said to him: ﴿You have certainly known that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence﴾ [al-Isrā' 102].
* Student: Pharaoh; this evidence is clear regarding him. For others than Pharaoh who denied (...), is there a sound proof that (...) with certainty (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, the proof is rational.
* Student: Legal (shar'ī); that is, there is none.
* The Shaykh: No, there is no legal one; because the legal proof cannot speak about a matter that has already occurred; for among those present now who deny, do they say there is no creator?
* Student: Only by analogy (...).
* The Shaykh: Only by analogy?! No, and by reason too: no sane person can claim that these things came into being without a cause at all. We have not known anyone who denied it, and we see that it is not possible either, and that if he denies it with his tongue, his heart acknowledges it, unless he is not sensible; that is, some people may be purely imitators and do not think, like the ordinary communists and others, who apparently do not reflect on these matters, because they have lived in an environment that from the outset says: there is only our worldly life, we die and live, and there is no resurrection and no lord and nothing at all. Such people may be deniers in the depths of their hearts or souls (...) but he ceased from opposition.
* Student: He ceased from opposition.
* The Shaykh: It does not follow that he believes; he may be arrogant and not believe.
* Student: (...) a proof.
* The Shaykh: On what?
* Student: On (...).
* The Shaykh: He was unable to oppose.
* Student: Yes, he acknowledged (...).
* The Shaykh: Because he said: "I give life and cause death," so he opposed with deception, then afterwards he was unable.
* Student: (...) he confessed.
* The Shaykh: No, he did not confess; because he did not say: "so he confessed."
* Student: He was stunned.
* The Shaykh: Stunned, unable. What does "stunned" mean?
* Student: Cut off (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, that. But it does not follow from the absence of the establishment of proof, or from the establishment of proof against the opponent, that he must acknowledge; he may be arrogant.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, now we are saying there is one who denies verbally.
* Student: No, in his heart.
* The Shaykh: No, the verse does not indicate that he denied in his heart even if he was stunned; there is no evidence that he denied in his heart, nor does it indicate that he acknowledged faith, nor that he denied the meaning; because when he said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾ [al-Baqarah 258], he did not say that he had no lord; he made himself a rival to Allah and said: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ [al-Baqarah 258], so the objection was presented to him that he could not escape. He mentioned three pretexts to clarify the matter against these pretexts: their denial, that his breast tightens, and that his tongue does not speak freely. Allah the Exalted showed that these do not affect the matter, and said: ﴿So go, both of you, with Our signs; indeed We are with you, listening. So come to Pharaoh and say: Indeed we are the messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 15–16]. They would comply with this command, because they know that Allah the Exalted is with them, hearing what Pharaoh says and what they say to him, and they carried out this message by the command of Allah, blessed and exalted.

It was also mentioned earlier that they asked him to send the Children of Israel with them. The author says: he should send them to Shām; but there is nothing in the Qur'an that indicates that; that is, they asked that he send the Children of Israel with them to Shām. Rather, the meaning of "sending" here is release from enslavement and bondage, because he was doing that to the Children of Israel.

Almighty Allah says, mentioning Pharaoh's reply to Musa: (﴿He said﴾, Pharaoh to Musa: ﴿Did we not raise you among us﴾). There is brevity (ijaz) in the verse, and according to the rhetoricians brevity is divided into two types: brevity by omission (ijaz al-hadhf) and brevity by condensation (ijaz al-ikhtisar). Which of them is present here?

* A student: Omission.

* The Shaykh: It is brevity by omission (ijaz al-hadhf). This is why He said: (﴿So they both went to him and said: Indeed, we are messengers of your Lord﴾), what was mentioned, and Pharaoh said to Musa, and so on. When Musa and his brother delivered the message, Pharaoh replied to this call: (﴿Did we not raise you among us﴾, in our homes, ﴿as a child﴾, a young boy close to infancy after being weaned). This is one point. ﴿And you remained among us for years of your life. And you did your deed that you did, and you were of the ungrateful﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 18-19]. That is: after all this, do you come and claim that you are the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds? The meaning is that he denies the lordship of Pharaoh. It is as if he is saying, after these three matters: it was more fitting for you to come apologizing and submissive, because we bestowed favour upon you, and because you wronged us by failing to acknowledge the favour.

He said: (﴿Did we not raise you among us﴾, in our homes, ﴿as a child﴾, a young boy close to infancy after being weaned). The story is well known from Surah al-Qasas: Allah inspired his mother, when she feared for him, to place him in a chest and cast him into the river, and she did so out of faith in Allah's promise. Then Allah decreed that this chest fell into the hands of Pharaoh's family, and they picked it up for a wisdom that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, intended, while they did not perceive it. When they picked him up, his mother sent his sister to follow the news: ﴿so she watched him from afar, and they did not perceive﴾ [al-Qasas 11], from a distance. Then she saw them seeking a wet-nurse for him, so she offered to them: ﴿Shall I direct you to a household that will rear him for you and they will be sincere to him?﴾ [al-Qasas 12]. So he was returned to his mother, even though he had not suckled the breast of any woman other than hers. This is part of the complete power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the fulfilment of His promise: He returned him to his mother before he was nourished by anything other than her milk, and he remained with her until she weaned him. And according to the situation, to whom would he return afterwards?

* Students: Pharaoh.

* The Shaykh: To the family of Pharaoh who had picked him up. He returned to them and grew up among them. This is part of the complete power of Allah, that this boy, whose downfall of Pharaoh would be because of him, grew up in Pharaoh's lap. It has been said that Pharaoh used to kill the sons of the Children of Israel out of fear of this boy, because the soothsayers told him: a man will appear among the Children of Israel through whom your kingdom will end, so he began killing their sons.

This, in any case, is among the Isra'iliyyat, of which we do not know whether it is true or not. As for his killing the sons and sparing the women, this is in the Qur'an. But was it a humiliation of the people and their enslavement, or fear of this boy? Allah knows best. In any case, he was raised by him, and Pharaoh would bestow this favour upon him: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾ That is: how then do you come with the opposite of what we want, and claim that you have a Lord who sent you? Secondly: ﴿And you remained among us for years of your life﴾, is it "sinin" or "sinina"?

* Students: Sinin.

* The Shaykh: Sinin, because it is attached to the sound masculine plural.

His saying: ﴿min 'umurika﴾ originally is a description (sifah) of "sinin"; its original form is: "labithta fina sinin min 'umurika" (you remained among us years of your life). But the grammatical rule is that when a description is placed before what it describes, it is parsed as a circumstantial (hal), because the hal is a description in meaning, and a description in the sense of a qualifier (na't) cannot precede the qualified noun. Therefore they said: the description of an indefinite noun, when placed before it, is parsed as a hal of it. This is the rule of the grammarians.

﴿min 'umurika sinin﴾: these years were thirty years, according to what the author and some exegetes said. But it is better to leave them undetermined as Allah left them undetermined. However, they estimated these thirty because Musa, peace be upon him, was granted prophethood at the age of forty, according to Allah's customary way in sending messengers. So they said: the thirty years were with Pharaoh; then he went to Madyan and remained among them for how long?

* Students: Ten years.

* The Shaykh: Ten years. Then Allah sent him. From here the years became thirty. But this is not necessarily so, because he may have been raised by Pharaoh for less than this, and then joined whom? The Children of Israel. Therefore we should not affirm definitively that it was thirty years; rather let us say as Allah said: ﴿sinin﴾, which is a plural, and the least plural is three years. But it appears that it was more, because three years may not contain that favour which Pharaoh bestowed.

It is said: (he would wear Pharaoh's clothing, ride his mounts, and he was called his son). That is why Pharaoh's wife said: ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us, or we may take him as a son﴾, and they did not perceive [al-Qasas 9].

* A student: Pharaoh's wife.

* The Shaykh: Pharaoh's wife: ﴿Do not kill him; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may take him as a son﴾. Yes indeed.

This is evidence that they took him as a son; that is, "perhaps he will benefit us" absolutely, even if we do not adopt him or take him as a son. It is known that a son will benefit, but Allah says: ﴿and they did not perceive﴾ [al-Qasas 9]: the matter was not as they expected, rather it was the opposite.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 19:

(﴿And you did your deed which you did﴾, which is his killing of the Copt) ﴿You did your deed﴾: he left it vague to magnify it. Vagueness (ibhām) sometimes comes for the sake of magnification, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Inevitable Reality (1), what is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ [al-Haqqah 1, 2], and His saying: ﴿Then there covered them of the sea that which covered them﴾ [Taha 78]. This is vagueness intended for magnification. Here He said ﴿you did your deed﴾ and did not say "you killed the Copt," as an indication of its magnitude. He attributed it to him as a matter of affirmation (taqrir), meaning: you did that deed which no one else does (or has done) except you, namely his killing of the Copt who was in a quarrel with the Israelite.

﴿And you did your deed which you did, and you were among the disbelievers﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 19]. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in ﴿you did﴾. ﴿And you were among the disbelievers﴾: disbelievers in whom? Not in Allah, since he (Musa) did not disbelieve in Allah; rather, [they were] disbelievers in Him by [following] Pharaoh, because Musa did not take him as a god as the Copts did. (﴿And you were among the disbelievers﴾, those who denied My favour upon you in raising you and not enslaving you.) This is what the author (the commentator Ibn Kathir / the author of the cited work) adopted, and that the intended meaning of disbelief here is ingratitude (kufr al-ni'mah), namely his denial of the favour Pharaoh had bestowed on him by raising him and not enslaving him as he enslaved the Children of Israel. But what should be said is that it is more general than what the author stated; indeed, even more important in Pharaoh's view is that he disbelieved in his lordship, so he did not worship him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 20:

(﴿Musa said﴾ "I did it then" — i.e., at that time — ﴿and I was among the astray﴾ concerning what Allah gave me of knowledge and messagehood after it)

﴿I did it then﴾: you know that the word "idhan" (then/in that case) refers to the future, because its origin is "idha" and it has been given nunation (tanwin); but here it can refer to the past. So the author's explanation of "idhan" as "hina'idhin" (at that time) is interpretation by meaning (al-tafsir bil-ma'na), not interpretation by wording (al-tafsir bil-lafz), since one particle is not explained by a particle that corresponds to it in meaning. Rather, it is interpretation by meaning; that is: "I did it at that time, I did it in the past," ﴿and I was among the astray﴾.

Some exegetes held that "idhan" retains its own sense here as a response to Pharaoh, in a mocking manner, as if he were saying: "Then I will do it," meaning: "I do not care about you. But I was among the ignorant ones regarding the ruling on killing." Perhaps this is closer to the truth: "idhan" is in its own usage, not in the sense of the past, and it is as though this was a reply to Pharaoh by way of belittling him and not caring, and that he does not mind him. His saying ﴿and I was among the astray﴾ is a response to Pharaoh's words to him: ﴿And you were among the disbelievers﴾.

As for His saying ﴿among the astray﴾, the commentator or the explainer says: "concerning what Allah gave me of knowledge and messagehood after it." So the intended meaning of "astray" here is ignorance. On this basis, straying (al-dalal) divides into two kinds: straying for which the doer or the one who strays is blamed, and straying for which he is not blamed. The straying that occurred, or with which Musa was characterized when he killed the Copt, is straying for which he is not blamed, because no revelation or messagehood had yet come to him at that time, so he was excused.

From here we learn that it is valid to describe those among the people of knowledge who deviate from what is correct as astray, but not with absolute straying for which they are blamed, when it is known that they are sincere advisers to Islam, but erred after exertion (ijtihad). An example of this is what passed with us in the chapter on the principles, that many of the people of knowledge are Ash'aris, who are known for their sincerity to Islam and their standing in truthfulness; nevertheless we describe them as astray, but not with the absolute straying that implies blame and disparagement. Rather, the intended meaning is opposing the correct position. Otherwise, you will find someone who is outraged if we say, for example, that Ibn Hajar is astray, or al-Nawawi is astray, and that many of the great scholars are mistaken in what is right, or in error in what they say, deviating from the correct position. But no, we say: it is not the absolute straying for which the doer is blamed, because straying with exertion is the pursuit of truth, and a person is not blamed for it even if he is described by it.

* Student: (...) "I will do it."

* The Shaykh: No, its original form cannot be "I will do it." He did it already, but: ﴿idhan﴾ is a response to the present situation, considering his answer to Pharaoh.

* Student: Then the clause of circumstance ﴿and I was among the astray﴾ (...).

* The Shaykh: No, because ﴿and I was among the astray﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) describing the subject in ﴿I did it﴾. Now ﴿idhan﴾ is not connected to "I did it"; it is connected to a response: "I will answer you then," ﴿I did it and I was among the astray﴾, meaning: considering his answer to Pharaoh, not on the basis that he did it then, since one cannot say "I did it then" as though he did it now, when he had done it earlier.

* Student: "I answer you then."

* The Shaykh: "I answer you then. So I did it, and I was among the astray." It thus conveys disregard and defiance toward Pharaoh, that he was unconcerned with him. He says ﴿and I was among the astray﴾. What is meant by "astray" here?

* The students: Ignorance.

* The Shaykh: The ignorance meant here is the ignorance that is not deliberate.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 21:

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So I fled from you when I feared you, then my Lord granted me wisdom﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 21], to the end of the verse. ﴿So I fled from you﴾. The reason for his fleeing from them was that a man came to him running and said: ﴿O Musa, indeed the chiefs are conferring about you to kill you, so leave; indeed I am to you of the sincere advisors﴾ [al-Qasas 20]. This man, as you know, is unidentified, since he said "a man came." But Musa accepted his report because of the presence of an indicator. What is the indicator?

* Student: That the Copt had killed someone.

* Shaykh: That the Copt had killed someone. Otherwise, the report of an unidentified man would not be accepted. Then this man confirmed his report by saying: ﴿So leave; indeed I am to you of the sincere advisors﴾ [al-Qasas 20]. So he left, fleeing in fear.

﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾. "Lamma" (when) is a temporal adverb meaning "when/at the time that." You know that "lamma" has several uses: it is used as a temporal adverb meaning "when," as an exceptive particle meaning "except," as a conditional, and as a negative. As for its use as a negative, what is the example in the words of Allah, the Exalted?

* Student: ﴿And faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat 14].

* Shaykh: ﴿But say, "We have submitted," for faith has not yet entered﴾ [al-Hujurat 14], meaning: it has not entered.

As for its use as a conditional, an example is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when there came to them a messenger from Allah confirming what was with them, a party of those who were given the Scripture threw away the Book of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 101]. ("And when there came to them... they threw away") This is conditional. As for its use meaning "except," an example is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq 4], meaning: no soul except that it has over it a guardian.

Here, ﴿lamma khiftukum﴾ is a noun meaning "when," so it is a temporal adverb: "when I feared you," that is, "at the time I feared you." ﴿Then my Lord granted me wisdom﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 21]. This supports what we previously pointed out: that words are understood as literal according to their context, and this is the basis of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, in holding that there is nothing in the Arabic language called "majaz" (metaphor) absolutely, because meaning is not an intrinsic property of a word; rather, a word has a meaning according to its context and the indicators of its circumstances.

* Student: The man mentioned in Surah al-Qasas, ﴿And there came a man from the farthest part of the city, running﴾ [al-Qasas 20], is not to be interpreted as the man in Surah Ghafir, ﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh said﴾ [Ghafir 28].

* Shaykh: That is not the apparent meaning, because that believing man came to Pharaoh with the message after he went to Madyan. As for the first, it is before he went to Madyan. It is not possible (...), because he is not specified. We do not know, it may be him, but our interpreting him as such means we affirm definitively that he is him, and that is not the case.

* Student: The grammatical analysis of ﴿lamma khiftukum﴾, "lamma..."

* Shaykh: That is, "when I feared you" — a temporal adverb meaning "when."

(﴿then my Lord granted me wisdom﴾, meaning knowledge, ﴿and made me of the messengers﴾.)

﴿Then He granted me﴾: gave me. His saying ﴿hukman﴾ means knowledge. However, interpreting "hukm" as "knowledge" may be objected to by someone who says there is a problem with it, because Allah, the Exalted, conjoins the two, as in ﴿And We gave him wisdom and knowledge﴾ [Yusuf 22], and conjunction requires difference. If that is the case, then one of them cannot be explained by the other. Let us examine whether this objection is correct, or whether it is said that they are among the words which, when combined, are distinct, and when separate, are combined. So when they are combined, they differ, and when one is used alone, the meaning of each becomes the meaning of the other.

﴿Then my Lord granted me wisdom and made me of the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 21]. "Hukm" is the judgment of a matter, and it is called "hukm," and there is no judgment except with knowledge. So is the explanation of "hukm" now by its concomitant or not? It is explained by its concomitant. When it is combined with knowledge, knowledge becomes the opposite of ignorance, and judgment is the application of that knowledge. What appears is that the intended meaning of "hukm" here is less than knowledge; that is, "hukm" means judgment, or that by which a person judges between people, and this is only with knowledge. So the author's explanation of it is an explanation by its concomitant, because knowledge is a necessary consequence of judgment, but judgment is not a necessary consequence of knowledge, since a person may know without judging.

His saying ﴿and made me of the messengers﴾ comes after Allah had revealed to him and given him knowledge and judgment; He also made him a messenger, entrusted with the message.

In His saying ﴿of the messengers﴾, rather than "and made me a messenger," there is a kind of alert to Pharaoh that he is not unprecedented among the messengers, and that he has brought no new matter; rather, there were messengers before him. Allah, the Exalted, mentioned in Surah Ghafir that the believing man said to them: ﴿And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs, but you remained in doubt about what he brought you﴾ [Ghafir 34]. It is as if he is saying to him: "And He made me of the messengers" whose news you have, so I am no novelty among the messengers.

﴿وَتِلْكَ نِعْمَةٌ تَمُنُّهَا عَلَيَّ﴾ [الشعراء ٢٢] أصلها: تمن بها علَيَّ. أي: تجعل بها منة عليَّ. ولكنه حذف حرف الجر وعُدي الفعل إليها، فـ﴿تَمُنُّهَا عَلَيَّ﴾ أي: تجعلها منة. ﴿أَنْ عَبَّدْتَ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾ يقول: (بيان لتلك، أي: اتخذتهم عبيدًا). وإذا كانت بيانًا لتلك، فتكون "أن" تفسيرية (an tafsiriyyah)، تفسيرًا لاسم الإشارة في قوله: ﴿تِلْكَ نِعْمَةٌ﴾. يعني: أي ﴿عَبَّدْتَ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾، أي: حين عبدت بني إسرائيل جعلت تربيتي عندك وليد النعمة. وفي الحقيقة أن هذا ليس بنعمة، لأن كون الإنسان لا يقتل هذا الرجل، وهو يقتل غيره عدوانًا، هل تكون هذه نعمة؟ لا. لماذا؟ لأن أصل قتل أولئك ظلم وجور، فكونه لا يقتل هذا الرجل ليس نعمة، غاية ما هنالك أنه لم يظلمه، فهو لم يدفع عنه ضررًا نازلًا به من غيره، ولم يجلب إليه نفعًا. فموسى يقول: كيف تَمُن عليَّ بهذه النعمة أن عبدت بني إسرائيل؟ يعني: ولم تستعبدني. فهذه ليست نعمة، لأن كون الإنسان لا يظلم هذا الرجل ويظلم ذاك ليس نعمة على من لم يظلم، إذ لم يسد إليه نفعًا، ولم يدفع عنه ضررًا. غاية ما هنالك أنه امتنع عن ظلمه، وامتناعه عن ظلمه نعمة على من؟ في الواقع على الظالم، على نفس الظالم، أن الله تعالى أنعم عليه فمنعه من ظلم هذا الرجل. ولهذا يقول: ﴿أَنْ عَبَّدْتَ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾ (ولم تستعبدني، لا نعمة لك بذلك لظلمك باستعبادهم)، فأنت الآن ما أعطيتني منة جديدة ونعمة جديدة حتى تمن بها.

* طالب: أقول: ما يكون قول (...) فرعون أنه أنعم بها عليه؟

* الشيخ: كيف؟

* الطالب: قوله: ﴿تِلْكَ نِعْمَةٌ﴾.

* الشيخ: إي، هو ينكر عليه، ولهذا يقول المؤلف: (وقدر بعضهم أول الكلام همزة استفهام للإنكار). هو ينكر عليه، يقول: كيف تَمُنُّ عليَّ بهذا الشيء؟ لأنك عبدت بني إسرائيل، وهذا ليس بنعمة.

* طالب: وإن فرعون يراها نعمة.

* الشيخ: إي، يراها نعمة. هذا الذي قال له: ﴿أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا وَلَبِثْتَ فِينَا مِنْ عُمُرِكَ سِنِينَ (١٨) وَفَعَلْتَ فَعْلَتَكَ﴾ [الشعراء ١٨، ١٩]، هو جعل هذه من النعم.

هنا يقول: ﴿وَتِلْكَ نِعْمَةٌ تَمُنُّهَا عَلَيَّ أَنْ عَبَّدْتَ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾، كونك عبدتهم، أي: جعلتهم عبيدًا له. ووجه الاستعباد أنه، والعياذ بالله، كان يقتل الرجال، فيبقى النساء بدون قَيِّم، والمرأة إذا بقيت بدون قَيِّم تُضطر إلى أن تخدم. ولهذا قال العلماء: إنه كان يستخدم النساء فيبقيهن، وبالضرورة إذا لم يكن لهن قيم سوف يلجأن إلى الأقباط لاستخدامهن.

وقوله: (قدر بعضهم أول الكلام همزة) ليس ببعيد، أنه قال: أَوَتِلْك نعمة تمنها علي أن عَبَّدْت بني إسرائيل؟ يعني: فليس لك علي نعمة.

* طالب: فرعون كان يمن عليه بهذه النعمة ويذكره بالماضي، فموسى عليه السلام يُعرض عن ذلك، ويحاول أن يقرره ويبين له شناعة عمله، (...) النعمة البسيطة التي أنعمتها علي أنستك ما عملته مع بني إسرائيل.

* الشيخ: إي نعم، هذا صحيح. لولا وجود (أن)، يعني أن هذه تبين المبهم في قوله: ﴿وَتِلْكَ نِعْمَةٌ تَمُنُّهَا عَلَيَّ﴾، يعني: فكأنه يقول: تَمُنُّ عليَّ بهذه النعمة حين عبدت بني إسرائيل، يعني: ولم تستعبدني، هذا المعنى. ولولا أن هذا المعنى ظاهر، لقلنا: إن موسى عليه الصلاة والسلام صرف نعمته عليه كالمتهكم به. كيف؟ يعني يقول: أين النعمة التي أنعمت بها علي، وأنت تعبد بني إسرائيل؟ لأن تعبيد بني إسرائيل خلاف النعمة في الواقع، ومن المعلوم أن موسى من بني إسرائيل، فتعبيد بني إسرائيل وهم قومه إذلال له. وهذا المعنى جيد في الحقيقة، أن نقول: ﴿وَتِلْكَ نِعْمَةٌ تَمُنُّهَا عَلَيَّ﴾ يعني: كيف تَمُنُّ عليَّ بهذه النعمة؟ يعني وأنت تُعَبِّد بني إسرائيل. ويكون هذا من باب ما يسمونه "ta'kid al-dhamm bi-ma yushbih al-madh" (توكيد الذم بما يشبه المدح). وحينئذ نبقي ﴿أَنْ عَبَّدْتَ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾ على أنها تفسير لتلك، يعني: أهذه النعمة التي تَمُنُّ عليَّ أن تعبد بني إسرائيل؟ فأين النعمة؟ فهذا معنى جيد، إن كنت تريد هذا فهذا معنى جيد.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 23–24:

(﴿Pharaoh said﴾) to Moses, ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ — meaning, the one you claimed you are a messenger of? That is, what is He? Since there is no way for created beings to know His essence, Exalted is He, and they know Him only through His attributes, Moses answered him with some of them. ﴿He said, "Lord of the heavens"﴾ — this statement that the author made in explaining the sentence is far, far from the truth. ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ It is well known that (mā) is used to ask about the reality of a thing. You say: "What is gold?" It is said, for example: it is a precious metal, and so on. You say, for example: "What is knowledge?" You say: the perception of a thing as it is, with certainty. So (mā) is used in origin to ask about the reality of something.

The author claims that Pharaoh asked about that reality, but that is not the case. Pharaoh asked about this lordship, because he said: ﴿Indeed, we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾. So what is this lordship that you claim Allah, Exalted is He, sent you with, while He is the Lord of the worlds? For if we said that he was asking about the reality of Allah, Exalted is He, it would follow that he had acknowledged Him, but he is asking about His reality, and he had not acknowledged Him so as to ask about the reality — about the reality of this Lord. Rather, he denies the Lord altogether.

So the question is for denial: what is the Lord of the worlds whom you claim sent you? That is, there is no Lord. Therefore the explanation the author adopted, based on what is known — that (mā), and it is also so according to the logicians, what is known in the Arabic language among the people of logic — that (mā) is used to ask about the essence and reality of a thing, so he said that Pharaoh asks about the essence and reality of the Creator, Exalted is He, but Moses, since he could not answer that, turned to explaining one of His attributes. Thus the answer from Moses would not correspond to the question, and this is called the style of the wise (ḥakīm), that the questioner is answered with other than what he expects. But what he said and what he adopted is not correct, just as Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, rejected it in his tafsir, and said: this meaning implies Pharaoh's acknowledgment of Allah, but he asks about the reality of this god. The correct view is that Moses, peace be upon him, answered with an answer that corresponds to the question, and that Pharaoh asks about this lordship which Moses claimed he was sent with by the Lord of the worlds. ﴿What is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ That is: what is the Lord of the worlds who sent you? It does not mean: "from what substance is He made"? No.

The answer: (﴿He said, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them"﴾ — that is, the Creator of that), and it is not sufficient to explain it as merely "the Creator"; it is the Creator of that, its Administrator, and the one who disposes of it, because a lord is not merely a creator; creation, management, and disposal are necessary. And His saying: ﴿the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ — is Pharaoh's lordship like this lordship? 

* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: No. And does it include, because Allah is his Lord? Yes, because the heavens and the earth and what is between them do not escape any one of them, and he is in the earth and what is between them. And it seems he also answered with this to indicate the invalidity of Pharaoh's worship, because Pharaoh did not create heavens, nor earth, nor what is between them, so who deserves lordship?

The Creator of that, its Administrator, and the one who disposes of it; because a lord is not sufficient merely as a creator, rather creation, management, and disposal are necessary.

And His saying: ﴿the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 24] — is Pharaoh's lordship like this lordship? No. And does it include, because Allah is his Lord? Yes, because the heavens and the earth and what is between them do not escape any one of them, and he is in the earth.

﴿and what is between them﴾. And it seems he also answered with this to indicate the invalidity of Pharaoh's worship, because Pharaoh did not create heavens, nor earth, nor what is between them, so who deserves (...)?

So it is appropriate to pause at ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾, then say: ﴿if you are certain﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 24], for the matter is clear; and for this reason the author estimated the answer, saying: (﴿if you are certain﴾ that He, Exalted is He, is their Creator, so believe in Him alone).

We only said that it has no connection to what precedes it, because if it were connected to what precedes it, the meaning would be that He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth if they are certain of that, and otherwise He is not the Lord of the heavens and the earth. This statement does not hold. Rather we say: the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them (...).

Then he said: ﴿if you are certain﴾, that is: among those who have certainty, so be certain of that, because no one can deny or repel that the heavens and the earth are created by Allah; no one can create them.

* Student: Is "in" (in) here conditional?

* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed, "in" here is conditional, and the response of the condition is omitted; either what the author estimated, or what we also said: "then be certain." And "then believe" and "be certain" have one meaning: believe in Him alone.
