(The passage opens with the words of the commentary's margin note:) (﴿قَالَ﴾ Pharaoh said ﴿لِمَنْ حَوْلَهُ﴾ to those around him, from among the nobles of his people, ﴿أَلَا تَسْتَمِعُونَ﴾ "Do you not listen?" — his reply, which did not correspond to the question.) Strange, this one?!

(﴿قَالَ﴾ Pharaoh said ﴿لِمَنْ حَوْلَهُ﴾ to those around him.)

* Student: (...)

* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed.

﴿قَالَ﴾ Pharaoh said, ﴿أَلَا تَسْتَمِعُونَ﴾ "Do you not listen?" The interrogative here is undoubtedly for mockery (tahakkum); meaning: "Do you not listen to this one who claims that the Lord of the worlds is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?!" That is, in reality, according to his own claim, the Lord of the worlds is Pharaoh, so he mocks him, saying: "Listen to this! He says: the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them!" Is he then wrong in his mockery or right? Wrong.

His real purpose in this was to magnify the matter and belittle Musa (peace be upon him), and to show that what he brought was not correct.

As for the author's opinion, ("his reply, which did not correspond to the question"), if the matter were so, Pharaoh would have been right in his objection, would he not? Because everyone who knows that a person answered with something other than what he was asked about understands that he is cut off from the argument and unable to repel it, and this is the furthest thing from the truth.

We say to the author and to anyone who follows his method: the reply of Musa, ﴿رَبُّ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا﴾ "the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them," does correspond to the question. Pharaoh never asked about the true reality and essence of the Creator, nor did this occur to his mind, nor did he care what He is made of; he was only concerned with his own conduct and what would become of it. So for this reply we say that it does correspond to the question.

And ﴿أَلَا تَسْتَمِعُونَ﴾ "Do you not listen?" is an interrogative for mockery, because he (i.e., Musa) brought a matter far from what Pharaoh wanted. Pharaoh, who says ﴿مَا رَبُّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ "What is the Lord of the worlds?", wanted Musa to say: "The Lord of the worlds is Pharaoh." But he said ﴿رَبُّ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 24]. Then he also made them look foolish by his saying ﴿إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُوقِنِينَ﴾ "if you are people of certainty," meaning: if you are among those possessing certainty and knowledge, then be certain of this.

The interrogative here, in ﴿أَلَا تَسْتَمِعُونَ﴾ "Do you not listen?", in this context, undoubtedly comes from someone like Pharaoh, who mocks Musa, who brought the truth, and whom Pharaoh cannot repel.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 26:

(﴿Said [Moses]: "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones."﴾ And this, although it falls within what came before, angers Pharaoh.)

Look: Moses, peace be upon him, employed a wise method. He first mentioned the general lordship over the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and then he moved to the particular lordship over Pharaoh, who claimed to be a lord. He said: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones.﴾ This is an indication that you came from fathers, or not?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: And whoever came from a father, how can he be a lord when he was himself created from a drop of semen? That is, it is as if he is saying: return to your origin. Allah the Exalted is your Lord, you who claim that you are lords.

﴿And the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones.﴾ Those from whom you came. He reminds them of their origin so that they remember that they were created, and that they are not fit to be lords. This is from the excellence of the answer. In reality, every answer that Moses gives is a conclusive proof that refutes him (Pharaoh), but, may Allah protect us, whoever is not granted success in the truth does not benefit from it and becomes arrogant toward it.

(﴿He said: "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones."﴾ And this, although it falls within what came before, angers Pharaoh.) That is, this is in reality a gentle statement by the author. If he had said: "And this is also the establishment of another proof against Pharaoh, that they are servants (of a Lord) and that they were created from the loins of their earliest fathers, and whoever is born in that condition does not deserve to be a lord and a god (...)."

That is: he answered the deed by saying that it was done out of ignorance.

Then he says: ﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 21]. It is as if he is saying to them: you did not spare any effort in punishing me for it, but I fled from you and you did not catch me (...). We did not say this, but now we say it; that is, he said: ﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 21]. It is as if he is saying to them: you did not spare any effort, but I escaped; I escaped the punishment by fleeing, and I cleared myself of the ignorance by the prophethood.

The answer to the third matter: it is as if he is saying: it is a leaving off of injustice with regard to me, and leaving off injustice is not counted as a favour, because a person is not entitled to it, so that we would say: he pardoned it and left it. Or it may be said: this is what the author followed.

However, there is another possibility: harm done to my people is harm done to me. So he now emphatically denies the favour in a manner resembling (...).

He says: that is, where is the favour, when you have enslaved the Children of Israel, who are my people?

So if it is assumed that I was spared by you from enslavement and oppression, I am one individual of a tribe and a people whom you have enslaved, so where is the favour?!

After that, the debate took place between him and Moses; Pharaoh asked the first question. This is the first question.

* Student: From Pharaoh to Moses?

* Shaykh: Yes. And does this question include a question about the reality and quiddity, or about something else?

* Student: He wants to establish...

* Shaykh: First tell me its meaning according to the author's opinion. A question about the reality is as if he is saying: what is its substance, what is its substance? What is its essence? What is its reality? Yes. But he is asking about what the author said, because one cannot ask about what the author said unless he has acknowledged it, and he did not acknowledge Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

So the interrogative is a denial: "What is the Lord of the worlds, and I am the Lord?!" How did Moses answer?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, ﴿the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 24].

What is the benefit of his saying: ﴿if you are certain﴾? Does it refer to what preceded; that is, that He is the Lord of these things if you are certain, and if you are not certain then He is not their Lord?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: That is, if you are among those who possess certainty, who are characterized by certainty regarding what they witness, then be certain of that.

How did Pharaoh respond?

* Student: That is, as if...

* Shaykh: The interrogative here: ﴿Do you not listen?﴾ What is its purpose?

* Student: Its purpose is mockery.

* Shaykh: Showing mockery and ridicule. On what did the author base this mockery and ridicule?

* Student: The author says: ("Do you not listen to this answer, which does not correspond to the question?")

* Shaykh: I asked him about the reality, and he answered me with attributes. And what is the correct view?

* Student: The correct view according to the sound opinion is that the answer is not to the question, but rather it is a denial of his answer that his Lord is the Lord of the heavens.

* Shaykh: Excellent. That is: "Do you not listen to this man who denied my lordship and claimed that there is a Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them?!"

* Student: No, it is said that he (...).

* Shaykh: Rather he is?

* Student: Pharaoh did not (...).

* Shaykh: It corresponds to the answer, yes.

* Student: Pharaoh's question...

* Shaykh: It corresponds to Moses' answer, and Moses' answer corresponds to Pharaoh's question.

After that, did he move on to another answer?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Good. Is this not included in "Lord of the heavens and the earth"?

* Student: Yes, it is included.

* Shaykh: But?

* Student: But mentioning this, and the implication is to remind them that they were created from the loins of their fathers, so no one deserves lordship (...).

* Shaykh: That is: this was like establishing proof of the impossibility of Pharaoh's lordship, and that Allah the Exalted and Majestic was the Lord of him and of his earliest forefathers from whom he came, so it is not possible for him to be a lord while he is himself a servant.

* Student: One does not say this (...).

* Shaykh: No, it is possible; this whole answer is consistent with wisdom, but it is not the wise method well known among the rhetoricians.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, Pharaoh did not ask in the second; he only mocked.

* Student: I meant the first.

* Shaykh: Where?

* Student: He said: "What is the Lord of the worlds?"

* Shaykh: No, the first answer is sound, the first answer is correct, and the second answer is correct but more specific than the first; that is, it is an answer that corresponds exactly to the question. But moving from this to that is from wisdom: he mentioned in the first the Lord of the heavens and the earth, then mentioned the direct lordship over these people.

* Student: Does Pharaoh not have a right when he asked with his words: ﴿Do you not listen?﴾?

* Shaykh: Yes, he does have one, indeed.

* Student: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers﴾ as a belittling of them, that they came from fathers...

* Shaykh: Yes, indeed, it is belittling and a clarification that lordship is not valid for them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 27:

He says: Allah said, "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan": ﴿He said, "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad."﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 27] Look: (inna) is for emphasis, and (lamajnun) the lam is also for emphasis, so he emphasised the madness of Musa by two means: (inna) and the lam.

In his saying ﴿Indeed, your messenger﴾ there is a mockery that is not hidden; meaning: your messenger is being mocked, because he denies his message and denies the lordship of the One who sent him. But this is by way of mockery of him. Then he did not attribute him to himself out of arrogance; he did not say, "Indeed, the messenger who has been sent to us," or "Indeed, our messenger," but he said, ﴿Indeed, your messenger﴾. This is haughtiness and arrogance from him and mockery of Musa. So the haughtiness, the arrogance and the disdain lie in attributing him to them; meaning, it is as if he himself is in a station too high to be sent to, and not in the manner of mockery. Then, attributing the message to them while he denies it is clear mockery of Musa.

As for his saying ﴿who has been sent to you﴾, he did not say, "whom the Lord of the worlds sent," although Musa had said, "Indeed, I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds"; this is because he did not permit himself to describe Allah, exalted is He, with lordship, nor in the manner of mockery.

As for his saying ﴿mad﴾: the majnun is one who has lost his reason. This is the practice of all those who denied the messengers: ﴿Thus, no messenger came to those before them except that they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ [al-Dhariyat 52] They say, "a sorcerer or a madman." And (aw) here is for indicating that one of the two may be said, not for indicating that both are said together; for they may say "a sorcerer" only, or "a madman" only, or "a sorcerer and a madman." This is what happened to Musa, peace be upon him, as will come shortly, God willing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 28:

﴿قَالَ﴾ Moses said: ﴿Lord of the east and the west and whatever is between them, if you would but understand.﴾ [Al-Shu'ara' 28] Meaning: He is the Lord of the east and the west. Is the intended meaning only the direction, or the direction together with what occurs in it, such as the rising of the sun, the moon, the stars and the like? There is no doubt that the intended meaning is the latter: the direction and what is in it.

Lord of the east and the west and what is between them. This is like the statement of Abraham to the one who argued with him: ﴿Abraham said, "Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west."﴾ [Al-Baqarah 258] So it is as if Moses, peace be upon him, turned to a matter that is apparent and clear, which is not possible to (...) ever: the Lord of the east and the west and what is between them.

What is between them includes what occurs of clouds, winds and other things, and this is a matter that no one denies. Therefore he said to them: ﴿if you would but understand﴾, because this matter is evident to people of reason.

Then, in his saying ﴿if you would but understand﴾ there is an implicit rebuke to them, as a response to their saying that he is ﴿indeed a madman﴾: that your messenger is indeed mad. It is as if he is saying: the madman is the one who denies these things. Therefore he said: ﴿if you would but understand﴾.

In his saying ﴿if you would but understand﴾ there is a display of strength from Moses, peace be upon him, and that he did not care about them: a man alone before a stubborn tyrant, saying this statement. In reality this is an unsettling statement; that is, a person says it only to someone who is his equal. But Moses, peace be upon him, when God said to him at the beginning: ﴿So go, both of you, with Our signs. Indeed, We are with you, listening.﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 15], he was confident in Allah, glorified and exalted, and certain that Pharaoh would not harm him, and so it was. The point is that the east, the west and what is between them are evidence through the signs in them. He said to them: ﴿if you would but understand﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 28]. This is one aspect.

Second: he intended to answer Pharaoh's saying: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad﴾. It is as if he is saying: the madman is the one who does not take these signs as evidence for the Lord, glorified and exalted.

﴿if you would but understand﴾ that it is so, then believe in Him alone, just as the author said earlier: ﴿if you are certain﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 24], that it is so, then believe in Him alone.

Pharaoh said to Moses: ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely place you among those imprisoned﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 29]. After he was defeated by the argument and the proof, he turned to force; that is, the authority of argument had failed him, so he turned to the authority of force and threat. For the one who is unable to answer argument with argument, what does he resort to? He resorts to force, if he has the power to do so, and this man had power over Moses. This is why he threatened him with his words: ﴿If you take a god other than me﴾. He did not say: "If you call to God only." That is, he wants him to refrain from calling to God all the more, and not to take any god besides him. In this there is evidence that Pharaoh denied that there could be any lord other than himself.

Also, his saying: ﴿I am your lord, the most high﴾ [An-Nazi'at 24] is a descriptive (explanatory) attribute and not a restrictive one, because he does not believe that there is any lord other than himself.

And his saying: ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely place you﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 29]. Here there are two things that require an answer: the conditional (shart) and the oath (qasam). The one present here is the answer to the oath or the answer to the conditional? 

* Student: The oath.

* Shaykh: What is the evidence?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Now, is what is present the answer to the conditional or the answer to the oath?

* Student: The conditional.

* Shaykh: No, the answer to the oath; because ﴿la-aj'alannaka﴾ is not the answer to a conditional, it is the answer to an oath, and this is why it is emphasized with the nun and the lam. So it is the answer to the oath, and this is the rule.

Ibn Malik says:

"Omit, when a conditional and an oath come together, the answer of whichever is placed later, for it is then obligatory to omit it."
Here a conditional and an oath have come together: the conditional (in) and the oath (wallah), which is omitted.
He says:

"Omit, when a conditional and an oath come together, the answer of whichever is placed later..."
Which of them is placed later here? The conditional is placed later, so the answer present is for the oath, and that is correct.

And his saying: ﴿If you take a god other than me﴾: ilahan (a god) in the sense of mal'uh (one who is worshipped), that is, ma'bud (one worthy of worship).

By "the worshipped" here is meant the one who deserves to be worshipped, and that is because of his lordship. He believes that he is the Lord, so he must be the god who is worshipped.

﴿I will surely place you among those imprisoned﴾. Notice ﴿among those imprisoned﴾; he did not say "I will imprison you." As God Most High said in the story of Joseph: ﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him for a time﴾ [Yusuf 35]. Rather he said: ﴿la-aj'alannaka min al-masjuniin﴾, as an increase in the threat to Moses, as if he were saying: "There are prisoners, and I am able to imprison people; so if you do not take me as god and you take a god other than me, I will place you among these prisoners."

(His prison was severe; a person is confined in a place underground, alone, seeing no one and hearing no one there.) This is not severe compared to the prisons we know today, for they are far worse than this. Pharaoh only said: ﴿I will surely place you among those imprisoned﴾; as for how he would imprison him, the verse does not address it. Moreover, even if it were known that his imprisonment was of this kind, this prison is not severe; rather, among prisons there is torture that is worse. We hear that, God forbid, a person is brought and placed in something like a barrel with nails in it and fire beneath it. How can this man sit? He cannot: if he sits, the hot nails tear him, and if he leans against one of the walls, it is the same. This, God forbid, is among the methods they practise. We also hear that among the methods is that they starve ferocious lions and then release them upon prisoners, who tear at them while they cannot defend themselves, because they have no power. Like what al-Hajjaj did to Jahdar ibn Malik: he was one of the Kharijites; he seized him, and he was very brave. When he seized him he imprisoned him and brought him and said: "We will throw you to the lion, and we will bind your hand, and you and the lion (...)." So he brought a lion and starved it for three days. Then he said to him: "Give me a sword and bind one of my hands however you wish." So he gave him the sword and bound one of his hands, then threw him to the lion, which had been hungry for three days and had not eaten. They say in its account: when the lion leapt upon him, he struck it in its neck with the sword with one hand, and the lion fell dead. Al-Hajjaj then released him for his strength and bravery.[[Al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya (12/526).]]

These methods, too, are among those that people of injustice, God forbid, resort to against prisoners.

The essential point is that the noble verse does not mention what he would do to him; rather, it states that he would be among the imprisoned, from among those who are imprisoned.

(Musa said to him: ﴿Even if I brought you something clear?﴾) That is, would you still do that even if I brought it?

We have already gone over the question of when the interrogative hamza is combined with a conjunction: is a clause to be supplied after it, with what follows the hamza coordinated to it, or is the hamza understood to come after the conjunction? We mentioned two positions among the scholars on this. We said the latter position is easier, because the first may lead you to cases where no such supplying is possible. With the latter, you say: the hamza is an interrogative and it comes first, and the waw is a conjunction which is first in meaning but second in pronunciation, and the clause is coordinated.

As for the view the author takes here, he treats the hamza as entering on something omitted: (would you do that even if I ﴿brought you something clear﴾). It is as if Musa, peace be upon him, had said to him: "Take it easy, do not imprison me. I have not brought falsehood, and I will establish proof of what I brought."

﴿Even if I brought you something clear?﴾ Part of God's kindness was that Pharaoh said: ﴿Then bring it.﴾ Given his tyranny and arrogance, the expected reply would have been: "Even if you bring me something clear, if you take a god other than me I will make you one of the imprisoned." But hearts are in the hand of God, the Mighty and Majestic. He softened the heart of this arrogant tyrant toward Musa when he said: ﴿Even if I brought you something clear?﴾ This softness may have a tangible cause: so that he would not be defeated before the chiefs around him. If Musa had offered them the path of right guidance and then Pharaoh had stubbornly said, "Even if you bring me this," he would have appeared before his chiefs as obstinate and defeated. So he said: ﴿Then bring it.﴾

Furthermore, one reason that may have moved him to this was that he wanted Musa to bring it so that its refutation, or the claim of its falsehood, would be carried out at his own hand. Musa might have brought it elsewhere and people would have been deceived by it according to his claim, so he wanted him to bring it before him so that he could claim its falsehood.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes, he is... No, it is far-fetched on its face, but it is possible... Because Musa did not say ﴿Even if I brought you something clear﴾ except that he was certain. It is possible that he would do what he said, as he did. As for Pharaoh's humbling himself and saying ﴿Then bring it﴾, this is undoubtedly from God's tafsir (interpretation), which may have known tangible causes.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes, it does not contradict that. But is there not a possibility in it? There is a possibility that he would bring it, because Musa said it only while certain of it.

We say that the aspect of softening, or that God made him soft toward it, is this: he did not say "Do not bring anything, I will imprison you even if you do not bring it," because his hypothetical bringing of something is a matter which may possibly occur. But Pharaoh yielded somewhat, for the reasons we mentioned:

First: that God, glorified and exalted, softened him, and God is capable of all things.

Second: tangible causes, so that it would not be said that his argument had been cut off, and that the man had offered him a path of right guidance and he refused it.

Third: so that the refutation of what Musa brings would be at his own hand, until it is made clear.

A third point too, if you wish to add it: he wanted to challenge him. Yet this does not prevent him from saying "Do not bring it," because he was able to say "Do not bring it" without challenging him. Because his challenge carries the possibility that Musa would bring it, and then Pharaoh's argument would be cut off.

﴿He said: "Then bring it, if you are of the truthful."﴾

The author says: (﴿something clear﴾, that is, a clear proof of my message).

﴿Something﴾ the author explained as proof, and ﴿clear﴾ as clear.

So is it from (abāna) in its transitive or intransitive form? It is intransitive.

Because we said that abāna meaning "to make manifest" is transitive, and abāna in the sense of (...), that is, "to become apparent," is intransitive.

His words: (clear as proof of my message). The author restricted it by saying "of my message," but it is better to say it is more general than that: it covers everything I have said of the message, and the description of God, blessed and exalted, as Lord of the worlds, Lord of the heavens and the earth, your Lord, the Lord of your forefathers, and the Lord of the east and the west. Yet the author's statement does not reject this if we say that what is meant by "message" is everything Musa brought.

(﴿He said﴾: Pharaoh said to him: ﴿Then bring it﴾) That is, this clear thing (﴿if you are of the truthful﴾ in it).

Is the conditional clause connected to what came before, or is it separate? It is connected, meaning: if you are of the truthful, then bring it.

In this kind of construction some grammarians say there is no need for a response to the condition, because what precedes it indicates it.

Others say the response to the condition is omitted, and what precedes it indicates it.

I know of no one who said that the response to the condition is what came before, because the response to the condition cannot precede the governing element (al-‘āmil).

But the correct view is the first: that such a construction does not need a response.

The difference between this and the one after it is that the latter says it must be supplied, but it was omitted because it is known.

We say: it is known, and it does not need a response at all. This is the correct view.

Something similar also occurs in oaths. An oath may come, an oath may come (...).

* * *

He said to him: ﴿Then bring it, if you are of the truthful.﴾ We mentioned that this submission from Pharaoh includes three matters. What are they?

Student: First (...) that God subjected him, and also that he wanted to cut off the argument before his people, and also that he did not want to appear weak before his people.

Shaykh: Yes, correct. Because he challenged him with his words?

Student: Because he challenged him, he said...

Shaykh: ﴿Then bring it, if you are of the truthful.﴾ Although in reality this challenge, were it not that God softened him, would not have been made, since it was possible for him to say what? That he say to him: "Do not bring it." And it was possible, after he challenged him, that Musa would bring it, and that would be a proof against Pharaoh. So he brought the two great signs: the sign of the staff and the sign of the hand.

And what did Pharaoh respond to them with? He responded with the same as he had at first: deception, claiming it was magic, and that he was a knowing magician, skilled in his magic.

Then he said: ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land with his magic; so what do you advise?﴾

﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾: he did not say "that he will drive me out" or "that he will drive us out," out of pride and self-exaltation, so as not to appear before Musa in a manner of weakness that threatens. Rather, he addressed his people with it.

Then he said: ﴿from your land﴾ to stir them up, because a person certainly cannot be driven out of his land by anyone. For this reason he said ﴿drive you out of your land﴾ and did not say "from the land of Egypt" or "from the earth." He was stirring them to confront Musa with what they would confront him with, and so that they would hate Musa, peace be upon him, and see him as an enemy who seeks to occupy.

And his words ﴿with his magic﴾: the bā’ is causal, that is, because of his magic.

Pharaoh here said ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾, and the chiefs did not say "with his magic." As for him, he said ﴿with his magic﴾ in order to rouse them to seek the magicians who would confront (...). In Surah al-A‘raf: ﴿The eminent ones of Pharaoh's folk said: "Indeed, this is a knowing magician. He wants to drive you out of your land; so what do you advise?"﴾ and they did not say "with his magic." The difference is that Pharaoh wanted to rouse them and incite them to confront Musa, peace be upon him.

His words ﴿so what do you advise?﴾: the meaning of "command" here is not a demand for action in a manner of superiority, because Pharaoh would not humble himself to his people by asking them for a command. Rather, the meaning of "command" is consultation. That is: "What do you advise me?" The one who is consulted is called a commander, because he directs; whoever consults him certainly seeks direction, so his advice becomes a command to act.

Student: If he submitted (...) his tyranny.

Shaykh: The consultation here is for his own benefit, because he wanted to test what they had, and he also wanted to show that they had weight, so that they would be encouraged in this matter (...).

﴿And draw your arm close to your side against fear﴾ [al-Qasas 32]. But this is not "draw" your arm to yourself from fear; this is ﴿Insert your hand into your bosom﴾ [al-Naml 12], because, God knows best, the bosom is in the front of the body, and it is not possible, if he threw it behind his back and then took it out, [for it to be seen]. Someone may say he did something to it that we did not witness, but this was before them and became apparent.

I used to imagine at first that, since the custom is that when the hand is inserted and hidden from the sun and air it becomes white, the whole skin hidden from a person is white while what is exposed to the sun and air is tanned. So perhaps, I used to imagine, since its insertion changed with such speed, and this is contrary to custom, for custom does not change except after a long time, that its change being so rapid indicates that it is not an ordinary matter but a matter contrary to custom, and this is one of God's signs.

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: Yes, combine them.

Student: The first to say it was Pharaoh, and people followed him.

Shaykh: They agreed with him in that.

Student: (...) from their saying...

Shaykh: (...) from their saying in agreement, or the first to say it was Pharaoh? But you know the great one, the chief of the people: when he says something, they say, "True, this is a magician." Now when the chief of the people says (...), the one who has it insists (...), so this is like that: when he said it, they said the same, agreeing with him.

Student: Shaykh, the sequence of the verses shows that it is from their saying.

Shaykh: Were it not for this, meaning if only one verse had come, we would say: "from their saying." But since two verses came, and it is also not possible for them to speak in his presence, because he had terrified them, he said, then he said, is it clear?

Student: (...) but the saying is attributed to him by way of (...).

Shaykh: No.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No, it is in reality agreement; because you say: "Imam Ahmad said such and such, and Shaykh al-Islam said the like, and Ibn al-Qayyim said the like." This is a saying. So agreement with a person is a saying. This is the nearest way to reconcile the verses. What do we say? They certainly were not speaking before he spoke. When he spoke, he said, "the eminent ones of Pharaoh's folk."

This shows us that the Qur'an transmitted the speech by its meaning. That is, God, exalted, transmitted the speech of these people by its meaning, not by its wording, because if it were the very wording, it would not have changed in a single instance.

(Musa said to him: ﴿Even if I brought you something clear?﴾) That is, would you still do that even if I brought it?

We have already gone over the question of when the interrogative hamza is combined with a conjunction: is a clause to be supplied after it, with what follows the hamza coordinated to it, or is the hamza understood to come after the conjunction? We mentioned two positions among the scholars on this. We said the latter position is easier, because the first may lead you to cases where no such supplying is possible. Rather, the meaning of "command" is consultation. That is: "What do you advise me?" The one who is consulted is called a commander, because he directs; whoever consults him certainly seeks direction, so his advice becomes a command to act.

Student: If he submitted (...) his tyranny.

Shaykh: The consultation here is for his own benefit, because he wanted to test what they had, and he also wanted to show that they had weight, so that they would be encouraged in this matter (...).

﴿And draw your arm close to your side against fear﴾ [al-Qasas 32]. But this is not "draw" your arm to yourself from fear; this is ﴿Insert your hand into your bosom﴾ [al-Naml 12], because, God knows best, the bosom is in the front of the body, and it is not possible, if he threw it behind his back and then took it out, [for it to be seen]. Someone may say he did something to it that we did not witness, but this was before them and became apparent.

I used to imagine at first that, since the custom is that when the hand is inserted and hidden from the sun and air it becomes white, the whole skin hidden from a person is white while what is exposed to the sun and air is tanned. So perhaps, I used to imagine, since its insertion changed with such speed, and this is contrary to custom, for custom does not change except after a long time, that its change being so rapid indicates that it is not an ordinary matter but a matter contrary to custom, and this is one of God's signs.

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: Yes, combine them.

Student: The first to say it was Pharaoh, and people followed him.

Shaykh: They agreed with him in that.

Student: (...) from their saying...

Student: Shaykh, the sequence of the verses shows that it is from their saying.

Shaykh: Were it not for this, meaning if only one verse had come, we would say: "from their saying." But since two verses came, and it is also not possible for them to speak in his presence, because he had terrified them, he said, then he said, is it clear?

Student: (...) but the saying is attributed to him by way of (...).

Shaykh: No.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No, it is in reality agreement; because you say: "Imam Ahmad said such and such, and Shaykh al-Islam said the like, and Ibn al-Qayyim said the like." This is a saying. (Musa said to him: ﴿Even if I brought you something clear?﴾) That is, would you still do that even if I brought it?

With the latter, you say: the hamza is an interrogative and it comes first, and the waw is a conjunction which is first in meaning but second in pronunciation, and the clause is coordinated.

It is as if Musa, peace be upon him, had said to him: "Take it easy, do not imprison me. I have not brought falsehood, and I will establish proof of what I brought."

﴿Even if I brought you something clear?﴾ Part of God's kindness was that Pharaoh said: ﴿Then bring it.﴾ Given his tyranny and arrogance, the expected reply would have been: "Even if you bring me something clear, if you take a god other than me I will make you one of the imprisoned." He softened the heart of this arrogant tyrant toward Musa when he said: ﴿Even if I brought you something clear?﴾ This softness may have a tangible cause: so that he would not be defeated before the chiefs around him. If Musa had offered them the path of right guidance and then Pharaoh had stubbornly said, "Even if you bring me this," he would have appeared before his chiefs as obstinate and defeated. So he said: ﴿Then bring it.﴾

Musa might have brought it elsewhere and people would have been deceived by it according to his claim, so he wanted him to bring it before him so that he could claim its falsehood.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes, he is... No, it is far-fetched on its face, but it is possible... Because Musa did not say ﴿Even if I brought you something clear﴾ except that he was certain. Student: (...).

﴿He said: "Then bring it, if you are of the truthful."﴾

* The Shaykh: (Put off his matter and [Pharaoh said], "Send [heralds] to the cities to gather [them]" [al-Shu'ara' 36]). When Allah wills a matter, He prepares its causes. Had Pharaoh been empowered over Musa and his brother, he would have finished them off, but Allah, glorified and exalted, has made a cause for everything.

The chiefs advised Pharaoh to postpone the matter of Musa and Harun, and to send to the cities (al-mada'in, plural of madina, "city") for [the purpose of] "gathering" (hashirin), meaning gathering people.

That is: he sends to the cities of Egypt someone to gather the sorcerers; hence the answer came: ﴿They will bring you every skilled sorcerer﴾.

It was expected that he would say "ya'tunaka" (they will come to you). So what is the difference between "ya'tuka" and "ya'tunaka"? (...) The difference between them, with regard to "ya'tuka," is that the nun is omitted. But what is the difference between them in meaning?

* Student: "Ya'tuka" and "ya'tunaka"; meaning: the same wording, without the jazm (apocope), meaning.

* The Shaykh: If he had said "ya'tunaka" or said "ya'tuka"...

* The Student: The answer to the imperative (jawab al-talab).

* The Shaykh: Which of them? When it is with the nun omitted?

* The Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: And if the nun comes.

* The Student: If the nun comes, it becomes (...).

* The Shaykh: No, he said: ﴿They will bring you every skilled sorcerer﴾.

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No. If he had said "ya'tunaka," it would have been a description of every knowing sorcerer; "hashirin ya'tunaka" would be a description of "hashirin": "gatherers who come to you," a description of "hashirin." Do you understand? It would be a description of "hashirin": that they bring you every knowing sorcerer.

But the intended meaning is otherwise, because "ya'tuka" is more emphatic than "ya'tunaka," since it is a response (jawab) to the imperative, which is for consultation.

"Ib'ath" (send) is also not a true command; rather it is an imperative of consultation. "Ib'ath... ya'tuka" means: merely by your sending, they will come to you with him. Do you understand?

But if it were a description of "hashirin" ("hashirin ya'tunaka"), it would be permissible that they might not come; the description of the gatherer is that he gathers and brings the sorcerers, but it may or may not be arranged for him.

As for when he says "ib'ath... ya'tuka," it becomes like a conditional and its consequence: that is, if your sending occurs, a result necessarily follows, which is that ﴿they will bring you every skilled knowing sorcerer﴾.

﴿Sahhar﴾: is it of the form of intensive adjective (sigha al-mubalagha), or is it of the form of relative attribution (al-nisba)?

As one says: bannā' (builder), najjār (carpenter), sanna' (craftsman); that is, because their craft is sorcery, and a person is not described by this attribute unless he is skilled in it. One does not call someone who built once "builder," nor someone who carpentered once "carpenter"; rather that is said of one who has mastered the profession and craft. So do you say that "sahhar" is an intensive form, or that it is a form of attribution?

* Student: What is the difference between them (...)?

* The Shaykh: The difference between them is clear: "sahhar" means one who practices sorcery much. But "sahhar" in the sense of attribution means one who has mastered this craft, since he is attributed to it. The apparent view is that attribution is preferable; that is, one who possesses sorcery and has mastered this profession, so it is for attribution.

What suffices in place of intensification is their saying: ﴿knowing﴾; that is, outstanding in sorcery.

* Student: Would it not be like the second, as we said: it is a form of attribution, in contrast to Pharaoh's saying: ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer﴾?

* The Shaykh: Yes, but Pharaoh did not use an intensive form or an attributive form; he said "sahir" only. But "'alim" is a second description, derived independently from "sahir."

Here they said: "sahhar" and "'alim"; therefore it may be preferred that it is intensive, and the attribution is understood from his saying "'alim."

(Musa "surpasses" in the knowledge of sorcery) meaning: he exceeds him. Accordingly, they requested that they bring sorcerers who would surpass Musa in quantity and in quality, or not?

And indeed this occurred: they brought the most skilled sorcerers and a great number. But that which is among the signs of Allah, glorified and exalted, is not like sorcery, which is imagination with no reality behind it.

Student: Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim (...).

* The Shaykh: (Put off his matter and [Pharaoh said], "Send [heralds] to the cities to gather [them]" [al-Shu'ara' 36]). When Allah wills a matter, He prepares its causes. Had Pharaoh been empowered over Musa and his brother, he would have finished them off, but Allah, glorified and exalted, has made a cause for everything.

The chiefs advised Pharaoh to postpone the matter of Musa and Harun, and to send to the cities (al-mada'in, plural of madina, "city") for [the purpose of] "gathering" (hashirin), meaning gathering people.

That is: he sends to the cities of Egypt someone to gather the sorcerers; hence the answer came: ﴿They will bring you every skilled sorcerer﴾.

It was expected that he would say "ya'tunaka" (they will come to you). So what is the difference between "ya'tuka" and "ya'tunaka"? (...) The difference between them, with regard to "ya'tuka," is that the nun is omitted. But what is the difference between them in meaning?

* Student: "Ya'tuka" and "ya'tunaka"; meaning: the same wording, without the jazm (apocope), meaning.

* The Shaykh: If he had said "ya'tunaka" or said "ya'tuka"...

* The Student: The answer to the imperative (jawab al-talab).

* The Shaykh: Which of them? When it is with the nun omitted?

* The Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: And if the nun comes.

* The Student: If the nun comes, it becomes (...).

* The Shaykh: No, he said: ﴿They will bring you every skilled sorcerer﴾.

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No. If he had said "ya'tunaka," it would have been a description of every knowing sorcerer; "hashirin ya'tunaka" would be a description of "hashirin": "gatherers who come to you," a description of "hashirin." Do you understand? It would be a description of "hashirin": that they bring you every knowing sorcerer.

But the intended meaning is otherwise, because "ya'tuka" is more emphatic than "ya'tunaka," since it is a response (jawab) to the imperative, which is for consultation.

"Ib'ath" (send) is also not a true command; rather it is an imperative of consultation. "Ib'ath... ya'tuka" means: merely by your sending, they will come to you with him. Do you understand?

But if it were a description of "hashirin" ("hashirin ya'tunaka"), it would be permissible that they might not come; the description of the gatherer is that he gathers and brings the sorcerers, but it may or may not be arranged for him.

As for when he says "ib'ath... ya'tuka," it becomes like a conditional and its consequence: that is, if your sending occurs, a result necessarily follows, which is that ﴿they will bring you every skilled knowing sorcerer﴾.

﴿Sahhar﴾: is it of the form of intensive adjective (sigha al-mubalagha), or is it of the form of relative attribution (al-nisba)?

As one says: bannā' (builder), najjār (carpenter), sanna' (craftsman); that is, because their craft is sorcery, and a person is not described by this attribute unless he is skilled in it. One does not call someone who built once "builder," nor someone who carpentered once "carpenter"; rather that is said of one who has mastered the profession and craft. So do you say that "sahhar" is an intensive form, or that it is a form of attribution?

* Student: What is the difference between them (...)?

* The Shaykh: The difference between them is clear: "sahhar" means one who practices sorcery much. But "sahhar" in the sense of attribution means one who has mastered this craft, since he is attributed to it. The apparent view is that attribution is preferable; that is, one who possesses sorcery and has mastered this profession, so it is for attribution.

"So the magicians were assembled for the appointed time of a known day."

The word ﴿جُمِعَ﴾ and ﴿السَّحَرَةُ﴾ — the definite article (ال) here is for generality (lil-'umum), meaning all the magicians. The one who gathered them is either Pharaoh, or the summoners (al-hashirun) who went to the cities to gather the people.

As for His saying ﴿لِمِيقَاتِ﴾, the lam (al-lam) here indicates a specified time (lil-tawqit), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَطَلِّقُوهُنَّ لِعِدَّتِهِنَّ﴾ [At-Talaq: 1], meaning: at the time of their waiting period ('iddah).

They were gathered for this day, ﴿لِمِيقَاتِ يَوْمٍ مَعْلُومٍ﴾, known among the people. And who set this day — glory be to Allah — who? The one who set this day was Musa. Musa is the one who proposed it. Look how the determination works! That is: Musa is the one who specifies the time and the place; ﴿مَوْعِدُكُمْ يَوْمُ الزِّينَةِ وَأَنْ يُحْشَرَ النَّاسُ ضُحًى﴾ [Ta-Ha: 59]. This is because he trusted in Allah's victory; and for this reason he promised them a day they call the Day of Adornment, which is like the 'Eid for the Muslims.

He also commanded that it be in the bright daytime, ﴿ضُحًى﴾, so that the people could be able to see and witness it at leisure and with tranquility.

﴿فَجُمِعَ السَّحَرَةُ لِمِيقَاتِ يَوْمٍ مَعْلُومٍ﴾ — and it is the time of mid-morning (duha) on the Day of Adornment.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 26, verses 39–40:**

﴿And it was said to the people, "Will you gather?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 39]. The speaker is unspecified, because the speakers were many. People were dispatched to the markets and the places of gathering, saying: ﴿Will you gather?﴾. The interrogative here is for command, meaning: "Gather!" Or it is for arousing eagerness, as in His saying, ﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ [al-Saff 10]. But the command reading is clearer. That is, they were ordered to gather. ﴿And it was said to the people, "Will you gather? (39) Perhaps we will follow the magicians if they are the victors"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 39–40]. According to my understanding, he (the author) says: "The interrogative is for urging them to listen, and the hope (tarajji) is on the assumption of their victory, so that they remain upon their religion and do not follow Musa."

What the author mentioned regarding the interrogative is possible. It is the eagerness-arousing reading that we have already pointed out, and it is also possible that it is for command, meaning: they ordered the people to gather.

He (Allah) said: ﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians﴾. ﴿Perhaps we﴾ means the Copts all together. ﴿Will follow the magicians﴾, rather than Musa, but with the condition ﴿if they are the victors﴾. This condition, in their assumption, is certain, and that the magicians will surely prevail.

In their saying, ﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians﴾, there is a display of partisanship that is not hidden. This is because what was obligatory for them was to say: "Perhaps we will follow the victor," not to say: ﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians﴾. The truth may be with Musa, and it may be with the magicians. Had they been granted success, they would have said: "Perhaps we will follow the victor or the truth." But they said: ﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians﴾, then they qualified it, saying: ﴿if they are the victors﴾. This is what is called *al-tahaffuz* (reservation, hedging) in the language of our age. That is, it is as if they had judged that victory belongs to the magicians, but with a reservation in their statement: ﴿if they are the victors﴾.

In His saying, ﴿al-ghalibin (the victors)﴾, there is a difficulty from the standpoint of grammatical parsing (*i'rab*). This is because (*hum*) is a pronoun, and the predicate should be in the nominative. Is it nominative or accusative? It is nominative. So why is it in the accusative here?

* A student: We say: (*hum*) is a separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*), which has no place in the grammatical structure.

* The Shaykh: Yes. Good. And *al-ghalibin*?

* The student: *Al-ghalibin* is the predicate of (*kana*).

* The Shaykh: The predicate of *kana*. Well done. Yes. So (*hum*) here is a separating pronoun, which has no grammatical position, and *al-ghalibin* is the predicate of *kana*, and it is known that the predicate of *kana* is in the accusative.

The benefit of the separating pronoun: it has benefits. What are they?

* A student: Distinguishing the adjective from the predicate. We say: *Zaydun al-fadilu* or *Zayd huwa al-fadil*.

* The Shaykh: When you say *Zayd al-fadil*, it may be an adjective (*na't*), and no predicate has come. But when you say *huwa al-fadil*...

* The student: We have determined that it is...

* The Shaykh: The predicate.

* The student: The predicate. And also one of its benefits is restriction (*al-hasr*)...

* The Shaykh: The subject in the predicate.

*Zayd huwa al-fadil* means: not anyone else.

* The student: And the third benefit is emphasis (*al-ta'kid*).

* The Shaykh: Emphasis. Because when you say *Zayd huwa al-fadil*, it is as if you are emphasizing that, emphasizing that he is the virtuous one and no other.

He said: ﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians, if they are the victors﴾. The interrogative is for urging them to gather.

His saying, ﴿Will you gather?﴾, means: gather, with encouragement and urging.

(And the hope on the assumption of their victory.) Where is the hope? ﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians﴾, on the assumption of their victory, so that they remain upon their religion and do not follow Musa.

Were those who went out to gather the people fair-minded or not?

* A student: No, because the first thing that prevents it is that there is partisanship in the claim, since they said: ﴿we will follow the magicians﴾. So they displayed following, and this shows their partisanship, and...

* The Shaykh: Yes, but I am asking: was there some kind of fairness in them, though not complete fairness?

* The student: (*La'allahum*): the saying (*la'allahum*) may contain something of...

* The Shaykh: No. ﴿Perhaps we will follow﴾ is a light matter, there is nothing in it. There is no fairness in it.

* The student: No fairness in it?!

* Another student: Yes, there is some fairness in it, because of their saying: ﴿if they are the victors﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿If they are the victors﴾ contains some fairness, because "if" (*in*), ﴿if they are the victors﴾, we will follow them, and otherwise not. But putting first the following of the magicians and hoping to follow them, this is what contains some partisanship. It was incumbent upon them not to (...) concerning the magicians at all, and to say: "Perhaps we will follow the victor."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 41–42:

Then he said: (﴿So when the magicians came﴾, meaning: to Pharaoh, ﴿they said﴾ to him, ﴿"Will we indeed have a reward"﴾ — with the two hamzas pronounced fully (tahqiq) and the second one eased (tashil), and with an alif inserted between them according to the two readings (tahqiq and tashil)); ﴿أَئِنَّ﴾ this is the full pronunciation (tahqiq). The easing of the second (tashil): ﴿أَاِنَّ﴾ is easy (...) the hamza and the yaa; inserting an alif between them in both ways: ﴿آئِنَّ﴾, ﴿آاِنَّ﴾ with its easing. So the recitation becomes four in this way.

﴿Surely we will have a reward, if we are the victors﴾. This lam is for emphasis (lam al-tawkid) ﴿لَأَجْرًا﴾, and the meaning of "reward" here is worldly recompense and nearness and closeness to him. Or do we say: worldly recompense only? But he added to them nearness and closeness to him: ﴿He said, "Yes, and indeed you will then be among those brought near."﴾

Here he says: ﴿أَئِنَّ لَنَا لَأَجْرًا﴾. If it is asked: how did the lam of emphasis enter upon the interrogative, when the interrogation has not yet been resolved (i.e., the matter is still unsettled)? How can it be emphasized? There are parallels to this in the Qur'an, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Are you indeed Joseph?﴾ [Yusuf 90]. How can emphasis be valid with an interrogative, when the questioner is asking? Until now the matter has not become clear to him as having occurred, so how can it be emphasized?

It is said: the emphasis here is intended to emphasize the answer, as if they were saying: "Will you confirm for us the reward? Will you confirm for us that you are Joseph?" As for the questioner himself, emphasis is not possible for him, because he is an inquirer asking; and there is no combining of the interrogative, which is ignorance, with the emphasis, which is certain knowledge.

Accordingly we say: the interrogative here is with an implied meaning of what? The answer: meaning, "Will you confirm for us that there is indeed a reward for us?"

﴿if we are the victors﴾. The answer: ﴿He said, "Yes"﴾. These people wanted the salary before the rank; they sought the reward, just as some people say when they are asked to be imam of the mosque: "Is there a salary, or a muezzin, or something like that?" Likewise they, since the position had now become, in their assumption, a right, and yet they said: if we prevail over falsehood, as they claimed, with the truth, ﴿Will we indeed have a reward?﴾ So he said to them: ﴿Yes﴾, meaning: you will have a reward.

And ﴿نَعَمْ﴾ (naam, "yes") is a particle of answer. It is said that the answer is a restated question, so the particle stands in for the question; meaning: "Yes, you will have a reward." Based on this rule, that the particle of answer is a repetition of the question: if it were said to a man, "Did you divorce your wife?" and he said, "Yes," he did not say, "She is divorced." [He said] "Yes, does she get divorced?"

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: She gets divorced even if he did not say, "You are divorced," because the particle of answer is a repetition of the question. Likewise, if he was asked, "Did you accept the marriage contract?" and he said, "Yes," the marriage is concluded. If he was asked, "Did you free your slave?" and he said, "Yes," the slave is freed. "Did you endow your house?" He said, "Yes."

If he intended to lie in such circumstances: if he was asked, "Did you endow your house?" and he said, "Yes," while lying; "Did you divorce your wife?" and he said, "Yes," while lying, does divorce, endowment, emancipation and the like take effect or not?

* Student: As for divorce, there is detail: the right of another takes effect, because it is judged by the outward.

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. It is said: he is responsible before God but his statement is not accepted in judgment. As for what is between him and God, if he is not brought to court, it is accepted; meaning: if his wife trusted him and said that when the man was asked, "Did you divorce your wife?" he said, "Yes," intending to deceive his companion, she remains with him, because what he claimed is possible. Is it possible or not?

* Student: It is possible.

* The Shaykh: It is possible; what he claimed is possible, and if it is possible and the one who has the right does not dispute it and confirms it, it is accepted from him. They said: Yes.

* Student: Yes. Is there another meaning for the interrogative?

* The Shaykh: No.

* Student: It is interrogative; meaning he is asking (...). One says, "Did you divorce your wife?" with surprise; yes, it is as if he is expressing surprise here.

* The Shaykh: "Yes" is a particle of answer.

* Student: A linguistic usage.

* The Shaykh: Neither linguistic nor customary usage; but "yes" is sometimes followed by saying, "What do you say?" Yes, what do you say?

* Student: Or is it interrogative?

* The Shaykh: No, in any case it is a particle of answer, and it does not come in language or custom as interrogative unless it is joined with something, such as "Yes, what do you say?" because it is as if he says: "Yes, bring what you have," (yes) asking for more.

* Student: The scholars said they call the learned man among them a sorcerer, citing His saying: ﴿And they said, "O sorcerer, invoke your Lord for us"﴾ [az-Zukhruf 49]. Is that correct?

* The Shaykh: No, that is not correct.

* Student: Or is it an accusation against Musa of being a sorcerer? They believed...

* The Shaykh: No, they believed this: ﴿O sorcerer﴾ based on their belief in it; and His saying: ﴿invoke your Lord for us﴾ is by way of mockery (tahakkum).

He said: ﴿He said, "Yes, and indeed you will then..."﴾ (﴿then﴾ meaning: at that time). But this interpretation is not correct: explaining ﴿idhan﴾ as "at that time" is not correct, because "at that time" refers to the past; rather it must be "then," meaning: if you overcome him, if you are the victors.

﴿among those brought near﴾, meaning: in my presence. So it is as if he added to what they asked for, what? He added nearness to him for them, and he only promised them this to encourage them in this matter; so he answered what they asked and more, to encourage them.

* Student: The tanwin, Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: The tanwin is a substitute for a clause, meaning: if you overcome them.

And His saying: ﴿And indeed you will then be among those brought near﴾ — the lam, what is its meaning?

* Student: Emphasis.

* The Shaykh: Emphasis.

He said: ﴿among those brought near﴾ is an indication that he would place them in his inner circle, since he did not say, "I will bring you near," but said, ﴿among those brought near﴾; meaning: you will be among the group of the inner circle, who are the people closest to me.
