In surah Ta-Ha: ﴿So decide what you will decide; you only decide about this worldly life﴾ [Ta-Ha 72]. That is: decide what you want. The most that can happen is that your torture will lead to death, and when it leads to death, the result is only this worldly life. This indicates that they were truthful in their faith and that their faith was firmly established. In this there is clear evidence of the signs of Allah, the Exalted, and of His power.

How could it be that in a single moment the great disbelief turned into deep faith? In an instant. As soon as they saw what Musa's staff did, they changed from disbelief to faith. This is why some scholars said: "They became disbelieving magicians in the morning, and in the evening they were righteous martyrs." This is true: they were righteous and pious, and among the strongest of people in faith and in striving in the way of Allah.

﴿Indeed, to our Lord we will return﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 50]. This is also evidence of their belief in resurrection, from their saying ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we will return﴾. They believe in meeting Allah, the Exalted, which is one of the fundamentals of faith.

(﴿Indeed, we hope﴾, that is, we aspire, ﴿that our Lord will forgive us our sins﴾, that is, because ﴿we were the first of the believers﴾ in our time.) ﴿We hope﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 51]: that is, we aspire and anticipate. This hope is praiseworthy in a servant, but when? When he has taken its means. If he has not taken its means, it is one of the vain wishes, as in the hadith: «The intelligent one is the one who holds himself accountable and works for what comes after death, and the incapable one is the one who follows his desires and wishes against Allah for vain hopes» [al-Tirmidhi (2459) and Ibn Majah (171), from the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws]. They affirmed that they hoped for Allah's forgiveness, because they had taken the means, which is faith after disbelief. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾ [Al-Anfal 38]. So they hoped this well-known hope because of its cause, and it is praiseworthy.

Their saying, may Allah be pleased with them: ﴿that our Lord will forgive us our sins﴾: al-ghafr (forgiveness) was previously explained as concealing the sin and pardoning it.

Their saying ﴿our sins﴾ is the plural of khati'ah (sin). Are khata'a and sayyi'at (evil deeds) the same thing, or is there a difference between them, or are they distinguished only when they are mentioned together?

* Students: Only when they are mentioned together.
* Shaykh: Only when they are mentioned together. They are distinguished, but when one of them is mentioned alone, it includes the other. In surah Al 'Imran: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, are signs for those of understanding. Who remember Allah standing, sitting and on their sides, and give thought to the creation of the heavens and the earth, [saying], "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; exalted are You, so protect us from the punishment of the Fire." … [They say], "Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, 'Believe in your Lord,' so we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins, remove from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die with the righteous"﴾ [Al 'Imran 190–193]. They distinguished between dhunub (sins) and sayyi'at (misdeeds). For dhunub they asked for forgiveness, and for sayyi'at they asked for expiation, because the sayyi'at are minor sins that righteous deeds expiate. The sayyi'at here refer to the major sins, which are removed not by expiation but only by forgiveness.

﴿That we were the first of the believers﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 51]: this is not an attitude of presuming upon Allah or claiming a favour over Him by being the first believers. Rather, it is a way of speaking of Allah's blessing, which they see as a cause and means of forgiveness of sins, because precedence in faith and in righteous deeds is a virtue and one of the causes of high rank. This is why Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward. But to all Allah has promised the best﴾ [Al-Hadid 10]. Precedence in faith and righteous deeds has its distinction and gives its possessor his rank. Is that correct?

* Student: His saying ﴿you believed in him﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 49], and in the verse of al-A'raf: ﴿you believed in him﴾ [Al-A'raf 123]?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Originally there is a difference between them. "Amana bihi" means he acknowledged it and confessed it with complete faith, and "amana lahu" implies the meaning of submitting (inqad).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: He submitted to him. It may be less, and it may be more. He submitted to him together with faith. When you combine the two verses here, the expression becomes more eloquent. That is, it is as if they believed in him with faith, then they believed in him and submitted to him.
* Student: ﴿So decide what you will decide. You only decide about this worldly life. Indeed, we have believed in our Lord that He may forgive us our sins and the magic to which you compelled us. And Allah is better and more enduring. Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell﴾ [Ta-Ha 72–74].
* Shaykh: You mean His saying ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord﴾.
* Student: ﴿And Allah is better and more enduring.﴾
* Shaykh: No, ﴿And Allah is better and more enduring﴾ is their own speech. Yes indeed. But ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾ may be their speech or the speech of Allah.
* Student: Here, these magicians (...), they are the ones who believed (...), or these were killed.
* Shaykh: Who?
* Student: The magicians who believed (...).
* Shaykh: They (...) of whom?
* Student: Afterwards Musa (...).
* Shaykh: No, the Children of Israel.
* Student: The Children of Israel. These were killed right away.
* Shaykh: Either they were killed right away, or nothing happened to them. But as for those who harmed him, they were his people.
* Student: Yes, they did not believe.
* Shaykh: Who?
* Student: The Children of Israel were not believers?

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verses 43–51 (part 3 of 4):**

* **The Shaykh:** In this treatment, they were not believers at all, or some of them were believers. I do not know. The basis is that the Torah was revealed afterward: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses the Book after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾ [al-Qasas 43].
* **Student:** Regarding Allah's words: ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾ (...). Because if he cuts off the right hand and the left remains, no person can lean on (...). Because if he cuts off one hand and one foot (...), one (...) cannot (...). Is this more severe (...)?
* **The Shaykh:** No. In one respect it is more severe, and in another respect it is lighter. In terms of severity, the pain is on both sides. In terms of lightness, and this is apparently what is intended here, because, as it appears, and Allah knows best, they were killed in the end.
* **The Student:** Apparently they were all like that.
* **The Shaykh:** Because some scholars' statement "martyrs of righteousness" indicates that they were killed. I do not know this now.
* **The Student:** (...) some scholars (...).
* **The Shaykh:** This needs verification.
* **The Student:** Apparently they were all like that.
* **The Shaykh:** All of them what?
* **The Student:** There was not a single one, for example.
* **The Shaykh:** Of the magicians?
* **The Student:** Yes.
* **The Shaykh:** They all believed. ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾. What is this word (al) here?
* **Students:** For generality.
* **The Shaykh:** For generality. They all believed, and their faith was complete, not yet incomplete.
* **Student:** "Whoever fears Allah, the Exalted, (receives) Paradise, not the service of Him."
* **The Shaykh:** Who says that?
* **The Student:** Some scholars (...).
* **The Shaykh:** No, is there "service" and "Paradise" in it?
* **The Student:** Because they did not do deeds.
* **The Shaykh:** First: the expression "His service" is not reported, and in reality it should not be used alongside worship. Allah did not praise people because they served Him; rather, because they are His servants. For this reason, this expression that is written in books of admonition must truly be taken into consideration.
Second: We say that every person who acts, acts for Allah, the Exalted, in devotion to Him and hoping for His reward. Allah described the best of creation and the highest in rank, Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and those with him, saying: ﴿You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and approval﴾ [al-Fath 29]. The Messenger (ﷺ) said, when a Bedouin said: "I do not do well with your murmuring nor the murmuring of Mu'adh, but I ask Allah for Paradise and seek refuge with Him from the Fire," "Around it we murmur." [[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (15898) and Abu Dawud (792), from a hadith of some of the Companions of the Prophet.]] Some of the "knowers" (ʿārifīn), as they say, say: "You must worship Allah for Allah's sake, not for the sake of your own portion." Who told you this? One who hopes for His reward, may He be blessed and exalted, is the reality, and this is what Allah described His servants with. This is what I said: "for His service, not His Paradise," right?
* **The Student:** "For His service, not His Paradise."
* **The Shaykh:** I say: that is, or they worship Allah in His service, not His Paradise. That is, they say: the best is to worship Allah for His service, not for His Paradise, and they consider the one who worships Allah for His Paradise to be deficient.
* **The Student:** "I worshipped Allah not for His Paradise, nor out of fear of His Fire, but out of love for His Essence."
* **Another student:** They say Ibn al-Farid, at the time of his death sickness, saw Paradise and began to cry out and shout: "Why did I do this? Why did I pray? Only out of love for You."
* **The Shaykh:** "Out of love for You," and he sees it in every (...). I seek refuge with Allah.
* **Student:** Combining between... he acts out of love for Allah, the Exalted, and seeking Paradise (...).
* **The Shaykh:** This is the reality, because reaching Paradise is reaching Allah, since the people of Paradise see Allah, the Exalted.
* **The Student:** I do not mean that a person's deed is only for the sake of Paradise. Perhaps his feeling is gratitude to Allah (...).
* **The Shaykh:** His feeling is what?
* **The Student:** His inner feeling of magnifying Allah, the Exalted, makes him act with this disposition. So if (...).
* **The Shaykh:** By Allah, I do not know. In reality, I think the best is what the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions followed.
* **The Student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Thankful to Allah.
* **The Student:** Thankful to Allah, the Exalted.
* **The Shaykh:** It does not contradict that one loves Allah and strives to reach His Paradise: ﴿You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and approval﴾.
* **Student:** And bounty is not except after approval.
* **The Shaykh:** Also, this bounty and approval include the love of Allah.
* **Student:** And then, Shaykh, the more love increases, the more reward increases for it.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, there is no doubt. A person is rewarded for love.
* **The Student:** ﴿Say: If you should love Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran 31].
* **The Shaykh:** Yes. No one denies the love of Allah. And no one denies that... Even your acting to reach the pleasure of Allah is love for Allah. Otherwise he would say: "Whether He is pleased or not, it does not matter; whether He grants bliss or not, it does not matter." But if he says: "No, act for Allah's own essence," like this (...), it is not correct.
* **Student:** He, may Allah have mercy on him, said in the benefits of these verses: The worship of believers is from the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, toward them, and this is from His words, glorified is He: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan 63].
* **The Shaykh:** Is this in your text?
* **Student:** In a second form.
* **The Shaykh:** What is it?
* **The Student:** That the servanthood of a person to Allah draws mercy from Allah to him.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, no, this is not that.
* **The Student:** He calls those who were granted these qualities because of His mercy.
* **The Shaykh:** This is close to it.
* **Student:** That the attribute of servanthood (...).
* **The Shaykh:** This is different.
* **Student:** That worship is a cause for mercy. Allah said: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾. So the attribution of worship to the name "the Most Merciful" specifically, not to others.
* **The Shaykh:** This means that a benefit is that they worship Allah to reach His mercy.
* **Student:** That among the attributes of the servants of the Most Merciful, His believing servants, is walking on the earth with tranquility and dignity: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan 63].
* **The Shaykh:** Ali has another benefit too, which is dividing servanthood into general and special, right?
* **Student:** (...) establishing special servanthood, which is the servanthood of the Prophet.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, and also perhaps we say: from this verse it is derived that describing a person with servanthood is one of the levels of perfection. For this reason He said: ﴿servants of the Most Merciful﴾.
* **Student:** Its honoring them, since He attributed them to Himself.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, indeed. This is also a benefit other than what I (...).
* **Student:** Yes, other than (...).
* **The Shaykh:** We say: the attribute of servanthood in general is one of the levels of perfection, from attributing them to Allah: ﴿servants of the Most Merciful﴾. This is from the category of honor and dignity.
* **Student:** His words: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾ (...).
* **The Shaykh:** They mentioned two benefits in it: First, that their worship is from Allah's mercy toward them. Second, that they bring this servanthood to the level of mercy.
* **Student:** We said: among the attributes of the servants of the Most Merciful, the believers, is walking on the earth with tranquility and dignity: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾.
Fifth: a veiled reference to the arrogant who walk on the earth exultantly, from His words: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾.
* **The Shaykh:** A veiled reference to their blame.
* **The Student:** To their blame, yes.
* **Another student:** We say here: among their attributes is not harming others: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾.
* **The Shaykh:** From where do we take it? From His words: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾.
* **The Student:** That is, from their disposition, that is, tranquility.
* **Another student:** ﴿And when the ignorant address them﴾.
* **The Student:** Yes, well done. ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾
* **The Shaykh:** But this is a description even if there is no one in the place: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾. Even if no one is around them, they fear harming anyone. And if we say tranquility and dignity include all possible forms...
* **The Student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** That they do not harm anyone by their walking.
* **Student:** (...) His words: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾.
* **The Shaykh:** That is, it includes physical and moral walking, right?
* **The Student:** Yes.
* **The Shaykh:** It is possible.
* **Student:** An encouragement. We mentioned it as an encouragement toward calmness and deliberation in all kinds of striving, including moral striving, such as seeking provision and knowledge.
* **The Shaykh:** What do you have?
* **Student:** Yes, the same: "who walk upon the earth." It shows an attribute of these virtuous people. As if Allah, the Exalted, answered a question that might arise: who are these servants, and why did they deserve this beautiful description, in that He attributed them to Himself? Among their attributes are humility, love of good, and distance from haughtiness and pride, which are not befitting except to Allah alone. Whoever wishes to be among the righteous servants must recognize one of their attributes, which is humility and gentleness of manner.
* **Another student:** Honor is among the attributes of believers: ﴿But to Allah belongs honor, and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8]. He says: distance from... means honor!
* **The Shaykh:** You mean self-pride?
* **The Student:** No, honor that is not honor (i.e., a false honor).
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, disbelief that is not disbelief.
* **The Student:** No, I mean honor that belongs to Allah.
* **The Shaykh:** You mean arrogance?
* **The Student:** Yes, arrogance.
* **The Shaykh:** In any case, I have an objection to this. Not from the side of this issue, but from the side that it came unconnected, as if it were speech (...).
The explanation of benefits is usually concentrated; it should not be like loose speech, as if we were speaking in a sermon. This is like a verbal explanation, and in terms of style it is deficient, though it is complete, meaning the speech has no deficiency in meaning. But in terms of style (...) keep the benefits concentrated so that the mind is not scattered and one can grasp them grain by grain.
* **Student:** In His words: ﴿they walk﴾, that the successful person can make the habit of walking into worship, and it is a habit (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, if they were paying attention to this, and that is apparent, it is apparent that they were paying attention to this, that is, it is not a common matter or from their disposition; rather it is deliberate.
* **Student:** Affirmation of the attribute of mercy for Allah, and affirmation that "the Most Merciful" is an attribute of Allah, the Exalted.
* **The Shaykh:** This is necessary. There is also in it the affirmation of the name "the Most Merciful" and the attribute of mercy. Correct.
* **Student:** His words: ﴿they walk﴾. He did not say: "and the servants of the Most Merciful who travel upon the earth in humility." In this there is an indication that the servants of the Most Merciful (...).
* **The Shaykh:** What is the difference between them?
* **The Student:** If he said "travel," perhaps they travel on their mounts, travel (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Even this, if a person travels on his mounts, it is not apparent. Even travel can be on two feet, and walking can be on foot or on a mount.
* **Student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** In any case, note this, what the brother said: affirmation of the name "the Most Merciful" and the attribute of mercy for Allah, the Exalted.
* **The Student:** Encouragement to forbearance from His words: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾, that they do not repay evil with its like, but say (...). And after that, a benefit: encouragement to forbearance, a veiled reference to the blame of ignorance and of people of sin, from His words: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾, that among the attributes of His believing servants (...), when the ignorant address them, is their commitment to speech by which they are safe from sin (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Good (...). Three benefits. What do you have?
* **Student:** I say: that when he mentioned the first (...) "peace" is appropriate to the state of the aggressor, and they may respond to them with a strong response suited to their state. Their forbearance is not always (...), that when they are treated ignorantly they respond with the appropriate response to the state of the aggressor (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Forbearance is possible, because forbearance does not mean pardon absolutely. Forbearance may also be called forbearance by not aggressing, and by this they are safe from sin if they do not aggress. But I also have a benefit more important than all of this, in reality?
* **The Student:** That Allah loves from His servants (...), and that it is not appropriate to confront the ignorant with ignorance (...). The Qur'an's explanation of this beautiful etiquette (...) and returning the offender with good. The legislation of pardoning the ignorant, that good treatment of creation is in addition to the Creator.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes indeed.
* **Student:** There is in it that (...) and aggression by speech against others is from ignorance.
* **The Shaykh:** Because of His words: ﴿when they address them﴾.
* **Student:** (...) the believer with wisdom.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, this, do I want this?
* **The Student:** And that the believer must bear harm.
* **The Shaykh:** Wisdom here is more important than forbearance, and this forbearance is a good condition. But wisdom is important, because their saying: ﴿they say, "Peace"﴾ does not say: if the ignorant address them, they fall silent. Rather it says: "they say," but "peace," by which they are safe, as we said in the explanation and commentary, from sin, harm, humiliation and abasement.
The point: peace from every side. If harshness (...) safety, they were harsh; if it was regarding those who turned away.
The point is that they do not neglect the matter, but they do not say a word whose outcome is evil; rather they say: "Peace."
* **Student:** A demonstration that these people do not avenge themselves when they hear speech from an ignorant person who does not reason, for how could it be right for this wise, rational man to take from one who does not reason? And there is evidence that ignorance and weakness of intellect are close to each other.
* **The Shaykh:** Close to each other?
* **The Student:** From His words.
* **The Shaykh:** Then ignorance here means one who behaves badly, not one who is not a scholar.
Now, how many benefits do you see in total from this sentence?
* **Students:** Four or five.
* **The Shaykh:** Four or five. Let us first repeat them. Come on, read them to us.
* **Student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** This is so long as forbearance is not silence and humiliation.
* **Student:** (...) wisdom, and a veiled reference to the blame of ignorance and people of evil from His words: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾, and that among the attributes of the believing servants of Allah, when the ignorant address them, is their commitment to speech by which they are safe from sin (...), harm, and forbearance.
* **The Shaykh:** Good, there is a benefit (...).
* **Student:** That the believer must bear harm.
* **Another student:** That treating people kindly is what pleases Allah.
* **The Shaykh:** Good.
* **Student:** Not derived from these verses.
* **The Shaykh:** Whoever reads them (...).
* **The Student:** It is derived, Shaykh.
* **The Shaykh:** From this itself, that we treat people kindly, from where?
* **Student:** Because He mentioned them among the attributes of His servants.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, but ﴿they say, "Peace"﴾ may not be their treating them kindly in terms of safety; their treatment may be with what they deserve, harm. Perhaps there is derived from it what Allah mentioned in Surah al-Shura: ﴿And those who, when tyranny strikes them, defend themselves﴾ [al-Shura 39], and that a man is not blamed if he opposes the ignorant with what he deserves. That is, silence is not good absolutely, and speech is not good absolutely; rather following what is kindest in that is the good, and "for every situation there is a statement." ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah 269]. A person may desire wisdom but not be granted success in it.
* **Student:** Is there not in it evidence for the permissibility of courtesy (mujamalah) in some situations? Because perhaps they will not be safe except with courtesy.
* **The Shaykh:** It does not contradict. Courtesy, as long as it is speech of peace (...) courtesy. For example, if they wanted to soften speech in opposition to the harshness of those people, and it is something by which they are safe, but a safety that is physical and moral, then there is no harm.
* **Student:** As long as it is not reprehensible.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, as long as it is not reprehensible.
* **The Student:** He gets angry.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, but the words ﴿when they address them﴾ indicate that the address is directed at them. As for if they insult Allah, no. In any case, ﴿they say, "Peace"﴾ is a measure of wisdom.
* **Student:** (...) we mentioned observing the state of the aggressor and responding to him in a way suited to the situation.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, this is from wisdom, because if you establish that this indicates their wisdom.
* **The Student:** This is among what indicates it.
* **The Shaykh:** The rest are forms.
* **Student:** Treating the ignorant in a manner befitting him is not (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Not what?
* **The Student:** Not (...).
* **The Shaykh:** This is following (...).
I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verses 43–51 (part 4 of 4):

* Among the lessons of the preceding verses: when Musa (peace be upon him) said, ﴿Throw down what you are about to throw﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 43], they threw down their ropes and staffs, and they sought help from one who could not help them, saying, ﴿By the might of Fir'awn, we are surely the victors﴾.
* Also in it: Musa (peace be upon him) threw his staff by the command of Allah, when He revealed to him that he should not fear, and that he should throw what was in his right hand.
* Also in it, among its lessons: when the truth becomes clear, the people most knowledgeable of it are those who know this truth. Musa (peace be upon him) was the first to whom it became clear that what he brought was the truth and was not magic. The sorcerers were the ones who knew magic and its falsehood. Whoever knows the truth is the one who knows falsehood. As for one who does not know falsehood, matters may become confused for him. For this reason it was said: "Things are made clear by their opposites."
* Also in it: the haste of the sorcerers to embrace faith, to the point that faith appeared to be something compelled. ﴿So the sorcerers were thrown down prostrating﴾, because of the strength of what they witnessed of the signs, with which they could not delay.
* Student: The last benefit you mentioned.
* Shaykh: I say: when they saw the signs, they were not able to delay in faith, so it was as if they were thrown down under compulsion.
* Also in it: the extent of Fir'awn's deception when he said, ﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic﴾, even though he knew that there was no connection between Musa and these sorcerers. But because of the strength of his deception, he wanted to disguise with this statement something that is not rational.
* Also in it: the force of his tyranny when he threatened them with cutting off their hands and feet on opposite sides, and then crucifixion.
* Also in it, among its lessons: the strength of faith of these sorcerers, who defied Fir'awn in his tyranny and said that there was no harm to them in what he threatened them with, because they would return to Allah, glorified and exalted be He, and He would give them a reward and recompense greater than what they lost of this worldly life. As He said in Surah Ta-Ha, ﴿Indeed, you decide only concerning this worldly life﴾ [Ta-Ha 72].
* Also in it: when faith is true, it becomes stronger than natural inclination. Love of the self is an innate matter, but faith leads a person to hold his self cheap in the cause of his religion.
* Also in it: the strength of hope these sorcerers placed in Allah, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿Indeed, we aspire that our Lord will forgive us our sins﴾.
* Also in it: evidence that precedence in faith is among the causes of forgiveness and elevation, by their saying, ﴿that we are the first of the believers﴾. The Book has also indicated this in the saying of Allah, exalted be He: ﴿Those of you who spent and fought before the conquest are not equal [to others]. They are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward. But to all Allah has promised the best﴾ [Al-Hadid 10].
When 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf and Khalid ibn al-Walid quarrelled, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Khalid, do not revile my companions. Slow down, Khalid, do not revile my companions. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of you were to spend gold equal to Mount Uhud, it would not reach a mudd of one of them, nor even half of it." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3673) and Muslim (2541 / 222), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]
* Also in it: an unrestricted statement is restricted by an indicator. Their saying, ﴿that we are the first of the believers﴾, is restricted, because what is meant is "the first of the believers" in their time. Otherwise, someone had believed before them. Or it means "the first of the believers from the family of Fir'awn," because someone had believed before them. So their saying, ﴿that we are the first of the believers﴾, means from the family of Fir'awn.
The author says "in our time," but this is not apparent. Rather, the apparent meaning is that it refers to the family of Fir'awn, because some of the Children of Israel had believed before that.
* Student: Did the believer from the family of Fir'awn believe before them?
* Shaykh: Perhaps he did not make it public, because He said, ﴿A man of the family of Fir'awn who concealed his faith﴾ [Ghafir 28].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verses 43–51 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Musa said to them﴾, after they had said to him: ﴿Either you throw, or we will be the ones who throw﴾ [al-A'raf 115]: ﴿Throw what you are going to throw.﴾ The imperative here is a permission to let them go first, so that through their throwing the truth may be made manifest.

As for his saying ﴿Throw what you are going to throw﴾, the author (al-Mu'allif) said, as in the verse: ﴿They said: "Either you throw, or we will be the ones who throw." He said: "Throw!"﴾ [al-A'raf 115–116]. The author says that this imperative is for permission, and it may also be for challenge. That is why he said ﴿Throw what you are going to throw﴾, with "what" (ma) in its general sense. That is, "Throw whatever you wish to throw; I do not care about it and I am not concerned with it."

This is shown by the fact that he asked them to be the ones who throw first, so that he would be the victor afterwards. For if he had thrown his staff first, what would they have done, with nothing in front of it? It became a manifest serpent, but there was nothing before it. So he commanded them to throw first, because he, upon him be peace, was confident in Allah's promise. He speaks from a position of strength, saying: "I do not care about you; throw whatever you want." ﴿Throw what you are going to throw.﴾ So the vagueness here is for emphasis: "Throw whatever you wish to throw."

In his saying ﴿what you are going to throw﴾, with the nominal sentence, there is evidence that whatever kind of throwing they were characterized by, he was not concerned with it.

Allah says: ﴿So they threw their ropes and their staffs, and said: "By the might of Pharaoh, we are surely the victors."﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 44] (I seek refuge in Allah).

﴿Their ropes﴾ means the ones with which they deceived people. ﴿Their staffs﴾ means those with which they deceived people. When they threw these ropes and staffs, they appeared to people as serpents and snakes.

Also, they appeared in great numbers, filling the valley. In reality, were they serpents and snakes or not? No. So is magic an illusion or a reality?
* Students: An illusion.
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: A reality.
* The Shaykh: Magic is a reality, but in terms of what it is applied to, it is an illusion. It is a reality because it affected sight: instead of the person seeing these ropes as ropes and staffs as staffs, he began to see them as serpents and snakes.
* A student: How do they leave him (...)?
* The Shaykh: Then this is a reality, but in relation to what is seen, it is not changed from its true nature. The ropes are ropes and the staffs are staffs. If someone whom the magic had not reached looked at them, he would see them as they really are: ropes and staffs.

It is mentioned that a magician sat with some people who were pollinating palm trees. Do you know what pollinating (bashara) is among us? It is taking dates after they have wilted slightly and placing them (...).

In short: one of the magicians came to these people while they were gathered around a cooking pot containing dates. He said to them: "I will walk on these dates and they will not be affected; I will walk in the middle of the pot and it will not affect me." They said: "That is impossible." He said: "It is possible." So he cast the magic and began walking in the middle of the pot in their sight, while he was walking outside it, circling around it. They were amazed. The one in the palm tree said: "He is lying to you; he is your magician." So he cast the magic on him. He said: "No, it is correct now; try its middle."

This is correct; that is, if it is woven, it is woven, but it is close to reality.

So magic affects the senses and a person's perception, but as far as the actual reality of the matter is concerned, it never affects it at all.
* A student: According to the magician's desire, for example, is its effect like that?
* The Shaykh: That is apparent, according to the magic he has. Just like the evil eye (al-'ayn): the one who casts the evil eye does to the afflicted person whatever he wants. That is why a man went to a person who had the evil eye, and this man who went was more afflicted by it than he was. This is a verified story (and if you wish to hear it, though it is somewhat long): there was a man with the evil eye who bargained over a camel with a person, and that person outdid him and bought the camel. He had camels in the open pasture (ra'iyah), so he sent the camel he had bought to the pasture. Allah, glorified and exalted, decreed that at the end of the day a violent wind arose, the camels were lost, and the camel he had sent was lost. His son also went to search for the camels and there was no news of him. The son of the man who had bought the camel, that very night, suffered pain in his eyes, so that he could not sleep at night or during the day, may Allah protect us. This continued for a long period, about fifteen days. Then the one who had cast the evil eye came to him and said: "O so-and-so, are you well? (...)" He said: "May Allah guide you. Is there no good in you (...)? Why have you come? What has happened?" He said: "What has happened is that so-and-so bargained with me over the camel, and I bought it; and who bought it? Here it is: my child and my two camels are lost, and the camel I bought is lost, and my eyes (...). I cannot sleep at night or during the day." He (the afflicted man) went out and went to the man who had cast the evil eye on him, and knocked on his door. He greeted him: "How are you?" So-and-so, and he clung to him. He said: "What (...) so-and-so, who has held him in his house for fifteen days? Now he cannot sleep at night or during the day, his camel is lost, and his child is lost. But choose one of three options: either we will pray for you at the afternoon (...), or I will keep you confined in your house and you will not leave it (...), or you will swear an oath to me that you will never harm them within such-and-such a distance of the markets." He said: "This is easier." So he swore to him that he would not harm them. He said: "Give me your cap." He gave him his cap, and he wet it with water, drank from it, and sprinkled it on his face, and his eyes, glory be to Allah the Mighty, were as if released from a shackle. Then news came after noon that the child and the two camels had come back, and the camel that was lost had come back to him. This is a certainty.

But the point is that the one with the evil eye is now brought to account. He (the afflicted man) said to him: "Choose one of three," and bring this one who bewitched him, who likewise bewitches as he wills.
* A student: Should the one with the evil eye be killed, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: No. The correct view is that he is not killed unless he intentionally kills.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: If he says, "I will kill so-and-so," then kill him.
* The student: Even if he causes harm without killing?
* The Shaykh: No. If he causes harm, he is imprisoned. He says it is obligatory to imprison him in every case. The one with the evil eye must be imprisoned in every case, as the scholars have said. But it is strange that this evil eye was well known in earlier times among people, and the rulers were strong; the emirs had stronger positions than today, even the emirs of the regions, and the judges were present. The statements of the jurists, also the Hanbalis (a school of jurisprudence), are that it is not far from what we say: this is a weaker opinion in the school, that these people must be imprisoned. But even so (...). Or if they were imprisoned, the evil would decrease.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What about it? Yes, because he did not kill him.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, if he killed him, if he intended it as well. He says: "I will kill him; I will kill so-and-so." But if he did not intend to kill and yet the person died, this is a mistake, and he must pay blood-money (diyah) for it.

However, some scholars say he is not killed even if he intentionally killed, because this weapon is a hidden, inner weapon. Others said: he is killed in the same manner, by one (...).
* A student: This is better: "Iron is only broken by iron."
* The Shaykh: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were afflicted﴾ [al-Nahl 126]. But one fears it would encourage those who carve (magic).
* A student: Is the treatment of the evil eye something a person may be afflicted with?
* The Shaykh: It is treated, may Allah bless you, by recitation, and treated by a physical treatment: the one who casts the evil eye is asked to perform ablution, wash his inner folds (maghabin), and what drips from him is taken and given to the afflicted person to drink, and it is poured over his head from above, on his back, and by Allah's permission he will be healed.

Among people now there is something that is not known from the Sunnah, but it has been tested: taking from his garments, whether a cap, a head-cloth, a vest, or trousers, washing them and taking the washing water, and the afflicted person drinks it and benefits from it, by Allah's permission.
* A student: (...) perhaps (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: It makes them imagine (...).
* The Shaykh: No, it cannot. Strangely, if he is challenged, he cannot (...).
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: If he is challenged, whether out of enmity or not out of enmity, because the evil eye only comes upon heedlessness, and it mostly comes from one who fears it. But if he is not challenged, he cannot.
* They say: people...
* A student: (...) for war.
* Another student: Or he says: (...).
* The Shaykh: It does affect; there is no doubt. Even (...) cars are well known among us.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, something similar happened to us: people in the valley of al-Qasr, between 'Unayzah and Buraydah, who were working. When they came out at midday they stopped and began to be deserted. That was thirty years ago. A car was coming from Buraydah heading to 'Unayzah, so some of them said to others: "By Allah, we will go (...), come on." He said: "No (...), let us leave, it is not (...)." They wanted to stand up and rush, but he said to them: "Sit down, do not go at all (...)," and (...) in al-Qasr, while they were departing (...) calmly. But (...) the body (budy), how often he saw (...), once (...). When they finished and came and arrived, he said: "By Allah, O people (...)." He said to him: "Fine, do you want (...)?" He said: "Only let him come down (...)." He said to them: "Those who call this one with us an evil-eyer, he said (...)."
* A student: Shaykh, what is the treatment from the Sunnah?
* The Shaykh: It is what we mentioned: first, he performs ablution and washes his inner folds, and it is sprinkled on this...
* A student: His inner folds, which are like the armpits.
* The Shaykh: Yes, like the armpits.
* The student: So, in addition to the ablution, the limbs?
* The Shaykh: Yes, but what is tested among people, what is well known to them, is the thing that touches his body directly. They claim that if the one with the evil eye prays the funeral prayer over the person, the harm is nullified. But this is not correct.
* A student: They say: real stories.
* The Shaykh: They say: and in some narrations, that he washes his inner folds.
* A student: Has the topic not been researched?
* The Shaykh: Only in Zad al-Ma'ad.
* The student: In the appendix (dhayl) of Zad al-Ma'ad.
* The Shaykh: I do not know.
* A student: The recitation (...) Ibn Taymiyyah.
* The Shaykh: Shaykh al-Islam (...).
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Perhaps it is found in the Shaykh's words.
* A student: (...) evil spirits (...) come out of the eye.
* The Shaykh: Correct. Its source is envy; that is why it was said regarding Allah's saying: ﴿And from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾ [al-Falaq 5] that it refers to the one with the evil eye when he casts it. Otherwise, there is no doubt that it comes from stinginess and concern over a thing and envy of another's possession.
* A student: But is it not every envier? The one with the evil eye?
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yesterday (...) our shaykh was teaching us at night between the two evening prayers, and some birds passed by, which I think they call ducks. I raised my head, and he said: "Here, hunting knowledge is better, or more excellent, than hunting birds." And it is true, there is no doubt. I affirm with certainty that a person who turns his attention with certainty, his thought goes away, and he does not turn except when directed by a command from whom? By the command of his heart. He cannot turn except by this.

* * *

I say: When the people were gathered at an appointment with Musa, upon him be peace: ﴿Musa said to them: "Throw what you are going to throw"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 43], after they had said: ﴿Either you throw, or we will be the ones who throw﴾ [al-A'raf 115].

We have mentioned that in the vagueness of ﴿Throw what you are going to throw﴾ there is an evident challenge: whatever you throw, I am not concerned with it.

﴿So they threw their ropes and their staffs﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 44].
* A student: Shaykh, their saying "if they are the victors" (...) does it not imply that they were doubtful about the magicians' victory over Musa?
* The Shaykh: Perhaps this is that they were doubtful; this is out of caution. But they did not say: "Perhaps we will follow the victor or the truth." ﴿The magicians.﴾ Then it is possible that their saying ﴿if they are the victors﴾ is a conditional clause that states the reality, meaning: they will prevail in every case.
* A student: Does "perhaps" (la'alla) negate that we are certain of this? ﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians if they are the victors.﴾ Their mention of the magicians means "perhaps," and we are not certain that they were doubtful?
* The Shaykh: Yes. When they said ﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians﴾, what should they have said?
* The student: "The victors."
* The Shaykh: Yes, "the victors." So when they said ﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians﴾, they also feared that the matter might be contrary to what they expected, and they said: ﴿if they are the victors﴾.

Then Allah, exalted, said: ﴿So they threw their ropes and their staffs﴾. The ropes (habal) is the plural of rope (habl), and the staffs ('isiy) is the plural of staff ('asa).

They threw those ropes and staffs in order to deceive people by their magic into thinking they were snakes and serpents. Even Musa, upon him be peace, was afraid and felt fear within himself when he saw these snakes and serpents coming towards him; he was afraid. But Allah said to him at that moment: ﴿We said: "Do not fear; indeed, you are the superior. And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have made."﴾ [Ta-Ha 68–69].

When they threw them, they said: ﴿By the might of Pharaoh, we are surely the victors﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 44]. The "ba'" (by) is causal.

''Izzat Fir'awn means his dominance and subjugation. In their mention of might here, there is evidence that they did not take pride in anything other than his might, and that they did not believe they could triumph except by his might.

Their saying ﴿we are surely the victors﴾ was emphasized with "inna" and the lam, because they believed at that moment that no one was stronger than Pharaoh, and that by his might they would certainly prevail. That is why they emphasized it with their saying ﴿we are surely the victors﴾.

Then they used the nominal sentence ﴿we are surely the victors﴾, as a sign that this victory would endure and continue, because the nominal sentence indicates stability, permanence, and continuity.

In his saying ﴿innā la-naḥnu﴾: if we parse "naḥnu" as a separating pronoun (ḍamīr faṣl), there is what is derived from the separating pronoun, which is emphasis, restriction, and separation. That is: "Indeed we are the victors, not others, by this great might which they believed in at that time." What do you say?
* A student: My question, Shaykh: "la'alla" (...) for causation: ﴿perhaps we will follow the magicians﴾.
* The Shaykh: Possibly, but for hope (tarajji) it is clearer.
* The student: Clearer than causation.
* The Shaykh: Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Then Musa threw his staff﴾ by a special revelation from Allah, as in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿We said: "Do not fear; indeed, you are the superior. And throw what is in your right hand, it will swallow what they have made."﴾ [Ta-Ha 68–69]. Musa threw his staff.

﴿Then behold, it swallowed﴾ (with the omission of one of the two tas from the original: tatalaqqaf, "it swallows") ﴿what they falsely produced﴾ [al-A'raf 117; al-Shu'ara' 45].

As for the reading "talaqqafu" (with the doubled ta), one of the two ta's is omitted; its original form is "tatalaqqafu," meaning "swallows." Both have the same meaning, but "talaqqafu" (with doubling) adds a meaning beyond "talqafu." It conveys pursuit: as if it kept pursuing until it had consumed them all. For when they were many in front of it, it did not pursue them; the reason it did not pursue them is that they were many. In which direction would it seize? But when they were destroyed and fewer, they became a rope here, a rope there, and a rope there, so it pursues them, following them.

His saying ﴿what they falsely produced﴾: they turn the truth upside down by their deception, so that they make their ropes and staffs appear as moving snakes.

﴿What they falsely produced﴾: "ifk" means lying. Is this a lie in action or in speech?
* Students: In action.
* The Shaykh: It is an active lie, because a spoken lie is by the tongue, which is informing about something that does not correspond to reality. An active lie is by action, which is a person displaying an act contrary to the reality. These people displayed these ropes and staffs as snakes, but they were not so; they were not snakes.

He says: this is a lie in action, because they displayed them as snakes when they were not such; they were only ropes and staffs.

Some scholars claimed that magic has no reality, and they cited the verse: ﴿It is imagined to him, by their magic, that they were moving﴾ [Ta-Ha 66].

The correct view is that it has a reality; its reality is this imagining (takhyil).
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, it affects perception and sensation and the like, but that it alters the realities of things, no; because that is one of the attributes of the Creator.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verses 43–51 (part 2 of 4):

When the magicians, who are the most knowledgeable of people about magic, its effects and its influence, saw what this staff did after Musa had thrown it down while they were watching, they knew that the matter was not magic. Their magic was the strongest and most extensive magic of all the magicians in Egypt, and magic was also widespread at that time. For this reason, what came to Musa was something resembling a kind of magic, but they knew that this was not magic and that it was beyond the capacity of magicians. So what happened? ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrating. They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun."﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 46–48].

﴿So the magicians were thrown down﴾, and it did not say, "So the magicians prostrated." This is as if the prostration was involuntary, because of the strength of what compelled them to it. That is, it was not as if it were a voluntary act, but because the motivating force was so strong, it was as if they had been thrown down without their choice.

﴿The magicians were thrown down﴾: the definite article in "al-sahara" (the magicians) denotes generality. That is, all the magicians, despite their skill and knowledge, were thrown down prostrating. Prostrating to whom? To Allah. The evidence is their saying, ﴿They said, "We have believed,"﴾ and they were not prostrating in honour of Musa's staff. No, because their declaration of faith is evidence that they were prostrating to Allah, the Exalted.

﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun."﴾ This substitution (badal) is one of the finest forms that can follow a general term. ﴿The Lord of the worlds﴾: because Musa used to say that he was the messenger of the Lord of the worlds, they said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds." Pharaoh also used to say that he was the Lord of the worlds, so by their saying ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun﴾ they excluded Pharaoh's lordship. For although Pharaoh claimed to be the Lord of the worlds, he is not the Lord of Musa and Harun, because Musa and Harun denied his lordship. Therefore this substitution is one of the finest ways of clarifying what is meant by "the Lord of the worlds."

Their saying ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾ rather than directly saying ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun﴾ indicates that they believed in Musa's prophethood, because Musa had said, "I am the messenger of the Lord of the worlds," and did not say, "I am the messenger of my Lord." He said, "the Lord of the worlds." This is the benefit of the substitution in His saying ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun﴾.

The order here, Musa before Harun, corresponds to reality, for Musa's rank is higher than Harun's, since Musa is among the ulu al-'azm (the messengers of firm resolve). However, the order differs in surah Ta-Ha: ﴿the Lord of Harun and Musa﴾ [Ta-Ha 70], for the sake of observing the fawasil (the rhyming verse-endings). This is evidence that the Noble Qur'an, and every eloquent speech, may observe the fawasil and rhythms, but in matters that are known. Here, it is known that Musa is superior, and no one imagines that Harun's rank is higher because he is mentioned in a particular order.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, but putting something first has its distinction. This is why the Messenger (ﷺ) said: «I begin with what Allah began with» [Muslim (1218/147) from the hadith of Jabir].

(﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun﴾: because they knew that what they had seen of the staff could not be achieved by magic.) Then, when they professed this faith and declared it openly, heedless of what would result from it, because true faith overcomes every natural impulse. The love of self is an innate, natural inclination, but faith overcomes it. This is why a person exposes himself to destruction when he goes out to fight in the way of Allah, knowing that the swords of the enemy may sever his neck, yet he does not care. Likewise, a person forgets the bonds of affection with his relatives, to the extent that a man may kill his father if he is a disbeliever.

So here they declared this openly, heedless of what would result. In my view, they knew that a great matter would result from it, because Pharaoh had brought them as his weapon. So if they betrayed him in this great gathering, which was the day of the festival, the punishment would be greater. Nevertheless, they were heedless of this, for the reason we mentioned earlier.

He said: ﴿He said, "Have you believed in him before I give you permission?"﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 49]. This is Pharaoh's speech. The word ﴿He said﴾: is it disconnected or connected to the previous sentence? Is it joined (waṣl) or separated (faṣl) from the earlier statement?

It is disconnected, because waṣl is conjunction by the letter "wa" (and), and anything other than that is faṣl. It is disconnected, but it indicates that this matter occurred immediately, as if it were a response to their action. That is, what was the outcome?

(﴿He said, "Have you believed in him?"﴾ is read with both hamzas pronounced: ﴿a'amantum﴾ and with the second hamza replaced by an alif: ﴿amantum﴾, and ﴿in him﴾.)

(﴿He said, "Have you believed in him before I give you permission?"﴾ "in him" refers to Musa, ﴿before I give you permission﴾, meaning I, ﴿for you﴾.) This is something that does not normally happen from these people or from anyone else: that someone should believe in the enemy of Pharaoh without his permission.

In His saying ﴿before I give you permission﴾ there is an indication that the man had gained complete control over them, and that they did not act in anything without his permission.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿Have you believed in him before I give you permission?﴾ is for denial and rebuke. ﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic﴾: observe the deception. He said, "How strange!" In reality this is a sign of his weakness. How could he be their chief who taught them magic, when they had been gathered from the cities, and were not even with Musa in his city? So it cannot be said that he taught them; rather, they were in distant cities.

And how could it be said that he is their chief who taught them magic, when they had placed their ropes and staffs to overcome him? For whoever taught them magic must surely be feared by them. And how could it be said that he taught them magic when they had sworn by the might of Pharaoh, ﴿By the might of Pharaoh, we will surely be the victors﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 44], while they know that Pharaoh is Musa's adversary? But this is a means of deceiving his people. As Allah said of his people: ﴿So he made his people feel foolish, and they obeyed him﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 54]. That is, their minds were nothing compared to Pharaoh's; they were light-minded and without thought, knowing nothing except that Pharaoh was their god.

﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 49]. We have said that this is false from the three or four aspects we mentioned, and that it is impossible. But this is undoubtedly a display of weakness on Pharaoh's part. It is as if he is saying: "You have united against me and conspired against me, you and your teacher." Then he resorted to threats, as was his habit, and said: (﴿Then you will soon know﴾ what I will inflict upon you) ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you all﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 49].

His saying ﴿Then you will soon know﴾ is a threat about an unspecified matter. We have mentioned that among the benefits of stating something in general and then specifying it is that it arouses the listener's eagerness to have this general matter explained. If it is a threat, the listener is eager for the explanation but is extremely afraid, because he does not know what this unspecified thing is that he has been promised. He explained it with ﴿I will surely cut off﴾, and the lam (emphatic particle) here is the response to an oath, as shown by the emphasis ﴿I will surely cut off﴾.

His saying ﴿your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾: "hands" and "feet" are plural forms of "yad" and "rijl." ﴿On opposite sides﴾ means in alternation. If he cuts off the right hand, he cuts off the left foot; if he cuts off the left hand, he cuts off the right foot. ﴿On opposite sides﴾ does not mean that I will oppose you by cutting off the hands of some of you and the feet of others. Rather, it applies to a single person: each one of you will have his hand and foot cut off on opposite sides. In our sharia, this is the prescribed punishment for highway robbers (qutta' al-tariq): their hands and feet are cut off on opposite sides.

﴿And I will surely crucify you all﴾: that is, after I do this, I will crucify you all, as He said in another verse: ﴿on the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ta-Ha 71]. This indicates that there were palm trees in Egypt. He had promised them this.

Salb (crucifixion) means binding. Is it a condition that the crucified person's arms be stretched out or not? It is not a condition. What matters is that he is bound tightly to the cross.

* Student: After death or before it?
* Shaykh: No, before death, because he said, "I will crucify you," ﴿and I will surely crucify you﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 49], so they...
* Student: Crucifixion in the verse about highway robbers.
* Shaykh: The crucifixion in the verse about highway robbers has been disputed among the scholars: is it before death or after?

The well-known position in our madhhab (school) is that it is after death, but the correct view is that it is before death. They are crucified before death, because if they are crucified before death they experience two kinds of pain: physical and psychological or emotional. But if they are crucified after death, they feel nothing at all. Moreover, crucifying them after death is, as the common people say, (...), of no benefit. This is why when it was said to Asma bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him and with her, that al-Hajjaj had done such and such to 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr after his death, she said, may Allah be pleased with her: "What harm is there to a sheep in skinning it after it is dead?" Because this does not have any effect.

Their reply was: ﴿They said, "No harm! Indeed, to our Lord we will return."﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 50].

(﴿No harm﴾: there is no harm to us in that.) How wonderful! That is, because of the strength of their faith they said: this does not harm us and has no effect. In this there is clear challenge, display of strength and courage: they were addressing the most arrogant man on earth, Pharaoh, and saying: "No harm, do whatever you want, it does not concern us." They were truthful that there was no harm for them in that, as long as this torture was for the sake of Allah. They were being tortured only for the sake of Allah, and this would never harm them. Rather, it would increase their rank. That is why their remembrance continues until the Day of Resurrection. Allah, the Exalted, praised them in the Qur'an, and their remembrance will remain until the Day of Resurrection. This is the greatest benefit.

(﴿Indeed, to our Lord﴾ after our death, in whatever manner it happens, ﴿we will return﴾: we will return in the Hereafter.) That is, whatever happens, even if we reach death, the end result is that we will return to our Lord. Our return to our Lord is better than this world, because they return to an everlasting bliss that nothing in worldly bliss can equal. In surah Ta-Ha: ﴿So decide what you will decide; you only decide about this worldly life﴾ [Ta-Ha 72]. That is: decide what you want. The most that can happen is that your torture will lead to death, and when it leads to death, the result is only this worldly life. This indicates that they were truthful in their faith and that their faith was firmly established. In this there is clear evidence of the signs of Allah, the Exalted, and of His power.

How could it be that in a single moment the great disbelief turned into deep faith? In an instant. As soon as they saw what Musa's staff did, they changed from disbelief to faith. This is why some scholars said: "They became disbelieving magicians in the morning, and in the evening they were righteous martyrs." This is true: they were righteous and pious, and among the strongest of people in faith and in striving in the way of Allah.

﴿Indeed, to our Lord we will return﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 50]. This is also evidence of their belief in resurrection, from their saying ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we will return﴾. They believe in meeting Allah, the Exalted, which is one of the fundamentals of faith.

(﴿Indeed, we hope﴾, that is, we aspire, ﴿that our Lord will forgive us our sins﴾, that is, because ﴿we were the first of the believers﴾ in our time.) ﴿We hope﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 51]: that is, we aspire and anticipate. This hope is praiseworthy in a servant, but when? When he has taken its means. If he has not taken its means, it is one of the vain wishes, as in the hadith: «The intelligent one is the one who holds himself accountable and works for what comes after death, and the incapable one is the one who follows his desires and wishes against Allah for vain hopes» [al-Tirmidhi (2459) and Ibn Majah (171), from the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws]. They affirmed that they hoped for Allah's forgiveness, because they had taken the means, which is faith after disbelief. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾ [Al-Anfal 38]. So they hoped this well-known hope because of its cause, and it is praiseworthy.

Their saying, may Allah be pleased with them: ﴿that our Lord will forgive us our sins﴾: al-ghafr (forgiveness) was previously explained as concealing the sin and pardoning it.

Their saying ﴿our sins﴾ is the plural of khati'ah (sin). Are khata'a and sayyi'at (evil deeds) the same thing, or is there a difference between them, or are they distinguished only when they are mentioned together?

* Students: Only when they are mentioned together.
* Shaykh: Only when they are mentioned together. They are distinguished, but when one of them is mentioned alone, it includes the other. In surah Al 'Imran: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, are signs for those of understanding. Who remember Allah standing, sitting and on their sides, and give thought to the creation of the heavens and the earth, [saying], "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; exalted are You, so protect us from the punishment of the Fire." … [They say], "Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, 'Believe in your Lord,' so we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins, remove from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die with the righteous"﴾ [Al 'Imran 190–193]. They distinguished between dhunub (sins) and sayyi'at (misdeeds). For dhunub they asked for forgiveness, and for sayyi'at they asked for expiation, because the sayyi'at are minor sins that righteous deeds expiate. The sayyi'at here refer to the major sins, which are removed not by expiation but only by forgiveness.

﴿That we were the first of the believers﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 51]: this is not an attitude of presuming upon Allah or claiming a favour over Him by being the first believers. Rather, it is a way of speaking of Allah's blessing, which they see as a cause and means of forgiveness of sins, because precedence in faith and in righteous deeds is a virtue and one of the causes of high rank. This is why Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward. But to all Allah has promised the best﴾ [Al-Hadid 10]. Precedence in faith and righteous deeds has its distinction and gives its possessor his rank. Is that correct?

* Student: His saying ﴿you believed in him﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 49], and in the verse of al-A'raf: ﴿you believed in him﴾ [Al-A'raf 123]?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Originally there is a difference between them. "Amana bihi" means he acknowledged it and confessed it with complete faith, and "amana lahu" implies the meaning of submitting (inqad).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: He submitted to him. It may be less, and it may be more. He submitted to him together with faith. When you combine the two verses here, the expression becomes more eloquent. That is, it is as if they believed in him with faith, then they believed in him and submitted to him.
* Student: ﴿So decide what you will decide. You only decide about this worldly life. Indeed, we have believed in our Lord that He may forgive us our sins and the magic to which you compelled us. And Allah is better and more enduring. Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell﴾ [Ta-Ha 72–74].
* Shaykh: You mean His saying ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord﴾.
* Student: ﴿And Allah is better and more enduring.﴾
* Shaykh: No, ﴿And Allah is better and more enduring﴾ is their own speech. Yes indeed. But ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾ may be their speech or the speech of Allah.
* Student: Here, these magicians (...), they are the ones who believed (...), or these were killed.
* Shaykh: Who?
* Student: The magicians who believed (...).
* Shaykh: They (...) of whom?
* Student: Afterwards Musa (...).
* Shaykh: No, the Children of Israel.
* Student: The Children of Israel. These were killed right away.
* Shaykh: Either they were killed right away, or nothing happened to them. But as for those who harmed him, they were his people.
* Student: Yes, they did not believe.
* Shaykh: Who?
* Student: The Children of Israel were not believers?

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verses 43–51 (part 3 of 4):**

* **The Shaykh:** In this treatment, they were not believers at all, or some of them were believers. I do not know. The basis is that the Torah was revealed afterward: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses the Book after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾ [al-Qasas 43].
* **Student:** Regarding Allah's words: ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾ (...). Because if he cuts off the right hand and the left remains, no person can lean on (...). Because if he cuts off one hand and one foot (...), one (...) cannot (...). Is this more severe (...)?
* **The Shaykh:** No. In one respect it is more severe, and in another respect it is lighter. In terms of severity, the pain is on both sides. In terms of lightness, and this is apparently what is intended here, because, as it appears, and Allah knows best, they were killed in the end.
* **The Student:** Apparently they were all like that.
* **The Shaykh:** Because some scholars' statement "martyrs of righteousness" indicates that they were killed. I do not know this now.
* **The Student:** (...) some scholars (...).
* **The Shaykh:** This needs verification.
* **The Student:** Apparently they were all like that.
* **The Shaykh:** All of them what?
* **The Student:** There was not a single one, for example.
* **The Shaykh:** Of the magicians?
* **The Student:** Yes.
* **The Shaykh:** They all believed. ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾. What is this word (al) here?
* **Students:** For generality.
* **The Shaykh:** For generality. They all believed, and their faith was complete, not yet incomplete.
* **Student:** "Whoever fears Allah, the Exalted, (receives) Paradise, not the service of Him."
* **The Shaykh:** Who says that?
* **The Student:** Some scholars (...).
* **The Shaykh:** No, is there "service" and "Paradise" in it?
* **The Student:** Because they did not do deeds.
* **The Shaykh:** First: the expression "His service" is not reported, and in reality it should not be used alongside worship. Allah did not praise people because they served Him; rather, because they are His servants. For this reason, this expression that is written in books of admonition must truly be taken into consideration.
Second: We say that every person who acts, acts for Allah, the Exalted, in devotion to Him and hoping for His reward. Allah described the best of creation and the highest in rank, Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and those with him, saying: ﴿You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and approval﴾ [al-Fath 29]. The Messenger (ﷺ) said, when a Bedouin said: "I do not do well with your murmuring nor the murmuring of Mu'adh, but I ask Allah for Paradise and seek refuge with Him from the Fire," "Around it we murmur." [[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (15898) and Abu Dawud (792), from a hadith of some of the Companions of the Prophet.]] Some of the "knowers" (ʿārifīn), as they say, say: "You must worship Allah for Allah's sake, not for the sake of your own portion." Who told you this? One who hopes for His reward, may He be blessed and exalted, is the reality, and this is what Allah described His servants with. This is what I said: "for His service, not His Paradise," right?
* **The Student:** "For His service, not His Paradise."
* **The Shaykh:** I say: that is, or they worship Allah in His service, not His Paradise. That is, they say: the best is to worship Allah for His service, not for His Paradise, and they consider the one who worships Allah for His Paradise to be deficient.
* **The Student:** "I worshipped Allah not for His Paradise, nor out of fear of His Fire, but out of love for His Essence."
* **Another student:** They say Ibn al-Farid, at the time of his death sickness, saw Paradise and began to cry out and shout: "Why did I do this? Why did I pray? Only out of love for You."
* **The Shaykh:** "Out of love for You," and he sees it in every (...). I seek refuge with Allah.
* **Student:** Combining between... he acts out of love for Allah, the Exalted, and seeking Paradise (...).
* **The Shaykh:** This is the reality, because reaching Paradise is reaching Allah, since the people of Paradise see Allah, the Exalted.
* **The Student:** I do not mean that a person's deed is only for the sake of Paradise. Perhaps his feeling is gratitude to Allah (...).
* **The Shaykh:** His feeling is what?
* **The Student:** His inner feeling of magnifying Allah, the Exalted, makes him act with this disposition. So if (...).
* **The Shaykh:** By Allah, I do not know. In reality, I think the best is what the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions followed.
* **The Student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Thankful to Allah.
* **The Student:** Thankful to Allah, the Exalted.
* **The Shaykh:** It does not contradict that one loves Allah and strives to reach His Paradise: ﴿You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and approval﴾.
* **Student:** And bounty is not except after approval.
* **The Shaykh:** Also, this bounty and approval include the love of Allah.
* **Student:** And then, Shaykh, the more love increases, the more reward increases for it.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, there is no doubt. A person is rewarded for love.
* **The Student:** ﴿Say: If you should love Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran 31].
* **The Shaykh:** Yes. No one denies the love of Allah. And no one denies that... Even your acting to reach the pleasure of Allah is love for Allah. Otherwise he would say: "Whether He is pleased or not, it does not matter; whether He grants bliss or not, it does not matter." But if he says: "No, act for Allah's own essence," like this (...), it is not correct.
* **Student:** He, may Allah have mercy on him, said in the benefits of these verses: The worship of believers is from the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, toward them, and this is from His words, glorified is He: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan 63].
* **The Shaykh:** Is this in your text?
* **Student:** In a second form.
* **The Shaykh:** What is it?
* **The Student:** That the servanthood of a person to Allah draws mercy from Allah to him.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, no, this is not that.
* **The Student:** He calls those who were granted these qualities because of His mercy.
* **The Shaykh:** This is close to it.
* **Student:** That the attribute of servanthood (...).
* **The Shaykh:** This is different.
* **Student:** That worship is a cause for mercy. Allah said: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾. So the attribution of worship to the name "the Most Merciful" specifically, not to others.
* **The Shaykh:** This means that a benefit is that they worship Allah to reach His mercy.
* **Student:** That among the attributes of the servants of the Most Merciful, His believing servants, is walking on the earth with tranquility and dignity: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan 63].
* **The Shaykh:** Ali has another benefit too, which is dividing servanthood into general and special, right?
* **Student:** (...) establishing special servanthood, which is the servanthood of the Prophet.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, and also perhaps we say: from this verse it is derived that describing a person with servanthood is one of the levels of perfection. For this reason He said: ﴿servants of the Most Merciful﴾.
* **Student:** Its honoring them, since He attributed them to Himself.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, indeed. This is also a benefit other than what I (...).
* **Student:** Yes, other than (...).
* **The Shaykh:** We say: the attribute of servanthood in general is one of the levels of perfection, from attributing them to Allah: ﴿servants of the Most Merciful﴾. This is from the category of honor and dignity.
* **Student:** His words: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾ (...).
* **The Shaykh:** They mentioned two benefits in it: First, that their worship is from Allah's mercy toward them. Second, that they bring this servanthood to the level of mercy.
* **Student:** We said: among the attributes of the servants of the Most Merciful, the believers, is walking on the earth with tranquility and dignity: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾.
Fifth: a veiled reference to the arrogant who walk on the earth exultantly, from His words: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾.
* **The Shaykh:** A veiled reference to their blame.
* **The Student:** To their blame, yes.
* **Another student:** We say here: among their attributes is not harming others: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾.
* **The Shaykh:** From where do we take it? From His words: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾.
* **The Student:** That is, from their disposition, that is, tranquility.
* **Another student:** ﴿And when the ignorant address them﴾.
* **The Student:** Yes, well done. ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾
* **The Shaykh:** But this is a description even if there is no one in the place: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾. Even if no one is around them, they fear harming anyone. And if we say tranquility and dignity include all possible forms...
* **The Student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** That they do not harm anyone by their walking.
* **Student:** (...) His words: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾.
* **The Shaykh:** That is, it includes physical and moral walking, right?
* **The Student:** Yes.
* **The Shaykh:** It is possible.
* **Student:** An encouragement. We mentioned it as an encouragement toward calmness and deliberation in all kinds of striving, including moral striving, such as seeking provision and knowledge.
* **The Shaykh:** What do you have?
* **Student:** Yes, the same: "who walk upon the earth." It shows an attribute of these virtuous people. As if Allah, the Exalted, answered a question that might arise: who are these servants, and why did they deserve this beautiful description, in that He attributed them to Himself? Among their attributes are humility, love of good, and distance from haughtiness and pride, which are not befitting except to Allah alone. Whoever wishes to be among the righteous servants must recognize one of their attributes, which is humility and gentleness of manner.
* **Another student:** Honor is among the attributes of believers: ﴿But to Allah belongs honor, and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8]. He says: distance from... means honor!
* **The Shaykh:** You mean self-pride?
* **The Student:** No, honor that is not honor (i.e., a false honor).
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, disbelief that is not disbelief.
* **The Student:** No, I mean honor that belongs to Allah.
* **The Shaykh:** You mean arrogance?
* **The Student:** Yes, arrogance.
* **The Shaykh:** In any case, I have an objection to this. Not from the side of this issue, but from the side that it came unconnected, as if it were speech (...).
The explanation of benefits is usually concentrated; it should not be like loose speech, as if we were speaking in a sermon. This is like a verbal explanation, and in terms of style it is deficient, though it is complete, meaning the speech has no deficiency in meaning. But in terms of style (...) keep the benefits concentrated so that the mind is not scattered and one can grasp them grain by grain.
* **Student:** In His words: ﴿they walk﴾, that the successful person can make the habit of walking into worship, and it is a habit (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, if they were paying attention to this, and that is apparent, it is apparent that they were paying attention to this, that is, it is not a common matter or from their disposition; rather it is deliberate.
* **Student:** Affirmation of the attribute of mercy for Allah, and affirmation that "the Most Merciful" is an attribute of Allah, the Exalted.
* **The Shaykh:** This is necessary. There is also in it the affirmation of the name "the Most Merciful" and the attribute of mercy. Correct.
* **Student:** His words: ﴿they walk﴾. He did not say: "and the servants of the Most Merciful who travel upon the earth in humility." In this there is an indication that the servants of the Most Merciful (...).
* **The Shaykh:** What is the difference between them?
* **The Student:** If he said "travel," perhaps they travel on their mounts, travel (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Even this, if a person travels on his mounts, it is not apparent. Even travel can be on two feet, and walking can be on foot or on a mount.
* **Student:** (...).
* **The Shaykh:** In any case, note this, what the brother said: affirmation of the name "the Most Merciful" and the attribute of mercy for Allah, the Exalted.
* **The Student:** Encouragement to forbearance from His words: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾, that they do not repay evil with its like, but say (...). And after that, a benefit: encouragement to forbearance, a veiled reference to the blame of ignorance and of people of sin, from His words: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾, that among the attributes of His believing servants (...), when the ignorant address them, is their commitment to speech by which they are safe from sin (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Good (...). Three benefits. What do you have?
* **Student:** I say: that when he mentioned the first (...) "peace" is appropriate to the state of the aggressor, and they may respond to them with a strong response suited to their state. Their forbearance is not always (...), that when they are treated ignorantly they respond with the appropriate response to the state of the aggressor (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Forbearance is possible, because forbearance does not mean pardon absolutely. Forbearance may also be called forbearance by not aggressing, and by this they are safe from sin if they do not aggress. But I also have a benefit more important than all of this, in reality?
* **The Student:** That Allah loves from His servants (...), and that it is not appropriate to confront the ignorant with ignorance (...). The Qur'an's explanation of this beautiful etiquette (...) and returning the offender with good.
