He said: ﴿Ta-llahi, in truth we were in clear error﴾: ﴿in﴾ — the author says: (it is a lightened form of "inna," and its noun is omitted; i.e., indeed it, namely the "ta'" [is]) ﴿we were in clear error﴾ (clear, manifest). ﴿Kunna﴾ is a past-tense verb; it was asked to indicate time (...)? Because what is meant is: we were in this world.

(﴿We were in clear error﴾ manifest, ﴿when﴾ where ﴿we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 98] in worship.) This is correct: this is the utmost of error, that a person equates a created being with the Creator in worship. Worship is not only bowing and prostration; even whoever obeys someone in making unlawful what Allah has made lawful, or making lawful what Allah has made unlawful, is thereby a worshipper of him, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and the Messiah, son of Mary﴾ [al-Tawbah 31]. 'Adi ibn Hatim said to the Prophet ﷺ: O Messenger of Allah, we do not worship them; that is, we do not worship our rabbis and our monks, meaning our scholars and our worshippers? The Prophet ﷺ said: «Do they not make unlawful what Allah has made lawful, and you make it unlawful, and make lawful what Allah has made unlawful, and you make it lawful?» He said: "Yes," 'Adi said it. He said: «That is their worship»[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3095), and al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (218), the wording is his, from the hadith of 'Adi ibn Hatim.]]. Those who apply the regulations of their governments while they contradict the Sharia will have an end on the Day of Resurrection like these people; that is, they will disown them and dispute with them, saying, arguing against themselves: ﴿By Allah, we were in clear error (97) when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾.

For example, a person is told by Allah in His Book and by the words of His Messenger ﷺ: "This is lawful," and then the ruler says to him: "This is unlawful and forbidden," so he forbids it, and considers it unlawful despite Allah's making it lawful for him. Without doubt he has taken this ruler as a god besides Allah, as a legislator.

Likewise, his Lord says to him, for example: "This is unlawful," and then this ruler comes and says: "The regulation or constitution requires its permissibility," so he makes it permissible. Without doubt he has also taken this ruler as a god besides Allah, and his end will be the end of those people; he will dispute with him on the Day of Resurrection and say to him: ﴿By Allah, we were in clear error (97) when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾.

For this reason, a authentic hadith states that the Prophet ﷺ said: «Obedience is only in what is right»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7145), and Muslim (1840 / 39) from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.]]; that is, obedience to the ruler in what is right as the person recognizes it. Just as the correct view is that if the ruler legislates regulations that oppose the Sharia of Allah, he becomes a disbeliever, by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44]. If the truth is made clear to him and it is said to him: "This is the ruling of Allah, and this regulation you have enacted contradicts the ruling," yet he insists after the truth has become clear to him, he becomes a disbeliever, and it is then permissible to rise against him to remove him from rule; because if he commits open disbelief (kufr bawah) about which there is a proof from Allah, it is permissible to confront him and rise against him, since it is not possible for any individual among people to rule the Muslims contrary to their Sharia. Rather, he must be rejected and action must be taken against him until he is removed from rule.

The summary is that Allah the Exalted says to those who have taken deities besides Him, whether it is worship of submission or worship of judgment, that they will be thrown into the Fire of Hell and will dispute therein, and the followers will say to the leaders: ﴿By Allah, we were in clear error (97) when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾.

(﴿And none led us astray﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 99] from guidance ﴿except the criminals﴾) and so on.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: If it admits interpretation (...); that is, whether the interpretation is from the agent or from (...), but the interpretation of the agent, if the truth is made clear to him, is permissible if it is evident.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: For example, if the ruler makes lawful, and some Islamic countries now make fornication lawful and set up a specific market for it; whoever wants it may go there. We have heard that in some Islamic countries, when a traveling passenger arrives, pictures of young women and men are presented to him, and it is asked: "Do you like this or that?" That is, permissibility of sodomy and permissibility of fornication. This is clear disbelief, it needs no interpretation.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is, how is it disbelief (...) because either (...), if he says disbelief, even if it is open (...) rising against him, or we see open disbelief, clear and manifest disbelief; "manifest" means that he committed it knowingly, and there is a proof from Allah, the Exalted, regarding it; meaning that the indication of the texts on this is that it is clear disbelief.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: (...) There is a difference between one who judges in a specific case, who may say: "I know Allah's ruling, but I opposed it for my desire or out of enmity toward the one judged against," and one who legislates, because the one who legislates writes laws; this means he has removed the legislated ruling and put in place a man-made ruling, so one must distinguish between the law and the act. A person who judges by other than what Allah revealed in a particular case may be driven by the desire of his own soul, or may be driven, for example, by supporting his companion or spiting his enemy if the one judged against is his enemy, or the ruling may stem from hatred of Allah's ruling. These three states correspond to the three verses.

As for the person who legislates and writes laws, what does that mean? That he did not accept Allah's ruling, because he replaced Allah's rulings with these laws. This is a disbeliever without doubt, and he is not included in the verse.
* Student: Whoever legislates (...)?
* Shaykh: No, he is not included in the three; he falls under one of them, which is judging by other than what Allah revealed: ﴿Or do they have partners who have legislated for them in religion that for which Allah has not given permission?﴾ [al-Shura 21].
* Student: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves, and then find within themselves no resistance against what you have decided, and submit in full submission﴾ [al-Nisa' 65] if (...)?
* Shaykh: It is not in every case; because negation of faith may be of two kinds. A person may come out of what was decided either out of aversion to Allah's ruling, the Exalted and Glorified, or out of aversion because it opposed his desire, not aversion to the ruling itself, like the calamities that now befall a person, which he dislikes, but he does not dislike Allah's decree in them.
* Student: (...) the legal ruling?
* Shaykh: Even the legal ruling, perhaps if it contradicts what some people are upon. Now some common people, when the legal ruling comes, apply it, but (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) but his faith is deficient, because in his heart and soul there is now resentment, and it is obligatory that a person open his breast to the rulings of Islam: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam, so that he is upon light from his Lord?﴾ [al-Zumar 22].
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: This is part of the punishment; because the point is that they dispute, they speak to the guards: ﴿Let your Lord decree upon us﴾ [al-Zukhruf 77], they curse one another: ﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾ [al-A'raf 38]. All of this is part of the punishment.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, they dispute and they are being punished, yes indeed.
* Student: This is not conceivable.
* Shaykh: Yes, but the states of the Hereafter are not measured by the states of this world. Is it not that the sun will draw near to the creatures on the Day of Resurrection by the distance of a mile? Now, if it moved even a fingertip from its place, it would burn the world to ashes (...), it will be on the Day of Resurrection a distance of a mile (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, the states of the Hereafter can never be measured by the states of this world.
* Student: Some (...) imagine (...).
* Shaykh: No, it cannot be imagined, just as the states of the barzakh: when a person dies, he sits up, is questioned, and is punished (...).

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿They will say, while they dispute therein: By Allah, we were certainly in clear error, when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds. And none led us astray except the criminals. So we have no intercessors, nor any devoted friend. So if only we had another return, we would be among the believers. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers. And indeed your Lord — He is the Exalted in Might, the Most Merciful.  The people of Noah denied the messengers. When their brother Noah said to them, "Will you not fear Allah? Indeed I am to you a trustworthy messenger. So fear Allah and obey me. And I do not ask you for any payment for it; my payment is only from the Lord of the worlds. So fear Allah and obey me." They said, "Shall we believe you while the lowest people follow you?" He said, "And what is my knowledge of what they used to do? Their account is only upon my Lord, if you could perceive. And I am not one to drive away the believers. I am only a clear warner." They said, "If you do not desist, O Noah, you will surely be among those stoned." He said, "My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment and save me and those with me of the believers." So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship. Then We drowned the remaining ones afterward. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers. And indeed your Lord — He is the Exalted in Might, the Most Merciful.﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 96–122].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said, explaining that it will not benefit a person on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 89]. So wealth and children will not benefit, ﴿except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart﴾. And in this exception (istithna', exception) is evidence that the matter depends on the heart, that it be sound.
As for its soundness, the author says: (from shirk and hypocrisy). But it is more general than that as well: its soundness from every action or statement. The heart has speech and action. Its speech is its affirmation (of faith), and its action is its movement out of hope, fear, love and other things.
* In the verse is the affirmation of resurrection, due to His saying: ﴿and do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾.
* Also in it: every person is in need of supplication, even the prophets, because Ibrahim, peace be upon him, supplicated to Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, with that.
* In it is evidence that on the Day of Resurrection wealth and children will not benefit, due to His saying: ﴿the Day when wealth and children will not benefit﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 88], contrary to what people were upon in this world, for wealth and children do benefit in the world, but in the Hereafter they will not benefit.
* In it is evidence of the virtue of the sound heart, because it is the means by which a person benefits from his wealth and children, based on the exception being connected (istithna' muttasil), and it is so.
* Also in it is evidence for the affirmation of Paradise, due to His saying: ﴿and Paradise will be brought near﴾, and that its people are the God-fearing, those who did what protects them from the punishment of Allah, by performing the commands and avoiding the prohibitions.
* In it is evidence for the affirmation of Hellfire, due to His saying: ﴿and Hellfire will be made apparent﴾.
* In it is evidence, when He distinguished between the two expressions regarding the bringing near of Paradise and the manifestation of Hellfire, evidence that mercy precedes wrath, because Paradise is brought close to the believers, whereas for those (the disbelievers) it appears to them, and they see it from afar: ﴿when it sees them from a distant place, they hear its raging and roaring﴾ [Al-Furqan 12]; so that they will be in fear and terror before they reach it.
* Also in it is evidence that the companions of the Blazing Fire are every ghawi (one who is deviant). And who is the ghawi?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed, (...) is the one who.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Ghawayah (deviance) is the opposite of... what is guidance? Guidance is the opposite of misguidance; ghawayah is the opposite of rushd (right guidance). The meaning is that what is intended by the ghawin (deviants) are those who turned away from the straight path. They turned away from it; they did not go astray from it. That is, they knew it but turned away from it, and we seek refuge in Allah.
* In it is evidence of the punishment of the companions of the Fire, both of the heart and of the body. From where is it taken?
* Student: The verse and what follows it.
* Shaykh: What?
* Student: ﴿And Hellfire will be made apparent to the deviants﴾.
* Shaykh: Not that. Specify for us the particular phrase for this verse.
* Student: The bodily punishment: ﴿and Hellfire will be made apparent﴾.
* Shaykh: Good, and the mental (heart) one?
* Student: The heart one: ﴿and it will be said to them﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿and it will be said to them﴾, well done.
* In it is evidence of (...) these worshippers of idols, to humiliate their idols: ﴿So they will be thrown into it, they and the deviants.﴾ And excluded from this is who? One who was worshipped while he was righteous, for he will not be thrown in, due to the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed those for whom the best reward from Us has preceded, they will be kept far from it. They will not hear its faintest sound﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 101–102].
* And in this is evidence that whoever follows Satan is not merely one of his followers, but one of his soldiers who accompany him, due to His saying: ﴿and the soldiers of Iblis﴾. This is because the one who follows a person strengthens him, supports him, and spreads what he wants, so he becomes like a soldier made subservient to him.
* And in this is evidence of the people of the Fire's immense regret when they say, while disputing with one another: ﴿By Allah, we were certainly in clear error, when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾. Here they swore and emphasized: ﴿By Allah﴾ is an oath; ﴿indeed we were﴾ — (in) is a lightened form of the heavy (inna), which conveys emphasis; and the lam in ﴿certainly in clear error﴾ is likewise. Although some grammarians call this lam the lam of (...), yet while it is distinguishing, it is also emphasizing. The meaning of (distinguishing) is that it distinguishes between (in) the negative and (in) the lightened form, because the form of (in) is one, and it is not made clear which of them is intended except by the presence of the lam. If the lam is absent, the sentence is impermissible unless context indicates otherwise.
I say: ﴿when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾. In their saying: ﴿By Allah, we were certainly in clear error, when we equated you﴾ there is an implicit acknowledgment that Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has no equal, because they denied and explained that they were in clear error when they equated these idols with the Lord, Blessed and Exalted, whom no one resembles in this attribute: ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾. These idols that they worship, they believe that divinity belongs only to those who worship them, whereas the Lord of the worlds is Lord of every single one.
* And among the benefits in His saying ﴿when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾: an indication of the clarity of the error, ﴿with the Lord of the worlds﴾; for it is impossible to equate one who has this description with one who deserves none of this description, ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾. These idols deserve no aspect of lordship whatsoever, let alone the general lordship over all the worlds.
* Then also in this verse: their profound acknowledgment of their own error, ﴿indeed we were in clear error﴾; that is, manifest and evident, in that ﴿we equated you﴾. But this acknowledgment and this affirmation of the Lord and this declaration of His transcendence above being equated with Him in that place will not benefit them, because the time has passed; the time for action was in this world, whereas now is the time of recompense.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 99:

He says: ("﴿And none misled us﴾ from the guidance, ﴿except the criminals﴾, that is, the devils"); meaning the devils of mankind and the jinn. It should be so, and "al-mujrim" (the criminal, one who commits crime) is the doer of crime. It is frequently applied in the Qur'an to the disbeliever. So the meaning is: none misled us except the people of disbelief and crime, who transgressed against us by this misguidance. But in reality, they did not transgress against them, because they are the ones who submitted to this disbelief. ﴿And when they argue with one another in the Fire, the weak will say to those who were arrogant, "Indeed, we were your followers, so will you relieve us of some portion of the Fire?" (47) Those who were arrogant will say, "Indeed, we are all in it"﴾ [Ghafir 47-48]. In Surah Saba' there are verses with this meaning: ﴿And those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant, "Rather, it was your plotting by night and day, when you were ordering us to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him." And they will conceal regret when they see the punishment, and We will put shackles around the necks of those who disbelieved. Are they recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾ [Saba' 33]. So the disbelievers who followed the arrogant have no excuse before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, even if they revile them and say that they are criminals, for that is not an excuse.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, for Allah the Exalted has given them intellect and perception, sent Messengers to them, and revealed Books to them, so there remains no proof for them to argue that these people misled them.

Allah the Exalted said: ("﴿except the criminals﴾, that is: the devils, or our forefathers whom we followed"). This applies if by the criminal is meant the one who is astray, whether he transgressed or did not transgress; for if they were their forefathers whom they followed, then they did not mislead them nor commit crime against them; these are the ones who committed crime against themselves. It is not far-fetched that the verse intends both meanings together, for they were led astray by two things:

Firstly: by those who call them, while alive, to misguidance.

Secondly: by those whom they imitate among the dead. But in the first case the crime lies upon them and upon those who misled them, while in the second it lies upon them alone, because those dead ones did not really commit crime against them, since the Messengers came to them and explained to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verses 100–105 (part 1 of 2):

(﴿So we have no intercessors﴾) as the believers have among the angels, the prophets and the believers. ﴿So we have no intercessors.﴾ Is the word (mā) interrogative or negative?
* Student: Negative.
* The Shaykh: Negative. The evidence is the emphatic (min) in ﴿no intercessors﴾. Its original form is "so we have intercessors," but (min) was brought in for emphasis.
The intercessor (shafi') is the one who mediates on behalf of another to bring about a benefit or to repel a harm. An example is the intercession of the Prophet (ﷺ) for the people of the Gathering that judgment be passed among them, which is intercession to repel harm and hardship. Another is his intercession for the people of Paradise that they enter Paradise, which is intercession to bring benefits.
So intercession (shafa'a) is mediation on behalf of another to bring a benefit or repel a harm. If you wish, you may say: by repelling harm or bringing good.
Why do they have no intercessors? Because of what condition for intercession?
* Student: Among the conditions of intercession (...).
* The Shaykh: And what else?
* Student: And that the one for whom intercession is made be a believer.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence?
* Student: The evidence is ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya' 28].
* The Shaykh: Yes. Those people are not approved by God, so they say: ﴿we have no intercessors﴾. That means: we have no one at all who intercedes, neither from the prophets nor from anyone else, because among the conditions of intercession is that God, blessed and exalted, be pleased with the one for whom intercession is made and with the intercessor. Is He pleased with the intercessor?
* Student: It follows a fortiori.
* The Shaykh: A fortiori, yes. If God's approval of the one for whom intercession is made is required, then His approval of the intercessor is required all the more.
As for permission, it is also a condition. Even when God is pleased with both this one and that one, permission is still necessary. God, blessed and exalted, does not permit intercession except for the one He is pleased with. So both conditions are required. One should not say, for example, that if He approves a person He must permit him. He may permit or He may not. But we know that He does not permit except for those whom He approves, and these people are not approved by God.
﴿So we have no intercessors (100). Nor a close friend.﴾ ﴿Nor a close friend﴾ is coordinated with ﴿intercessors﴾ according to the wording. If it were coordinated according to the grammatical position, it would be (nor a close friend, with a nominative ending), because ﴿intercessors﴾ is in the position of a subject.
﴿A close friend﴾: the friend (ṣadīq) is the one whose affection is sincere toward you. That is, a companion whose love is true is called a friend. He is more specific than a companion (ṣāḥib), so every friend is a companion, but not every companion is a friend.
As for the (ḥamīm), he is the close relative, or one who exaggerates in friendship to the point that he is tender toward you, and then the close relative is tender toward you. The author says: (that is, he is concerned with our affair), because a close and intimate friend, tender and compassionate, or a relative, is concerned with the affair of his companion as he is concerned with his friend's.
Now, is this description (ḥamīm) a descriptive qualifier (ṣifa kāshifa) or a restrictive qualifier (ṣifa muqayyada)? It is descriptive if we say: there is no friend who is not ḥamīm, so it is a descriptive qualifier. If we say: a person may be a friend without being ḥamīm, then the qualifier is restrictive, on condition that we take ḥamīm here to mean "relative," because a person may be a friend without being a relative. If we take ḥamīm to mean the tender one who is like a relative because of his affection and compassion, then it is descriptive. But if we say (ḥamīm) means "relative," it becomes restrictive, because not every friend is a relative.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. How? If we say (nor a close friend ḥamīm), these become two qualities: friendship and kinship, correct? So the quality of kinship does not carry the meaning of the quality of friendship. A person can be a friend without being a relative, and there is no obstacle.
* Student: On the Day of Resurrection.
* The Shaykh: (...) On the Day of Resurrection, but kinship will not benefit him, nor friendship.
﴿Nor a close friend. So if only we had a return (a return to the world)﴾, ﴿then we would be among the believers﴾. (If only) expresses a wish. That is, we do not have a return, meaning a return to the world. ﴿Then we would be﴾: the (fa) indicates causation. (We would be) is in the subjunctive after an implied (an) that follows the causative (fa), because the wish came first. For this reason he says: (lau here expresses a wish, and (nakūna, "we would be") is its answer).
﴿If only that we had a return﴾ means: would that we had a return, ﴿then we would be among the believers﴾. They did not say (layta, "would that") because the situation is one of humility and submission. (Lau) in expressing a wish is softer than (layta), because (layta) is explicit in making a request, while (lau) contains some gentleness and indirectness. This is like when you say to a person who wished to visit you: "If only you would visit me." This (lau) is clearly for expressing a wish, but it is a gentle, indirect and courteous wish, and the situation here calls for it, because they are in a state of humiliation, may God protect us, and submission. So they did not say, "Would that we could return," but they said: ﴿If only that we had a return, then we would be among the believers﴾. However, in Surah al-An'am they say: ﴿Would that we could be returned, and not deny the signs of our Lord, and be among the believers﴾ [al-An'am 27].
It is said that the way to reconcile these is that they sometimes say this and sometimes say that. But which came first, (layta) or (lau)? Apparently (layta) came first. That is, it seems they begin with a resolute wish, and then, if it is not granted, they return to submission and gentle expression.
If they were returned, would they go back? God, mighty and majestic, says in Surah al-An'am: ﴿But there has appeared to them what they had been concealing before. And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars﴾ [al-An'am 28]. This is the true report. That is, their statement that if we return we will be among the believers is a false statement. The true report is ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden. And indeed they are liars﴾ in their claim: ﴿we would be returned and would not deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be among the believers﴾.
* Student: In the same context (...). Is the act of God ﴿If they were returned, they would return﴾?
* The Shaykh: No. Apparently it is the act of God, perhaps (...). At that hour they say it truthfully, but God informed us that if they were returned they would return to disbelief.
﴿If only that we had a return, then we would be among the believers﴾: that is, among those who affirm the truth (...) who are committed to action, because faith alone does not benefit if it does not entail action, so it is not true faith. For this reason we say: the disbelievers who (...) are believers. ﴿They denied them, though their souls were convinced of them﴾ [al-Naml 14]. But because they do not submit, they did not benefit from their faith. Is Iblis a believer or not?
* Students: A believer.
* The Shaykh: In the sense of affirming the truth, he is a believer. But he was arrogant, so his faith did not benefit him. I recall that when the first man went up into space from Russia and observed the universe, he declared that this universe has a Manager. Then his companions came...
No, he becomes more severe than others when the matter becomes clear to him. Now it is clear to him (...).
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) even (...) from him.
* Student: If we say, for example, that faith is speech, action and belief, then on this basis we exclude everyone who, for example, said it with his tongue or believed it in his heart, like Iblis and Pharaoh.
* The Shaykh: If he does not submit, yes. If he does not submit, then he is not a believer, that is known.
For this reason we have said: faith is affirmation that entails acceptance and submission: acceptance of the report and submission to the command (...). This is faith. As for a person who merely says, "I believe in God, and I acknowledge that God exists and that He has messengers," but does not act, this faith does not benefit him.
* Student: Essentially, it does not take place in the self.
* The Shaykh: It is faith, because the faith that benefits is what you mentioned. As for faith, it applies to mere affirmation. (...) this one believes in something but is a disbeliever in other things. Legally valid faith is what benefits. We say: this one is not a believer, meaning not a believer in the legal sense. But linguistically he is a believer.
* Student: Honorable Shaykh, everyone who is arrogant is worse.
* The Shaykh: (...) because the one to whom the truth becomes clear and who is arrogant toward it, his disbelief is disbelief of obstinacy. And the one who does not know the truth and is now acting in the manner of the people of disbelief, his disbelief is disbelief of denial.
Now, the Christians in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ), that is, before his mission, are considered astray. After he was sent and the truth became clear to them, they become those who have incurred anger, since there is no difference between them and the Jews. Each of them was given good news of Muhammad (ﷺ). God says describing the Messenger: ﴿Whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-A'raf 157], which is well known. Their disbelief is the same. For this reason it is not correct for us to say: ﴿You will surely find the most intense of the people in animosity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate others with God, and you will find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, "We are Christians"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 82]. This does not apply to our time, nor to times long before it, because God explained the reason: ﴿That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant (82). And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of what they have recognized of the truth. They say, "Our Lord, we have believed, so register us among the witnesses"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 82–83]. Now among them are righteous people and monks who are arrogant toward the truth, calling to misguidance, may God protect us. So this description cannot apply to them. Their enmity now toward the Muslims and toward those who believe, especially toward those who believe and not only the Muslims, is evident. They never forget the raids of the believers against them in their own homeland, and they never forget the Crusades, and they never forget the great conquest that took place in the lands of their people, for all the lands of Rome were taken, and all the Romans are Christians, taken at the hands of the Muslims.
God, exalted, says: (﴿﴿Indeed, in that﴾﴾), referring to what was mentioned of the story of Abraham and his people, ﴿is a sign, but most of them were not believers (103). And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 103–104]. This has been discussed before, but we must know that when God says about something that in it is a sign, we must not take it only at face value. Let us reflect on what these signs are.
His saying ﴿In that is a sign﴾: is the intended reference the whole story or each part of the story? The reference is undoubtedly to the whole, so there is a sign in each part of it, and in the combination of these parts together there is also a sign. So the sign is distributed over each part, and the sign is also the collection of all these things together.
The important thing is that when God says to you, ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign﴾, you must reflect, ponder and take lessons, so that this sign becomes manifest.
His saying ﴿but most of them were not believers﴾: it was mentioned before that the more likely reference of the pronoun in ﴿most of them﴾ is to those who were in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ).
His saying ﴿but most of them were not believers﴾: is this Hijazi or Tamimi usage?
* Student: This is Hijazi.
* Another student: This is Hijazi, but (...).
* The Shaykh: That is correct. For this reason some students mistakenly think that (mā) is the operative word, but the correct view is that what operates is (kāna, "was"), because if you make (mā) the operative word, you make (kāna) superfluous. The original principle is that there is no superfluity (...) it is a negation of existence: ﴿but most of them were not believers﴾, meaning most of them were not among us.
Then God, exalted, says: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 105]. The author intends to give an answer about the feminine form of the verb while the subject is masculine.
﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers.﴾ First, Noah (peace be upon him) is the first messenger God sent to the people of the earth. The first messenger sent to the people of the earth was Noah (peace be upon him). Adam was the first prophet to receive revelation, for he was undoubtedly a prophet, and Noah was the first messenger. Adam was a prophet out of necessity, because he had to worship God, and there is no worship of God except by what has been legislated, and no legislation except by revelation. But he was not sent as a messenger, because there was no need for that, since people were in agreement. When they differed, God sent the messengers: ﴿Mankind was one community, and God sent prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners﴾ [al-Baqarah 213]. In the recitation of Ibn 'Abbas it is: ﴿So they differed﴾, and this sentence is unnecessary, because it is understood from His saying: ﴿And He sent down with them the Book in truth to judge between the people concerning that over which they differed﴾ [al-Baqarah 213].
In any case, in the time of Adam there was no need for messengership, only prophethood. He worshipped God, and his children did as well. Indeed, his children followed him in that by mutual agreement. When the community grew and spread over the earth, they differed, and the need became pressing, indeed a necessity, for sending messengers. So God sent Noah, who was the first messenger God sent to the people of the earth, as His saying indicates: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾ [al-Nisa' 163]. As the authentic and explicit hadith of intercession says, they go to Noah and say to him, among the things they seek through him: "You are the first messenger God sent to the people of the earth" (agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4476) and Muslim (193/322), from the hadith of Anas). But if we say that he was the first messenger God sent to the people of the earth, do we say that he was sent to all mankind?
Then it is necessary to reconcile this with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I was sent to all mankind" (agreed upon; al-Bukhari (438) and Muslim (521), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah).
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: They say "the first messenger." Being first is only valid with exclusivity, is that not so?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: Because if someone else shared it with him, he would not be the first. He and another would both be the first.
A speaker might say: perhaps someone was sent in his time, sent during his lifetime but to a different place. We may also say that the word "first" is taken at face value, and that he was sent to people only because at that time people were one community, few in number and not yet widely spread over the earth. So these people were in the position of the people among the messengers who came after him.
By this approach we are spared another difficulty, which is that God drowned all the people of the earth in the time of Noah except those who believed with him. For it would be asked: how could they be drowned when no messenger had been sent to them? If Noah had not been a messenger to them, they would not all have been drowned.
It is permissible to say that perhaps those to whom he was sent in his time also denied their messengers. But the apparent meaning of the verses is that those who drowned were drowned because of Noah's supplication.
In any case, this is a problem that has been debated among scholars since ancient times. They answered that Noah (peace be upon him) had a message to all people at that time as an incidental matter, not as a primary aim. There is a difference between one who comes to different nations, where a messenger is sent to each nation and then it is said to all these nations: you must follow this messenger so that you become one community, and one who was sent only to his own people, one nation only. For his being sent to all of them is by coincidence and incidentally, not by intention. Through this the distinction between Muhammad (ﷺ) and Noah (peace be upon him) becomes clear, and we are spared the difficulty. We say: Noah was sent to his people, and there were no different nations that needed to unite under one messenger as was the case in the time of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). His being sent to all people at that time was not a matter of intention, but of coincidence and incidence, meaning that it happened that all people were confined to the people of Noah. Here, his message was not intended to encompass all nations, unlike the message of the Prophet (ﷺ), for his message was intended to be comprehensive, so that Jews, Christians, Magians and idolaters would all unite in one community. This is due to the difference between the two kinds of generality: intentional generality and incidental, coincidental generality.

This is Noah. Allah says: "The people of Noah denied the messengers." We know that they denied only one messenger, Noah, don't we? No one came before him, so how can we say they denied this one and that one? The author answers this by saying: (because their denial of him is their denial of the messengers as a whole) that is, the messengers, (since they all share in bringing tawhid (monotheism)). When all of them share in bringing the worship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and in standing firm in obedience to Him, they become one kind. Denying one member of that kind is denying all of them. They did not deny Noah because his name was Noah. They denied Noah because he came and said that he was from the Lord of the worlds. Based on this, if Hud came, would they deny him or not?

* Student: Yes, they would deny him.

* Shaykh: Yes, there is no difference. If Salih came, they would deny him. If Musa came, they would deny him. If Muhammad came, they would deny him. Why? Because they denied the kind, not the individual, since he brought what contradicts what they were upon. So they deny all the messengers.

So today we say to the Christians who claim to believe in 'Isa (peace be upon him): you disbelieve in him and deny him. Why? Because they denied Muhammad (ﷺ). Especially since their messenger, 'Isa (ﷺ), gave them the good news of him, as Allah says: ﴿And a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff 6]. Would he give them good news of someone who has no connection to them? He would not give them good news of someone who has no connection to them. Consider: if a child is born to so-and-so, would I come to you and say, "Rejoice at the birth of so-and-so's child," when there is no relationship between you and him? If a man arrived to distribute gifts to the family of so-and-so, would I give you good news of his arrival? Never. And if I had given you such news, it would be considered foolishness. So 'Isa gave them good news only because he was a messenger to them. For this reason he said: ﴿And a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾, meaning he specified him by name so that no doubt would remain afterward. But, and Allah forbid, they disbelieved in the Prophet (peace be upon him) and so became among the disbelievers in 'Isa son of Maryam.

As for the Jews, their disbelief in Muhammad (peace be upon him) is also disbelief in Musa and in the Torah, in which the Messenger of Allah was found written among them: ﴿They know him as they know their own sons﴾ [al-Baqarah 146], just as a person knows his son. They recognize Muhammad (ﷺ) by his description, but it is arrogance, and Allah forbid.

* Student: Is ﴿اسْمُهُ أَحْمَدُ﴾ a proper name or a description?

* Shaykh: Not a description; it is a proper name, because the Messenger called himself Ahmad in other hadiths. It is a proper name.

* Student: Shaykh, regarding Adam, we say he was a prophet but not a messenger, meaning that he was given revelation of the law and he worshipped by it?

* Shaykh: He worshipped by it, and no one disagreed about that.

* Student: Then how did his children receive it (...)?

* Shaykh: They saw him act and so they acted. It is the habit of people to imitate those older than themselves, and there were no obstacles or distinctions preventing them from imitating him.

* Student: Could there be verbal matters in it that need explanation?

* Shaykh: He could make them understand. He would make them understand from his deeds and his words. If they saw him speak and act, they would speak and act like him.

* Student: So he became a messenger?

* Shaykh: No. The one who is sent (mursal) is one who is conveyed and charged with a duty, but he was not charged with that. For this reason we say, for example: Did the jinn benefit from the message of Musa? The known position among the scholars is that it did not reach them, and that no one was sent to the jinn except Muhammad (ﷺ) (...). ﴿O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Musa, confirming what came before it﴾ [al-Ahqaf 30]. This shows that they were benefiting from the Book of Musa.

* Student: What is the evidence of the scholars that the earlier messengers (...), since Allah, glory be to Him, says: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat 56]?

* Shaykh: They say: a prophet is sent to his people, and his people are his tribe and those connected to them. The jinn are not of his kind, so they are not of his people.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Correct. This does not indicate that the message is general to the jinn, because the jinn are not human. But the fact that the Messenger (peace be upon him) met with them, made appointments with them, recited the Qur'an to them, and informed them of what it contains indicates that he was sent to them.

* Student: (...) meaning there is no negation in it (...) was sent (...).

* Shaykh: No. (...) he is sent to his people, and the jinn are not among them.

* Student: The jinn who live among people?

* Shaykh: No. I agree (...) from mankind and the jinn. Even if he said "from the jinn," there would be some reservation in the soul about it, because the jinn are not his people.

* Student: They only live among a people.

* Shaykh: Even if they live among them, if they live among a people they do not become part of them.

* Student: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat 56] (...) worship (...) by desire, except by a law.

* Shaykh: We still have the word "by a law" (bi-shar'). They worship Allah by a law (...). But are there messengers among them or not? This question is also a matter of dispute among the scholars. Some say there are messengers among them, based on His saying: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you﴾ [al-An'am 130]. ﴿Messengers from among you﴾. A messenger must be of the same kind as those to whom he is sent, based on His saying: ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [al-An'am 9]. And it is not possible for a human to be sent to the jinn.

Others say: His saying ﴿from among you﴾ refers to the addressees considered as a group. ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind﴾ addresses two groups, and the pronoun in ﴿from among you﴾ refers to one of the two.

This is like what they claimed, as in: ﴿He released the two seas, meeting side by side. Between them is a barrier they do not transgress. So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny? From them emerge pearls and coral﴾ [al-Rahman 19-22]. They claimed that pearls and coral come out only from the salt water, though the correct view is that they come out of both. In any case, referring a pronoun to one member of a group when the whole group is absent is linguistically permissible.

Some say that the messengers mentioned here are the warners (nudhur), and they were called messengers because of their resemblance to them. Without doubt, the warners come to the jinn just as they come to mankind.

* Student: Shaykh, (...) the preponderant view (...).

* Shaykh: The preponderant view is that there is no messenger among them, based on the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed﴾ [Yusuf 109], and the jinn are not called men.

* Student: It is established in a hadith that one of the two sons of Adam killed (...), and this indicates (...).

* Shaykh: Yes indeed. There is no doubt that transgression is unavoidable. This (...), but this does not necessarily mean that he is arrogant toward the worship of Allah (...) that he does not pray, does not fast, does not worship, just as (...) transgression is found in many worshippers.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No (...). But the prophets; because the prophet is other than the messenger. The prophet is one to whom revelation was sent.

* Student: (...) because revelation was not sent to (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿As We revealed to Noah﴾ [al-Nisa 163], meaning with him, because the revelation that is compared to the revelation of Muhammad (peace be upon him) is that which came to Noah and those after him. The revelation compared to Allah's revelation to His messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) is that which was given to Noah and those after him. Why? Because it is revelation joined with a human being.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: (...) it is fundamentally, the basis is (...).

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, but Adam (peace be upon him) is not like the revelation Allah sent to Muhammad (peace be upon him). It was a special revelation only, without a duty to convey it.

* Student: (...) informing that he would (...)?

* Shaykh: If he says that he was not negligent, that is the end of it. He said this arrogantly.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: If it becomes general, we say: No. Allah has given you good news, O Christians, through the tongue of your prophet 'Isa, of Muhammad.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: We say: If you do not believe anything except that he informed that a messenger would be sent, then this is from the misguidance of his people who misled him. Otherwise, there is no doubt; we have no doubt that 'Isa gave good news of Muhammad (peace be upon him), gave them the good news (...) the good tidings.

* Student: Ibn al-Qayyim (...).

* Shaykh: There is no doubt about it. Whoever denies any messenger is denying Allah, or describing Allah with what does not befit Him, because Allah supports the messenger with signs. If that is established, it would follow that Allah does not exist, or that He, Allah forbid, is treacherous, or something similar.

* * *

Allah the Exalted said, regarding the benefits mentioned earlier:

* First: the negation of intercession for those who deny the messengers, that they will not be interceded for. From where is this derived?

* Student: ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ [al-Shu'ara 100].

* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿So we have no intercessors.﴾

* Among its benefits also: the mutual cursing of these people toward one another.

* Student: ﴿By Allah, we were in clear error, when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds. And none misled us except the criminals﴾ [al-Shu'ara 97-99].

* Shaykh: This is a condemnation of them, in that they misled them, and in that they are criminals.

* And in it is evidence for the negation of likening Allah (to creation).

* Student: Their saying: ﴿when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds.﴾

* Shaykh: ﴿Indeed we were in clear error, when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara 97-98].

This likening (...) is it likening the Creator to the created, or the created to the Creator?

* Student: Likening the created to the Creator.

* Shaykh: The created to the Creator, yes.

* And it is derived from this hadith: the affirmation of intercession for the believers.

* Student: From His saying: ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ [al-Shu'ara 100]. They negated that they would have intercessors (...).

* Shaykh: Yes. It seems they saw that believers intercede for one another, so they said: "We have no intercessors, nor a close friend."

* And in it is evidence of the extreme regret that afflicts these people on that Day.

* Student: From His saying (...) if he returned to the world.

* Shaykh: If we returned to the world: ﴿So if only we had another chance, we would be among the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara 102]. Is this wish true, that if they returned they would be believers?

* Student: No.

* Shaykh: What is the evidence?

* Student: Because Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am 28].

* Shaykh: He said: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars.﴾

Now, who is Noah (peace be upon him)?

* Student: Is he the first of Allah's messengers?

* Shaykh: The first messenger Allah sent.

* Student: The first messenger Allah sent to the earth.

* Shaykh: What is the evidence?

* Student: The evidence is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾ [al-Nisa 163]. So His revealing to Noah (...).

* Shaykh: (...) what is the indication from the verse?

* Student: ﴿As We revealed to Noah﴾: just as revelation was sent to you and you are a messenger to these people, Noah was sent before him.

* Shaykh: It does not follow from his being before the Messenger (peace be upon him) that he is the first of the messengers.

* Student: ﴿As We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him.﴾

* Shaykh: ﴿And the prophets after him﴾, yes, this.

* Student: It indicates that he was before them.

* Shaykh: Also, in the "Hadith of Intercession": "You are the first messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth," which is explicit. How do we reconcile this with His saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara 105], even though he was the first of the messengers?

* Student: The message of the prophets is one. Those who denied Noah (peace be upon him) did not deny him as an individual, or because his name was Noah, but because what he brought was tawhid. So if every prophet had brought tawhid, they would have denied him too, and so they are deniers of the messengers. Or, because he remained among his people for nine hundred and fifty years, it is as if they were many messengers.

* Shaykh: Yes, good.

* And it is derived from this noble verse: that denying the truth from one person is denying it from all persons.

* Student: His saying: ﴿the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara 105].

* Shaykh: ﴿The messengers﴾, even though only one denied him. But in reality they denied the truth, whether it was brought by Noah or someone else, and for this reason they became deniers of all the messengers.

* And in it is evidence that Noah was sent to all people.

* Student: Because the people of Noah were the first of mankind.

* Shaykh: How?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: This is not sufficient.

* Student: Because of His saying: ﴿The people of Noah﴾ [al-Shu'ara 105], and He did not say: "their brother."

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: (...).

* Student: (...) "their brother."

* Shaykh: Many said "their brother," all (...) "their brother," except Shu'ayb.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: There is evidence that Noah was sent to all people.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: (...) what is the indication of this? I say it like this, so what is the indication?

* Student: His saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara 105]. They denied the messengers in general, so it indicates that they were a collective of the messengers (...).

* Shaykh: No.

Since we have said he is the first of the messengers, the first messenger and sent to his people, meaning there was no one else, if there had been another messenger he would share the priority.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: We established that Noah... the difficulty with Noah, we explained it as the messenger whom Allah sent first among the messengers.

* Student: Someone might say: Yes, ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara 105]: the people to whom he was sent alone, and there are peoples to whom he was not sent.

* Shaykh: That is not possible. This is why we said yesterday: it is possible that Allah sent other messengers after Noah's time to other peoples, so he would not be sent to all people. But in any case, since he was the first to be sent to these people, there would be no messenger other than him.

We have said that this does not contradict the generality of the message of the Messenger (peace be upon him), because at that time there were none except his people: ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾ [al-Saffat 77]. This was not intentional; it happened by coincidence.

The meaning of "happened by coincidence" is that when Allah sent him, there was no one on earth except his people. As for the Messenger (peace be upon him), the peoples are many: the Children of Israel, the Arabs, and other nations, and yet he was sent to all of them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verses 100–105 (part 1 of 2):

(﴿So we have no intercessors﴾) as the believers have among the angels, the prophets and the believers. ﴿So we have no intercessors.﴾ Is the word (mā) interrogative or negative?
* Student: Negative.
* The Shaykh: Negative. The evidence is the emphatic (min) in ﴿no intercessors﴾. Its original form is "so we have intercessors," but (min) was brought in for emphasis.
The intercessor (shafi') is the one who mediates on behalf of another to bring about a benefit or to repel a harm. An example is the intercession of the Prophet (ﷺ) for the people of the Gathering that judgment be passed among them, which is intercession to repel harm and hardship. Another is his intercession for the people of Paradise that they enter Paradise, which is intercession to bring benefits.
So intercession (shafa'a) is mediation on behalf of another to bring a benefit or repel a harm. If you wish, you may say: by repelling harm or bringing good.
Why do they have no intercessors? Because of what condition for intercession?
* Student: Among the conditions of intercession (...).
* The Shaykh: And what else?
* Student: And that the one for whom intercession is made be a believer.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence?
* Student: The evidence is ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya' 28].
* The Shaykh: Yes. Those people are not approved by God, so they say: ﴿we have no intercessors﴾. That means: we have no one at all who intercedes, neither from the prophets nor from anyone else, because among the conditions of intercession is that God, blessed and exalted, be pleased with the one for whom intercession is made and with the intercessor. Is He pleased with the intercessor?
* Student: It follows a fortiori.
* The Shaykh: A fortiori, yes. If God's approval of the one for whom intercession is made is required, then His approval of the intercessor is required all the more.
As for permission, it is also a condition. Even when God is pleased with both this one and that one, permission is still necessary. God, blessed and exalted, does not permit intercession except for the one He is pleased with. So both conditions are required. One should not say, for example, that if He approves a person He must permit him. He may permit or He may not. But we know that He does not permit except for those whom He approves, and these people are not approved by God.
﴿So we have no intercessors (100). Nor a close friend.﴾ ﴿Nor a close friend﴾ is coordinated with ﴿intercessors﴾ according to the wording. If it were coordinated according to the grammatical position, it would be (nor a close friend, with a nominative ending), because ﴿intercessors﴾ is in the position of a subject.
﴿A close friend﴾: the friend (ṣadīq) is the one whose affection is sincere toward you. That is, a companion whose love is true is called a friend. He is more specific than a companion (ṣāḥib), so every friend is a companion, but not every companion is a friend.
As for the (ḥamīm), he is the close relative, or one who exaggerates in friendship to the point that he is tender toward you, and then the close relative is tender toward you. The author says: (that is, he is concerned with our affair), because a close and intimate friend, tender and compassionate, or a relative, is concerned with the affair of his companion as he is concerned with his friend's.
Now, is this description (ḥamīm) a descriptive qualifier (ṣifa kāshifa) or a restrictive qualifier (ṣifa muqayyada)? It is descriptive if we say: there is no friend who is not ḥamīm, so it is a descriptive qualifier. If we say: a person may be a friend without being ḥamīm, then the qualifier is restrictive, on condition that we take ḥamīm here to mean "relative," because a person may be a friend without being a relative. If we take ḥamīm to mean the tender one who is like a relative because of his affection and compassion, then it is descriptive. But if we say (ḥamīm) means "relative," it becomes restrictive, because not every friend is a relative.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. How? If we say (nor a close friend ḥamīm), these become two qualities: friendship and kinship, correct? So the quality of kinship does not carry the meaning of the quality of friendship. A person can be a friend without being a relative, and there is no obstacle.
* Student: On the Day of Resurrection.
* The Shaykh: (...) On the Day of Resurrection, but kinship will not benefit him, nor friendship.
﴿Nor a close friend. So if only we had a return (a return to the world)﴾, ﴿then we would be among the believers﴾. (If only) expresses a wish. That is, we do not have a return, meaning a return to the world. ﴿Then we would be﴾: the (fa) indicates causation. (We would be) is in the subjunctive after an implied (an) that follows the causative (fa), because the wish came first. For this reason he says: (lau here expresses a wish, and (nakūna, "we would be") is its answer).
﴿If only that we had a return﴾ means: would that we had a return, ﴿then we would be among the believers﴾. They did not say (layta, "would that") because the situation is one of humility and submission. (Lau) in expressing a wish is softer than (layta), because (layta) is explicit in making a request, while (lau) contains some gentleness and indirectness. This is like when you say to a person who wished to visit you: "If only you would visit me." This (lau) is clearly for expressing a wish, but it is a gentle, indirect and courteous wish, and the situation here calls for it, because they are in a state of humiliation, may God protect us, and submission. So they did not say, "Would that we could return," but they said: ﴿If only that we had a return, then we would be among the believers﴾. However, in Surah al-An'am they say: ﴿Would that we could be returned, and not deny the signs of our Lord, and be among the believers﴾ [al-An'am 27].
It is said that the way to reconcile these is that they sometimes say this and sometimes say that. But which came first, (layta) or (lau)? Apparently (layta) came first. That is, it seems they begin with a resolute wish, and then, if it is not granted, they return to submission and gentle expression.
If they were returned, would they go back? God, mighty and majestic, says in Surah al-An'am: ﴿But there has appeared to them what they had been concealing before. And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars﴾ [al-An'am 28]. This is the true report. That is, their statement that if we return we will be among the believers is a false statement. The true report is ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden. And indeed they are liars﴾ in their claim: ﴿we would be returned and would not deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be among the believers﴾.
* Student: In the same context (...). Is the act of God ﴿If they were returned, they would return﴾?
* The Shaykh: No. Apparently it is the act of God, perhaps (...). At that hour they say it truthfully, but God informed us that if they were returned they would return to disbelief.
﴿If only that we had a return, then we would be among the believers﴾: that is, among those who affirm the truth (...) who are committed to action, because faith alone does not benefit if it does not entail action, so it is not true faith. For this reason we say: the disbelievers who (...) are believers. ﴿They denied them, though their souls were convinced of them﴾ [al-Naml 14]. But because they do not submit, they did not benefit from their faith. Is Iblis a believer or not?
* Students: A believer.
* The Shaykh: In the sense of affirming the truth, he is a believer. But he was arrogant, so his faith did not benefit him. I recall that when the first man went up into space from Russia and observed the universe, he declared that this universe has a Manager. Then his companions came...
No, he becomes more severe than others when the matter becomes clear to him. Now it is clear to him (...).
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) even (...) from him.
* Student: If we say, for example, that faith is speech, action and belief, then on this basis we exclude everyone who, for example, said it with his tongue or believed it in his heart, like Iblis and Pharaoh.
* The Shaykh: If he does not submit, yes. If he does not submit, then he is not a believer, that is known.
For this reason we have said: faith is affirmation that entails acceptance and submission: acceptance of the report and submission to the command (...). This is faith. As for a person who merely says, "I believe in God, and I acknowledge that God exists and that He has messengers," but does not act, this faith does not benefit him.
* Student: Essentially, it does not take place in the self.
* The Shaykh: It is faith, because the faith that benefits is what you mentioned. As for faith, it applies to mere affirmation. (...) this one believes in something but is a disbeliever in other things. Legally valid faith is what benefits. We say: this one is not a believer, meaning not a believer in the legal sense. But linguistically he is a believer.
* Student: Honorable Shaykh, everyone who is arrogant is worse.
* The Shaykh: (...) because the one to whom the truth becomes clear and who is arrogant toward it, his disbelief is disbelief of obstinacy. And the one who does not know the truth and is now acting in the manner of the people of disbelief, his disbelief is disbelief of denial.
Now, the Christians in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ), that is, before his mission, are considered astray. After he was sent and the truth became clear to them, they become those who have incurred anger, since there is no difference between them and the Jews. Each of them was given good news of Muhammad (ﷺ). God says describing the Messenger: ﴿Whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-A'raf 157], which is well known. Their disbelief is the same. For this reason it is not correct for us to say: ﴿You will surely find the most intense of the people in animosity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate others with God, and you will find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, "We are Christians"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 82]. This does not apply to our time, nor to times long before it, because God explained the reason: ﴿That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant (82). And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of what they have recognized of the truth. They say, "Our Lord, we have believed, so register us among the witnesses"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 82–83]. Now among them are righteous people and monks who are arrogant toward the truth, calling to misguidance, may God protect us. So this description cannot apply to them. Their enmity now toward the Muslims and toward those who believe, especially toward those who believe and not only the Muslims, is evident. They never forget the raids of the believers against them in their own homeland, and they never forget the Crusades, and they never forget the great conquest that took place in the lands of their people, for all the lands of Rome were taken, and all the Romans are Christians, taken at the hands of the Muslims.
God, exalted, says: (﴿﴿Indeed, in that﴾﴾), referring to what was mentioned of the story of Abraham and his people, ﴿is a sign, but most of them were not believers (103). And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 103–104]. This has been discussed before, but we must know that when God says about something that in it is a sign, we must not take it only at face value. Let us reflect on what these signs are.
His saying ﴿In that is a sign﴾: is the intended reference the whole story or each part of the story? The reference is undoubtedly to the whole, so there is a sign in each part of it, and in the combination of these parts together there is also a sign. So the sign is distributed over each part, and the sign is also the collection of all these things together.
The important thing is that when God says to you, ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign﴾, you must reflect, ponder and take lessons, so that this sign becomes manifest.
His saying ﴿but most of them were not believers﴾: it was mentioned before that the more likely reference of the pronoun in ﴿most of them﴾ is to those who were in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ).
His saying ﴿but most of them were not believers﴾: is this Hijazi or Tamimi usage?
* Student: This is Hijazi.
* Another student: This is Hijazi, but (...).
* The Shaykh: That is correct. For this reason some students mistakenly think that (mā) is the operative word, but the correct view is that what operates is (kāna, "was"), because if you make (mā) the operative word, you make (kāna) superfluous. The original principle is that there is no superfluity (...) it is a negation of existence: ﴿but most of them were not believers﴾, meaning most of them were not among us.
Then God, exalted, says: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 105]. The author intends to give an answer about the feminine form of the verb while the subject is masculine.
﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers.﴾ First, Noah (peace be upon him) is the first messenger God sent to the people of the earth. The first messenger sent to the people of the earth was Noah (peace be upon him). Adam was the first prophet to receive revelation, for he was undoubtedly a prophet, and Noah was the first messenger. Adam was a prophet out of necessity, because he had to worship God, and there is no worship of God except by what has been legislated, and no legislation except by revelation. But he was not sent as a messenger, because there was no need for that, since people were in agreement. When they differed, God sent the messengers: ﴿Mankind was one community, and God sent prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners﴾ [al-Baqarah 213]. In the recitation of Ibn 'Abbas it is: ﴿So they differed﴾, and this sentence is unnecessary, because it is understood from His saying: ﴿And He sent down with them the Book in truth to judge between the people concerning that over which they differed﴾ [al-Baqarah 213].
In any case, in the time of Adam there was no need for messengership, only prophethood. He worshipped God, and his children did as well. Indeed, his children followed him in that by mutual agreement. When the community grew and spread over the earth, they differed, and the need became pressing, indeed a necessity, for sending messengers. So God sent Noah, who was the first messenger God sent to the people of the earth, as His saying indicates: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾ [al-Nisa' 163]. As the authentic and explicit hadith of intercession says, they go to Noah and say to him, among the things they seek through him: "You are the first messenger God sent to the people of the earth" (agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4476) and Muslim (193/322), from the hadith of Anas). But if we say that he was the first messenger God sent to the people of the earth, do we say that he was sent to all mankind?
Then it is necessary to reconcile this with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I was sent to all mankind" (agreed upon; al-Bukhari (438) and Muslim (521), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah).
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: They say "the first messenger." Being first is only valid with exclusivity, is that not so?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: Because if someone else shared it with him, he would not be the first. He and another would both be the first.
A speaker might say: perhaps someone was sent in his time, sent during his lifetime but to a different place. We may also say that the word "first" is taken at face value, and that he was sent to people only because at that time people were one community, few in number and not yet widely spread over the earth. So these people were in the position of the people among the messengers who came after him.
By this approach we are spared another difficulty, which is that God drowned all the people of the earth in the time of Noah except those who believed with him. For it would be asked: how could they be drowned when no messenger had been sent to them? If Noah had not been a messenger to them, they would not all have been drowned.
It is permissible to say that perhaps those to whom he was sent in his time also denied their messengers. But the apparent meaning of the verses is that those who drowned were drowned because of Noah's supplication.
In any case, this is a problem that has been debated among scholars since ancient times. They answered that Noah (peace be upon him) had a message to all people at that time as an incidental matter, not as a primary aim. There is a difference between one who comes to different nations, where a messenger is sent to each nation and then it is said to all these nations: you must follow this messenger so that you become one community, and one who was sent only to his own people, one nation only. For his being sent to all of them is by coincidence and incidentally, not by intention. Through this the distinction between Muhammad (ﷺ) and Noah (peace be upon him) becomes clear, and we are spared the difficulty. We say: Noah was sent to his people, and there were no different nations that needed to unite under one messenger as was the case in the time of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). His being sent to all people at that time was not a matter of intention, but of coincidence and incidence, meaning that it happened that all people were confined to the people of Noah. Here, his message was not intended to encompass all nations, unlike the message of the Prophet (ﷺ), for his message was intended to be comprehensive, so that Jews, Christians, Magians and idolaters would all unite in one community. This is due to the difference between the two kinds of generality: intentional generality and incidental, coincidental generality.

This is Noah. Allah says: "The people of Noah denied the messengers." We know that they denied only one messenger, Noah, don't we? No one came before him, so how can we say they denied this one and that one? The author answers this by saying: (because their denial of him is their denial of the messengers as a whole) that is, the messengers, (since they all share in bringing tawhid (monotheism)). When all of them share in bringing the worship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and in standing firm in obedience to Him, they become one kind. Denying one member of that kind is denying all of them. They did not deny Noah because his name was Noah. They denied Noah because he came and said that he was from the Lord of the worlds. Based on this, if Hud came, would they deny him or not?

* Student: Yes, they would deny him.

* Shaykh: Yes, there is no difference. If Salih came, they would deny him. If Musa came, they would deny him. If Muhammad came, they would deny him. Why? Because they denied the kind, not the individual, since he brought what contradicts what they were upon. So they deny all the messengers.

So today we say to the Christians who claim to believe in 'Isa (peace be upon him): you disbelieve in him and deny him. Why? Because they denied Muhammad (ﷺ). Especially since their messenger, 'Isa (ﷺ), gave them the good news of him, as Allah says: ﴿And a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff 6]. Would he give them good news of someone who has no connection to them? He would not give them good news of someone who has no connection to them. Consider: if a child is born to so-and-so, would I come to you and say, "Rejoice at the birth of so-and-so's child," when there is no relationship between you and him? If a man arrived to distribute gifts to the family of so-and-so, would I give you good news of his arrival? Never. And if I had given you such news, it would be considered foolishness. So 'Isa gave them good news only because he was a messenger to them. For this reason he said: ﴿And a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾, meaning he specified him by name so that no doubt would remain afterward. But, and Allah forbid, they disbelieved in the Prophet (peace be upon him) and so became among the disbelievers in 'Isa son of Maryam.

As for the Jews, their disbelief in Muhammad (peace be upon him) is also disbelief in Musa and in the Torah, in which the Messenger of Allah was found written among them: ﴿They know him as they know their own sons﴾ [al-Baqarah 146], just as a person knows his son. They recognize Muhammad (ﷺ) by his description, but it is arrogance, and Allah forbid.

* Student: Is ﴿اسْمُهُ أَحْمَدُ﴾ a proper name or a description?

* Shaykh: Not a description; it is a proper name, because the Messenger called himself Ahmad in other hadiths. It is a proper name.

* Student: Shaykh, regarding Adam, we say he was a prophet but not a messenger, meaning that he was given revelation of the law and he worshipped by it?

* Shaykh: He worshipped by it, and no one disagreed about that.

* Student: Could there be verbal matters in it that need explanation?

* Shaykh: He could make them understand. He would make them understand from his deeds and his words. If they saw him speak and act, they would speak and act like him.

In any case, referring a pronoun to one member of a group when the whole group is absent is linguistically permissible.

Since we have said he is the first of the messengers, the first messenger and sent to his people, meaning there was no one else, if there had been another messenger he would share the priority.

* Shaykh: We established that Noah... the difficulty with Noah, we explained it as the messenger whom Allah sent first among the messengers.

* Student: Someone might say: Yes, ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara 105]: the people to whom he was sent alone, and there are peoples to whom he was not sent.

* Shaykh: That is not possible. This is why we said yesterday: it is possible that Allah sent other messengers after Noah's time to other peoples, so he would not be sent to all people. But in any case, since he was the first to be sent to these people, there would be no messenger other than him.

We have said that this does not contradict the generality of the message of the Messenger (peace be upon him), because at that time there were none except his people: ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾ [al-Saffat 77]. This was not intentional; it happened by coincidence.

The meaning of "happened by coincidence" is that when Allah sent him, there was no one on earth except his people. As for the Messenger (peace be upon him), the peoples are many: the Children of Israel, the Arabs, and other nations, and yet he was sent to all of them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verses 100–105 (part 1 of 2):

(﴿So we have no intercessors﴾) as the believers have among the angels, the prophets and the believers. ﴿So we have no intercessors.﴾ Is the word (mā) interrogative or negative?
* Student: Negative.
* The Shaykh: Negative. The evidence is the emphatic (min) in ﴿no intercessors﴾. Its original form is "so we have intercessors," but (min) was brought in for emphasis.
The intercessor (shafi') is the one who mediates on behalf of another to bring about a benefit or to repel a harm. An example is the intercession of the Prophet (ﷺ) for the people of the Gathering that judgment be passed among them, which is intercession to repel harm and hardship. Another is his intercession for the people of Paradise that they enter Paradise, which is intercession to bring benefits.
So intercession (shafa'a) is mediation on behalf of another to bring a benefit or repel a harm. If you wish, you may say: by repelling harm or bringing good.
Why do they have no intercessors? Because of what condition for intercession?
* Student: Among the conditions of intercession (...).
* The Shaykh: And what else?
* Student: And that the one for whom intercession is made be a believer.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence?
* Student: The evidence is ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya' 28].
* The Shaykh: Yes. Those people are not approved by God, so they say: ﴿we have no intercessors﴾. That means: we have no one at all who intercedes, neither from the prophets nor from anyone else, because among the conditions of intercession is that God, blessed and exalted, be pleased with the one for whom intercession is made and with the intercessor. Is He pleased with the intercessor?
* Student: It follows a fortiori.
* The Shaykh: A fortiori, yes. If God's approval of the one for whom intercession is made is required, then His approval of the intercessor is required all the more.
As for permission, it is also a condition. Even when God is pleased with both this one and that one, permission is still necessary. God, blessed and exalted, does not permit intercession except for the one He is pleased with. So both conditions are required. One should not say, for example, that if He approves a person He must permit him. He may permit or He may not. But we know that He does not permit except for those whom He approves, and these people are not approved by God.
﴿So we have no intercessors (100). Nor a close friend.﴾ ﴿Nor a close friend﴾ is coordinated with ﴿intercessors﴾ according to the wording. If it were coordinated according to the grammatical position, it would be (nor a close friend, with a nominative ending), because ﴿intercessors﴾ is in the position of a subject.
﴿A close friend﴾: the friend (ṣadīq) is the one whose affection is sincere toward you. That is, a companion whose love is true is called a friend. He is more specific than a companion (ṣāḥib), so every friend is a companion, but not every companion is a friend.
