Was their due right from me to be driven away or to be honoured? To be honoured.

What the people of Noah said, and he was the first of the messengers, was also said by the people of Muhammad (ﷺ), who is the last of the messengers. So God Most High said to him: ﴿And restrain yourself to remain with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance, and let not your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾ [al-Kahf 28]. And God Most High said: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance﴾ [al-An'am 52].

This is the practice of those who deny the messengers. They have nothing to rely on except deception, misleading, and embellished speech that deceives none but the blind.

Regarding ﴿And I am not one to drive away the believers﴾:

* In this there is evidence that a person should draw close to every believer, and choose for himself the best companions, as the Sunnah (the prophetic tradition) enjoins by encouraging the choice of a righteous companion [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2101) and Muslim (2628/146), from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of the righteous companion and the bad companion is like the bearer of musk and the blacksmith's bellows..."]].

* Also in it is evidence that one should show loyalty to the believers and draw near to them, and that this is the practice of the prophets.

* Also in it is patience with what one encounters from believers in the way of harshness and lowliness of occupation and other things.

* Also in it is humility toward the believers and not troubling them, even if they are of low standing among people. The Messenger (ﷺ), the most honoured of creation in rank with God and the most exalted in status, was rebuked by God Most High concerning a blind man: ﴿He frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him. And what would make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself, or be reminded, and the reminder would benefit him﴾ [Abasa 1–4].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 115:

﴿إِنْ أَنَا﴾ (﴿﴿إِنْ﴾ ﴾ ما ﴿﴿إِلَّا نَذِيرٌ مُبِينٌ﴾ ﴾) [الشعراء: ١١٥] 

Ibn 'Uthaymin's comment on the words "نَذِيرٌ": The meaning of nadhir (warner) has already been explained: it is one who informs of what is feared, that is, notification combined with warning. This is inidhar (warning).

As for his words "مُبِينٌ" (clear/manifest): the author (al-Mu'allif) took it as coming from (abana), used intransitively rather than transitively, although it may also be from (abana) used transitively, in which case it means "one who makes clear" (muzhir), meaning: I make clear what I have brought, so I am a warner who makes things clear to the people.

"They said" — meaning: when they saw his firm resolve, peace be upon him, and that he would not drive away the believers at their demand, and that these lowly people were not accountable for anything of their reckoning, since their reckoning rests with Allah alone, and they are believers, they resorted to force and said: ("If you do not desist, O Nuh, you will surely be among the stoned.") [ash-Shu'ara: 116] — that is, from what you say to us, "and you will surely be among those stoned," with stones or with abuse.

"If you do not desist" — there is a difficulty here from the standpoint of grammar (i'rab), because it contains both an oath (qasam) and a conditional (shart), and both require an answer (jawab). So where is the answer to the conditional, and where is the answer to the oath?

* A student: When an oath and a conditional are combined, the answer belongs to the one that comes later, and the answer of the later one dispenses with the answer of the earlier one.

* Another student: We say: "la-takunanna" (surely you will be) is the answer to the conditional; as for the answer to the oath, the one swearing sometimes dispenses with it.

* The Shaykh: No, this is an error. Ibn Malik says:

"When a conditional and an oath come together, omit the answer of whichever comes later; it is then what is required to be omitted."

Also, "la-takunanna" cannot be the answer to a conditional, because the lam cannot be attached to the answer of a conditional; it is attached only to the answer of an oath.

In any case, the rule among the grammarians is that when a conditional and an oath come together, the answer that is omitted is the answer of the one that comes later. So if you say: "In kunta—wallahi—darabtuka" (If you were—by Allah—I struck you), you do not say "la-adribannaka," because the conditional comes first. But if you say: "Wallahi in kunta darabtuka" (By Allah, if you struck me), that is not correct; you say "la-adribannaka."

"If you do not desist, O Nuh, you will surely be among the stoned" — they, may Allah protect us, emphasized what they intended for his stoning with three emphatics: the oath, the lam, and the nun of emphasis. Then they went to extremes in threat and intimidation when they said "among the stoned," and did not say "we will stone you," as if they were saying: those who came before you were stoned, so we will stone you along with them.

As for his saying "with stones or with speech," which is closer? Stones are closer, because stoning with speech is rarely used. Moreover, threatening with it from people who regard themselves as speaking from a position of strength is not fitting to the situation. So the correct reading is: "you will surely be among the stoned," meaning with stones. And Allah knows best.

* * *

(...) peace be upon him, and that Allah informed that his people denied the messengers. The author mentioned two possibilities: either because they denied monotheism, and this tawhid is the category of all that the messengers were sent with, so denying one member of the category is denying the whole category, and this is the more correct view; or because his stay among them was long, so it was as if they had denied many messengers. It has also been mentioned in the story that, out of their arrogance, they said: ﴿"Shall we believe you, when the lowest have followed you?"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 111], meaning: we do not believe you, because those who followed you are the lowest according to our view, as they said in Surat Hud: ﴿"We see none following you except those who are our lowest, in immature judgment"﴾ [Hud: 27].

Also in it is that he said to them: ﴿"And I have no knowledge of what they used to do"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 112], meaning: what knowledge do I have of their deeds that they perform? I have only the outward appearance of their affair, and their inner state is up to Allah. The outward appearance of their affair is that they are good and righteous, and they are not "the lowest" as these people claim. But after this they threatened him, may Allah protect us, with stoning, as a threat and a display of strength, in their saying: ﴿"you will surely be among the stoned"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 116]. This is more emphatic than their saying "we will stone you," because it contains intimidation, since he is not the first to be stoned; rather, others were stoned before him.

Then he turned to Allah, glorified and exalted, and ﴿"said: My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. So decide between me and them with a decision"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 117–118]. This supplication combines the three causes of answer: calling upon Allah by the name of Lordship, ﴿"My Lord"﴾; mentioning the state that calls for and warrants the supplication, ﴿"indeed my people have denied me"﴾; and the request, ﴿"So decide between me and them with a decision, and save me and those with me of the believers"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 118].

First: his saying ﴿"My Lord, indeed my people"﴾. Lordship, as we have passed over, is divided into two kinds: general and specific. This is of the specific kind, indeed one of the most particular forms of lordship, since it is Allah's lordship over His messengers.

Also in it is his saying ﴿"indeed my people have denied me"﴾, a display of his own weakness, meaning: he is the weaker party. Since he said "indeed my people," it was fitting that they should have confirmed him, because they are his people; but, may Allah protect us, they became deniers of him. So his condition calls for greater compassion, since his own people are the ones who denied him. Furthermore, it calls for their being punished more severely, since they are his people; it was incumbent upon them to believe him and to protect him from harm, so how could they be the ones who harm him!

This is like Allah's saying: ﴿"By the star when it sets. Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred"﴾ [an-Najm: 1–2]. He did not say "the prophet" or "the messenger," but said "your companion," meaning the one you know, and whose sound judgment and trustworthiness you know. How then do you deny what he has brought you of the ascension!

He said: ﴿"indeed my people have denied me"﴾, meaning they attributed lying to me, and they said: he denied him (kadhdhaba) and he lied to him (kadhaba). The difference between them:

* A student: "Kadhaba-hu" means he informed him of something contrary to reality, and "kadhdhaba-hu" means he did not believe what he brought.

* The Shaykh: He attributed lying to him. Good. And "kadhaba-hu" means he told him a lie.

﴿"My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. So decide between me and them"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 117–118]. The "fa" is for causation. "Decide between me" is outwardly an imperative, but when addressed to Allah it is called a supplication, since a command is issued only by one who stands above the one commanded, and the seeker is not above what he seeks; moreover, Allah, Majestic and Exalted, is above all things.

(﴿"So decide between me and them with a decision"﴾: i.e., judge.) The judgment is called a "fath" (opening) because the matter is opened and made clear by it, and one party is separated from the other. This decision consists in saving him and those with him of the believers and destroying them. His salvation and that of the believers with him is stated explicitly; as for their destruction, there is no salvation except from ruin. This is the decision that Nuh requested: that Allah destroy his people and save him and those with him of the believers. Allah said of him in Surat Nuh: ﴿"My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant. Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will not beget except a wicked, ungrateful one"﴾ [Nuh: 26–27].

As for this verse, ﴿"indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants"﴾: someone may say: does Nuh inform Allah of reality? Is Allah not knowing of it?

The answer: Yes, He knows it, but his intention, peace be upon him, was to state what moved him to this supplication: that by his belief he thinks or holds that if He leaves them, they will beget only a wicked, ungrateful one. Otherwise Allah is Knowing of them. So this is like an excuse for that general request: ﴿"My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant."﴾

Then he said: ﴿"and save me and those with me of the believers"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 118]. This "with me" is not companionship in the sense of mixing, as is well known; rather, it is companionship of sharing in deed and belief. The believers (...) the believers were sharing with him in belief and action. This shows that the "with" (ma'iyyah) is not as those who distort [the attributes] understood the "with" of Allah, glorified and exalted, as implying sharing in place or mixing; this is not so.

His saying ﴿"and those with me of the believers"﴾ is to clarify the ambiguity of "those with me"; since "man" is a relative pronoun, and a relative pronoun requires clarification, and its clarification is either from its relative clause or from something else.

"They said" — meaning: when they saw his firm resolve, peace be upon him, and that he would not drive away the believers at their demand, and that these lowly people were not accountable for anything of their reckoning, since their reckoning rests with Allah alone, and they are believers, they resorted to force and said: ("If you do not desist, O Nuh, you will surely be among the stoned.") [ash-Shu'ara: 116] — that is, from what you say to us, "and you will surely be among those stoned," with stones or with abuse.

Then he turned to Allah, glorified and exalted, and ﴿"said: My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. So decide between me and them with a decision"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 117–118]. This supplication combines the three causes of answer: calling upon Allah by the name of Lordship, ﴿"My Lord"﴾; mentioning the state that calls for and warrants the supplication, ﴿"indeed my people have denied me"﴾; and the request, ﴿"So decide between me and them with a decision, and save me and those with me of the believers"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 118].

First: his saying ﴿"My Lord, indeed my people"﴾. Lordship, as we have passed over, is divided into two kinds: general and specific. This is of the specific kind, indeed one of the most particular forms of lordship, since it is Allah's lordship over His messengers.

Also in it is his saying ﴿"indeed my people have denied me"﴾, a display of his own weakness, meaning: he is the weaker party. Since he said "indeed my people," it was fitting that they should have confirmed him, because they are his people; but, may Allah protect us, they became deniers of him. So his condition calls for greater compassion, since his own people are the ones who denied him. Furthermore, it calls for their being punished more severely, since they are his people; it was incumbent upon them to believe him and to protect him from harm, so how could they be the ones who harm him!

This is like Allah's saying: ﴿"By the star when it sets. Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred"﴾ [an-Najm: 1–2]. He did not say "the prophet" or "the messenger," but said "your companion," meaning the one you know, and whose sound judgment and trustworthiness you know. How then do you deny what he has brought you of the ascension!

He said: ﴿"indeed my people have denied me"﴾, meaning they attributed lying to me, and they said: he denied him (kadhdhaba) and he lied to him (kadhaba). The difference between them:

* A student: "Kadhaba-hu" means he informed him of something contrary to reality, and "kadhdhaba-hu" means he did not believe what he brought.

* The Shaykh: He attributed lying to him. Good. And "kadhaba-hu" means he told him a lie.

﴿"My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. So decide between me and them"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 117–118]. The "fa" is for causation. "Decide between me" is outwardly an imperative, but when addressed to Allah it is called a supplication, since a command is issued only by one who stands above the one commanded, and the seeker is not above what he seeks; moreover, Allah, Majestic and Exalted, is above all things.

(﴿"So decide between me and them with a decision"﴾: i.e., judge.) The judgment is called a "fath" (opening) because the matter is opened and made clear by it, and one party is separated from the other. This decision consists in saving him and those with him of the believers and destroying them. His salvation and that of the believers with him is stated explicitly; as for their destruction, there is no salvation except from ruin. This is the decision that Nuh requested: that Allah destroy his people and save him and those with him of the believers. Allah said of him in Surat Nuh: ﴿"My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant. Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will not beget except a wicked, ungrateful one"﴾ [Nuh: 26–27].

As for this verse, ﴿"indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants"﴾: someone may say: does Nuh inform Allah of reality? Is Allah not knowing of it?

The answer: Yes, He knows it, but his intention, peace be upon him, was to state what moved him to this supplication: that by his belief he thinks or holds that if He leaves them, they will beget only a wicked, ungrateful one. Otherwise Allah is Knowing of them. So this is like an excuse for that general request: ﴿"My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant."﴾

Then he said: ﴿"and save me and those with me of the believers"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 118]. This "with me" is not companionship in the sense of mixing, as is well known; rather, it is companionship of sharing in deed and belief. The believers (...) the believers were sharing with him in belief and action. This shows that the "with" (ma'iyyah) is not as those who distort [the attributes] understood the "with" of Allah, glorified and exalted, as implying sharing in place or mixing; this is not so.

His saying ﴿"and those with me of the believers"﴾ is to clarify the ambiguity of "those with me"; since "man" is a relative pronoun, and a relative pronoun requires clarification, and its clarification is either from its relative clause or from something else.

"They said" — meaning: when they saw his firm resolve, peace be upon him, and that he would not drive away the believers at their demand, and that these lowly people were not accountable for anything of their reckoning, since their reckoning rests with Allah alone, and they are believers, they resorted to force and said: ("If you do not desist, O Nuh, you will surely be among the stoned.") [ash-Shu'ara: 116] — that is, from what you say to us, "and you will surely be among those stoned," with stones or with abuse.

"If you do not desist" — there is a difficulty here from the standpoint of grammar (i'rab), because it contains both an oath (qasam) and a conditional (shart), and both require an answer (jawab). So where is the answer to the conditional, and where is the answer to the oath?

* A student: When an oath and a conditional are combined, the answer belongs to the one that comes later, and the answer of the later one dispenses with the answer of the earlier one.

* Another student: We say: "la-takunanna" (surely you will be) is the answer to the conditional; as for the answer to the oath, the one swearing sometimes dispenses with it.

* The Shaykh: No, this is an error. Ibn Malik says:

"When a conditional and an oath come together, omit the answer of whichever comes later; it is then what is required to be omitted."

Also, "la-takunanna" cannot be the answer to a conditional, because the lam cannot be attached to the answer of a conditional; it is attached only to the answer of an oath.

In any case, the rule among the grammarians is that when a conditional and an oath come together, the answer that is omitted is the answer of the one that comes later. So if you say: "In kunta—wallahi—darabtuka" (If you were—by Allah—I struck you), you do not say "la-adribannaka," because the conditional comes first. But if you say: "Wallahi in kunta darabtuka" (By Allah, if you struck me), that is not correct; you say "la-adribannaka."

"If you do not desist, O Nuh, you will surely be among the stoned" — they, may Allah protect us, emphasized what they intended for his stoning with three emphatics: the oath, the lam, and the nun of emphasis. Then they went to extremes in threat and intimidation when they said "among the stoned," and did not say "we will stone you," as if they were saying: those who came before you were stoned, so we will stone you along with them.

As for his saying "with stones or with speech," which is closer? Stones are closer, because stoning with speech is rarely used. Moreover, threatening with it from people who regard themselves as speaking from a position of strength is not fitting to the situation. So the correct reading is: "you will surely be among the stoned," meaning with stones. And Allah knows best.

* * *

(...) peace be upon him, and that Allah informed that his people denied the messengers. The author mentioned two possibilities: either because they denied monotheism, and this tawhid is the category of all that the messengers were sent with, so denying one member of the category is denying the whole category, and this is the more correct view; or because his stay among them was long, so it was as if they had denied many messengers. It has also been mentioned in the story that, out of their arrogance, they said: ﴿"Shall we believe you, when the lowest have followed you?"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 111], meaning: we do not believe you, because those who followed you are the lowest according to our view, as they said in Surat Hud: ﴿"We see none following you except those who are our lowest, in immature judgment"﴾ [Hud: 27].

Also in it is that he said to them: ﴿"And I have no knowledge of what they used to do"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 112], meaning: what knowledge do I have of their deeds that they perform? I have only the outward appearance of their affair, and their inner state is up to Allah. The outward appearance of their affair is that they are good and righteous, and they are not "the lowest" as these people claim. But after this they threatened him, may Allah protect us, with stoning, as a threat and a display of strength, in their saying: ﴿"you will surely be among the stoned"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 116]. This is more emphatic than their saying "we will stone you," because it contains intimidation, since he is not the first to be stoned; rather, others were stoned before him.

Then he turned to Allah, glorified and exalted, and ﴿"said: My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. So decide between me and them with a decision"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 117–118]. This supplication combines the three causes of answer: calling upon Allah by the name of Lordship, ﴿"My Lord"﴾; mentioning the state that calls for and warrants the supplication, ﴿"indeed my people have denied me"﴾; and the request, ﴿"So decide between me and them with a decision, and save me and those with me of the believers"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 118].

First: his saying ﴿"My Lord, indeed my people"﴾. Lordship, as we have passed over, is divided into two kinds: general and specific. This is of the specific kind, indeed one of the most particular forms of lordship, since it is Allah's lordship over His messengers.

Also in it is his saying ﴿"indeed my people have denied me"﴾, a display of his own weakness, meaning: he is the weaker party. Since he said "indeed my people," it was fitting that they should have confirmed him, because they are his people; but, may Allah protect us, they became deniers of him. So his condition calls for greater compassion, since his own people are the ones who denied him. Furthermore, it calls for their being punished more severely, since they are his people; it was incumbent upon them to believe him and to protect him from harm, so how could they be the ones who harm him!

This is like Allah's saying: ﴿"By the star when it sets. Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred"﴾ [an-Najm: 1–2]. He did not say "the prophet" or "the messenger," but said "your companion," meaning the one you know, and whose sound judgment and trustworthiness you know. How then do you deny what he has brought you of the ascension!

He said: ﴿"indeed my people have denied me"﴾, meaning they attributed lying to me, and they said: he denied him (kadhdhaba) and he lied to him (kadhaba). The difference between them:

* A student: "Kadhaba-hu" means he informed him of something contrary to reality, and "kadhdhaba-hu" means he did not believe what he brought.

* The Shaykh: He attributed lying to him. Good. And "kadhaba-hu" means he told him a lie.

﴿"My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. So decide between me and them"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 117–118]. The "fa" is for causation. "Decide between me" is outwardly an imperative, but when addressed to Allah it is called a supplication, since a command is issued only by one who stands above the one commanded, and the seeker is not above what he seeks; moreover, Allah, Majestic and Exalted, is above all things.

(﴿"So decide between me and them with a decision"﴾: i.e., judge.) The judgment is called a "fath" (opening) because the matter is opened and made clear by it, and one party is separated from the other. This decision consists in saving him and those with him of the believers and destroying them. His salvation and that of the believers with him is stated explicitly; as for their destruction, there is no salvation except from ruin. This is the decision that Nuh requested: that Allah destroy his people and save him and those with him of the believers. Allah said of him in Surat Nuh: ﴿"My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant. Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will not beget except a wicked, ungrateful one"﴾ [Nuh: 26–27].

As for this verse, ﴿"indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants"﴾: someone may say: does Nuh inform Allah of reality? Is Allah not knowing of it?

The answer: Yes, He knows it, but his intention, peace be upon him, was to state what moved him to this supplication: that by his belief he thinks or holds that if He leaves them, they will beget only a wicked, ungrateful one. Otherwise Allah is Knowing of them. So this is like an excuse for that general request: ﴿"My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant."﴾

Then he said: ﴿"and save me and those with me of the believers"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 118]. This "with me" is not companionship in the sense of mixing, as is well known; rather, it is companionship of sharing in deed and belief. The believers (...) the believers were sharing with him in belief and action. This shows that the "with" (ma'iyyah) is not as those who distort [the attributes] understood the "with" of Allah, glorified and exalted, as implying sharing in place or mixing; this is not so.

His saying ﴿"and those with me of the believers"﴾ is to clarify the ambiguity of "those with me"; since "man" is a relative pronoun, and a relative pronoun requires clarification, and its clarification is either from its relative clause or from something else.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We saved him﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 119]. The fa' (فاء) here indicates causation (السببية), meaning: "Because of their supplication, We saved him." Besides indicating causation, it also indicates sequence (التعقيب).

He said: ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 119]. Here He said ﴿and those with him﴾ (وَمَنْ مَعَهُ), although his supplication was ﴿and those of the believers who are with me﴾ (وَمَنْ مَعِيَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ). The phrase (من معه) is more general. What is the wisdom in that?

* Student: He took along some animals, and he took a pair of each kind, and these cannot be described as believers.

* The Shaykh: Perhaps he did not intend them either. Nuh (عليه الصلاة والسلام) in his supplication, as far as it appears, did not have in mind that Allah would save these other creatures; rather he said: ﴿and those of the believers who are with me﴾.

But this raises a question: why did He say ﴿وَمَنْ مَعَهُ﴾ — "man" (من) — and not "wa-ma ma'ahu" (وما معه)?

* Student: Taghlib (التغليب, giving precedence to the rational).

* The Shaykh: It is by way of taghlib, and also because he himself only prayed for those who were with him. So it is as if Allah, glorified and exalted, gave precedence to the side of the rational beings, since he only supplicated for their salvation. Thus this is more fitting for the correspondence of the response to the request.

As for His words ﴿in the laden ship﴾ (فِي الْفُلْكِ الْمَشْحُونِ): the ship (الفلك) that Nuh built or made, in the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Allah the Exalted also said: ﴿And We carried him on a vessel of planks and nails﴾ [al-Qamar 13]. Here He said ﴿in the ship﴾, and there He said ﴿of planks and nails﴾ (ذَاتِ أَلْوَاحٍ وَدُسُرٍ). Which is more concise? The "ship" (al-fulk) is undoubtedly more concise, shorter than "of planks and nails." But the surah of ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾ [al-Qamar 1], as is well known, has its verse-endings and pauses, and the phrase appropriate to them is "of planks and nails" (ذات ألواح ودسر). Moreover, there is a meaningful benefit in it, namely the explanation of the materials of this ship: that it is of planks and nails; so that this is evidence that it is sound, and so that whoever does not know may learn the craft of shipbuilding. The craft at that time had not developed to this degree. The upshot is that the reason it is mentioned in detail there and here it is mentioned (...).

As for his words (﴿الْمَشْحُونِ﴾ — "filled with people, animals and birds"): are birds not animals? Yes, but coordinating them with it is by way of mentioning the specific after the general (عطف الخاص على العام).

* Student: Are birds animals?

* The Shaykh: Yes, even human beings are animals, but the human being is a "rational speaking animal" (حيوان ناطق), as the logicians say.

It seems he means by "animal" that which walks on two legs, and by "bird" that which flies on two wings; otherwise, had he said "and the animals," it would have sufficed.

As for His words ﴿in the laden ship﴾, we have often noted that al-fulk is a noun of genus (اسم جنس) which includes, by its wording, both the singular and the plural; that is, this word is suitable for both the plural and the singular. ﴿Until when you are in the ships and they sail with them with a favorable wind﴾ [Yunus 22] — here "wa-jarayna" (وَجَرَيْنَ) — did He intend by al-fulk the plural or the singular?

* Student: The plural.

* The Shaykh: ﴿Do you not see that the ship (al-fulk) runs in the sea﴾ [Luqman 31] — this?

* Student: Plural.

* The Shaykh: No, He intended the singular. Had it been plural, He would have said "tajrina" (تجرين).

* Student: He intended the genus of the ship.

* The Shaykh: No, He intended the singular here; the wording is singular now, but it is meant as a genus. You cannot say: "al-insan" is singular but genus. Otherwise the meaning would be that al-fulk is applied to the plural and the singular with a single application, and one could not distinguish whether the plural or the singular is intended, or (...) the singular from the plural, except by context.

Almighty God said: (﴿Then We drowned the rest﴾) [al-Shu'ara' 26:120], i.e., after their deliverance, ﴿the rest﴾, from his people.

Those who were saved, as Allah the Exalted said in Surah Hud, were few: ﴿And none believed with him except a few﴾ [Hud 11:40]. Look, his wife and his son, one of his sons, were not saved, because he was a disbeliever. And he (peace be upon him) had said: ﴿My Lord, save me and my family from among the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:118], right? In the other verse, Allah said to him: ﴿We said: Carry in it two of every kind, and your family﴾ [Hud 11:40]. But Allah made an exception: ﴿except those against whom the word has already preceded﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:27]. However, he (peace be upon him) called upon Allah, the Exalted, in compassion and hoping for His mercy: ﴿So he said: My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges﴾ [Hud 11:45]. Then Allah, the Exalted, said to him: ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose work was other than righteous﴾ [Hud 11:46].

The answer here is problematic. The statement ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose work was other than righteous﴾ was phrased this way, because what preceded would require saying: "He is not of your family," since we made an exception, for example, ﴿except those against whom the word has already preceded﴾. But if it had been said that way, because the word had preceded concerning him, he would have asked: "And why has the word preceded concerning him?" So He mentioned the final result, which is that he did work that was not righteous, or ﴿work other than righteous, so do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge﴾ [Hud 11:46], and so on.

* Student: What (...) "work other than righteous"?

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: The grammatical explanation of the reading (...).

* The Shaykh: It has two explanations: ﴿Indeed, it﴾, i.e., your request, ﴿is work other than righteous﴾, because you asked for what is not permissible.

Or ﴿Indeed, it﴾, i.e., the son, ﴿is work other than righteous﴾ by way of intensification: meaning, he is a doer of unrighteous deeds, so the verbal noun is applied to him, as one says: "So-and-so is justice (ʿadl), and so-and-so is approval (riḍā)," meaning he is just and approved. So the meaning is that he is one possessing unrighteous work.

This possibility is supported by the reading, which is not among the seven canonical readings: ﴿Indeed, he did (ʿamila) other than righteous work, so do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge﴾.

Were those who were saved the ones who remained of the people of the earth? No, they are not; rather, the descendants of Noah are those who remained. As for those among the believers who were with him, they perished, and no offspring remained for them, because of the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We made his descendants the remaining ones﴾ [al-Saffat 37:77]. For this reason it is said that Noah (peace be upon him) is the second father of mankind; the first father is Adam, and this is the second, because all of the children of Adam died, and none remained except his descendants. ﴿And We made his descendants they﴾, and this "they" (hum) is a pronoun of separation that conveys restriction and exclusivity: they are the ones who remained. The historians say, meaning they say, that they are three: Sam, Ham, and Japheth. And Allah knows best whether these are their names or not, and whether they are three or more or fewer; this is only the speech of the historians. The point is that what we are certain of is that no one remained on the earth except the descendants of Noah (peace be upon him), so he is the second father.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 26, verses 121–122:

﴿Indeed, in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers. (121) And indeed, your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Most Merciful.﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 120, 121] And their drowning is a great sign. That is, Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, opened the gates of the heaven with pouring water, ﴿So We opened⦆ [al-Qamar 11]. Both ﴿fataḥna﴾ and ﴿fattaḥna﴾ are recitations (qira'at) from the seven canonical readings, and ﴿fattaḥna﴾ is more emphatic than ﴿fataḥna﴾.

Allah opened the gates of the heaven with pouring water, that is, descending with force, intensity and abundance.

﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾ [al-Qamar 12]. The grammarians (al-mu'rabun, those who study i'rab, grammatical inflection) say: the original form is "fajarna 'uyun al-ard" (We caused the springs of the earth to gush forth), (...) and the object was transposed (mahwulah 'an maf'ul). In reality, "fajarna al-ard 'uyunan" (We caused the earth to gush forth springs) is more eloquent and more magnificent. That is, as if the entire earth became springs. It is more eloquent than "fajarna 'uyun al-ard", for "'uyun al-ard" (...) ten springs, no more, would have been the case had it been "fajarna 'uyun al-ard". But: "fajarna al-ard 'uyunan" means all of it became springs, to the extent that the oven (al-tannur) began to boil with water. And the oven, as you know, is the furthest thing from water, because it is the place where fire is kindled, and the place of kindling fire is extremely dry, yet by the permission of Allah it began to boil.

The water met in a matter that had been decreed, until it reached the peaks of the mountains. All the people drowned except those who were in this ship. At that point, the words of Nuh to his people were fulfilled: ﴿If you ridicule us, then we ridicule you just as you ridicule [us]. (38) So you will soon know who will receive a punishment that will disgrace him and upon whom will descend a lasting punishment.﴾ [Hud 38, 39] (...) The ship now, the real ship, is for those who are on it, and it is as if I see them looking down at those [who drowned] through its windows while they are swimming in this water and drowning, while these [in the ship] are safe from it.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ More than whom? According to the view of the author (al-mu'allif), most of the people of Nuh were believers. But the more correct view is that "most of them" refers to those among whom the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent.

His statement: ﴿وَمَا كَانَ أَكْثَرُهُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("and most of them were not believers"). Is this the Hijazi "ma" (which works like "laysa"), with "kana" being superfluous (za'ida)? Or is the "ma" negative and "kana" original, with its grammatical function belonging to "kana"?

* Student: The function belongs to "kana", as we mentioned.

* Shaykh: The function belongs to "kana", as we mentioned, because the original state is the absence of superfluity. If you make the function belong to "ma", it becomes necessary to make "kana" superfluous. But if you make the function belong to "kana", "ma" remains a negation as it is.

﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Most Merciful.﴾ Al-'Aziz is the one who combines dominant, overpowering might, and al-Rahim is the one with perfect mercy. But because He, glory be to Him, combines might and mercy, mercy is placed where it belongs and might is placed where it belongs.

And how many types of 'izza (might) is Allah described with?

* Student: 'Izzat al-qadr (might of decree), 'izzat al-qahr (might of subjugation), 'izzat al-imtina' (might of invulnerability).

* Shaykh: The might of decree, the might of subjugation, and the might of invulnerability.

What is the meaning of the might of decree?

* Student: That Allah, glory be to Him, has a lofty station that none of His creatures resemble.

* Shaykh: "Dhu 'izz al-qadr" means that His decree has no equal, just as you say: "this is 'aziz", meaning it does not exist (in abundance).

The might of subjugation?

* Student: That Allah, glory be to Him, overpowers whoever else among His creatures, or (...).

* Shaykh: He overpowers them and prevails over them.

Alright, and the might of invulnerability?

* Student: That none of His creatures can reach Him...

* Shaykh: With harm.

* Student: With harm, or any...

* Shaykh: That is, every harm or deficiency is impossible for Him.

And regarding this last meaning they said: from this is their saying "ard 'azzaz" (hard, firm land). We call it "'izz", meaning solid, strong, impregnable, not soft or yielding.

As for al-Rahim, its meaning is the one whose mercy reaches His creation. That is, al-Rahim is other than al-Rahman.

All of Ahl al-Sunnah affirm that mercy is truly an attribute of Allah, while others interpret it to mean kindness (al-ihsan) or the will to show kindness (iradat al-ihsan), that is, they turn it to its necessary consequence. How? Because mercy is tenderness of heart (al-ruqqa), and Allah, glory be to Him, is free of such tenderness. It is said: who told you that Allah is exempt from the tenderness of mercy? Allah, glory be to Him, has mercy on His servant, meaning He is compassionate toward him. And what prevents this? Is the harsh person the praiseworthy one, or the gentle one? There is no doubt that the gentle one is the praiseworthy one.

Furthermore, we say: the gentleness of a human being is not the gentleness of Allah, glory be to Him, because a human's gentleness is sometimes caused by weakness and inability. For this reason a person sometimes shows mercy to one who does not deserve it, because he has nothing but the mere emotion of softness, whose cause is weakness. As for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, His mercy is the mercy of strength and the mercy of wisdom. For this reason He punishes the people of the Fire with that great punishment, while He is the Most Merciful of the merciful. This indicates that the mercy of the Creator is not like the mercy of the created.

﴿Indeed, in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers. (121) And indeed, your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Most Merciful.﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 120, 121] And their drowning is a great sign. Both ﴿fataḥna﴾ and ﴿fattaḥna﴾ are recitations (qira'at) from the seven canonical readings, and ﴿fattaḥna﴾ is more emphatic than ﴿fataḥna﴾.

Allah opened the gates of the heaven with pouring water, that is, descending with force, intensity and abundance.

﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾ [al-Qamar 12]. The grammarians (al-mu'rabun, those who study i'rab, grammatical inflection) say: the original form is "fajarna 'uyun al-ard" (We caused the springs of the earth to gush forth), (...) and the object was transposed (mahwulah 'an maf'ul). In reality, "fajarna al-ard 'uyunan" (We caused the earth to gush forth springs) is more eloquent and more magnificent. That is, as if the entire earth became springs. It is more eloquent than "fajarna 'uyun al-ard", for "'uyun al-ard" (...) ten springs, no more, would have been the case had it been "fajarna 'uyun al-ard". But: "fajarna al-ard 'uyunan" means all of it became springs, to the extent that the oven (al-tannur) began to boil with water. And the oven, as you know, is the furthest thing from water, because it is the place where fire is kindled, and the place of kindling fire is extremely dry, yet by the permission of Allah it began to boil.

The water met in a matter that had been decreed, until it reached the peaks of the mountains. All the people drowned except those who were in this ship. At that point, the words of Nuh to his people were fulfilled: ﴿If you ridicule us, then we ridicule you just as you ridicule [us]. (38) So you will soon know who will receive a punishment that will disgrace him and upon whom will descend a lasting punishment.﴾ [Hud 38, 39] (...) The ship now, the real ship, is for those who are on it, and it is as if I see them looking down at those [who drowned] through its windows while they are swimming in this water and drowning, while these [in the ship] are safe from it.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ More than whom? According to the view of the author (al-mu'allif), most of the people of Nuh were believers. But the more correct view is that "most of them" refers to those among whom the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent.

His statement: ﴿وَمَا كَانَ أَكْثَرُهُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("and most of them were not believers"). Is this the Hijazi "ma" (which works like "laysa"), with "kana" being superfluous (za'ida)? Or is the "ma" negative and "kana" original, with its grammatical function belonging to "kana"?

* Student: The function belongs to "kana", as we mentioned.

* Shaykh: The function belongs to "kana", as we mentioned, because the original state is the absence of superfluity. If you make the function belong to "ma", it becomes necessary to make "kana" superfluous. But if you make the function belong to "kana", "ma" remains a negation as it is.

﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Most Merciful.﴾ Al-'Aziz is the one who combines dominant, overpowering might, and al-Rahim is the one with perfect mercy. But because He, glory be to Him, combines might and mercy, mercy is placed where it belongs and might is placed where it belongs.

And how many types of 'izza (might) is Allah described with?

* Student: 'Izzat al-qadr (might of decree), 'izzat al-qahr (might of subjugation), 'izzat al-imtina' (might of invulnerability).

* Shaykh: The might of decree, the might of subjugation, and the might of invulnerability.

What is the meaning of the might of decree?

* Student: That Allah, glory be to Him, has a lofty station that none of His creatures resemble.

* Shaykh: "Dhu 'izz al-qadr" means that His decree has no equal, just as you say: "this is 'aziz", meaning it does not exist (in abundance).

The might of subjugation?

* Student: That Allah, glory be to Him, overpowers whoever else among His creatures, or (...).

* Shaykh: He overpowers them and prevails over them.

Alright, and the might of invulnerability?

* Student: That none of His creatures can reach Him...

* Shaykh: With harm.

* Student: With harm, or any...

* Shaykh: That is, every harm or deficiency is impossible for Him.

And regarding this last meaning they said: from this is their saying "ard 'azzaz" (hard, firm land). We call it "'izz", meaning solid, strong, impregnable, not soft or yielding.

As for al-Rahim, its meaning is the one whose mercy reaches His creation. That is, al-Rahim is other than al-Rahman.

All of Ahl al-Sunnah affirm that mercy is truly an attribute of Allah, while others interpret it to mean kindness (al-ihsan) or the will to show kindness (iradat al-ihsan), that is, they turn it to its necessary consequence. How? Because mercy is tenderness of heart (al-ruqqa), and Allah, glory be to Him, is free of such tenderness. It is said: who told you that Allah is exempt from the tenderness of mercy? Allah, glory be to Him, has mercy on His servant, meaning He is compassionate toward him. And what prevents this? Is the harsh person the praiseworthy one, or the gentle one? There is no doubt that the gentle one is the praiseworthy one.

Furthermore, we say: the gentleness of a human being is not the gentleness of Allah, glory be to Him, because a human's gentleness is sometimes caused by weakness and inability. For this reason a person sometimes shows mercy to one who does not deserve it, because he has nothing but the mere emotion of softness, whose cause is weakness. As for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, His mercy is the mercy of strength and the mercy of wisdom. For this reason He punishes the people of the Fire with that great punishment, while He is the Most Merciful of the merciful. This indicates that the mercy of the Creator is not like the mercy of the created.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verses 123–124:

He says: ﴿The 'Ad denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 123]. 'Ad are the people of Hud, and for this reason He says: ﴿When their brother Hud said to them, "Will you not fear Allah?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 124]. And where were these people located?

* Student: In the Empty Quarter (al-Rub' al-Khali).

* Shaykh: In the Empty Quarter. Good. And in al-Ahqaf, ﴿And mention the brother of 'Ad, when he warned his people in al-Ahqaf﴾ [al-Ahqaf 21]. These people are well known for strength and power, to the extent that they said: ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15], as if they were dominant. As for the exaggeration that the exegetes mention, when they give dates for the enormous size of their bodies and their strength, Allah knows best about it. What is certain, without doubt, is that they were a strong people and were arrogant, meaning hard-hearted and physically strong. So they are known for strength. But Allah, exalted is He, wanted to rebuke them and establish the proof against them by His saying: ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created them﴾ [Fussilat 15]. That is, they lower their heads. ﴿Who created them﴾: they are created, and He is the Creator. It is therefore necessary that the Creator be higher than the created, and that the created be in His grip. This is the wisdom in His saying: ﴿that Allah, who created them﴾, and He did not say: "that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth." Yes, the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of people, but in order to make them lower their heads even more: ﴿created them﴾; they themselves are created (...).

* * *
They denied Nuh (peace be upon him) and Hud (peace be upon him), even though he gave them this advice: ﴿When their brother Hud said to them, "Will you not fear Allah?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 124]. It has already been mentioned that the interrogation here is either for urging (tahdid, i.e., exhortation) on (...), for exhortation, or it is an interrogation meaning reproach, that is, he rebukes them for not being God-fearing: (A-la tattaqun), so that the hamza alone and the la alone are separated. This is if we take it as an interrogation meaning reproach. But if we take it as exhortation, we say: (ala) together, we parse them together.
﴿Will you not fear—﴾ whom?

* Student: Allah.

* Shaykh: "Will you not fear Allah?" Because this sentence is abbreviated, and it is known that he used to command them, for example: "Fear Allah" (...).

* Student: Does the verse ﴿The people of Nuh denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 105] not support (...) that their intended meaning is not that he (...)?

* Shaykh: Yes indeed, this is among the things that (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 125–128 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 125] "Indeed, I am to you a messenger" means: sent to you from Allah, the Exalted. The placing of "to you" (lakum) first indicates exclusivity, meaning: sent specifically to you, i.e., every messenger is sent only to his own people.

His saying ﴿trustworthy﴾ means: one who possesses trustworthiness; Allah, the Exalted, has entrusted me with His message.

If someone says: these two descriptions, ﴿a trustworthy messenger﴾, are merely a claim, and they deny that he is a trustworthy messenger, rather they say that he is a liar..

His saying ﴿trustworthy﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 125]: that is, one who possesses trustworthiness; Allah, the Exalted, has entrusted me with His message.

If someone says: these two descriptions are ﴿a trustworthy messenger﴾ while they deny that he is a trustworthy messenger, rather they say that he is a liar and a traitor, so is the claim alone sufficient to establish proof against them? The answer: No. But this claim is supported by signs from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no messenger whom Allah sent except that he was given what led people to believe based on its like" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7274) and Muslim (152 / 239) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. So it is not merely a call; because a mere call is easy to reject, but it is a call supported and strengthened by Allah, the Exalted, with clear signs by which people believe. In this, it is as if, when he said with such certainty, ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 125], this statement made with certainty is evidence of the strength of his signs, and that he had with him signs that caused him to express himself with this decisive expression. In this is evidence that the message is the greatest proof of a person's trustworthiness, isn't it? Because had he not been trustworthy, Allah, the Exalted, would not have entrusted him with the revelation which contains the judgment of people to happiness and misery, and even the judgment of making lawful their wealth, their women, and their blood. So if the messengers, peace be upon them, were not the greatest of people in trustworthiness, Allah would not have entrusted them with this great revelation.
* Student: Could their saying be a claim, because they said, ﴿O Hud, you have brought us no clear evidence, and we will not leave our gods on your word﴾ [Hud 53].
* The Shaykh: Yes, denying these is obstinacy. ﴿So fear Allah and obey me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 126], returning in meaning to his saying ﴿Will you not fear Allah?﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 124]; meaning: since I am a trustworthy messenger, do what I command you of righteousness, and I urge you to it. ﴿Fear Allah and obey me﴾: he did not say "and fear me," because he does not possess any benefit or harm for himself, nor for anyone else. The duty of people toward the messengers is not to fear the messengers but to obey them. For this reason, no messenger is reported to have said to his people, "fear me"; rather, they command them to obey. As for fear, reverence and dread, to whom is it owed? To Allah, the Exalted: ﴿so fear Allah﴾.

This taqwa (fear of Allah; God-consciousness) has been explained to us many times as taking a shield against the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, and that this is the most comprehensive of what has been said about taqwa, and they have many expressions regarding it.

His saying ﴿and obey me﴾: What is obedience (ta'ah)? The origin of ta'ah is submission (al-infiqad), and from it their saying: "this she-camel is tame (tawʿ) to its owner," i.e., submissive and docile to him. It is also explained as conforming to a command. So we say: conforming to a command out of submission to the one who commands; for conforming to a command may be out of submission to the commander, and it may be out of compulsion, and the latter is not obedience.

﴿So fear Allah and obey me﴾: in this noble verse is the obligation of fearing Allah and the obligation of obeying His Messenger, because obedience to His Messenger is obedience to Him: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [An-Nisa' 80].

(﴿And I do not ask you for any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 127])
﴿And I do not ask you for it﴾: that is, for what I say to you, or ﴿for it﴾ meaning for conveying the message; the meanings are close. That is, I am not saying: give me something; rather I command you with that in which your good lies. Had I asked you a reward for that, you would have had a proof to refuse; but I do not ask you for any reward, meaning recompense and compensation, ﴿my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾.

(﴿my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾) In this is perfect sincerity; that is, I do not want a reward except from Allah, the Exalted.

In His saying ﴿only from the Lord of the worlds﴾, the scholars say that the particle "ʿalā" (upon/from) indicates obligation; that is, He did not say "my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds," but said ﴿upon the Lord of the worlds﴾. Is anything obligatory upon Allah, the Exalted?
The answer: As for us obligating Him, no; but as for Him obligating Himself out of generosity, there is no objection to this. Ibn al-Qayyim said:

*Nothing is due to the servants from Him as an obligation,*
*Yet He has made obligatory the great and lofty reward.*
*Nay, no deed is lost before Him*
*If it is with sincerity and excellence.*
*If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are blessed, it is by His bounty,*
*And praise belongs to the Bestower.*

And the verses that come after these three verses (...) are restrictive of previous verses:

*Nothing is due to the servants from Him as an obligation,*
*Nay, no effort is lost before Him.*
*If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are blessed, it is by His bounty,*
*And He is the Generous, the Vast.*

These two verses are absolute, but Ibn al-Qayyim said:

*Nothing is due to the servants from Him as an obligation,*
*Yet He has made obligatory the great and lofty reward.*

(Nay, no deed is lost before Him) he restricted it by his saying (if it is with sincerity and excellence). Excellence is following (the Sunnah). As for if it is not with sincerity and excellence, it is lost. ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [Al-Kahf 110].

He says: ﴿So fear Allah and obey me. (126) And I do not ask you for any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 126–127]. (﴿Do you build on every high place﴾: a high place; ﴿a sign﴾: a building as a landmark for passersby; ﴿you mock﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 128]: at those who pass by you and you ridicule them) to the end.

He says: ﴿Do you build on every high place a sign﴾. ﴿A sign﴾ means: a landmark. But is it a landmark on the road as the author said? This is possible, although the context does not support it, yet it is not excluded by it; but it is not supported by it. Or the intended meaning of ﴿a sign﴾ is: a sign of your strength and your power. This is the closer view, and for this reason He said ﴿on every high place﴾; meaning that you intend by these buildings to be a sign, an evidence and a proof of your strength. His saying ﴿you mock﴾: you take these as play, because you have no benefit in them except mere play and displaying greatness and displaying strength; and there is no doubt that a person displaying his strength is play and corruption.

Based on this, it becomes clear to us that those who try to reach the stars and launch these moons which you do not find on earth are exactly like the people of 'Ad; that is, the method is the same, though the style differs. They do these things as signs and as play, since they do not benefit from them in what they were created for. ﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth﴾ [Al-Baqarah 29], in the sky; but what is on the earth is created for us to benefit from directly, while what is in the sky is subjected to our interests, yet we do not benefit from it directly. So the beneficial thing we benefit from directly is what is on the earth.

For this reason some people say: why do you try to reach the sky while you are unable to solve your problems on earth? This is true, but it is merely play and boasting, and that we are strong, and that we have reached such-and-such; even though they are the people of Hud. And these contemporary people also lose enormous sums on these matters, so it becomes play, because everything in which a person exhausts his body, wealth and thought without benefit is play with no use. Rather, if he intends by it displaying greatness and arrogance over creation, it also becomes corruption; so it becomes a positive matter, not merely a negative one, yes positive because it is corruption. He is rejecting this matter upon them: ﴿Do you build on every high place a sign, mocking?﴾

As for what the author, may Allah have mercy on him, took—that they make landmarks for passersby so that when they pass by them they mock them—this is far from the context; although the context does not prohibit it, it does not support it. So the correct view in this verse is that they build great buildings showing their strength and power in play, because they benefit from them only in displaying greatness, and this is without doubt play. ﴿And you take for yourselves palaces﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 129], to the end.

If you reflect on the human being: the first human is the last human, or the last human is the first human, but the style differs. ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed. (29) And when they passed by them, they winked at one another. (30) And when they returned to their own people, they returned jesting. (31) And when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are misguided"﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 29–32].

These matters, applied to the present time, exist; but the word "misguided" (...) "backward" or "conservative" or the like; or is it the same thing? So the human being in reality—the mindset is the same, but the style differs in keeping with the times, or is it the same thing? And Allah knows best.

* Student: "You will certainly follow the ways of those before you" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7320) and Muslim (2669 / 6) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri]. Is it correct what some people say: that the animals in the time of Noah were fewer kinds than today, and that this is due to the mating of some of them producing other forms, and from them new forms are born?
* The Shaykh: Since the verse does not state either this or that: ﴿two of every pair﴾ [Hud 40]; meaning, of every one of the existing creatures. We do not know; there is no doubt the origin did not come into existence as a new origin, but perhaps, as you said, by reproduction or the mating of some of them with others they differ. Although they say: it is well known among them that what results from the mating of some (...) with others does not reproduce; whatever arose from reproduction does not reproduce. This is known among them, and for this reason the mule cannot (...). Yes indeed.
* Student: From where comes the abundance of mules?
* The Shaykh: From the mating of donkeys with mares.
* Student: Shaykh 'Abd al-Rahman said: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Ya-Sin 41]; he said that "the ship" includes even airplanes (...), and he said the proof is that it says ﴿We carried their offspring﴾ and did not say "We carried them."
* The Shaykh: Read the verses that come before it.
* Student: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth; We have brought it to life and brought forth from it grain, from which they eat. (33) And We placed therein gardens of palms and grapevines and caused to gush forth therein springs (34) That they may eat of its fruit and that which their hands have made. Then will they not be grateful? (35) Glorified is He who created all the pairs from what the earth grows and from themselves and from that which they do not know. (36) And a sign for them is the night; We remove from it the day, and they are in darkness. (37) And the sun runs toward its stationary point. That is the decree of the Exalted in Might, the Knowing. (38) And the moon—We have determined for it phases until it returns like the old dry date stalk. (39) It is not for the sun to reach the moon, nor does the night overtake the day; but each, in an orbit, is swimming. (40) And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship. (41)﴾ [Ya-Sin 33–41].
* The Shaykh: The truth is that what prevents this is His saying ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾, and "offspring" (dhurriyyah) comes later, does it not?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: How can it be a sign for them when they came before it? For this reason most of the exegetes disagree with this view. He says: ﴿their offspring﴾ means the offspring of their father, that is Noah, peace be upon him. Some said that "offspring" here means "fathers," but using "dhurriyyah" to mean "fathers" is far-fetched in the Arabic language. Rather, its use to mean "their offspring," i.e., the offspring from whom they arose, so the attribution is not to the offspring that arose from them, but to the offspring from which they arose, which is the offspring of their father Noah, "We carried them in the laden ship." This is more appropriate, because in reality, making it "a sign for them that We carried their offspring" refers to later offspring who came after, or it would be a sign for those who had died; this is far-fetched (...). The Shaykh's statement—I do not see any basis for it.
* Student: (...) it is only applied to airplanes, cars...
* The Shaykh: No, it may apply; because the whale (...) and for this Allah, the Exalted, limited means of conveyance to this: ﴿And He has made for you of the ships and cattle that which you ride﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 12]. So "the ship" is what we make, and "the cattle" is what Allah creates. But the point is that it being a sign for them while they are looking, and the offspring being after them.
* Student: He says: this address is to the later people, and their earlier offspring, the ones who were not found in the time of (...), were carried on what?
* The Shaykh: (...) the signs existing in his time. If we are carried on airplanes, cars and vessels, these would not be signs for those (earlier people). Moreover, the word "We carried" requires interpreting it as "We will carry." Then, if it is "We will carry," it would be a sign for them only in the sense of a promise from Allah, not something they witnessed.
* Student: Would it not be that these conveyances are a sign for you, and likewise, with the passing of time, a sign?
* The Shaykh: A sign for whom?
* Student: For your offspring; that you were carried upon them, and will be carried...
* The Shaykh: Yes, that does not contradict; but airplanes and cars—the offspring existing in the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him, how can ﴿that We carried their offspring﴾ apply to them except by interpreting it as "then We carry"? And if it is by interpreting it as "then We carry," it would not be a sign for them except in the sense that it is a promise from Allah and they trust in it. Allah, the Exalted, does not address these obstinate people with what His promise entails only; rather He addresses them with a sign they witness or which is known to them, such that they cannot deny it. In reality, this passed by me in the Shaykh's words, but it has no basis. The correct view is to say: ﴿We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾, meaning the offspring from which they descended. The attribution—as the grammarians say—is for the slightest connection; their fathers are "offspring" in relation to Noah. As for the claim that "offspring" comes in its literal meaning of "fathers" (...).
* In the story of Noah: ﴿My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. (117) So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 117–118], and so on. What is derived from this sentence?
* Student: The attribution of "people" to him.
* The Shaykh: That is, from every (...) ﴿My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. (117) So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment﴾.
* Student: First: seeking refuge in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, supplicating against them, and mentioning the reasons that led to the supplication against them.
* The Shaykh: In His saying?
* Student: ﴿Indeed my people have denied me. (117) So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment﴾.
* The Shaykh: This is supplication; is it among the etiquettes of supplication?
* Student: Among the etiquettes of supplication: first, he called upon Allah with the attribute of Lordship, and also mentioned the circumstances and the conditions to Allah, the Exalted...

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 26, verses 125–128 (part 2 of 2):

* The Shaykh: This means mentioning the circumstance that calls for the supplication.
* Student: ﴿He said, "My Lord, my people have denied me."﴾
* The Shaykh: No. It also means mentioning the thing requested. The one who supplicates sometimes mentions only the request, sometimes praises Allah along with mentioning the request, sometimes praises Allah and mentions his own situation and the request, and sometimes mentions only his own situation. ﴿"My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You might send down to me."﴾ [Al-Qasas: 24]. So the point is that among the etiquettes of supplication there are three things. What are they?
* Student: Seeking a means (tawassul) through the attributes of Allah, and also describing one's situation and the request.
* The Shaykh: What is the benefit of his saying ﴿"my people have denied me"﴾, in attributing the people to himself?
* Student: The benefit of attributing the people to him is that the proof is established against them to the greatest degree, because a prophet was sent to them from among them, to his own people, and a man from another tribe was not sent to them.
* The Shaykh: That means increasing the condemnation of them.
* Student: Increasing the condemnation of them.
* The Shaykh: Since they denied him while he was one of them. There is a second benefit in it as well.
* Student: Another benefit: so that it serves as an excuse before Him, that he did not ask for their destruction.
* The Shaykh: That means magnifying the trial upon him, because when his own people deny him it becomes harder and greater for him. So in it is the magnifying of the trial upon him, so that it becomes the strongest means of his supplication being answered. What is derived from his saying: ﴿"So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment"﴾?
* Student: It means: judge between them.
* The Shaykh: Its meaning is that He judges between them by destroying them. Is such a supplication permissible?
* Student: Yes, because they deserve destruction.
* The Shaykh: That means it is derived from it that when despair sets in, it is permissible for a person to supplicate against those who deny and obstinately oppose. Did our Sharia approve of this or oppose it?
* Student: Our Sharia approved it. It only preferred not supplicating against them, unless it is established that they will not go straight and will not believe, in which case supplication is prescribed.
* The Shaykh: What is your evidence?
* Student: The evidence for the non-legitimacy of supplicating except when there is a need is: "The Prophet ﷺ, when Gabriel came down to him and said: If you wish, I will close the two mountains upon them. He said: 'Rather, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins someone who worships Allah alone, associating nothing with Him.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3231) and Muslim (1795/111), from 'A'isha, with the wording: "The angel of the mountains called to me and greeted me, then said: O Muhammad, Allah has heard the words of your people to you, and I am the angel of the mountains, and your Lord has sent me to you so that you may command me with your command. What do you wish? If you wish, I will close the two mountains upon them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: 'Rather, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins those who worship Allah alone, associating nothing with Him.'"]] Or as the Prophet ﷺ said, this noble Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, but he did not prohibit...that a person supplicates against...
* The Shaykh: Now I am asking?
* Student: So the prescribed course is not to supplicate...
* The Shaykh: Does that mean our Sharia came contrary to that?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Alright, is there a more explicit evidence than this?
* Student: The explicit evidence on that is: "The Prophet ﷺ, when he supplicated against them in the prayer, saying: 'O Allah, destroy so-and-so bin so-and-so, and so-and-so bin so-and-so,' the verse was revealed to him: ﴿"You have no part in the affair, whether He turns to them in forgiveness or punishes them, for indeed they are wrongdoers."﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 128], so he refrained from them."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (4560) and Muslim (675/294), from Abu Hurayrah: ...and he would say in some of his prayers, in the dawn prayer, "O Allah, curse so-and-so and so-and-so," referring to some tribes of the Arabs, until Allah revealed ﴿"You have no part in the affair"﴾, the verse. The wording is al-Bukhari's.]]
* The Shaykh: Yes. Our Sharia commanded patience and not supplicating against them. But it may be said: the Sharia of Noah, upon him be prayers and peace, differs from our Sharia, and there is no objection to Sharias differing on such a matter. Also, Noah, upon him be prayers and peace, remained among his people for how long? A thousand years less fifty years, and every time he called them they increased in obstinacy and arrogance, so there remained no benefit in (...) against them. But he did not emigrate from them as Jonah did; rather he remained among them until Allah seized them.
* Student: The fact that the Messenger ﷺ supplicated against the leaders of Quraysh, does that not indicate the permissibility of supplicating against...
* The Shaykh: Yes, but in the end he was prohibited from it. Nor did he supplicate against the leaders of Quraysh in Makkah before he emigrated. In the end he was prohibited; that is: ﴿"You have no part in the affair"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 128] (...).
What is derived from His saying: ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 119]?
* Student: The command includes (...) the salvation of the believers and those who boarded with them in the ship from among the animals.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it means a choice from Him that Allah, glorified and exalted, saved those with him from the believers in response to his supplication, and He also saved others that they need for their existence: ﴿"two of every kind, two of each"﴾ [Hud: 40].
Is it derived from the noble verse that the ship was loaded (with its cargo of creatures)?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: From where?
* Student: ﴿"and those with him in the laden ship"﴾. First He described it as laden, then the ship is defined with the article "al-", which is for definiteness...
* The Shaykh: The one that indicates perfection, meaning.
* Student: Perfection, yes.
* The Shaykh: And that it is laden also indicates its strength, because what is not strong, if it were loaded, would sink and be destroyed.
* Student: Then His saying: ﴿"So We saved him and those with him"﴾ means many, certainly.
* The Shaykh: No, the discussion is about the laden ship, meaning filled, and despite that it held steady, and Allah saved through it those with him.
Now in the story of Hud, first: Hud, upon him be prayers and peace, was among a tribe called 'Ad, and their dwellings were located where?
* Student: In al-Ahqaf.
* The Shaykh: Yes. And for what were they known?
* Student: They were known for strength and tyranny, to the point that they said: ﴿"Who is mightier than us in strength?"﴾ [Fussilat: 15], as mentioned in the Qur'an.
* The Shaykh: Well said. What is derived from His saying: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾?
* Student: That the message includes trustworthiness, because a human being, who is a man, does not send anyone except one whom he trusts, so how about the Creator?!
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. That means it is derived from this that all the bearers of messages are trustworthy; that is, sending cannot be sound except with a trustworthy person who is relied upon.
We raised an objection to this. What is the objection?
* Student: That if the messenger, or the one sent, is trustworthy, it is not necessary to believe him, because we know him by his trustworthiness, except by a proof or a sign that indicates his message (...) by his trustworthiness rather than the sign or miracle that indicates...
* The Shaykh: No, that is not an objection. We raised an objection regarding His saying: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾.
* Student: The restriction, we said: the exclusivity is for him...
* The Shaykh: No, we raised an objection, we made clear what it is, and we answered it.
* Student: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes. We said: this is a claim from him that it is so. They say: you are not a messenger and you are not trustworthy, rather they denied him. So how can this statement be made into an argument: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger (125). So fear Allah"﴾, so that because I am a trustworthy messenger, you should fear Allah?
* Student: He does not mention that, rather the signs.
* The Shaykh: Yes. We said: this claim is not a bare claim. You only mentioned the answer and did not mention the objection. The most important thing is the objection, that someone says: how did he argue against them with what he claimed for himself? We say: this claim is accompanied by evidence.
* What is derived from this verse: the permissibility of a person describing himself with praise for a beneficial purpose, like His saying: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾. This was also reported from the Prophet ﷺ, when he said: "I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say this without boasting."[[Narrated by at-Tirmidhi (3148) and Ibn Majah (4308), from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] And similar praise was also reported from the Companions, such as the saying of Ibn Mas'ud: "If I knew that anyone knew the Book of Allah better than I do, and that a camel could reach him, I would travel to him, or I would journey to him."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5002) and Muslim (2463/115), from Ibn Mas'ud.]] And similar things, but on the condition that the person's purpose in that is the benefit.
* And it is derived from this: that piety (taqwa) is not attributed to a created being, unlike obedience; based on His saying: ﴿"So fear Allah and obey me"﴾. There is no harm in my saying: I obeyed so-and-so. But it is not permissible to say: fear so-and-so, in the sense of the taqwa that entails humility.
* In this there is evidence of the sincerity of the Messengers to Allah in His saying: ﴿"And I do not ask you for any reward for it"﴾.
* And in it also: a person reckoning his deed with Allah, not as humiliation before Allah in this deed or as a favor upon Him by it, but reckoning it with Him in hope of His reward. Based on His saying: ﴿"My reward is only from the Lord of the worlds"﴾.
* And in this is evidence of the tyranny of 'Ad and their love of pride and grandeur, in what their prophet denounced them for: ﴿"Do you build on every high place a monument for no purpose?"﴾.
* And in it is evidence that a person should have a sound purpose behind his deed, especially a great and enormous work, and that his purpose not be vain or for show. Based on His saying: ﴿"you build in vain"﴾. This is the point of criticism: it is not that they build on every high place a monument, but that doing so is in vain, and this is the object of censure and blame.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 125–128 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 125] "Indeed, I am to you a messenger" means: sent to you from Allah, the Exalted. The placing of "to you" (lakum) first indicates exclusivity, meaning: sent specifically to you, i.e., every messenger is sent only to his own people.

His saying ﴿trustworthy﴾ means: one who possesses trustworthiness; Allah, the Exalted, has entrusted me with His message.

If someone says: these two descriptions, ﴿a trustworthy messenger﴾, are merely a claim, and they deny that he is a trustworthy messenger, rather they say that he is a liar..

His saying ﴿trustworthy﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 125]: that is, one who possesses trustworthiness; Allah, the Exalted, has entrusted me with His message.

If someone says: these two descriptions are ﴿a trustworthy messenger﴾ while they deny that he is a trustworthy messenger, rather they say that he is a liar and a traitor, so is the claim alone sufficient to establish proof against them? The answer: No. But this claim is supported by signs from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no messenger whom Allah sent except that he was given what led people to believe based on its like" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7274) and Muslim (152 / 239) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. So it is not merely a call; because a mere call is easy to reject, but it is a call supported and strengthened by Allah, the Exalted, with clear signs by which people believe. In this, it is as if, when he said with such certainty, ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 125], this statement made with certainty is evidence of the strength of his signs, and that he had with him signs that caused him to express himself with this decisive expression. In this is evidence that the message is the greatest proof of a person's trustworthiness, isn't it? Because had he not been trustworthy, Allah, the Exalted, would not have entrusted him with the revelation which contains the judgment of people to happiness and misery, and even the judgment of making lawful their wealth, their women, and their blood. So if the messengers, peace be upon them, were not the greatest of people in trustworthiness, Allah would not have entrusted them with this great revelation.
* Student: Could their saying be a claim, because they said, ﴿O Hud, you have brought us no clear evidence, and we will not leave our gods on your word﴾ [Hud 53].
* The Shaykh: Yes, denying these is obstinacy. ﴿So fear Allah and obey me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 126], returning in meaning to his saying ﴿Will you not fear Allah?﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 124]; meaning: since I am a trustworthy messenger, do what I command you of righteousness, and I urge you to it. ﴿Fear Allah and obey me﴾: he did not say "and fear me," because he does not possess any benefit or harm for himself, nor for anyone else. The duty of people toward the messengers is not to fear the messengers but to obey them.
