For this reason, no messenger is reported to have said to his people, "fear me"; rather, they command them to obey. As for fear, reverence and dread, to whom is it owed? To Allah, the Exalted: ﴿so fear Allah﴾.

This taqwa (fear of Allah; God-consciousness) has been explained to us many times as taking a shield against the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, and that this is the most comprehensive of what has been said about taqwa, and they have many expressions regarding it.

His saying ﴿and obey me﴾: What is obedience (ta'ah)? The origin of ta'ah is submission (al-infiqad), and from it their saying: "this she-camel is tame (tawʿ) to its owner," i.e., submissive and docile to him. It is also explained as conforming to a command. So we say: conforming to a command out of submission to the one who commands; for conforming to a command may be out of submission to the commander, and it may be out of compulsion, and the latter is not obedience.

﴿So fear Allah and obey me﴾: in this noble verse is the obligation of fearing Allah and the obligation of obeying His Messenger, because obedience to His Messenger is obedience to Him: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [An-Nisa' 80].

(﴿And I do not ask you for any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 127])
﴿And I do not ask you for it﴾: that is, for what I say to you, or ﴿for it﴾ meaning for conveying the message; the meanings are close. That is, I am not saying: give me something; rather I command you with that in which your good lies. Had I asked you a reward for that, you would have had a proof to refuse; but I do not ask you for any reward, meaning recompense and compensation, ﴿my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾.

(﴿my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾) In this is perfect sincerity; that is, I do not want a reward except from Allah, the Exalted.

In His saying ﴿only from the Lord of the worlds﴾, the scholars say that the particle "ʿalā" (upon/from) indicates obligation; that is, He did not say "my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds," but said ﴿upon the Lord of the worlds﴾. Is anything obligatory upon Allah, the Exalted?
The answer: As for us obligating Him, no; but as for Him obligating Himself out of generosity, there is no objection to this. Ibn al-Qayyim said:

*Nothing is due to the servants from Him as an obligation,*
*Yet He has made obligatory the great and lofty reward.*
*Nay, no deed is lost before Him*
*If it is with sincerity and excellence.*
*If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are blessed, it is by His bounty,*
*And praise belongs to the Bestower.*

And the verses that come after these three verses (...) are restrictive of previous verses:

*Nothing is due to the servants from Him as an obligation,*
*Nay, no effort is lost before Him.*
*If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are blessed, it is by His bounty,*
*And He is the Generous, the Vast.*

These two verses are absolute, but Ibn al-Qayyim said:

*Nothing is due to the servants from Him as an obligation,*
*Yet He has made obligatory the great and lofty reward.*

(Nay, no deed is lost before Him) he restricted it by his saying (if it is with sincerity and excellence). Excellence is following (the Sunnah). As for if it is not with sincerity and excellence, it is lost. ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [Al-Kahf 110].

He says: ﴿So fear Allah and obey me. (126) And I do not ask you for any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 126–127]. (﴿Do you build on every high place﴾: a high place; ﴿a sign﴾: a building as a landmark for passersby; ﴿you mock﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 128]: at those who pass by you and you ridicule them) to the end.

He says: ﴿Do you build on every high place a sign﴾. ﴿A sign﴾ means: a landmark. But is it a landmark on the road as the author said? This is possible, although the context does not support it, yet it is not excluded by it; but it is not supported by it. Or the intended meaning of ﴿a sign﴾ is: a sign of your strength and your power. This is the closer view, and for this reason He said ﴿on every high place﴾; meaning that you intend by these buildings to be a sign, an evidence and a proof of your strength. His saying ﴿you mock﴾: you take these as play, because you have no benefit in them except mere play and displaying greatness and displaying strength; and there is no doubt that a person displaying his strength is play and corruption.

Based on this, it becomes clear to us that those who try to reach the stars and launch these moons which you do not find on earth are exactly like the people of 'Ad; that is, the method is the same, though the style differs. They do these things as signs and as play, since they do not benefit from them in what they were created for. ﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth﴾ [Al-Baqarah 29], in the sky; but what is on the earth is created for us to benefit from directly, while what is in the sky is subjected to our interests, yet we do not benefit from it directly. So the beneficial thing we benefit from directly is what is on the earth.

For this reason some people say: why do you try to reach the sky while you are unable to solve your problems on earth? This is true, but it is merely play and boasting, and that we are strong, and that we have reached such-and-such; even though they are the people of Hud. And these contemporary people also lose enormous sums on these matters, so it becomes play, because everything in which a person exhausts his body, wealth and thought without benefit is play with no use. Rather, if he intends by it displaying greatness and arrogance over creation, it also becomes corruption; so it becomes a positive matter, not merely a negative one, yes positive because it is corruption. He is rejecting this matter upon them: ﴿Do you build on every high place a sign, mocking?﴾

As for what the author, may Allah have mercy on him, took—that they make landmarks for passersby so that when they pass by them they mock them—this is far from the context; although the context does not prohibit it, it does not support it. So the correct view in this verse is that they build great buildings showing their strength and power in play, because they benefit from them only in displaying greatness, and this is without doubt play. ﴿And you take for yourselves palaces﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 129], to the end.

If you reflect on the human being: the first human is the last human, or the last human is the first human, but the style differs. ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed. (29) And when they passed by them, they winked at one another. (30) And when they returned to their own people, they returned jesting. (31) And when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are misguided"﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 29–32].

These matters, applied to the present time, exist; but the word "misguided" (...) "backward" or "conservative" or the like; or is it the same thing? So the human being in reality—the mindset is the same, but the style differs in keeping with the times, or is it the same thing? And Allah knows best.

* Student: "You will certainly follow the ways of those before you" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7320) and Muslim (2669 / 6) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri]. Is it correct what some people say: that the animals in the time of Noah were fewer kinds than today, and that this is due to the mating of some of them producing other forms, and from them new forms are born?
* The Shaykh: Since the verse does not state either this or that: ﴿two of every pair﴾ [Hud 40]; meaning, of every one of the existing creatures. We do not know; there is no doubt the origin did not come into existence as a new origin, but perhaps, as you said, by reproduction or the mating of some of them with others they differ. Although they say: it is well known among them that what results from the mating of some (...) with others does not reproduce; whatever arose from reproduction does not reproduce. This is known among them, and for this reason the mule cannot (...). Yes indeed.
* Student: From where comes the abundance of mules?
* The Shaykh: From the mating of donkeys with mares.
* Student: Shaykh 'Abd al-Rahman said: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Ya-Sin 41]; he said that "the ship" includes even airplanes (...), and he said the proof is that it says ﴿We carried their offspring﴾ and did not say "We carried them."
* The Shaykh: Read the verses that come before it.
* Student: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth; We have brought it to life and brought forth from it grain, from which they eat. (33) And We placed therein gardens of palms and grapevines and caused to gush forth therein springs (34) That they may eat of its fruit and that which their hands have made. Then will they not be grateful? (35) Glorified is He who created all the pairs from what the earth grows and from themselves and from that which they do not know. (36) And a sign for them is the night; We remove from it the day, and they are in darkness. (37) And the sun runs toward its stationary point. That is the decree of the Exalted in Might, the Knowing. (38) And the moon—We have determined for it phases until it returns like the old dry date stalk. (39) It is not for the sun to reach the moon, nor does the night overtake the day; but each, in an orbit, is swimming. (40) And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship. (41)﴾ [Ya-Sin 33–41].
* The Shaykh: The truth is that what prevents this is His saying ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾, and "offspring" (dhurriyyah) comes later, does it not?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: How can it be a sign for them when they came before it? For this reason most of the exegetes disagree with this view. He says: ﴿their offspring﴾ means the offspring of their father, that is Noah, peace be upon him. Some said that "offspring" here means "fathers," but using "dhurriyyah" to mean "fathers" is far-fetched in the Arabic language. Rather, its use to mean "their offspring," i.e., the offspring from whom they arose, so the attribution is not to the offspring that arose from them, but to the offspring from which they arose, which is the offspring of their father Noah, "We carried them in the laden ship." This is more appropriate, because in reality, making it "a sign for them that We carried their offspring" refers to later offspring who came after, or it would be a sign for those who had died; this is far-fetched (...). The Shaykh's statement—I do not see any basis for it.
* Student: (...) it is only applied to airplanes, cars...
* The Shaykh: No, it may apply; because the whale (...) and for this Allah, the Exalted, limited means of conveyance to this: ﴿And He has made for you of the ships and cattle that which you ride﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 12]. So "the ship" is what we make, and "the cattle" is what Allah creates. But the point is that it being a sign for them while they are looking, and the offspring being after them.
* Student: He says: this address is to the later people, and their earlier offspring, the ones who were not found in the time of (...), were carried on what?
* The Shaykh: (...) the signs existing in his time. If we are carried on airplanes, cars and vessels, these would not be signs for those (earlier people). Moreover, the word "We carried" requires interpreting it as "We will carry." Then, if it is "We will carry," it would be a sign for them only in the sense of a promise from Allah, not something they witnessed.
* Student: Would it not be that these conveyances are a sign for you, and likewise, with the passing of time, a sign?
* The Shaykh: A sign for whom?
* Student: For your offspring; that you were carried upon them, and will be carried...
* The Shaykh: Yes, that does not contradict; but airplanes and cars—the offspring existing in the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him, how can ﴿that We carried their offspring﴾ apply to them except by interpreting it as "then We carry"? And if it is by interpreting it as "then We carry," it would not be a sign for them except in the sense that it is a promise from Allah and they trust in it. Allah, the Exalted, does not address these obstinate people with what His promise entails only; rather He addresses them with a sign they witness or which is known to them, such that they cannot deny it. In reality, this passed by me in the Shaykh's words, but it has no basis. The correct view is to say: ﴿We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾, meaning the offspring from which they descended. The attribution—as the grammarians say—is for the slightest connection; their fathers are "offspring" in relation to Noah. As for the claim that "offspring" comes in its literal meaning of "fathers" (...).
* In the story of Noah: ﴿My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. (117) So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 117–118], and so on. What is derived from this sentence?
* Student: The attribution of "people" to him.
* The Shaykh: That is, from every (...) ﴿My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. (117) So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment﴾.
* Student: First: seeking refuge in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, supplicating against them, and mentioning the reasons that led to the supplication against them.
* The Shaykh: In His saying?
* Student: ﴿Indeed my people have denied me. (117) So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment﴾.
* The Shaykh: This is supplication; is it among the etiquettes of supplication?
* Student: Among the etiquettes of supplication: first, he called upon Allah with the attribute of Lordship, and also mentioned the circumstances and the conditions to Allah, the Exalted...

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 26, verses 125–128 (part 2 of 2):

* The Shaykh: This means mentioning the circumstance that calls for the supplication.
* Student: ﴿He said, "My Lord, my people have denied me."﴾
* The Shaykh: No. It also means mentioning the thing requested. The one who supplicates sometimes mentions only the request, sometimes praises Allah along with mentioning the request, sometimes praises Allah and mentions his own situation and the request, and sometimes mentions only his own situation. ﴿"My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You might send down to me."﴾ [Al-Qasas: 24]. So the point is that among the etiquettes of supplication there are three things. What are they?
* Student: Seeking a means (tawassul) through the attributes of Allah, and also describing one's situation and the request.
* The Shaykh: What is the benefit of his saying ﴿"my people have denied me"﴾, in attributing the people to himself?
* Student: The benefit of attributing the people to him is that the proof is established against them to the greatest degree, because a prophet was sent to them from among them, to his own people, and a man from another tribe was not sent to them.
* The Shaykh: That means increasing the condemnation of them.
* Student: Increasing the condemnation of them.
* The Shaykh: Since they denied him while he was one of them. There is a second benefit in it as well.
* Student: Another benefit: so that it serves as an excuse before Him, that he did not ask for their destruction.
* The Shaykh: That means magnifying the trial upon him, because when his own people deny him it becomes harder and greater for him. So in it is the magnifying of the trial upon him, so that it becomes the strongest means of his supplication being answered. What is derived from his saying: ﴿"So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment"﴾?
* Student: It means: judge between them.
* The Shaykh: Its meaning is that He judges between them by destroying them. Is such a supplication permissible?
* Student: Yes, because they deserve destruction.
* The Shaykh: That means it is derived from it that when despair sets in, it is permissible for a person to supplicate against those who deny and obstinately oppose. Did our Sharia approve of this or oppose it?
* Student: Our Sharia approved it. It only preferred not supplicating against them, unless it is established that they will not go straight and will not believe, in which case supplication is prescribed.
* The Shaykh: What is your evidence?
* Student: The evidence for the non-legitimacy of supplicating except when there is a need is: "The Prophet ﷺ, when Gabriel came down to him and said: If you wish, I will close the two mountains upon them. He said: 'Rather, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins someone who worships Allah alone, associating nothing with Him.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3231) and Muslim (1795/111), from 'A'isha, with the wording: "The angel of the mountains called to me and greeted me, then said: O Muhammad, Allah has heard the words of your people to you, and I am the angel of the mountains, and your Lord has sent me to you so that you may command me with your command. What do you wish? If you wish, I will close the two mountains upon them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: 'Rather, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins those who worship Allah alone, associating nothing with Him.'"]] Or as the Prophet ﷺ said, this noble Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, but he did not prohibit...that a person supplicates against...
* The Shaykh: Now I am asking?
* Student: So the prescribed course is not to supplicate...
* The Shaykh: Does that mean our Sharia came contrary to that?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Alright, is there a more explicit evidence than this?
* Student: The explicit evidence on that is: "The Prophet ﷺ, when he supplicated against them in the prayer, saying: 'O Allah, destroy so-and-so bin so-and-so, and so-and-so bin so-and-so,' the verse was revealed to him: ﴿"You have no part in the affair, whether He turns to them in forgiveness or punishes them, for indeed they are wrongdoers."﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 128], so he refrained from them."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (4560) and Muslim (675/294), from Abu Hurayrah: ...and he would say in some of his prayers, in the dawn prayer, "O Allah, curse so-and-so and so-and-so," referring to some tribes of the Arabs, until Allah revealed ﴿"You have no part in the affair"﴾, the verse. The wording is al-Bukhari's.]]
* The Shaykh: Yes. Our Sharia commanded patience and not supplicating against them. But it may be said: the Sharia of Noah, upon him be prayers and peace, differs from our Sharia, and there is no objection to Sharias differing on such a matter. Also, Noah, upon him be prayers and peace, remained among his people for how long? A thousand years less fifty years, and every time he called them they increased in obstinacy and arrogance, so there remained no benefit in (...) against them. But he did not emigrate from them as Jonah did; rather he remained among them until Allah seized them.
* Student: The fact that the Messenger ﷺ supplicated against the leaders of Quraysh, does that not indicate the permissibility of supplicating against...
* The Shaykh: Yes, but in the end he was prohibited from it. Nor did he supplicate against the leaders of Quraysh in Makkah before he emigrated. In the end he was prohibited; that is: ﴿"You have no part in the affair"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 128] (...).
What is derived from His saying: ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 119]?
* Student: The command includes (...) the salvation of the believers and those who boarded with them in the ship from among the animals.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it means a choice from Him that Allah, glorified and exalted, saved those with him from the believers in response to his supplication, and He also saved others that they need for their existence: ﴿"two of every kind, two of each"﴾ [Hud: 40].
Is it derived from the noble verse that the ship was loaded (with its cargo of creatures)?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: From where?
* Student: ﴿"and those with him in the laden ship"﴾. First He described it as laden, then the ship is defined with the article "al-", which is for definiteness...
* The Shaykh: The one that indicates perfection, meaning.
* Student: Perfection, yes.
* The Shaykh: And that it is laden also indicates its strength, because what is not strong, if it were loaded, would sink and be destroyed.
* Student: Then His saying: ﴿"So We saved him and those with him"﴾ means many, certainly.
* The Shaykh: No, the discussion is about the laden ship, meaning filled, and despite that it held steady, and Allah saved through it those with him.
Now in the story of Hud, first: Hud, upon him be prayers and peace, was among a tribe called 'Ad, and their dwellings were located where?
* Student: In al-Ahqaf.
* The Shaykh: Yes. And for what were they known?
* Student: They were known for strength and tyranny, to the point that they said: ﴿"Who is mightier than us in strength?"﴾ [Fussilat: 15], as mentioned in the Qur'an.
* The Shaykh: Well said. What is derived from His saying: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾?
* Student: That the message includes trustworthiness, because a human being, who is a man, does not send anyone except one whom he trusts, so how about the Creator?!
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. That means it is derived from this that all the bearers of messages are trustworthy; that is, sending cannot be sound except with a trustworthy person who is relied upon.
We raised an objection to this. What is the objection?
* Student: That if the messenger, or the one sent, is trustworthy, it is not necessary to believe him, because we know him by his trustworthiness, except by a proof or a sign that indicates his message (...) by his trustworthiness rather than the sign or miracle that indicates...
* The Shaykh: No, that is not an objection. We raised an objection regarding His saying: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾.
* Student: The restriction, we said: the exclusivity is for him...
* The Shaykh: No, we raised an objection, we made clear what it is, and we answered it.
* Student: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes. We said: this is a claim from him that it is so. They say: you are not a messenger and you are not trustworthy, rather they denied him. So how can this statement be made into an argument: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger (125). So fear Allah"﴾, so that because I am a trustworthy messenger, you should fear Allah?
* Student: He does not mention that, rather the signs.
* The Shaykh: Yes. We said: this claim is not a bare claim. You only mentioned the answer and did not mention the objection. The most important thing is the objection, that someone says: how did he argue against them with what he claimed for himself? We say: this claim is accompanied by evidence.
* What is derived from this verse: the permissibility of a person describing himself with praise for a beneficial purpose, like His saying: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾. This was also reported from the Prophet ﷺ, when he said: "I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say this without boasting."[[Narrated by at-Tirmidhi (3148) and Ibn Majah (4308), from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] And similar praise was also reported from the Companions, such as the saying of Ibn Mas'ud: "If I knew that anyone knew the Book of Allah better than I do, and that a camel could reach him, I would travel to him, or I would journey to him."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5002) and Muslim (2463/115), from Ibn Mas'ud.]] And similar things, but on the condition that the person's purpose in that is the benefit.
* And it is derived from this: that piety (taqwa) is not attributed to a created being, unlike obedience; based on His saying: ﴿"So fear Allah and obey me"﴾. There is no harm in my saying: I obeyed so-and-so. But it is not permissible to say: fear so-and-so, in the sense of the taqwa that entails humility.
* In this there is evidence of the sincerity of the Messengers to Allah in His saying: ﴿"And I do not ask you for any reward for it"﴾.
* And in it also: a person reckoning his deed with Allah, not as humiliation before Allah in this deed or as a favor upon Him by it, but reckoning it with Him in hope of His reward. Based on His saying: ﴿"My reward is only from the Lord of the worlds"﴾.
* And in this is evidence of the tyranny of 'Ad and their love of pride and grandeur, in what their prophet denounced them for: ﴿"Do you build on every high place a monument for no purpose?"﴾.
* And in it is evidence that a person should have a sound purpose behind his deed, especially a great and enormous work, and that his purpose not be vain or for show. Based on His saying: ﴿"you build in vain"﴾. This is the point of criticism: it is not that they build on every high place a monument, but that doing so is in vain, and this is the object of censure and blame.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 125–128 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 125] "Indeed, I am to you a messenger" means: sent to you from Allah, the Exalted. The placing of "to you" (lakum) first indicates exclusivity, meaning: sent specifically to you, i.e., every messenger is sent only to his own people.

His saying ﴿trustworthy﴾ means: one who possesses trustworthiness; Allah, the Exalted, has entrusted me with His message.

If someone says: these two descriptions, ﴿a trustworthy messenger﴾, are merely a claim, and they deny that he is a trustworthy messenger, rather they say that he is a liar..

His saying ﴿trustworthy﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 125]: that is, one who possesses trustworthiness; Allah, the Exalted, has entrusted me with His message.

If someone says: these two descriptions are ﴿a trustworthy messenger﴾ while they deny that he is a trustworthy messenger, rather they say that he is a liar and a traitor, so is the claim alone sufficient to establish proof against them? The answer: No. But this claim is supported by signs from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no messenger whom Allah sent except that he was given what led people to believe based on its like" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7274) and Muslim (152 / 239) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. So it is not merely a call; because a mere call is easy to reject, but it is a call supported and strengthened by Allah, the Exalted, with clear signs by which people believe. In this, it is as if, when he said with such certainty, ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 125], this statement made with certainty is evidence of the strength of his signs, and that he had with him signs that caused him to express himself with this decisive expression. In this is evidence that the message is the greatest proof of a person's trustworthiness, isn't it? Because had he not been trustworthy, Allah, the Exalted, would not have entrusted him with the revelation which contains the judgment of people to happiness and misery, and even the judgment of making lawful their wealth, their women, and their blood. So if the messengers, peace be upon them, were not the greatest of people in trustworthiness, Allah would not have entrusted them with this great revelation.
* Student: Could their saying be a claim, because they said, ﴿O Hud, you have brought us no clear evidence, and we will not leave our gods on your word﴾ [Hud 53].
* The Shaykh: Yes, denying these is obstinacy. ﴿So fear Allah and obey me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 126], returning in meaning to his saying ﴿Will you not fear Allah?﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 124]; meaning: since I am a trustworthy messenger, do what I command you of righteousness, and I urge you to it. ﴿Fear Allah and obey me﴾: he did not say "and fear me," because he does not possess any benefit or harm for himself, nor for anyone else. The duty of people toward the messengers is not to fear the messengers but to obey them. For this reason, no messenger is reported to have said to his people, "fear me"; rather, they command them to obey. As for fear, reverence and dread, to whom is it owed? To Allah, the Exalted: ﴿so fear Allah﴾.

This taqwa (fear of Allah; God-consciousness) has been explained to us many times as taking a shield against the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, and that this is the most comprehensive of what has been said about taqwa, and they have many expressions regarding it.

His saying ﴿and obey me﴾: What is obedience (ta'ah)? The origin of ta'ah is submission (al-infiqad), and from it their saying: "this she-camel is tame (tawʿ) to its owner," i.e., submissive and docile to him. It is also explained as conforming to a command. So we say: conforming to a command out of submission to the one who commands; for conforming to a command may be out of submission to the commander, and it may be out of compulsion, and the latter is not obedience.

﴿So fear Allah and obey me﴾: in this noble verse is the obligation of fearing Allah and the obligation of obeying His Messenger, because obedience to His Messenger is obedience to Him: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [An-Nisa' 80].

(﴿And I do not ask you for any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 127])
﴿And I do not ask you for it﴾: that is, for what I say to you, or ﴿for it﴾ meaning for conveying the message; the meanings are close. That is, I am not saying: give me something; rather I command you with that in which your good lies. Had I asked you a reward for that, you would have had a proof to refuse; but I do not ask you for any reward, meaning recompense and compensation, ﴿my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾.

(﴿my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾) In this is perfect sincerity; that is, I do not want a reward except from Allah, the Exalted.

In His saying ﴿only from the Lord of the worlds﴾, the scholars say that the particle "ʿalā" (upon/from) indicates obligation; that is, He did not say "my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds," but said ﴿upon the Lord of the worlds﴾. Is anything obligatory upon Allah, the Exalted?
The answer: As for us obligating Him, no; but as for Him obligating Himself out of generosity, there is no objection to this. Ibn al-Qayyim said:

*Nothing is due to the servants from Him as an obligation,*
*Yet He has made obligatory the great and lofty reward.*
*Nay, no deed is lost before Him*
*If it is with sincerity and excellence.*
*If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are blessed, it is by His bounty,*
*And praise belongs to the Bestower.*

And the verses that come after these three verses (...) are restrictive of previous verses:

*Nothing is due to the servants from Him as an obligation,*
*Nay, no effort is lost before Him.*
*If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are blessed, it is by His bounty,*
*And He is the Generous, the Vast.*

These two verses are absolute, but Ibn al-Qayyim said:

*Nothing is due to the servants from Him as an obligation,*
*Yet He has made obligatory the great and lofty reward.*

(Nay, no deed is lost before Him) he restricted it by his saying (if it is with sincerity and excellence). Excellence is following (the Sunnah). As for if it is not with sincerity and excellence, it is lost. ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [Al-Kahf 110].

He says: ﴿So fear Allah and obey me. (126) And I do not ask you for any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 126–127]. (﴿Do you build on every high place﴾: a high place; ﴿a sign﴾: a building as a landmark for passersby; ﴿you mock﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 128]: at those who pass by you and you ridicule them) to the end.

He says: ﴿Do you build on every high place a sign﴾. ﴿A sign﴾ means: a landmark. But is it a landmark on the road as the author said? This is possible, although the context does not support it, yet it is not excluded by it; but it is not supported by it. Or the intended meaning of ﴿a sign﴾ is: a sign of your strength and your power. This is the closer view, and for this reason He said ﴿on every high place﴾; meaning that you intend by these buildings to be a sign, an evidence and a proof of your strength. His saying ﴿you mock﴾: you take these as play, because you have no benefit in them except mere play and displaying greatness and displaying strength; and there is no doubt that a person displaying his strength is play and corruption.

Based on this, it becomes clear to us that those who try to reach the stars and launch these moons which you do not find on earth are exactly like the people of 'Ad; that is, the method is the same, though the style differs. They do these things as signs and as play, since they do not benefit from them in what they were created for. ﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth﴾ [Al-Baqarah 29], in the sky; but what is on the earth is created for us to benefit from directly, while what is in the sky is subjected to our interests, yet we do not benefit from it directly. So the beneficial thing we benefit from directly is what is on the earth.

For this reason some people say: why do you try to reach the sky while you are unable to solve your problems on earth? This is true, but it is merely play and boasting, and that we are strong, and that we have reached such-and-such; even though they are the people of Hud. And these contemporary people also lose enormous sums on these matters, so it becomes play, because everything in which a person exhausts his body, wealth and thought without benefit is play with no use. Rather, if he intends by it displaying greatness and arrogance over creation, it also becomes corruption; so it becomes a positive matter, not merely a negative one, yes positive because it is corruption. He is rejecting this matter upon them: ﴿Do you build on every high place a sign, mocking?﴾

As for what the author, may Allah have mercy on him, took—that they make landmarks for passersby so that when they pass by them they mock them—this is far from the context; although the context does not prohibit it, it does not support it. So the correct view in this verse is that they build great buildings showing their strength and power in play, because they benefit from them only in displaying greatness, and this is without doubt play. ﴿And you take for yourselves palaces﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 129], to the end.

If you reflect on the human being: the first human is the last human, or the last human is the first human, but the style differs. ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed. (29) And when they passed by them, they winked at one another. (30) And when they returned to their own people, they returned jesting. (31) And when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are misguided"﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 29–32].

These matters, applied to the present time, exist; but the word "misguided" (...) "backward" or "conservative" or the like; or is it the same thing? So the human being in reality—the mindset is the same, but the style differs in keeping with the times, or is it the same thing? And Allah knows best.

* Student: "You will certainly follow the ways of those before you" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7320) and Muslim (2669 / 6) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri]. Is it correct what some people say: that the animals in the time of Noah were fewer kinds than today, and that this is due to the mating of some of them producing other forms, and from them new forms are born?
* The Shaykh: Since the verse does not state either this or that: ﴿two of every pair﴾ [Hud 40]; meaning, of every one of the existing creatures. We do not know; there is no doubt the origin did not come into existence as a new origin, but perhaps, as you said, by reproduction or the mating of some of them with others they differ. Although they say: it is well known among them that what results from the mating of some (...) with others does not reproduce; whatever arose from reproduction does not reproduce. This is known among them, and for this reason the mule cannot (...). Yes indeed.
* Student: From where comes the abundance of mules?
* The Shaykh: From the mating of donkeys with mares.
* Student: Shaykh 'Abd al-Rahman said: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Ya-Sin 41]; he said that "the ship" includes even airplanes (...), and he said the proof is that it says ﴿We carried their offspring﴾ and did not say "We carried them."
* The Shaykh: Read the verses that come before it.
* Student: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth; We have brought it to life and brought forth from it grain, from which they eat. (33) And We placed therein gardens of palms and grapevines and caused to gush forth therein springs (34) That they may eat of its fruit and that which their hands have made. Then will they not be grateful? (35) Glorified is He who created all the pairs from what the earth grows and from themselves and from that which they do not know. (36) And a sign for them is the night; We remove from it the day, and they are in darkness. (37) And the sun runs toward its stationary point. That is the decree of the Exalted in Might, the Knowing. (38) And the moon—We have determined for it phases until it returns like the old dry date stalk. (39) It is not for the sun to reach the moon, nor does the night overtake the day; but each, in an orbit, is swimming. (40) And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship. (41)﴾ [Ya-Sin 33–41].
* The Shaykh: The truth is that what prevents this is His saying ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾, and "offspring" (dhurriyyah) comes later, does it not?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: How can it be a sign for them when they came before it? For this reason most of the exegetes disagree with this view. He says: ﴿their offspring﴾ means the offspring of their father, that is Noah, peace be upon him. Some said that "offspring" here means "fathers," but using "dhurriyyah" to mean "fathers" is far-fetched in the Arabic language. Rather, its use to mean "their offspring," i.e., the offspring from whom they arose, so the attribution is not to the offspring that arose from them, but to the offspring from which they arose, which is the offspring of their father Noah, "We carried them in the laden ship." This is more appropriate, because in reality, making it "a sign for them that We carried their offspring" refers to later offspring who came after, or it would be a sign for those who had died; this is far-fetched (...). The Shaykh's statement—I do not see any basis for it.
* Student: (...) it is only applied to airplanes, cars...
* The Shaykh: No, it may apply; because the whale (...) and for this Allah, the Exalted, limited means of conveyance to this: ﴿And He has made for you of the ships and cattle that which you ride﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 12]. So "the ship" is what we make, and "the cattle" is what Allah creates. But the point is that it being a sign for them while they are looking, and the offspring being after them.
* Student: He says: this address is to the later people, and their earlier offspring, the ones who were not found in the time of (...), were carried on what?
* The Shaykh: (...) the signs existing in his time. If we are carried on airplanes, cars and vessels, these would not be signs for those (earlier people). Moreover, the word "We carried" requires interpreting it as "We will carry." Then, if it is "We will carry," it would be a sign for them only in the sense of a promise from Allah, not something they witnessed.
* Student: Would it not be that these conveyances are a sign for you, and likewise, with the passing of time, a sign?
* The Shaykh: A sign for whom?
* Student: For your offspring; that you were carried upon them, and will be carried...
* The Shaykh: Yes, that does not contradict; but airplanes and cars—the offspring existing in the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him, how can ﴿that We carried their offspring﴾ apply to them except by interpreting it as "then We carry"? And if it is by interpreting it as "then We carry," it would not be a sign for them except in the sense that it is a promise from Allah and they trust in it. Allah, the Exalted, does not address these obstinate people with what His promise entails only; rather He addresses them with a sign they witness or which is known to them, such that they cannot deny it. In reality, this passed by me in the Shaykh's words, but it has no basis. The correct view is to say: ﴿We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾, meaning the offspring from which they descended. The attribution—as the grammarians say—is for the slightest connection; their fathers are "offspring" in relation to Noah. As for the claim that "offspring" comes in its literal meaning of "fathers" (...).
* In the story of Noah: ﴿My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. (117) So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 117–118], and so on. What is derived from this sentence?
* Student: The attribution of "people" to him.
* The Shaykh: That is, from every (...) ﴿My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. (117) So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment﴾.
* Student: First: seeking refuge in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, supplicating against them, and mentioning the reasons that led to the supplication against them.
* The Shaykh: In His saying?
* Student: ﴿Indeed my people have denied me. (117) So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment﴾.
* The Shaykh: This is supplication; is it among the etiquettes of supplication?
* Student: Among the etiquettes of supplication: first, he called upon Allah with the attribute of Lordship, and also mentioned the circumstances and the conditions to Allah, the Exalted...

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 26, verses 125–128 (part 2 of 2):

* The Shaykh: This means mentioning the circumstance that calls for the supplication.
* Student: ﴿He said, "My Lord, my people have denied me."﴾
* The Shaykh: No. It also means mentioning the thing requested. The one who supplicates sometimes mentions only the request, sometimes praises Allah along with mentioning the request, sometimes praises Allah and mentions his own situation and the request, and sometimes mentions only his own situation. ﴿"My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You might send down to me."﴾ [Al-Qasas: 24]. So the point is that among the etiquettes of supplication there are three things. What are they?
* Student: Seeking a means (tawassul) through the attributes of Allah, and also describing one's situation and the request.
* The Shaykh: What is the benefit of his saying ﴿"my people have denied me"﴾, in attributing the people to himself?
* Student: The benefit of attributing the people to him is that the proof is established against them to the greatest degree, because a prophet was sent to them from among them, to his own people, and a man from another tribe was not sent to them.
* The Shaykh: That means increasing the condemnation of them.
* Student: Increasing the condemnation of them.
* The Shaykh: Since they denied him while he was one of them. There is a second benefit in it as well.
* Student: Another benefit: so that it serves as an excuse before Him, that he did not ask for their destruction.
* The Shaykh: That means magnifying the trial upon him, because when his own people deny him it becomes harder and greater for him. So in it is the magnifying of the trial upon him, so that it becomes the strongest means of his supplication being answered. What is derived from his saying: ﴿"So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment"﴾?
* Student: It means: judge between them.
* The Shaykh: Its meaning is that He judges between them by destroying them. Is such a supplication permissible?
* Student: Yes, because they deserve destruction.
* The Shaykh: That means it is derived from it that when despair sets in, it is permissible for a person to supplicate against those who deny and obstinately oppose. Did our Sharia approve of this or oppose it?
* Student: Our Sharia approved it. It only preferred not supplicating against them, unless it is established that they will not go straight and will not believe, in which case supplication is prescribed.
* The Shaykh: What is your evidence?
* Student: The evidence for the non-legitimacy of supplicating except when there is a need is: "The Prophet ﷺ, when Gabriel came down to him and said: If you wish, I will close the two mountains upon them. He said: 'Rather, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins someone who worships Allah alone, associating nothing with Him.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3231) and Muslim (1795/111), from 'A'isha, with the wording: "The angel of the mountains called to me and greeted me, then said: O Muhammad, Allah has heard the words of your people to you, and I am the angel of the mountains, and your Lord has sent me to you so that you may command me with your command. What do you wish? If you wish, I will close the two mountains upon them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: 'Rather, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins those who worship Allah alone, associating nothing with Him.'"]] Or as the Prophet ﷺ said, this noble Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, but he did not prohibit...that a person supplicates against...
* The Shaykh: Now I am asking?
* Student: So the prescribed course is not to supplicate...
* The Shaykh: Does that mean our Sharia came contrary to that?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Alright, is there a more explicit evidence than this?
* Student: The explicit evidence on that is: "The Prophet ﷺ, when he supplicated against them in the prayer, saying: 'O Allah, destroy so-and-so bin so-and-so, and so-and-so bin so-and-so,' the verse was revealed to him: ﴿"You have no part in the affair, whether He turns to them in forgiveness or punishes them, for indeed they are wrongdoers."﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 128], so he refrained from them."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (4560) and Muslim (675/294), from Abu Hurayrah: ...and he would say in some of his prayers, in the dawn prayer, "O Allah, curse so-and-so and so-and-so," referring to some tribes of the Arabs, until Allah revealed ﴿"You have no part in the affair"﴾, the verse. The wording is al-Bukhari's.]]
* The Shaykh: Yes. Our Sharia commanded patience and not supplicating against them. But it may be said: the Sharia of Noah, upon him be prayers and peace, differs from our Sharia, and there is no objection to Sharias differing on such a matter. Also, Noah, upon him be prayers and peace, remained among his people for how long? A thousand years less fifty years, and every time he called them they increased in obstinacy and arrogance, so there remained no benefit in (...) against them. But he did not emigrate from them as Jonah did; rather he remained among them until Allah seized them.
* Student: The fact that the Messenger ﷺ supplicated against the leaders of Quraysh, does that not indicate the permissibility of supplicating against...
* The Shaykh: Yes, but in the end he was prohibited from it. Nor did he supplicate against the leaders of Quraysh in Makkah before he emigrated. In the end he was prohibited; that is: ﴿"You have no part in the affair"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 128] (...).
What is derived from His saying: ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 119]?
* Student: The command includes (...) the salvation of the believers and those who boarded with them in the ship from among the animals.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it means a choice from Him that Allah, glorified and exalted, saved those with him from the believers in response to his supplication, and He also saved others that they need for their existence: ﴿"two of every kind, two of each"﴾ [Hud: 40].
Is it derived from the noble verse that the ship was loaded (with its cargo of creatures)?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: From where?
* Student: ﴿"and those with him in the laden ship"﴾. First He described it as laden, then the ship is defined with the article "al-", which is for definiteness...
* The Shaykh: The one that indicates perfection, meaning.
* Student: Perfection, yes.
* The Shaykh: And that it is laden also indicates its strength, because what is not strong, if it were loaded, would sink and be destroyed.
* Student: Then His saying: ﴿"So We saved him and those with him"﴾ means many, certainly.
* The Shaykh: No, the discussion is about the laden ship, meaning filled, and despite that it held steady, and Allah saved through it those with him.
Now in the story of Hud, first: Hud, upon him be prayers and peace, was among a tribe called 'Ad, and their dwellings were located where?
* Student: In al-Ahqaf.
* The Shaykh: Yes. And for what were they known?
* Student: They were known for strength and tyranny, to the point that they said: ﴿"Who is mightier than us in strength?"﴾ [Fussilat: 15], as mentioned in the Qur'an.
* The Shaykh: Well said. What is derived from His saying: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾?
* Student: That the message includes trustworthiness, because a human being, who is a man, does not send anyone except one whom he trusts, so how about the Creator?!
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. That means it is derived from this that all the bearers of messages are trustworthy; that is, sending cannot be sound except with a trustworthy person who is relied upon.
We raised an objection to this. What is the objection?
* Student: That if the messenger, or the one sent, is trustworthy, it is not necessary to believe him, because we know him by his trustworthiness, except by a proof or a sign that indicates his message (...) by his trustworthiness rather than the sign or miracle that indicates...
* The Shaykh: No, that is not an objection. We raised an objection regarding His saying: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾.
* Student: The restriction, we said: the exclusivity is for him...
* The Shaykh: No, we raised an objection, we made clear what it is, and we answered it.
* Student: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes. We said: this is a claim from him that it is so. They say: you are not a messenger and you are not trustworthy, rather they denied him. So how can this statement be made into an argument: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger (125). So fear Allah"﴾, so that because I am a trustworthy messenger, you should fear Allah?
* Student: He does not mention that, rather the signs.
* The Shaykh: Yes. We said: this claim is not a bare claim. You only mentioned the answer and did not mention the objection. The most important thing is the objection, that someone says: how did he argue against them with what he claimed for himself? We say: this claim is accompanied by evidence.
* What is derived from this verse: the permissibility of a person describing himself with praise for a beneficial purpose, like His saying: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾. This was also reported from the Prophet ﷺ, when he said: "I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say this without boasting."[[Narrated by at-Tirmidhi (3148) and Ibn Majah (4308), from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] And similar praise was also reported from the Companions, such as the saying of Ibn Mas'ud: "If I knew that anyone knew the Book of Allah better than I do, and that a camel could reach him, I would travel to him, or I would journey to him."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5002) and Muslim (2463/115), from Ibn Mas'ud.]] And similar things, but on the condition that the person's purpose in that is the benefit.
* And it is derived from this: that piety (taqwa) is not attributed to a created being, unlike obedience; based on His saying: ﴿"So fear Allah and obey me"﴾. There is no harm in my saying: I obeyed so-and-so. But it is not permissible to say: fear so-and-so, in the sense of the taqwa that entails humility.
* In this there is evidence of the sincerity of the Messengers to Allah in His saying: ﴿"And I do not ask you for any reward for it"﴾.
* And in it also: a person reckoning his deed with Allah, not as humiliation before Allah in this deed or as a favor upon Him by it, but reckoning it with Him in hope of His reward. Based on His saying: ﴿"My reward is only from the Lord of the worlds"﴾.
* And in this is evidence of the tyranny of 'Ad and their love of pride and grandeur, in what their prophet denounced them for: ﴿"Do you build on every high place a monument for no purpose?"﴾.
* And in it is evidence that a person should have a sound purpose behind his deed, especially a great and enormous work, and that his purpose not be vain or for show. Based on His saying: ﴿"you build in vain"﴾. This is the point of criticism: it is not that they build on every high place a monument, but that doing so is in vain, and this is the object of censure and blame.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 125–128 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 125] "Indeed, I am to you a messenger" means: sent to you from Allah, the Exalted. The placing of "to you" (lakum) first indicates exclusivity, meaning: sent specifically to you, i.e., every messenger is sent only to his own people.

His saying ﴿trustworthy﴾ means: one who possesses trustworthiness; Allah, the Exalted, has entrusted me with His message.

If someone says: these two descriptions, ﴿a trustworthy messenger﴾, are merely a claim, and they deny that he is a trustworthy messenger, rather they say that he is a liar..

His saying ﴿trustworthy﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 125]: that is, one who possesses trustworthiness; Allah, the Exalted, has entrusted me with His message.

If someone says: these two descriptions are ﴿a trustworthy messenger﴾ while they deny that he is a trustworthy messenger, rather they say that he is a liar and a traitor, so is the claim alone sufficient to establish proof against them? The answer: No. But this claim is supported by signs from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no messenger whom Allah sent except that he was given what led people to believe based on its like" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7274) and Muslim (152 / 239) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. So it is not merely a call; because a mere call is easy to reject, but it is a call supported and strengthened by Allah, the Exalted, with clear signs by which people believe. In this, it is as if, when he said with such certainty, ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 125], this statement made with certainty is evidence of the strength of his signs, and that he had with him signs that caused him to express himself with this decisive expression. In this is evidence that the message is the greatest proof of a person's trustworthiness, isn't it? Because had he not been trustworthy, Allah, the Exalted, would not have entrusted him with the revelation which contains the judgment of people to happiness and misery, and even the judgment of making lawful their wealth, their women, and their blood. So if the messengers, peace be upon them, were not the greatest of people in trustworthiness, Allah would not have entrusted them with this great revelation.
* Student: Could their saying be a claim, because they said, ﴿O Hud, you have brought us no clear evidence, and we will not leave our gods on your word﴾ [Hud 53].
* The Shaykh: Yes, denying these is obstinacy. ﴿So fear Allah and obey me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 126], returning in meaning to his saying ﴿Will you not fear Allah?﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 124]; meaning: since I am a trustworthy messenger, do what I command you of righteousness, and I urge you to it. ﴿Fear Allah and obey me﴾: he did not say "and fear me," because he does not possess any benefit or harm for himself, nor for anyone else. The duty of people toward the messengers is not to fear the messengers but to obey them. For this reason, no messenger is reported to have said to his people, "fear me"; rather, they command them to obey. As for fear, reverence and dread, to whom is it owed? To Allah, the Exalted: ﴿so fear Allah﴾.

This taqwa (fear of Allah; God-consciousness) has been explained to us many times as taking a shield against the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, and that this is the most comprehensive of what has been said about taqwa, and they have many expressions regarding it.

His saying ﴿and obey me﴾: What is obedience (ta'ah)? The origin of ta'ah is submission (al-infiqad), and from it their saying: "this she-camel is tame (tawʿ) to its owner," i.e., submissive and docile to him. It is also explained as conforming to a command. So we say: conforming to a command out of submission to the one who commands; for conforming to a command may be out of submission to the commander, and it may be out of compulsion, and the latter is not obedience.

﴿So fear Allah and obey me﴾: in this noble verse is the obligation of fearing Allah and the obligation of obeying His Messenger, because obedience to His Messenger is obedience to Him: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [An-Nisa' 80].

(﴿And I do not ask you for any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 127])
﴿And I do not ask you for it﴾: that is, for what I say to you, or ﴿for it﴾ meaning for conveying the message; the meanings are close. That is, I am not saying: give me something; rather I command you with that in which your good lies. Had I asked you a reward for that, you would have had a proof to refuse; but I do not ask you for any reward, meaning recompense and compensation, ﴿my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾.

(﴿my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾) In this is perfect sincerity; that is, I do not want a reward except from Allah, the Exalted.

In His saying ﴿only from the Lord of the worlds﴾, the scholars say that the particle "ʿalā" (upon/from) indicates obligation; that is, He did not say "my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds," but said ﴿upon the Lord of the worlds﴾. Is anything obligatory upon Allah, the Exalted?
The answer: As for us obligating Him, no; but as for Him obligating Himself out of generosity, there is no objection to this. Ibn al-Qayyim said:

*Nothing is due to the servants from Him as an obligation,*
*Yet He has made obligatory the great and lofty reward.*
*Nay, no deed is lost before Him*
*If it is with sincerity and excellence.*
*If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are blessed, it is by His bounty,*
*And praise belongs to the Bestower.*

And the verses that come after these three verses (...) are restrictive of previous verses:

*Nothing is due to the servants from Him as an obligation,*
*Nay, no effort is lost before Him.*
*If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are blessed, it is by His bounty,*
*And He is the Generous, the Vast.*

These two verses are absolute, but Ibn al-Qayyim said:

*Nothing is due to the servants from Him as an obligation,*
*Yet He has made obligatory the great and lofty reward.*

(Nay, no deed is lost before Him) he restricted it by his saying (if it is with sincerity and excellence). Excellence is following (the Sunnah). As for if it is not with sincerity and excellence, it is lost. ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [Al-Kahf 110].

He says: ﴿So fear Allah and obey me. (126) And I do not ask you for any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 126–127]. (﴿Do you build on every high place﴾: a high place; ﴿a sign﴾: a building as a landmark for passersby; ﴿you mock﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 128]: at those who pass by you and you ridicule them) to the end.

He says: ﴿Do you build on every high place a sign﴾. ﴿A sign﴾ means: a landmark. But is it a landmark on the road as the author said? This is possible, although the context does not support it, yet it is not excluded by it; but it is not supported by it. Or the intended meaning of ﴿a sign﴾ is: a sign of your strength and your power. This is the closer view, and for this reason He said ﴿on every high place﴾; meaning that you intend by these buildings to be a sign, an evidence and a proof of your strength. His saying ﴿you mock﴾: you take these as play, because you have no benefit in them except mere play and displaying greatness and displaying strength; and there is no doubt that a person displaying his strength is play and corruption.

Based on this, it becomes clear to us that those who try to reach the stars and launch these moons which you do not find on earth are exactly like the people of 'Ad; that is, the method is the same, though the style differs. They do these things as signs and as play, since they do not benefit from them in what they were created for. ﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth﴾ [Al-Baqarah 29], in the sky; but what is on the earth is created for us to benefit from directly, while what is in the sky is subjected to our interests, yet we do not benefit from it directly. So the beneficial thing we benefit from directly is what is on the earth.

For this reason some people say: why do you try to reach the sky while you are unable to solve your problems on earth? This is true, but it is merely play and boasting, and that we are strong, and that we have reached such-and-such; even though they are the people of Hud. And these contemporary people also lose enormous sums on these matters, so it becomes play, because everything in which a person exhausts his body, wealth and thought without benefit is play with no use. Rather, if he intends by it displaying greatness and arrogance over creation, it also becomes corruption; so it becomes a positive matter, not merely a negative one, yes positive because it is corruption. He is rejecting this matter upon them: ﴿Do you build on every high place a sign, mocking?﴾

As for what the author, may Allah have mercy on him, took—that they make landmarks for passersby so that when they pass by them they mock them—this is far from the context; although the context does not prohibit it, it does not support it. So the correct view in this verse is that they build great buildings showing their strength and power in play, because they benefit from them only in displaying greatness, and this is without doubt play. ﴿And you take for yourselves palaces﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 129], to the end.

If you reflect on the human being: the first human is the last human, or the last human is the first human, but the style differs. ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed. (29) And when they passed by them, they winked at one another. (30) And when they returned to their own people, they returned jesting. (31) And when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are misguided"﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 29–32].

These matters, applied to the present time, exist; but the word "misguided" (...) "backward" or "conservative" or the like; or is it the same thing? So the human being in reality—the mindset is the same, but the style differs in keeping with the times, or is it the same thing? And Allah knows best.

* Student: "You will certainly follow the ways of those before you" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7320) and Muslim (2669 / 6) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri]. Is it correct what some people say: that the animals in the time of Noah were fewer kinds than today, and that this is due to the mating of some of them producing other forms, and from them new forms are born?
* The Shaykh: Since the verse does not state either this or that: ﴿two of every pair﴾ [Hud 40]; meaning, of every one of the existing creatures. We do not know; there is no doubt the origin did not come into existence as a new origin, but perhaps, as you said, by reproduction or the mating of some of them with others they differ. Although they say: it is well known among them that what results from the mating of some (...) with others does not reproduce; whatever arose from reproduction does not reproduce. This is known among them, and for this reason the mule cannot (...). Yes indeed.
* Student: From where comes the abundance of mules?
* The Shaykh: From the mating of donkeys with mares.
* Student: Shaykh 'Abd al-Rahman said: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Ya-Sin 41]; he said that "the ship" includes even airplanes (...), and he said the proof is that it says ﴿We carried their offspring﴾ and did not say "We carried them."
* The Shaykh: Read the verses that come before it.
* Student: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth; We have brought it to life and brought forth from it grain, from which they eat. (33) And We placed therein gardens of palms and grapevines and caused to gush forth therein springs (34) That they may eat of its fruit and that which their hands have made. Then will they not be grateful? (35) Glorified is He who created all the pairs from what the earth grows and from themselves and from that which they do not know. (36) And a sign for them is the night; We remove from it the day, and they are in darkness. (37) And the sun runs toward its stationary point. That is the decree of the Exalted in Might, the Knowing. (38) And the moon—We have determined for it phases until it returns like the old dry date stalk. (39) It is not for the sun to reach the moon, nor does the night overtake the day; but each, in an orbit, is swimming. (40) And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship. (41)﴾ [Ya-Sin 33–41].
* The Shaykh: The truth is that what prevents this is His saying ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾, and "offspring" (dhurriyyah) comes later, does it not?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: How can it be a sign for them when they came before it? For this reason most of the exegetes disagree with this view. He says: ﴿their offspring﴾ means the offspring of their father, that is Noah, peace be upon him. Some said that "offspring" here means "fathers," but using "dhurriyyah" to mean "fathers" is far-fetched in the Arabic language. Rather, its use to mean "their offspring," i.e., the offspring from whom they arose, so the attribution is not to the offspring that arose from them, but to the offspring from which they arose, which is the offspring of their father Noah, "We carried them in the laden ship." This is more appropriate, because in reality, making it "a sign for them that We carried their offspring" refers to later offspring who came after, or it would be a sign for those who had died; this is far-fetched (...). The Shaykh's statement—I do not see any basis for it.
* Student: (...) it is only applied to airplanes, cars...
* The Shaykh: No, it may apply; because the whale (...) and for this Allah, the Exalted, limited means of conveyance to this: ﴿And He has made for you of the ships and cattle that which you ride﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 12]. So "the ship" is what we make, and "the cattle" is what Allah creates. But the point is that it being a sign for them while they are looking, and the offspring being after them.
* Student: He says: this address is to the later people, and their earlier offspring, the ones who were not found in the time of (...), were carried on what?
* The Shaykh: (...) the signs existing in his time. If we are carried on airplanes, cars and vessels, these would not be signs for those (earlier people). Moreover, the word "We carried" requires interpreting it as "We will carry." Then, if it is "We will carry," it would be a sign for them only in the sense of a promise from Allah, not something they witnessed.
* Student: Would it not be that these conveyances are a sign for you, and likewise, with the passing of time, a sign?
* The Shaykh: A sign for whom?
* Student: For your offspring; that you were carried upon them, and will be carried...
* The Shaykh: Yes, that does not contradict; but airplanes and cars—the offspring existing in the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him, how can ﴿that We carried their offspring﴾ apply to them except by interpreting it as "then We carry"? And if it is by interpreting it as "then We carry," it would not be a sign for them except in the sense that it is a promise from Allah and they trust in it. Allah, the Exalted, does not address these obstinate people with what His promise entails only; rather He addresses them with a sign they witness or which is known to them, such that they cannot deny it. In reality, this passed by me in the Shaykh's words, but it has no basis. The correct view is to say: ﴿We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾, meaning the offspring from which they descended. The attribution—as the grammarians say—is for the slightest connection; their fathers are "offspring" in relation to Noah. As for the claim that "offspring" comes in its literal meaning of "fathers" (...).
* In the story of Noah: ﴿My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. (117) So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 117–118], and so on. What is derived from this sentence?
* Student: The attribution of "people" to him.
* The Shaykh: That is, from every (...) ﴿My Lord, indeed my people have denied me. (117) So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment﴾.
* Student: First: seeking refuge in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, supplicating against them, and mentioning the reasons that led to the supplication against them.
* The Shaykh: In His saying?
* Student: ﴿Indeed my people have denied me. (117) So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment﴾.
* The Shaykh: This is supplication; is it among the etiquettes of supplication?
* Student: Among the etiquettes of supplication: first, he called upon Allah with the attribute of Lordship, and also mentioned the circumstances and the conditions to Allah, the Exalted...

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 26, verses 125–128 (part 2 of 2):

* The Shaykh: This means mentioning the circumstance that calls for the supplication.
* Student: ﴿He said, "My Lord, my people have denied me."﴾
* The Shaykh: No. It also means mentioning the thing requested. The one who supplicates sometimes mentions only the request, sometimes praises Allah along with mentioning the request, sometimes praises Allah and mentions his own situation and the request, and sometimes mentions only his own situation. ﴿"My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You might send down to me."﴾ [Al-Qasas: 24]. So the point is that among the etiquettes of supplication there are three things. What are they?
* Student: Seeking a means (tawassul) through the attributes of Allah, and also describing one's situation and the request.
* The Shaykh: What is the benefit of his saying ﴿"my people have denied me"﴾, in attributing the people to himself?
* Student: The benefit of attributing the people to him is that the proof is established against them to the greatest degree, because a prophet was sent to them from among them, to his own people, and a man from another tribe was not sent to them.
* The Shaykh: That means increasing the condemnation of them.
* Student: Increasing the condemnation of them.
* The Shaykh: Since they denied him while he was one of them. There is a second benefit in it as well.
* Student: Another benefit: so that it serves as an excuse before Him, that he did not ask for their destruction.
* The Shaykh: That means magnifying the trial upon him, because when his own people deny him it becomes harder and greater for him. So in it is the magnifying of the trial upon him, so that it becomes the strongest means of his supplication being answered. What is derived from his saying: ﴿"So judge between me and them with a decisive judgment"﴾?
* Student: It means: judge between them.
* The Shaykh: Its meaning is that He judges between them by destroying them. Is such a supplication permissible?
* Student: Yes, because they deserve destruction.
* The Shaykh: That means it is derived from it that when despair sets in, it is permissible for a person to supplicate against those who deny and obstinately oppose. Did our Sharia approve of this or oppose it?
* Student: Our Sharia approved it. It only preferred not supplicating against them, unless it is established that they will not go straight and will not believe, in which case supplication is prescribed.
* The Shaykh: What is your evidence?
* Student: The evidence for the non-legitimacy of supplicating except when there is a need is: "The Prophet ﷺ, when Gabriel came down to him and said: If you wish, I will close the two mountains upon them. He said: 'Rather, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins someone who worships Allah alone, associating nothing with Him.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3231) and Muslim (1795/111), from 'A'isha, with the wording: "The angel of the mountains called to me and greeted me, then said: O Muhammad, Allah has heard the words of your people to you, and I am the angel of the mountains, and your Lord has sent me to you so that you may command me with your command. What do you wish? If you wish, I will close the two mountains upon them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: 'Rather, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins those who worship Allah alone, associating nothing with Him.'"]] Or as the Prophet ﷺ said, this noble Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, but he did not prohibit...that a person supplicates against...
* The Shaykh: Now I am asking?
* Student: So the prescribed course is not to supplicate...
* The Shaykh: Does that mean our Sharia came contrary to that?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Alright, is there a more explicit evidence than this?
* Student: The explicit evidence on that is: "The Prophet ﷺ, when he supplicated against them in the prayer, saying: 'O Allah, destroy so-and-so bin so-and-so, and so-and-so bin so-and-so,' the verse was revealed to him: ﴿"You have no part in the affair, whether He turns to them in forgiveness or punishes them, for indeed they are wrongdoers."﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 128], so he refrained from them."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (4560) and Muslim (675/294), from Abu Hurayrah: ...and he would say in some of his prayers, in the dawn prayer, "O Allah, curse so-and-so and so-and-so," referring to some tribes of the Arabs, until Allah revealed ﴿"You have no part in the affair"﴾, the verse. The wording is al-Bukhari's.]]
* The Shaykh: Yes. Our Sharia commanded patience and not supplicating against them. But it may be said: the Sharia of Noah, upon him be prayers and peace, differs from our Sharia, and there is no objection to Sharias differing on such a matter. Also, Noah, upon him be prayers and peace, remained among his people for how long? A thousand years less fifty years, and every time he called them they increased in obstinacy and arrogance, so there remained no benefit in (...) against them. But he did not emigrate from them as Jonah did; rather he remained among them until Allah seized them.
* Student: The fact that the Messenger ﷺ supplicated against the leaders of Quraysh, does that not indicate the permissibility of supplicating against...
* The Shaykh: Yes, but in the end he was prohibited from it. Nor did he supplicate against the leaders of Quraysh in Makkah before he emigrated. In the end he was prohibited; that is: ﴿"You have no part in the affair"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 128] (...).
What is derived from His saying: ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 119]?
* Student: The command includes (...) the salvation of the believers and those who boarded with them in the ship from among the animals.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it means a choice from Him that Allah, glorified and exalted, saved those with him from the believers in response to his supplication, and He also saved others that they need for their existence: ﴿"two of every kind, two of each"﴾ [Hud: 40].
Is it derived from the noble verse that the ship was loaded (with its cargo of creatures)?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: From where?
* Student: ﴿"and those with him in the laden ship"﴾. First He described it as laden, then the ship is defined with the article "al-", which is for definiteness...
* The Shaykh: The one that indicates perfection, meaning.
* Student: Perfection, yes.
* The Shaykh: And that it is laden also indicates its strength, because what is not strong, if it were loaded, would sink and be destroyed.
* Student: Then His saying: ﴿"So We saved him and those with him"﴾ means many, certainly.
* The Shaykh: No, the discussion is about the laden ship, meaning filled, and despite that it held steady, and Allah saved through it those with him.
Now in the story of Hud, first: Hud, upon him be prayers and peace, was among a tribe called 'Ad, and their dwellings were located where?
* Student: In al-Ahqaf.
* The Shaykh: Yes. And for what were they known?
* Student: They were known for strength and tyranny, to the point that they said: ﴿"Who is mightier than us in strength?"﴾ [Fussilat: 15], as mentioned in the Qur'an.
* The Shaykh: Well said. What is derived from His saying: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾?
* Student: That the message includes trustworthiness, because a human being, who is a man, does not send anyone except one whom he trusts, so how about the Creator?!
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. That means it is derived from this that all the bearers of messages are trustworthy; that is, sending cannot be sound except with a trustworthy person who is relied upon.
We raised an objection to this. What is the objection?
* Student: That if the messenger, or the one sent, is trustworthy, it is not necessary to believe him, because we know him by his trustworthiness, except by a proof or a sign that indicates his message (...) by his trustworthiness rather than the sign or miracle that indicates...
* The Shaykh: No, that is not an objection. We raised an objection regarding His saying: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾.
* Student: The restriction, we said: the exclusivity is for him...
* The Shaykh: No, we raised an objection, we made clear what it is, and we answered it.
* Student: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes. We said: this is a claim from him that it is so. They say: you are not a messenger and you are not trustworthy, rather they denied him. So how can this statement be made into an argument: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger (125). So fear Allah"﴾, so that because I am a trustworthy messenger, you should fear Allah?
* Student: He does not mention that, rather the signs.
* The Shaykh: Yes. We said: this claim is not a bare claim. You only mentioned the answer and did not mention the objection. The most important thing is the objection, that someone says: how did he argue against them with what he claimed for himself? We say: this claim is accompanied by evidence.
* What is derived from this verse: the permissibility of a person describing himself with praise for a beneficial purpose, like His saying: ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾.
