* The student: ﴿And do not obey the command of the extravagant, (151) Who cause corruption on earth and do not reform. (152) They said, "You are only of those bewitched. (153) You are not but a human like us, so bring a sign, if you should be of the truthful." (154) He said, "This is a she-camel; for her is a share of water, and for you is a share of water on a known day. (155) And do not touch her with harm, lest there seize you the punishment of a tremendous day." (156) But they hamstrung her, and so they became regretful. (157) So the punishment seized them. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers. (158) And indeed, your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 151–159].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan.

Regarding what remains of the story of Hud, peace be upon him: * It is derived from it that the caller (da'i) should remind the one he calls of Allah's blessings upon him. From where is this derived?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes. What is the wisdom in reminding him of blessings?

* Student: Because blessings require gratitude and obedience to the Bestower.

* Shaykh: Yes, and also, rationally, this is implied: whoever does good to you, it is rationally good that you obey him in what he commands you.

* And among the benefits of what was mentioned: these blessings with which Allah supplies the servant require that he fulfill taqwa of Allah, because His saying: ﴿And fear the One who has provided you with what you know﴾ makes the command to taqwa the consequence. So blessings should require the servant's taqwa toward his Lord, blessed and exalted, not arrogance, insolence, and distance from Allah. This is based on His saying: ﴿And fear the One who has provided you﴾, where He turned away from saying "fear Allah" to what was mentioned, indicating that this is a great cause for the obligation of taqwa.

* And among the benefits in the verse also: the clarification that the caller, when combining the mention of blessings, should combine the call (...). From where is this derived?

* Student: From His saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾.

* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾.

* And also in it: that when the situation is more fitting, it is appropriate not to state it explicitly; based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear﴾. He did not say: "You will be struck by a tremendous day," but said ﴿I fear﴾, like one anticipating it without certainty, because the situation requires that; and every situation has its own discourse.

* And in it is evidence that Allah, glorified and exalted, may seal the heart of the servant so that he does not benefit from admonition; based on His saying: ﴿It is all the same for us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers﴾. This is if the statement from him was not a lie. If it was a lie, there is no evidence in it for that; meaning, if the matter is true as they say, that they are alike whether they are admonished or not, then it indicates that the servant, may Allah protect us, when what he does covers his heart, will not benefit from admonition. But if it was a lie, it indicates the arrogance of these people and the severity of their haughtiness toward the truth.

* And in this is evidence, in the expression of His saying: ﴿Whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers﴾, of the eloquence of the Qur'an. From where is this derived (...)?

* Student: (...) then the second clause ﴿or are not among the admonishers﴾ means..

* Shaykh: "Or" is the counterpart to it.

* Student: "Or are you..".

* Shaykh: Among those who admonish.

* Student: Among those who admonish, or you are not one of them..

* Shaykh: ("You are not one of them") is present in ﴿or are not among the admonishers﴾.

* Student: Yes, indeed, it combined the two clauses in one verse.

* Shaykh: That is, it combined the two meanings in two words, because in reality there are four meanings: "you admonished or you did not admonish," "you were among the admonishers or you were not," in two words; because from each word it omitted what corresponds to it, the meaning of the other indicating it.

* And in the verse is evidence that the opponents of the messengers have no argument except clinging to what their predecessors were upon. From where is this derived?

* Student: ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the earlier ones﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the earlier ones﴾ according to the reading ﴿khuluq al-awwalin﴾, following what the author adopted. As for the second reading ﴿khalq al-awwalin﴾, it is derived from it: that these people did not limit themselves to denying their prophet, but went beyond to denying others as well, even though the earlier messengers had not demanded that of them. Yet, due to their obstinacy and arrogance, they denied even the earlier ones, so that they could say: this is not an innovated matter, but rather the practice of those who came before.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿So they denied him, and We destroyed them﴾. In this is evidence that denial is a cause of destruction. Therefore the believer who takes lessons from the stories of the earlier prophets should beware of this, i.e., of denial, because if he does it, he will be destroyed.

Then, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾, what has preceded applies.

Then he said to them: (﴿And fear Him who has provided you with what you know﴾, i.e., bestowed favours upon you). ﴿And fear Him who﴾: here he used a descriptive clause, because ﴿Who has provided you﴾ is a relative noun whose clause functions like a derived noun; meaning: "fear the One who supplies you," and a derived noun or active participle is an explicit description. Thus he moved from the attribute of divinity to the attribute of lordship that particularly reached them, namely ﴿Who has provided you﴾, because God's supplying His creatures with blessings is a requirement of lordship.

His saying ﴿Who has provided you with what you know﴾ also brings this description as a means of establishing the proof against them, for whoever has provided you with these blessings is more deserving of being feared. His saying ﴿with what you know﴾ is vague, because (mā, "what") is a relative pronoun, and a relative pronoun is vague and general. He then specified it with His saying ﴿He has provided you with livestock﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 133]. We have mentioned that among the benefits of specifying after a general statement, or clarifying after a vague one, are several benefits. Among its benefits, what are they? 
* Student: Alerting the addressee (...).
* Shaykh: How does it alert him?
* Student: If, for example, he reads ﴿He has provided you with what you know (132). He has provided you with livestock﴾, he feels at ease, then he is alerted if he was heedless, because the context has changed, moving from the vague to the clarified. It is clear that there is an alert in it.
Second, there is also an element of arousing interest, because a person loves to find out. When the matter is left vague to him and then becomes clear, he longs for it and it settles firmly in his mind.
* Shaykh: (...) the fixing of a thing in the mind, because when it comes vague, the mind yearns for it, and when it is explained to him afterward, it becomes firmly rooted. Good, what next?
* Student: (...) the judgment upon him.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, this is in the manifest noun in place of the pronoun.
* Student: It is not emphasis of this meaning.
* Shaykh: How is it emphasis?
* Student: Because its line in (...) he mentioned it explicitly, then emphasized it.
* Shaykh: You mean giving it attention?
* Student: Giving it attention.
* Shaykh: Giving it attention, yes. This is among its benefits: attention, because his leaving it vague and then clarifying it, or summarizing it and then detailing it, is so that the person longs for it (...) for it, meaning it is a matter that receives attention. Just as there is also emphasis in it, because it was mentioned twice: once vaguely and once in detail or clarified. So the benefits are three:
The first benefit: arousing the listener's or addressee's desire to understand this meaning.
The second: fixing the meaning firmly in the mind.
The third: showing that it is given attention.
The fourth: emphasizing it by mentioning it twice, once summarily and once in detail, or vaguely and then clearly.

His saying ﴿He has provided you with what you know﴾ also: he did not say "He has provided you with livestock and sons" from the outset. With respect to this verse specifically, he showed them that God has provided them with something they cannot deny, because they know it. He placed ﴿what you know﴾ before mentioning the blessings bestowed, in order to establish the proof against them: these are blessings clearly understood by them, or not? They are understood and known, so they cannot deny them. First: ﴿He has provided you with livestock and sons﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 133], and ﴿gardens and springs﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 134]. (Livestock, *an'ām*) is the plural of (*ni'am*), or the plural of (*na'am*), meaning camels. If you say that the plural of (*ni'mah*) is (*ni'am*), and the plural of *ni'am* is *an'ām*, then the intended meaning of *an'ām* becomes broader than camels, as though he says: "with many blessings."

His saying ﴿and sons﴾...
* Student: (...) cattle are among the livestock.
* Shaykh: It is well known that it refers to camels only, but when one says "the beasts of livestock" it includes all three: "A camel of red hue is better for you than..." [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (2942), and Muslim (2406/34), from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd.]]

He said: ﴿and sons﴾: male offspring. He singled out sons because they are more distinguished in a person's honour, and because their offspring form a tribe, whereas the children of daughters belong to others and do not form a tribe (...) a household.
His saying ﴿and gardens﴾: orchards; ﴿and springs﴾: rivers. This indicates that (...) of water, if there are orchards and there are rivers. Perhaps this is also suggested by the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): "The Hour will not come until the Arabian Peninsula returns to meadows and rivers" [[Narrated by Muslim (157/60), from Abū Hurayrah.]]. His saying "until it returns" refers to a return after a beginning. These *jannāt* are orchards, not merely a single garden, because it is not called *jannah* unless it has many trees and crops, such that whoever is in it is concealed and covered by it.

*'Uyūn* is the plural of *'ayn*. The author's statement that they are rivers is by consideration of their flowing; otherwise *'uyūn* are what gush forth from the earth, whereas rivers, as is well known, do not gush from the earth but come from rains, snow and other sources.

﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ (in this world and the Hereafter, if you disobey me); meaning: if you persist in what you are upon of disbelief in these great blessings, then I fear for you the punishment of that day. His saying ﴿tremendous﴾ is an attribute of the day. But he says "in this world and the Hereafter," describing this punishment as tremendous in this world relative to what is other than it, and its tremendousness in the Hereafter is clear, because it is greatest in the Hereafter. ﴿They said﴾ in reply after this reminder of blessings and this warning: the answer: ﴿It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers.﴾ I seek refuge in God! Great arrogance! ﴿All the same﴾ means "equal," and it is a predicate placed first; and ﴿whether you admonish﴾, this interrogative clause is interpreted as a verbal noun as subject placed after: i.e., your admonition and its absence are the same. This is one of the positions where it is interpreted as a verbal noun without a verbal particle, because here it is interpreted as a verbal noun even though an interrogative particle precedes it; after "same," this is how it is treated: it and what follows are interpreted as a noun. ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn 6]; i.e., your seeking forgiveness and its absence. ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah 6]; i.e., your warning and its absence.

Well, they say: ﴿It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers﴾, meaning: we will not heed your admonition at all. See how haughty they are! "Whether you have admonished in fact or have not been among the admonishers": it did not matter whether you abandon admonition or not, because they said: "It is the same for us whether you admonish or do not admonish, ﴿or you were not among the admonishers﴾." The commentator said "at all" (*aslan*), meaning: your being an admonisher is not our concern, nor whether you are an admonisher or not, nor whether you actually admonish us or do not; the whole matter is the same to us.

They said this because a person may not care about a preacher because he is not qualified, and may not care about him out of obstinacy. When they said ﴿or you were not among the admonishers﴾, this indicates that they were stubborn even if you were from among those who are not qualified to admonish, or you admonished while being of those qualified. In this there is a clear eloquence of the Qur'an: they said, "It is the same to us whether you admonish or do not admonish," but perhaps they might say that he does admonish but is not qualified. However, when they said ﴿or you were not among the admonishers﴾, meaning you were not of those deserving to be described by this attribute, the two clauses become almost complete in themselves: "whether you admonished or did not admonish; whether you were an admonisher or were not an admonisher." That is, pairing ﴿you admonished﴾, which indicates the action, with "you were not among the admonishers," which indicates the attribute of being an admonisher.

From this it is derived that in each clause what corresponds to the other has been omitted for brevity, since it is clear. What then is the implied sense? "Whether you admonished or did not admonish; whether you were an admonisher deserving that people turn to you and take from you, or were not an admonisher." This is the utmost of the eloquence of the Qur'an, and for them it is the utmost of arrogance and indifference to their admonition. Have you now understood the wisdom? That He said ﴿or you were not among the admonishers﴾ and did not say "or you did not admonish," so that from each clause or word is taken what corresponds to it, ﴿or you were not among the admonishers﴾.

(﴿In truth﴾ "mā," *in* here is negating), (﴿this﴾ which you threaten us with, ﴿is nothing but the fabrication of the former peoples﴾; i.e., their invention and lies), meaning that you, O Hūd, have brought us nothing but a matter fabricated by those before you, so they denied him and those before him as well, and said: "This is the custom of the ancients," their *khuluq* meaning their fabrication, invention and falsehood, just as God said about Abraham: ﴿and you invent a falsehood﴾ [al-'Ankabūt 17]; i.e., you fabricate it.

﴿This is nothing but the custom of the ancients﴾ (with *khalq*). In another reading with the *kh* and *l* vowelled, ﴿khuluq﴾, and this reading is Sab'iyyah (of the seven canonical readings), based on the author's rule: when he says "it is read" (*quri'a*), it refers to an irregular reading, and "in another reading" refers to one of the seven.

(i.e., what we are upon, namely that there is no resurrection, is nothing but the custom of the ancients; i.e., their nature and habit). The author, on the second reading, holds that the demonstrative refers not to Hūd's statement but to what they were upon; and on the reading *khuluq*, he holds that it refers to Hūd's statement. The context of the verse indicates that it refers to Hūd's statement, whether with a damma or a fatha on the *kh*. As for the fatha, it is clear: ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the ancients﴾. As for the damma, it is also clear: as though they say, "What you have brought is the custom of the ancients before you," i.e., their practice, the earlier prophets. On this view the reference of the demonstrative is one; but on the author's opinion, ﴿this is nothing but the custom of the ancients﴾ is meant as an argument they put forward: "We found our fathers on a religion, and we will remain upon what our fathers were upon." The verse is open to both, but the first is more apparent: first, because the two readings explain one another; second, because they intend to refute his statement, not to justify their conduct.

﴿This is nothing but the custom of the ancients. And we will not be punished﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 137–138]. This is a denial of his statement ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾; as though they say: "What you feared has no basis, so we will not be punished."

Reflect on this expression, emphasized with the *bi-* in His saying ﴿And we will not be punished﴾. They did not say "wa-mā naḥnu mu'adhdhabīn" (with an unemphasized construction) but used the descriptive ﴿bi-mu'adhdhabīn﴾ in a nominal sentence, to indicate the absolute negation of this; because the nominal sentence indicates the establishment of its predicate. Accordingly, they have denied that they would be punished and claimed that they would never be punished. ﴿And we will not be punished﴾. But this is as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The incapable one is he who follows his desires and wishes vain wishes against God" [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhī (2459) and Ibn Mājah (4260), from Shaddād ibn Aws.]]. These people, may God protect us, followed their desires and wished vain wishes against God, if they were believers in resurrection; we do not know, perhaps they were deniers of it, saying there is no resurrection, no reckoning and no punishment.

﴿So they denied him, and We destroyed them﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 139]; i.e., by this statement which came from them, the description applies to them: they denied Hūd, so they deserved the punishment. For this reason He used *fa-* (then): ﴿so We destroyed them﴾ in this world by the wind. ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers﴾. God destroyed them by the wind.

Among the wonders is that God, glorified and praised, destroyed them at a time when they were longing for mercy, for they had been afflicted with drought and famine and had remained for a period awaiting relief through rain. When God sent this wind, ﴿they saw it as a cloud approaching their valleys, and said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain"﴾ [al-Aḥqāf 24], so they rejoiced at it and thought relief was near, but it was relief for Hūd and vengeance upon them. God said: ﴿Rather, it is what you sought to hasten: a wind in which is a painful punishment (24), destroying everything by the command of its Lord, so that by morning nothing could be seen but their dwellings﴾ [al-Aḥqāf 24–25]. This wind which God sent upon 'Ād contains a sign of God, glorified and exalted: these strong, mighty people, proud of their strength over others, were destroyed by the gentlest of things, the wind. Then they were destroyed while hoping as well, because they noticed that when punishment comes while a person expects blessing, what is it? It is more severe; likewise when punishment comes while a person is in blessing, it is also more severe and more painful, may God protect us.

In His saying ﴿So We destroyed them﴾ to the end there is an admonition for us regarding what we sometimes hear of these destructive storms that uproot trees, ruin homes, destroy crops and destroy lives too. But, regrettably, many of us fit God's saying: ﴿And if they should see a piece of the sky falling, they would say: "A layered cloud"﴾ [al-Ṭūr 44]. This is a natural matter, nothing of note. People now hear of earthquakes, hear of these storms and hear of great floods, yet they do not attribute them to God's wrath, but attribute them to natural causes. Therefore a person is not affected by them at all, as though they were nothing. Whereas when we were young and heard that the earth had shaken upon someone, we trembled while we were safe in our homes, because no one told us: "This is a natural matter, this is something of no concern, this is an event that is bound to happen." Just as with the eclipse: in the past, when the moon was eclipsed (I remember it), people felt great awe and fear, and came in large numbers to the mosques, men and women, in prayer, weeping and fear. Now, no; it is as though it is nothing. You find one watching television for songs, and another listening to songs on the radio. Except that, thank God, the last time the moon was eclipsed this year, our media became somewhat more upright: they broadcast the eclipse prayer on television, people watched it, and they benefited from it greatly, because most of the foreigners in the Kingdom know nothing whatsoever about eclipses, since over there they do not pray; rather, we hear that they go out (...) sing (...).
* Student: Yes, they sing (...).
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Their saying: we have not benefited from the verse that they denied Hūd's message. This verse contains obstinacy. In other verses it is established that they also did not believe Hūd: ﴿And those were 'Ād, who denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant﴾ [Hūd 59].
* Shaykh: And they did not believe him out of obstinacy.
* Student: His saying: ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 135]: does this not indicate that it refers to the Day of Resurrection specifically, since I fear for you a tremendous punishment?
* Shaykh: No, even the day on which the punishment occurs in this world (...).
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: It is not necessary.
* Student: (...) there is no lightening in it.
* Shaykh: (...) because ﴿day﴾ here is not specified; if he had said "the punishment of the day," even if he said "the day," it could be generic.
* Student: On this basis, when the message reached them, it seems they were saying: ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the ancients﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 137].
* Shaykh: Yes, (...) in the people of Noah (...) in Surah al-A'rāf he made it explicit: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾ [al-A'rāf 69].
* Student: But He left them, for example, the succession on earth; all of the people of Noah were there, for example people from here and there from tribes.
* Shaykh: It is known that when the people of Noah perished, only their descendants remained (...), these are among them.
* Student: Meaning, from them; because they are all...

* Shaykh: No, not all of them. The apparent meaning is that people multiplied quickly, and Allah knows best. Of course you know that these people were saved by their faith, so they remained upon the truth for a long time, because they had not multiplied, nor had their desires divided them. So they remained upon the truth for a long time. Then, after that, this development occurred, people increased, and every nation came to need a messenger, so Allah sent a messenger.

* Student: (...) ﴿The 'Ad denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 123], (...) its wording: "The earlier ones denied the messengers," ﴿This is nothing but the custom (khuluq) of the earlier ones﴾ or ﴿the creation (khalq) of the earlier ones﴾.

* Shaykh: Yes. It supports that what is meant by khuluq is the custom of the earlier ones, the practice of earlier messengers (...). They too respond to his words; they do not justify their position. They mention his words as being fabricated (mukhtalaq), or as something imitated from others that has no basis.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: How?

* Student: ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication (ikhtilaq)﴾ [Sad 7].

* Shaykh: ﴿Ikhtilaq﴾; meaning: lying. (...) khalq carries the meaning of lying, and it carries the meaning of creating/originating.

* Student: What is the wisdom in some messengers or some nations being mentioned repeatedly in the Qur'an, while some messengers are never mentioned at all?

* Shaykh: Allah, glorified and exalted, only mentioned the messengers who surrounded the Arabs, those whose accounts they knew. But this is stronger. As for those in America, for example, and in the far reaches of Asia, none of them were mentioned. But we know that Allah sent messengers to them: ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24]. However, Allah, glorified and exalted, only mentioned from the messengers those who were around the Peninsula.

* Student: Does this not indicate that those mentioned in the Qur'an are superior to others?

* Shaykh: No, because those others were not mentioned, so we know nothing about them. Rather, the five possessors of resolve (ulu al-'azm) are without doubt superior to others.

* Student: (...) you did not discover it except recently.

* Shaykh: What we had not discovered except recently.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: The point is that those continents, they discovered them only recently, but they existed before; they existed long ago.

* Student: (...) recently.

* Shaykh: Yes. The point is that they, may Allah keep you safe, undoubtedly exist, and people live in them. It is mentioned that Shaykh al-Islam spoke about this and said: there must be someone on the opposite side of the surface of the earth (...), since the earth cannot be traversed without habitation.

* The student: ﴿And do not obey the command of the extravagant, (151) Who cause corruption on earth and do not reform. (152) They said, "You are only of those bewitched. (153) You are not but a human like us, so bring a sign, if you should be of the truthful." Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers. (158) And indeed, your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 151–159].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan.

* Shaykh: ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the earlier ones﴾ according to the reading ﴿khuluq al-awwalin﴾, following what the author adopted. As for the second reading ﴿khalq al-awwalin﴾, it is derived from it: that these people did not limit themselves to denying their prophet, but went beyond to denying others as well, even though the earlier messengers had not demanded that of them. Yet, due to their obstinacy and arrogance, they denied even the earlier ones, so that they could say: this is not an innovated matter, but rather the practice of those who came before.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿So they denied him, and We destroyed them﴾. In this is evidence that denial is a cause of destruction. Therefore the believer who takes lessons from the stories of the earlier prophets should beware of this, i.e., of denial, because if he does it, he will be destroyed.

Then, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾, what has preceded applies.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Thamūd denied the messengers.﴾ This is the third story that Allah, blessed and exalted, always mentions when recounting the stories of the prophets. They come in order after the people of Hūd: Hūd comes before Ṣāliḥ, and Ṣāliḥ after Hūd. So He says: ﴿Thamūd denied the messengers.﴾ Thamūd is the well-known tribe whose dwellings were in the north of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and they are now called Madā'in Ṣāliḥ, though originally they were called al-Ḥijr. Allah, blessed and exalted, had given these people strength, power, and skill in craftsmanship, and for this reason they were given a sign suited to their condition, which is the she-camel, as will be mentioned, Allah willing.

He says: ﴿Thamūd denied the messengers.﴾ They only denied one messenger, but we have already mentioned that the messengers came with one call, so denying one of them is a denial of the category in general. These people who deny a messenger did not deny him for his own person or self, but they denied him for his call, and this call brought by this specific messenger is a call common to all the messengers. Thus it is as though they denied the very category of this message, and it holds true of them that they are deniers of all the messengers.

﴿When their brother Ṣāliḥ said to them⦅﴾: The word ﴿إِذْ﴾ (idh, "when") here is either causal (lit. "because") or an adverbial clause indicating the time of the denial; that is, the denial took place in this story. ﴿When their brother Ṣāliḥ said to them: "Will you not be God-fearing?"﴾ He called him their brother despite the distance between believer and disbeliever, because of kinship by lineage, not brotherhood in religion.

﴿When their brother Ṣāliḥ said to them, "Will you not be God-fearing? (142) Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger. (143) So fear Allah and obey me."﴾ All these sentences have already been discussed, along with the objections raised concerning his saying: ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾ and the answer to them. (﴿And I do not ask you any wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾) All of this too has already been covered.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 26, verses 146–153:

He said: (﴿Will you be left secure in what is here,﴾ of goodness, ﴿among gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿and crops and palm trees with delicate spathes﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 146–148], soft and pliant.)

﴿Will you be left secure in what is here﴾: ﴿in what﴾ means "in that which"; ﴿here﴾ refers to their place, because their place is as Salih, upon him be prayers and peace, described it: ﴿gardens and springs, and crops and palm trees with delicate spathes﴾. The interrogative in His words ﴿Will you be left﴾ (istifham, interrogation) is for warning. That is, do you think you will be left? No, you will not be left. It is a negation that carries a warning.

His words ﴿Will you be left﴾ are in the passive voice (mabni lil-majhul), because the agent is known. Who is the agent? Allah, glorified and exalted. That is, will Allah leave you in what is here?

His words ﴿in what is here, secure﴾ and so on to the end are a reminder of Allah's blessing upon them, and that they cannot be left in this state without a command or a prohibition. This is like His saying: ﴿Does man think he will be left neglected?﴾ [al-Qiyamah 36], and ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun 115]. He said ﴿secure in what is here﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the waw in ﴿you will be left﴾, meaning while you are secure. The one who is secure (al-amin) is the one who is free from fear.

* In this there is evidence of their settlement in their homelands and their security. Security together with abundant provision are the ultimate blessings of this life.

He said: ﴿secure, among gardens and springs﴾. (Al-jannat) is the plural of jannah, which is orchards with many trees, because it covers (yastur) those within it. His words ﴿and springs﴾ is the plural of ('ayn), which is flowing water without the need for buckets or water-wheels. ﴿and crops and palm trees with delicate spathes﴾: this mentions the crops and palms after the gardens by way of ataf al-khass 'ala al-'amm (specific after general, conjunction of the particular over the general), for the sake of emphasis on them, since otherwise they are included within the gardens, because the crops are among them and so are the palms. ﴿palm trees with delicate spathes﴾: (tal') means what it sends forth. His words ﴿delicate﴾ are explained as (soft, pliant). And so it is, for the spathe of the palm is among the softest and most delicate of things. It has been said that al-hadim means al-nadid (arranged in layers), as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿For it are spathes arranged in layers, a provision for the servants﴾ [Qaf 10–11]. That is, it is arranged in order and not scattered, so that it is easy to take and pick.

His words ﴿palm trees with delicate spathes﴾: this clause, ﴿its spathes are delicate﴾, what is its place in i'rab (grammatical analysis)?

* Student: It is an adjectival description of the palm trees, in the genitive position.

* Shaykh: Yes, in the genitive position: ﴿and palm trees with delicate spathes﴾. The spathe was singled out over the other benefits of the palm despite its many benefits, because it is the ultimate of what is benefited from it. Otherwise there are many other benefits in it. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ compared the believer to it because of its abundant good and benefits. This is with regard to the crops and cultivation.

As for construction and dwellings, He said: (﴿And you carve homes out of the mountains, skilfully﴾ — insolent (fari-hin). In one reading it is ﴿fari-hin﴾, skilled.) ﴿And you carve homes out of the mountains﴾: the meaning of carving them from the mountains is that they make the house from the mountain itself. It does not mean that they carve stones and then build with them. No, rather they make the house itself from the mountain, shaping the mountain as they wish. This is evidence of their capability and of their complete knowledge of engineering, because the thing is not in front of you but is inside the rock, and mountains and boulders require strong thought: how to make it, how to shape it, (...), and how to make (...), and so on. This is evidence of their strength and their skill in engineering.

The word ﴿fari-hin﴾ means insolent. It is an adjective of the form (sifah mushabbahah, quality-attribute form). ﴿Fari-hin﴾ with the lengthened vowel is an active participle (ism fa'il), and the meaning intended is skill. The difference between the two readings has a benefit: the word combines both meanings. They would be characterized by both matters: insolence, according to the reading with the short vowel, and skill, according to the reading with the long vowel. This is one of the benefits of the variety of readings, since variety of readings has many benefits, among them this matter: that a single word comprises two meanings.

﴿Fari-hin﴾ [149], ﴿so fear Allah and obey me﴾. This sentence, as we said regarding the story of 'Ad, is either built upon what was mentioned, or it repeats what came before. On the first view it is ta'sis (establishing a new meaning), and on the second it is tawkid (emphasis). The situation is very important and requires that this phrase be repeated: the fear of Allah and obedience to the Messenger ﷺ.

﴿So fear Allah and obey me﴾ [150], ﴿and do not obey the command of the extravagant﴾ [151], ﴿who cause corruption in the land and do not reform﴾. This is a command and a prohibition: a command to fear Allah and obey Him, but a prohibition against obeying the command of the extravagant. Is "amr" (command) singular or is it the plural of "awamir" (commands)?

* Students: Awamir (commands).

* Shaykh: It is the singular of the commands; that is, do not obey their command. Why did he not say "do not obey them," when he said ﴿so fear Allah and obey me﴾, and did not say "and obey my command"? Here he said ﴿and do not obey the command of the extravagant who cause corruption in the land and do not reform.﴾ Would it not have been possible for him to say "and do not obey the extravagant in their corruption"?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, he forbids them from obeying.

* Student: Yes, the obedience to the command of the extravagant (...).

* Shaykh: Good (...).

* Student: That is, the elders of the people and the notables, and that he commands them so that it would be more eloquent than if he had said "do not obey them."

* Shaykh: Good. The saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said: Will you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah"?﴾ [Ghafir 28]. He did not say "Will you kill Musa." Why?

* Student: Because he is speaking indirectly, since he is concealing his faith, so he does not want them to know Musa (...) ﴿because he says, "My Lord is Allah"﴾.

* Shaykh: They know Musa..

* Student: They know Musa, but he distances the closeness of his relationship with Musa (...) "as for me, I do not know him" (...).

* Shaykh: If he had mentioned him by his proper name, it would have been said: this is a personal relationship between him and him. So he made him indefinite, as if he did not know him: ﴿a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah."﴾ This is similar to it. If he had said "do not obey the extravagant themselves," it might be said that this is out of enmity between him and them, so that he does not want them to be obeyed, and he commanded obedience to himself. But when he said "the command of the extravagant," it is as if he were saying: I am not concerned whether this comes from so-and-so or so-and-so; rather the matter is that it is a command from an extravagant person. This is what has become clear to me, in order to avoid the accusation that he does not want the extravagant themselves, since the prohibition of obeying them was directed toward their persons. So he made the prohibition against obeying their command, which is a command of extravagance and corruption.

His words ﴿the extravagant﴾ mean those who exceed the limit. The extravagant one is the one who goes beyond the limit. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Eat and drink, but do not be extravagant﴾ [al-A'raf 31]: do not exceed the limit in quantity or in quality.

Then He said ﴿who cause corruption in the land﴾. This description is clarifying (kashifah) and not restrictive (qayd), because every extravagant person causes corruption in the land, so the description is clarifying. His words ﴿they cause corruption in the land﴾ mean they are a cause of its corruption, or that sins themselves are corruption. That is, either they are corruption, so they corrupt by way of attributing the thing to its cause, or sins are a cause of corruption, or they are themselves corruption.

(﴿and do not reform﴾ by obedience to Allah), nor by anything else. In His words ﴿they cause corruption and do not reform﴾ there is evidence of (...) their corruption, and that there is no reform in them. The negation here is intended to deny reform while affirming the complete opposite, which is corruption: ﴿they cause corruption and do not reform﴾.

His words (by obedience to Allah): obedience itself is undoubtedly reform, and it is also a cause of reform, for obedience to Allah, exalted is He, is the cause of the righteousness of everything: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl 97]. And what was their answer? ﴿They said: You are only one of the bewitched﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 153]. They accused him of being bewitched. (Musahharin) is more emphatic than (mashur). Also their saying ﴿You are only﴾ is a restriction (hasr) covering all states: that is, your condition never departs from this description: ﴿You are only one of the bewitched.﴾

The author said: (Those who cast a great deal of magic, until it overcame their reason.) This, may Allah protect us, is their answer, just as many people have answered in this way. Indeed, every prophet has been told the like: ﴿Thus no messenger came to those before them except that they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ [al-Dhariyat 52]. That is because they have no proof. Every person who has no proof resorts only to abuse and insult, thinking that by this he will turn people away from his opponent, since he is unable to confront him. But the person who has a proof does not resort to insult and abuse. For this reason some scholars are criticized for their habit of abuse and insult toward their opponents, as is done by whom? Ibn Hazm, may Allah have mercy on him and pardon him. That is, if he had argued calmly it would have been better for him. As for abuse and insult among people who are like him and who seek the truth, this is not fitting for them, nor for the common person, let alone the scholar. The aim is not to attack the person; the aim is the statement, so that it may be refuted (...).

But the enemies of the messengers have nothing with which to counter what the messengers brought, so they always resort to abuse and insult. (﴿You are not﴾ also ﴿except a human like us﴾.) As for the first, ﴿You are only one of the bewitched﴾, it is a lie without doubt. Indeed he is among the most intelligent of people, upon him be prayers and peace. Had he not been the most intelligent of his people, Allah would not have placed the message in him: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am 124]. He is the most intelligent of them, the most trustworthy of them, and the most patient of them.

But ﴿You are only a human like us﴾: is this correct or not? This is correct. He is only a human like us. But this reason (...) is what prevents him from being a messenger. For this reason the messengers said to their people, who argued against them with this proof: ﴿We are only humans like you, but Allah bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants. It was not for us to bring you an authority except by the permission of Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 11]. This is the answer to this doubt. It is a doubt, yet they made it into a proof. It is said: if he is a human like you, what prevents Allah from bestowing the message upon him? In reality there is no obstacle. Also, it is not possible for Allah to send anyone to mankind except from among mankind. Even if He had made him an angel, as they suggested, He would have made him appear in the form of a man, and the matter would have returned to these people in a confused and ambiguous state, so they would have gained nothing from it.

This is one of the benefits of the variety of readings, since variety of readings has many benefits, among them this matter: that a single word comprises two meanings.

﴿Fari-hin﴾ [149], ﴿so fear Allah and obey me﴾. This sentence, as we said regarding the story of 'Ad, is either built upon what was mentioned, or it repeats what came before. On the first view it is ta'sis (establishing a new meaning), and on the second it is tawkid (emphasis). The situation is very important and requires that this phrase be repeated: the fear of Allah and obedience to the Messenger ﷺ.

This is a command and a prohibition: a command to fear Allah and obey Him, but a prohibition against obeying the command of the extravagant. Is "amr" (command) singular or is it the plural of "awamir" (commands)?

* Students: Awamir (commands).

* Shaykh: It is the singular of the commands; that is, do not obey their command. Why did he not say "do not obey them," when he said ﴿so fear Allah and obey me﴾, and did not say "and obey my command"? * Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, he forbids them from obeying.

* Student: Yes, the obedience to the command of the extravagant (...).

* Shaykh: Good (...).

* Student: That is, the elders of the people and the notables, and that he commands them so that it would be more eloquent than if he had said "do not obey them."

That is, either they are corruption, so they corrupt by way of attributing the thing to its cause, or sins are a cause of corruption, or they are themselves corruption.

(﴿and do not reform﴾ by obedience to Allah), nor by anything else. The negation here is intended to deny reform while affirming the complete opposite, which is corruption: ﴿they cause corruption and do not reform﴾.

His words (by obedience to Allah): obedience itself is undoubtedly reform, and it is also a cause of reform, for obedience to Allah, exalted is He, is the cause of the righteousness of everything: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl 97]. But the person who has a proof does not resort to insult and abuse. For this reason some scholars are criticized for their habit of abuse and insult toward their opponents, as is done by whom? Ibn Hazm, may Allah have mercy on him and pardon him. That is, if he had argued calmly it would have been better for him. As for abuse and insult among people who are like him and who seek the truth, this is not fitting for them, nor for the common person, let alone the scholar. The aim is not to attack the person; the aim is the statement, so that it may be refuted (...).

The interrogative in His words ﴿Will you be left﴾ (istifham, interrogation) is for warning. That is, do you think you will be left? No, you will not be left. It is a negation that carries a warning.

His words ﴿Will you be left﴾ are in the passive voice (mabni lil-majhul), because the agent is known. Who is the agent? Allah, glorified and exalted. That is, will Allah leave you in what is here?

His words ﴿in what is here, secure﴾ and so on to the end are a reminder of Allah's blessing upon them, and that they cannot be left in this state without a command or a prohibition. This is like His saying: ﴿Does man think he will be left neglected?﴾ [al-Qiyamah 36], and ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun 115]. He said ﴿secure in what is here﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the waw in ﴿you will be left﴾, meaning while you are secure. The one who is secure (al-amin) is the one who is free from fear.

* In this there is evidence of their settlement in their homelands and their security. Security together with abundant provision are the ultimate blessings of this life.

He said: ﴿secure, among gardens and springs﴾. (Al-jannat) is the plural of jannah, which is orchards with many trees, because it covers (yastur) those within it. His words ﴿and springs﴾ is the plural of ('ayn), which is flowing water without the need for buckets or water-wheels. ﴿and crops and palm trees with delicate spathes﴾: this mentions the crops and palms after the gardens by way of ataf al-khass 'ala al-'amm (specific after general, conjunction of the particular over the general), for the sake of emphasis on them, since otherwise they are included within the gardens, because the crops are among them and so are the palms. ﴿palm trees with delicate spathes﴾: (tal') means what it sends forth. His words ﴿delicate﴾ are explained as (soft, pliant). And so it is, for the spathe of the palm is among the softest and most delicate of things. It has been said that al-hadim means al-nadid (arranged in layers), as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿For it are spathes arranged in layers, a provision for the servants﴾ [Qaf 10–11]. That is, it is arranged in order and not scattered, so that it is easy to take and pick.

His words ﴿palm trees with delicate spathes﴾: this clause, ﴿its spathes are delicate﴾, what is its place in i'rab (grammatical analysis)?

* Student: It is an adjectival description of the palm trees, in the genitive position.

* Shaykh: Yes, in the genitive position: ﴿and palm trees with delicate spathes﴾. The spathe was singled out over the other benefits of the palm despite its many benefits, because it is the ultimate of what is benefited from it. Otherwise there are many other benefits in it. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ compared the believer to it because of its abundant good and benefits. This is with regard to the crops and cultivation.

As for construction and dwellings, He said: (﴿And you carve homes out of the mountains, skilfully﴾ — insolent (fari-hin). In one reading it is ﴿fari-hin﴾, skilled.) ﴿And you carve homes out of the mountains﴾: the meaning of carving them from the mountains is that they make the house from the mountain itself. It does not mean that they carve stones and then build with them. No, rather they make the house itself from the mountain, shaping the mountain as they wish. This is evidence of their capability and of their complete knowledge of engineering, because the thing is not in front of you but is inside the rock, and mountains and boulders require strong thought: how to make it, how to shape it, (...), and how to make (...), and so on. This is evidence of their strength and their skill in engineering.

The word ﴿fari-hin﴾ means insolent. It is an adjective of the form (sifah mushabbahah, quality-attribute form). ﴿Fari-hin﴾ with the lengthened vowel is an active participle (ism fa'il), and the meaning intended is skill. The difference between the two readings has a benefit: the word combines both meanings. They would be characterized by both matters: insolence, according to the reading with the short vowel, and skill, according to the reading with the long vowel. This is one of the benefits of the variety of readings, since variety of readings has many benefits, among them this matter: that a single word comprises two meanings.

﴿Fari-hin﴾ [149], ﴿so fear Allah and obey me﴾. This sentence, as we said regarding the story of 'Ad, is either built upon what was mentioned, or it repeats what came before. On the first view it is ta'sis (establishing a new meaning), and on the second it is tawkid (emphasis). The situation is very important and requires that this phrase be repeated: the fear of Allah and obedience to the Messenger ﷺ.

﴿So fear Allah and obey me﴾ [150], ﴿and do not obey the command of the extravagant﴾ [151], ﴿who cause corruption in the land and do not reform﴾. This is a command and a prohibition: a command to fear Allah and obey Him, but a prohibition against obeying the command of the extravagant. Is "amr" (command) singular or is it the plural of "awamir" (commands)?

* Students: Awamir (commands).

* Shaykh: It is the singular of the commands; that is, do not obey their command. Why did he not say "do not obey them," when he said ﴿so fear Allah and obey me﴾, and did not say "and obey my command"? Here he said ﴿and do not obey the command of the extravagant who cause corruption in the land and do not reform.﴾ Would it not have been possible for him to say "and do not obey the extravagant in their corruption"?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, he forbids them from obeying.

* Student: Yes, the obedience to the command of the extravagant (...).

* Shaykh: Good (...).

* Student: That is, the elders of the people and the notables, and that he commands them so that it would be more eloquent than if he had said "do not obey them."

* Shaykh: Good. The saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said: Will you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah"?﴾ [Ghafir 28]. He did not say "Will you kill Musa." Why?

* Student: Because he is speaking indirectly, since he is concealing his faith, so he does not want them to know Musa (...) ﴿because he says, "My Lord is Allah"﴾.

* Shaykh: They know Musa..

* Student: They know Musa, but he distances the closeness of his relationship with Musa (...) "as for me, I do not know him" (...).

* Shaykh: If he had mentioned him by his proper name, it would have been said: this is a personal relationship between him and him. So he made him indefinite, as if he did not know him: ﴿a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah."﴾ This is similar to it. If he had said "do not obey the extravagant themselves," it might be said that this is out of enmity between him and them, so that he does not want them to be obeyed, and he commanded obedience to himself. But when he said "the command of the extravagant," it is as if he were saying: I am not concerned whether this comes from so-and-so or so-and-so; rather the matter is that it is a command from an extravagant person. This is what has become clear to me, in order to avoid the accusation that he does not want the extravagant themselves, since the prohibition of obeying them was directed toward their persons. So he made the prohibition against obeying their command, which is a command of extravagance and corruption.

His words ﴿the extravagant﴾ mean those who exceed the limit. The extravagant one is the one who goes beyond the limit. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Eat and drink, but do not be extravagant﴾ [al-A'raf 31]: do not exceed the limit in quantity or in quality.

Then He said ﴿who cause corruption in the land﴾. This description is clarifying (kashifah) and not restrictive (qayd), because every extravagant person causes corruption in the land, so the description is clarifying. His words ﴿they cause corruption in the land﴾ mean they are a cause of its corruption, or that sins themselves are corruption. That is, either they are corruption, so they corrupt by way of attributing the thing to its cause, or sins are a cause of corruption, or they are themselves corruption.

(﴿and do not reform﴾ by obedience to Allah), nor by anything else. In His words ﴿they cause corruption and do not reform﴾ there is evidence of (...) their corruption, and that there is no reform in them. The negation here is intended to deny reform while affirming the complete opposite, which is corruption: ﴿they cause corruption and do not reform﴾.

His words (by obedience to Allah): obedience itself is undoubtedly reform, and it is also a cause of reform, for obedience to Allah, exalted is He, is the cause of the righteousness of everything: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl 97]. And what was their answer? ﴿They said: You are only one of the bewitched﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 153]. They accused him of being bewitched. (Musahharin) is more emphatic than (mashur). Also their saying ﴿You are only﴾ is a restriction (hasr) covering all states: that is, your condition never departs from this description: ﴿You are only one of the bewitched.﴾

The author said: (Those who cast a great deal of magic, until it overcame their reason.) This, may Allah protect us, is their answer, just as many people have answered in this way. Indeed, every prophet has been told the like: ﴿Thus no messenger came to those before them except that they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ [al-Dhariyat 52]. That is because they have no proof. Every person who has no proof resorts only to abuse and insult, thinking that by this he will turn people away from his opponent, since he is unable to confront him. But the person who has a proof does not resort to insult and abuse. For this reason some scholars are criticized for their habit of abuse and insult toward their opponents, as is done by whom? Ibn Hazm, may Allah have mercy on him and pardon him. That is, if he had argued calmly it would have been better for him. As for abuse and insult among people who are like him and who seek the truth, this is not fitting for them, nor for the common person, let alone the scholar. The aim is not to attack the person; the aim is the statement, so that it may be refuted (...).

But the enemies of the messengers have nothing with which to counter what the messengers brought, so they always resort to abuse and insult. (﴿You are not﴾ also ﴿except a human like us﴾.) As for the first, ﴿You are only one of the bewitched﴾, it is a lie without doubt. Indeed he is among the most intelligent of people, upon him be prayers and peace. Had he not been the most intelligent of his people, Allah would not have placed the message in him: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am 124]. He is the most intelligent of them, the most trustworthy of them, and the most patient of them.

But ﴿You are only a human like us﴾: is this correct or not? This is correct. He is only a human like us. But this reason (...) is what prevents him from being a messenger. For this reason the messengers said to their people, who argued against them with this proof: ﴿We are only humans like you, but Allah bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants. It was not for us to bring you an authority except by the permission of Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 11]. This is the answer to this doubt. It is a doubt, yet they made it into a proof. It is said: if he is a human like you, what prevents Allah from bestowing the message upon him? In reality there is no obstacle. Also, it is not possible for Allah to send anyone to mankind except from among mankind. Even if He had made him an angel, as they suggested, He would have made him appear in the form of a man, and the matter would have returned to these people in a confused and ambiguous state, so they would have gained nothing from it.

(﴿and do not reform﴾ by obedience to Allah), nor by anything else. But the person who has a proof does not resort to insult and abuse. For this reason some scholars are criticized for their habit of abuse and insult toward their opponents, as is done by whom? Ibn Hazm, may Allah have mercy on him and pardon him. That is, if he had argued calmly it would have been better for him. As for abuse and insult among people who are like him and who seek the truth, this is not fitting for them, nor for the common person, let alone the scholar. The aim is not to attack the person; the aim is the statement, so that it may be refuted (...).

But the enemies of the messengers have nothing with which to counter what the messengers brought, so they always resort to abuse and insult. (﴿You are not﴾ also ﴿except a human like us﴾.) As for the first, ﴿You are only one of the bewitched﴾, it is a lie without doubt. Indeed he is among the most intelligent of people, upon him be prayers and peace. Had he not been the most intelligent of his people, Allah would not have placed the message in him: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am 124]. He is the most intelligent of them, the most trustworthy of them, and the most patient of them.

But ﴿You are only a human like us﴾: is this correct or not? This is correct. He is only a human like us. But this reason (...) is what prevents him from being a messenger. For this reason the messengers said to their people, who argued against them with this proof: ﴿We are only humans like you, but Allah bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants. It was not for us to bring you an authority except by the permission of Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 11]. This is the answer to this doubt. It is a doubt, yet they made it into a proof. It is said: if he is a human like you, what prevents Allah from bestowing the message upon him? In reality there is no obstacle. Also, it is not possible for Allah to send anyone to mankind except from among mankind. Even if He had made him an angel, as they suggested, He would have made him appear in the form of a man, and the matter would have returned to these people in a confused and ambiguous state, so they would have gained nothing from it.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿You are only a human being like us, so bring a sign, if you are of the truthful﴾ in your messengership).

That is, had they limited themselves to the second clause, "You are only a human being like us, so bring a sign," it would have been a sound statement. For every person who is visited by a man like himself and says, "I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds," will be asked: "Bring a sign and evidence." Otherwise, every liar could claim prophethood and make lawful the blood and wealth of others by this false claim. So His saying, ﴿so bring a sign﴾, is clear. But does the command here mean a challenge (tahaddi) or a request for guidance (istirshad)? It appears from their situation that it means a challenge; that is, that he cannot bring a sign, in the sense of their saying that he is bewitched. ﴿So bring a sign, if you are of the truthful﴾ in your messengership. The words ﴿if you are of the truthful﴾ indicate their deeming it unlikely that he is so, and that they intend this as a challenge to him. He answered them with His saying: ﴿This is a she-camel; she has a turn of drinking﴾. This is the sign, and this she-camel is greater than what they fashion from stone and what they cultivate in crops and plant in trees, because she came forth unlike other she-camels; she was not like the familiar camels known to them.

What is the aspect of her being a sign? ﴿She has a turn of drinking, and you have a turn of drinking on a known day﴾. This is the aspect of the sign in this she-camel. As for what has come in the Isra'iliyyat (narrations from the Israelite traditions) that she emerged from a rock, this has no basis. Had she been like that, it would have been mentioned in the Qur'an, because her emerging from a rock, and she being an animal, is a stronger, more manifest and clearer sign than her having a turn of drinking while they have a turn of drinking. So the correct statement is: this she-camel is a she-camel, born of she-camels, but she has a distinction over others, and this is the great distinction: ﴿She has a turn of drinking, and you have a turn of drinking on a known day﴾. How can she have a turn of drinking and you have a turn of drinking? That is, she drinks from this well: she comes and drinks. On the next day she goes off and grazes..

The correct statement is: this she-camel is a she-camel born of she-camels, but she has a distinction over others, and this is the great distinction: ﴿She has a turn of drinking, and you have a turn of drinking on a known day﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 155]. How can she have a turn of drinking and you have a turn of drinking? That is, she drinks from this well: she comes and drinks. On the next day she goes off and grazes. But on the day she drinks, the people of knowledge said: whoever gave her a bucket of water was given a bucket of milk in return, so they would drink milk one day and water the next day. They took this milk from this camel, and this is without doubt among the signs of Allah, since no she-camel of this kind exists.

As for His saying: ﴿and you have a turn of drinking on a known day﴾, it is as if this turn of drinking was fixed to a time they set for themselves, so that it would not be confused for someone who is not in the town. Even if a person is outside the town, he knows that the day is the she-camel's day or that the day is the people's day, so he comes and draws water from this well, or on the she-camel's day he comes and drinks from her milk. This is the benefit of His saying: ﴿and you have a turn of drinking on a known day﴾.

The words ﴿if you are of the truthful﴾ indicate their deeming it unlikely that he is so, and that they intend this as a challenge to him. He answered them with His saying: ﴿This is a she-camel; she has a turn of drinking﴾. This is the sign, and this she-camel is greater than what they fashion from stone and what they cultivate in crops and plant in trees, because she came forth unlike other she-camels; she was not like the familiar camels known to them.

What is the aspect of her being a sign? ﴿She has a turn of drinking, and you have a turn of drinking on a known day﴾. This is the aspect of the sign in this she-camel. As for what has come in the Isra'iliyyat (narrations from the Israelite traditions) that she emerged from a rock, this has no basis. Had she been like that, it would have been mentioned in the Qur'an, because her emerging from a rock, and she being an animal, is a stronger, more manifest and clearer sign than her having a turn of drinking while they have a turn of drinking. So the correct statement is: this she-camel is a she-camel, born of she-camels, but she has a distinction over others, and this is the great distinction: ﴿She has a turn of drinking, and you have a turn of drinking on a known day﴾. How can she have a turn of drinking and you have a turn of drinking? That is, she drinks from this well: she comes and drinks. On the next day she goes off and grazes..

The correct statement is: this she-camel is a she-camel born of she-camels, but she has a distinction over others, and this is the great distinction: ﴿She has a turn of drinking, and you have a turn of drinking on a known day﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 155]. How can she have a turn of drinking and you have a turn of drinking? That is, she drinks from this well: she comes and drinks. On the next day she goes off and grazes. But on the day she drinks, the people of knowledge said: whoever gave her a bucket of water was given a bucket of milk in return, so they would drink milk one day and water the next day. They took this milk from this camel, and this is without doubt among the signs of Allah, since no she-camel of this kind exists.

As for His saying: ﴿and you have a turn of drinking on a known day﴾, it is as if this turn of drinking was fixed to a time they set for themselves, so that it would not be confused for someone who is not in the town. Even if a person is outside the town, he knows that the day is the she-camel's day or that the day is the people's day, so he comes and draws water from this well, or on the she-camel's day he comes and drinks from her milk. This is the benefit of His saying: ﴿and you have a turn of drinking on a known day﴾.

﴿ ﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verse 156:

﴿And do not touch them with harm, lest there seize you the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 156] The author says: it is "tremendous" (due to the greatness of the punishment); meaning, the day itself is not the tremendous one, but because the punishment occurs in it, it became tremendous.

"Tremendous" (ʿaẓīm) is a descriptor of the day. Is "tremendous" a descriptor of praise or a descriptor of blame?

* Student: According to the context, it is a descriptor of blame.

* The Shaykh: Yes, but in reality it is a descriptor of praise, and an indication of the strength of what it describes. Even if it is a punishment, it indicates the strength of the punishment; if it is good, it indicates the strength of that good. The point is that greatness, as a meaning among meanings, indicates perfection and praise, whether it is in a punishment or in a blessing.

As for His saying: ﴿punishment of a tremendous day﴾, many people avoid describing a created thing as "tremendous," but in truth there is no basis for this. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And she has a tremendous throne﴾ [al-Naml 23], ﴿About what are they asking each other? About the tremendous news﴾ [al-Naba' 1–2], ﴿And indeed, it is a tremendous oath, if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 76]. So Allah the Exalted described Himself, His speech and His revelation as tremendous, and He also described some of His creatures with it, which indicates that there is no harm in it.

Some people also avoided saying "al-mu'azzam" (the one who is magnified), and this too should not be avoided; the reason is that the one who is magnified is not necessarily tremendous. One may be magnified who is not tremendous, and he is lower in rank than the tremendous. So if it is permissible to apply "tremendous" (ʿaẓīm) absolutely, then "magnified" (muʿaẓẓam) is all the more permissible.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 26, verses 157–159 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Exalted said: (﴿So they hamstrung her﴾, meaning some of them hamstrung her with their consent. ﴿So they became regretful﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 157] over hamstringing her. ﴿So the punishment seized them﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 158], the one promised to them, and they perished).

He said: "Do not touch her with harm," but they touched her with the worst harm, we seek refuge in Allah. They hamstrung the she-camel. And what is the meaning of ʿaqr (hamstringing)? The apparent meaning is that it refers to killing, not merely cutting the legs. Rather, they destroyed her, so they were punished with the like of what they had committed. "They became regretful." Were they regretful for the sin they had committed, or were they regretful for the benefit they had lost from her?

* Student: Both. They lost the benefit, and the punishment came upon them.

* The Shaykh: The punishment came after that, until now. The apparent meaning is that they regretted the worldly benefit they had lost, because if they had regretted the sin, they would have been repentant and would not have been destroyed. But they regretted. Consider: yesterday we drank milk, and today the milk is gone from us. So the apparent meaning is that this regret was only on account of the loss of the worldly purpose. And how long did they remain after that?

* Student: Three days.

* The Shaykh: Yes, three days. The wisdom behind these three days, Allah knows best, is that perhaps they would repent, but they did not repent. From this has been derived the rule on requesting an apostate to repent: how many days? Three days. If he repents, well and good; otherwise the prescribed punishment (hadd) is carried out on him. There is a difference of opinion among the scholars on this issue. The important point is that these people did not regret committing the disobedience. Had they regretted it, that would have been repentance. But they regretted only the worldly portion they had lost, so the promised punishment seized them and they perished, except that Allah saved Salih and those with him.

As for His saying ﴿So they hamstrung her﴾: it is well known that not all of them hamstrung her, but because it was done with the consent of all, including their leaders, it was attributed to all of them. You know that the act of a group within a community is considered the act of everyone if the rest do not object. If they stay silent and do not denounce it, it is attributed to all. For this reason, Allah addresses the Jews in the time of the Messenger ﷺ, reminding them of what their predecessors did, and speaks to them as if they were the doers, because they are one community. So if they do not reject what their predecessors did, it is attributed to all of them.

﴿So the punishment seized them﴾, the one promised. What was the punishment that seized them?

* Students: A cry.

* The Shaykh: And a quake. A cry and a quake together. Allah shook the earth beneath them, and Gabriel cried out at them, and they died. They were found in their homes, prostrate, lifeless, we seek refuge in Allah, fallen as one soul. In this is proof of the perfect power of Allah the Exalted, and that Allah is over all things powerful: ﴿And Allah is not to be frustrated by anything in the heavens or on the earth; indeed He is ever Knowing and Competent﴾ [Fatir 44].

If we, the Muslims, understood and truly believed, we would not be in the state we are in now. That is, we would not fear people more than we fear Allah. Today the leaders of the Muslims, unfortunately, fear people more than they fear Allah, and so they flatter people regarding the rulings of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Had they taken pride in the honor of their religion, people would have feared them.

For this reason they say: a person must fear and be shaken, but either he fears Allah or he fears other than Allah. If he fears Allah, all things fear him, and if he fears other than Allah, that fear takes control of him. This is true, it is the truth: whoever fears Allah, everything fears him, and whoever is mindful of Allah, everything is mindful of him. And the reverse is the reverse.

So it is incumbent upon all of us to be confident in the promise of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, not looking at the immediate causes. It is true that if we looked at things with purely material vision, we could not speak with these people, or challenge them in implementing the Shariah and fighting them. But we must not look only at these immediate causes. We must look at other causes beyond matter. Is that not so?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: For this reason, whoever looks only at these visible natural causes will not succeed in his affairs. When the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, fought the Persians and the Romans, did they look at these causes?

* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: Not at all. They would besiege a great city for a period, then go out in the morning and glorify Allah (takbir). When they glorified Allah, the walls would crumble. This is a widely transmitted report about them in history: they would besiege a city for some time, then when they glorified Allah the Exalted, it was as if cannons and bombs were shattering those walls. But it was a glorification that came from the heart.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers. And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 158, 159].

* Student: The people of Salih, did they believe, I mean, setting aside the hamstringing of the she-camel, did they believe in Allah and follow him?

* The Shaykh: No, only a few of them did.

* Student: Then how (...)?

* The Shaykh: How?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, I mean Allah granting them respite for three days means that we grant the disbelievers three days. But the original disbelievers under the Islamic Shariah have special rulings, such as their being permitted to remain upon payment of the jizya (poll tax), for example. As for others who are not permitted to remain upon their religion, namely the apostate (murtadd), they are given three days. So the matter is disputed. Furthermore, apostasy varies: some forms of apostasy may be given respite, and others may not.

* Student: Then let us mention from this the people of Salih. I mean, did they (...), I mean, did they go, or did she die in her place?

* The Shaykh: Yes, (...). The apparent meaning is that every person died in his house.

* Student: In his house?

* The Shaykh: That is the apparent meaning, yes.

* Student: And whoever was overtaken by death at (...)?

* The Shaykh: (...).

* Student: As for the whole tribe, they drank from one well. It is known that they had gardens and crops. Did they not also have rivers?

* The Shaykh: No, because this well is the one suitable for drinking.

* Student: And the others?

* The Shaykh: The others are not fit for drinking.

* Student: The drinking was specified to this well.

* The Shaykh: To this well. For this reason He divided it: ﴿For her is a share of water, and for you is a share of a known day﴾. There is also no objection to this well irrigating everything they have. That is not prohibited. But the closer view, Allah knows best, is that the gardens were spread with springs, and this well was the one from which they took their drinking water.

* Student: ﴿But as for Thamud, they were destroyed by the Overwhelming Blast﴾ [al-Haqqah 5]. It has been said: the quake, or something similar?

* The Shaykh: The apparent meaning is that it is a name for all of it, meaning by what overpowered them.

* Student: By what overpowered them, meaning it overwhelmed them?

* The Shaykh: Yes, it overwhelmed them.

* Student: Shaykh, what was the reason the Messenger ﷺ forbade (...)?

* The Shaykh: Its reasoning (...), because using this water leads to settling in it and feeling at ease. When the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, passed by it, he passed quickly with his head covered, and he said: "If you are not weeping, do not enter upon these people, lest what befell them befall you."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (433) and Muslim (2980/38), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. The wording of Muslim: "Do not enter upon these tormented people unless you are weeping. If you are not weeping, do not enter upon them, lest what befell them befall you."]] So the matter is not trivial. It is strange that many people today, may Allah guide us and them, go there for sightseeing and recreation. This is forbidden, it is not permissible. And the saying of Allah the Mighty and Majestic does not contradict this: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, and it became clear to you how We dealt with them, and We set forth parables for you﴾ [Ibrahim 45]. The reason it does not contradict is that...

* Student: The disbelievers (...).

* The Shaykh: The meaning is that their deeds do not indicate permissibility, meaning that the place being inhabited (...). Or it may be said that our Shariah has come with the opposite, prohibiting it. As for the statement of some people: "The whole earth is never free of nations that denied," we say: yes, the earth is never free of nations that denied. But who says that this specific place is the place of a denying nation? Is it permissible now to go down to al-Ahqaf?

* Student: It is not permissible (...).

* The Shaykh: It is permissible, because their dwellings are not known precisely. But the dwellings of Thamud still exist precisely as they are now. When a person enters them, it is as if he is entering them at that time. For this reason the Messenger forbade entering them except while weeping, and he said: "If you are not weeping, do not enter upon them."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (433) and Muslim (2980/38), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] But today people say: they enter with cameras.

* Student: They also travel to a place that is to be feared.

* The Shaykh: No, traveling for the sake of worship is not objectionable.

* Student: For the sake of worship.

* The Shaykh: Yes, traveling for the sake of worship. Some people travel for trade and for other than trade, but traveling for recreation is forbidden.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, is this not permissible?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: What is the case with the one who goes there? The one who goes there, there is no harm. It may be said that this is not harmful, though the matter requires consideration. It may be said that taking lessons from what is in the Qur'an is more eloquent than taking lessons from what is in its (the place's) worldly reality. The matter requires consideration, but it is lighter than the one who goes for recreation and sightseeing. Hearts have hardened.

* Student: Is it not traveling if the intention is worship?

* The Shaykh: No, because he did not intend that specific spot. The original principle is that a person intends a specific spot and travels to it (...). For example, if he says: "I will travel to the Mosque of Riyadh because it is an old mosque that kings have frequented," (...), "I will travel to it," this is forbidden, not permissible. Or traveling to the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus because it is the mosque of the caliphs: we say it is not permissible, it is forbidden.

* Student: For lesson and admonition (...).

* The Shaykh: No. This may be like what we said at the beginning: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, and it became clear to you﴾ [Ibrahim 45]. It only indicates... But ﴿Say: Travel through the earth and observe﴾ [al-Naml 69]. This may be the case if we say that travel in the physical sense includes (...).

* Student: But on condition of weeping?

* The Shaykh: On condition of weeping, yes, on condition that the person takes a lesson.

* Student: He specified the dwellings of Thamud from all regions of the earth.

* The Shaykh: The original principle is that we do not have a specific place indicating that these are the dwellings of that people, except like the town of Lot. For Allah says: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning, and at night. Will you not reason?﴾ [al-Saffat 137, 138]. But Allah rebuked those who pass by and do not take heed.

* Student: The drinking from (...) of Thamud, the cause is need. So if a person were given (...)?

* The Shaykh: Without (...).

* Student: He drinks from it.

* The Shaykh: Yes, that is known.

* Student: If he were given water from (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is permissible. Even the well of the she-camel, we say it is permissible, because the Muslims used to drink from it without objection. The well of the she-camel...

* Student: Is it known?

* The Shaykh: It was known in earlier times. I do not know now, by Allah, whether it is still known or not. And in the earlier period, according to the words of the jurists, it was known. It was a large well that pilgrims coming from Syria used to visit.
